prompt: Write the career advice post you wish someone had handed you as a young software engineer fresh out of college: the stuff about how the industry and business actually work that no CS degree or career center covers. Be blunt and practical.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
You came out of college trained to solve problems that already have a specification. Work is mostly the opposite. The problem is fuzzy, the constraints are political, the timeline is arbitrary, and the people around you have incentives you did not design. Your degree taught you to reason about correctness. Your job will be to decide what correctness is worth, for whom, and under what deadline.

The first thing to internalize is that software is not a pure technical artifact. It is a business instrument. A feature exists to change behavior, reduce cost, lower risk, or make money. A refactor exists to make future work cheaper or safer. A migration exists because the current system is becoming too expensive to operate or too risky to change. If you cannot connect your work to one of those, you are not doing engineering yet; you are doing exercises.

That does not mean every line of code must be directly monetizable. It means the system you build is a liability and an asset at the same time. It can generate revenue, but it also requires headcount, cloud spend, on-call attention, and organizational trust. A beautiful microservice that no one can operate is a bad microservice. A boring database table that lets the business run for five years is good engineering.

Your early instinct will be to make the code elegant. Often that is the wrong first move. The first version should be clear, testable, and good enough to answer the question. If you spend two weeks building a perfect search index before finding out that users mostly needed to export a CSV, you have not saved time. You have delayed learning. The cost of being wrong early is usually lower than the cost of being elegantly wrong late.

But “good enough” is not a license to be careless. It is a professional judgment. You need to know where the load-bearing walls are. If you are touching payments, authentication, data migration, or anything that can corrupt user state, slow down. Write the test that would have caught the bug. Add the log line that will tell you what happened. Make the deploy reversible. A production incident is not just an embarrassment; it is a tax on future trust. People remember which engineers make them nervous.

Observability matters more than most junior engineers expect. If you cannot see whether your code is running, how often it fails, and what it is doing under load, you do not control it. A change that ships with no metrics is a rumor. You want to be able to say, “Before this change, latency was X and errors were Y. After, they are Z.” That sentence is worth more in a performance review than any adjective.

Visibility is not a soft skill. It is infrastructure for your career. In a company, work that is invisible is work that did not happen. If you solved a hard problem and no one outside your immediate pair knows about it, the organization got the benefit but you did not get the reputation. Write the design doc. Write the postmortem. Write the internal blog post. In standup, do not say “working on it.” Say what you changed, what you measured, what is blocked, and what you expect next. People promote engineers they understand. You make yourself understandable by leaving a paper trail.

This is where the word “politics” becomes useful if you stop using it as an insult. Every company allocates scarce resources: budget, headcount, engineering time, executive attention. Projects compete. Teams compete. If your project is important to you but not connected to a metric or goal that your manager cares about, it is fragile. When the next priority shifts, it will be cut. Learn what your organization is actually optimizing for this quarter. Is it growth? Gross margin? Retention? Platform reliability? Compliance? The answer changes what “done” means.

You also need to learn the difference between a mentor and a sponsor. A mentor gives you advice. A sponsor puts your name in the room when decisions are being made. Most junior engineers have mentors and no sponsors. A sponsor is usually someone who has seen you do reliable, high-quality work and can vouch for you. You earn that by being easy to bet on: clear communication, honest estimates, follow-through, and no dramatic failures. Do not ask for a sponsor directly. Ask for feedback, take it seriously, and then make the next piece of work easier to recommend.

Customers matter. If you only talk to engineers, you will build a closed ecosystem of assumptions. Read support tickets. Sit in on sales calls if you can. Ask what users actually did, not what they say they want. A big customer requesting a feature is a signal, not a requirement. The feature may be a workaround for a broken workflow, a one-off need, or a competitive threat. The question “what job are they trying to get done?” is worth more than the feature request itself. Engineers who understand the customer become harder to replace because they can evaluate tradeoffs that pure technologists cannot see.

Promotions are not rewards for surviving years. They are bets on your ability to operate at a larger radius of impact. A junior engineer completes well-defined tasks. A mid-level engineer owns a project from design through launch. A senior engineer identifies problems that no one has formally assigned and leads people without formal authority. A staff engineer shapes what the team is trying to do. The jump is not “know more languages.” It is that you stop waiting to be told what is important.

The most useful promotion artifact is not a list of features. It is a story about a problem, your judgment, the tradeoffs, and the outcome. “I reduced checkout errors by 18%” is better than “I improved checkout.” “I convinced the team to delay the new dashboard because the data pipeline was unreliable, and we avoided two incidents during peak season” is better than “I was reliable.” You need evidence of leverage: time saved, risk reduced, revenue protected, other engineers unblocked, decision quality improved.

Do not confuse scope with importance. Owning a large system is not automatically senior work if you are just maintaining it. Identifying a subtle reliability issue, instrumenting it, and changing the team’s practice around it can be more valuable. Conversely, shipping a large feature with no learning, no measurement, and no improvement in process is not a promotion story. It is a receipt.

Your learning strategy should change after college. Stop consuming content at the same rate you were producing assignments. Tutorials create familiarity, not judgment. The best training is reading production code, especially code you did not write. Ask what would break if a dependency failed. Ask why the abstraction exists. Ask what the last incident taught. Then build something real, even if it is small: an internal tool, a script that saves your team an hour a week, a side project with actual users. The goal is to experience the full loop: idea, constraint, implementation, failure, feedback, revision.

If a tool saves five minutes for one person twice a week, it is a convenience. If it saves an hour for ten people every day, it is a business case. Start there. Junior engineers often think they need to build a distributed system to prove themselves. More often, they need to make a painful manual process disappear and document the result.

The job market is lumpy and not very personal. An offer is not a verdict on your soul. A rejection is not a diagnosis. Companies hire for risk reduction as much as talent. They want to know you will show up, communicate, and not require constant supervision. That is why interviews test basic problem-solving and communication so heavily: they are proxies for future cost. When negotiating, understand the whole package. Base salary is predictable. Sign-on is one-time. Equity is a bet, often a bad one unless the company is close to a liquidity event or you genuinely believe in the upside. A higher title at a smaller company may be less portable than a plain title at a company whose name opens doors.

Layoffs are a business cycle, not a moral ranking. Companies grow, overhire, revenue slows, and they cut. If you are caught in one, it is not evidence that you were bad. It is evidence that your cost was not protected at that moment. The practical response is boring: keep skills current, keep relationships warm, keep savings, and do not let your identity fuse with one employer. The engineers who recover fastest are the ones who can describe what they did in plain language to someone who is not on their team.

Artificial intelligence is changing the leverage curve, and you should take that seriously without becoming a hype victim. Writing boilerplate code is becoming less scarce. Judgment is becoming more valuable. You need to be good at specifying what should be built, verifying that the output is correct, understanding the system around it, and knowing when a generated patch is dangerous. The engineer who treats AI as a shortcut to looking busy will be exposed quickly. The engineer who uses it to expand the amount of reliable work they can ship will have an advantage.

The hardest objection to all of this is that it sounds like a recipe for becoming a political operator who happens to write code. That is a real failure mode. If you optimize only for visibility and alignment, you become replaceable the moment a better-connected person arrives. If you optimize only for technical purity, you become a hobbyist with a paycheck. The durable position is being genuinely good at hard technical work and genuinely good at making that work matter. Those are not opposites. The best engineers are dangerous because they can do both.

In your next one-on-one, bring one page. What you shipped. What you measured. What you learned. What you are unsure about. What you need from your manager. No apology, no performance. That page is the smallest unit of professional trust. Build it until it is boring.
rejected:
Your degree proves you can pass tests. It does not prove you can ship software, manage stakeholders, or survive a layoff. The gap between "knows algorithms" and "is a valuable employee" is filled by unglamorous skills.

### You are a liability until you are useful

For the first six months, you will break things. You will waste senior engineers' time asking questions they can answer with five minutes of debugging. This is not a moral failing; it is the cost of entry. Your job is to minimize the cost.

Read the codebase before asking. Search the internal wiki or Slack history. If you still don't know, ask a specific question: "I tried X and Y, but I’m stuck on Z." Vague questions like "How does this work?" are an insult to your senior colleagues' time.

Speed matters less than correctness. A junior engineer who ships a bug-free feature in two days is worth more than one who ships a buggy feature in two hours. Trust is the currency of engineering. You spend it every time you cut a corner.

### The business is the boss, not the tech

You are not building a product; you are building a cost center that generates revenue. If your feature does not move a business metric—conversion, retention, churn, revenue—it is a liability, no matter how elegant the architecture.

Learn to say no. Stakeholders will ask for things that are technically difficult or strategically irrelevant. Do not just say "no." Say, "We can do that, but it will take three weeks and delay the login page, which is driving 40% of our revenue. Which do you want to prioritize?" Make them choose.

### Code is not the product

The product is the outcome. If your API is beautiful but the frontend crashes on load, you have failed. If your database is optimized but the user has to click through six screens to buy, you have failed.

Talk to users. Read support tickets. Sit in on sales calls. If you don't understand why a customer is angry, you don't understand your code. Empathy is a technical skill.

### Leverage is everything

Coding is only one form of leverage. Writing clear documentation is leverage. Automating your own manual tasks is leverage. Teaching a junior engineer how to debug is leverage.

If you solve a problem once, you are a good engineer. If you solve it so no one else ever has to, you are a great engineer. If you build a tool that lets ten people solve it, you are a leader.

### Your reputation is a compound interest account

People remember who you are to work with. They remember if you were helpful, if you took ownership of mistakes, and if you were reliable.

Never blame a teammate. If a deployment failed, say "I missed the config change," not "You didn't update the config." Taking blame when it isn't yours is a rare and powerful display of confidence.

### The industry is a lottery

Your first job is not your life's work. It is a training ground. You will likely be laid off. You will likely hate a company. You will likely work on projects that go nowhere.

Do not optimize for the title. Optimize for the skills. A "Senior Engineer" at a dying company is worth less than a "Software Engineer" at a company that is growing and solving hard problems.

Learn to sell yourself. Your resume is a sales document. Your interview is a sales meeting. You are not applying for a job; you are proposing a partnership. You have value. State it plainly.

prompt: I run a company with a big, ugly legacy codebase, and everyone keeps saying we should rewrite it all in whatever framework is fashionable. Write a candid first-person post from someone who tried a big rewrite and what they concluded about it.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I did the rewrite.

Our legacy system was a Django monolith that had been growing for eleven years. It had about 412,000 lines of Python, 88,000 lines of JavaScript, 1,900 database migrations, and fourteen cron jobs whose purposes only a couple of people fully understood. The most frightening file was `billing_engine.py`, four thousand three hundred lines long, last touched by an engineer who no longer worked there. Some views were simple. Some were crimes. We had a table called `customer_preferences` with sixty-one boolean columns, and nobody could tell you what half of them meant without reading the code that used them.

Everyone who interviewed us said the same thing: you do not have a product problem, you have an architecture problem. Build the next platform on the modern stack. We chose TypeScript, React, Node, Postgres, and Kubernetes. I like that sentence now because it sounds so reasonable.

We stopped most feature work on the old system. Nine engineers went to the new platform. The first eight weeks were pleasant. We wrote clean services. Our pull requests were small. Our tests were green. We had a dashboard. We looked like a software company.

Then we started implementing real money.

The first casualty was a discount. In the old system, a customer got two percent off if the order was placed before 2 p.m. and shipped from warehouse seven. No ticket explained it. No comment did. We asked the account manager who knew the customer. He said it was a workaround from 2016 for a freight contract that had expired in 2018. The customer still expected it. We had to port the workaround.

That was the smallest one.

The big ones were in the data. Our old Postgres schema had views that encoded business rules, triggers that wrote audit rows, and a materialized view that updated at 3 a.m. It had also absorbed ten years of customer-specific behavior. When we tried to move the customer ledger to the new database, we found that some balances were not balances. They were promises, offsets, and credits that only made sense if you read the old code and then talked to the support team that had created them.

We built a sync job. Then we built a reconciliation job. Then we built a page to investigate mismatches. The new system and the old system disagreed about tax in eleven states. One integration partner sent webhooks in a format that only the old parser understood, because they had been told not to change it after we complained in 2019.

By month ten, we had two codebases and a bridge between them. The bridge had its own bugs.

The team split made it worse. The people on the new platform stopped reading the old code because it was embarrassing. The people left on the old system stopped answering questions because they were being treated like an archive. We had a domain expert who knew the refund rules, but he was not on the rewrite. He was on the old system, handling production incidents. He knew things, but the new team did not know what to ask.

We tried to measure progress. Story points were useless. We started tracking lead time from a business request to a safe change. For simple features, it improved. For anything touching billing, it got worse. After we cut over the first major workflow, we had three severe incidents in six weeks: duplicate charges, a webhook retry loop, and a batch job that marked unpaid invoices as paid. Each one had a cause that existed only in the old system.

I have the spreadsheet. The rewrite cost about $3.8 million in direct engineering and contractor spend over nineteen months, before the product work we deferred. The new platform used more compute than the old one because we had small services talking to each other to do things the old system did in one transaction. We were paying for cleanliness and still paying for the old building.

The strongest case against my conclusion is that the legacy code was already impossible to maintain. That was true in parts. If we had kept doing only local patches, we would have died slowly. I am not defending the old codebase. It was a mess.

But a rewrite does not remove the mess. It moves it into assumptions. You can redesign the code, but you cannot redesign the business rules from memory. You have to discover them by running the old system, reading its data, and asking awkward questions. A greenfield project makes that discovery feel optional for a while. Then it comes due.

I do not know if another year would have saved it. I suspect we could have finished something that worked, but I also suspect the business would not have waited. The customers did not care that we were building a better foundation. They cared that refunds were slow and the invoice PDF was wrong.

I would do it differently now. I would not stop work on the old system. I would pick the smallest dangerous domain, probably refunds or entitlements, and add characterization tests around the current behavior. I would wrap the old logic behind an interface, then replace one seam at a time. I would keep one deployable system until the new one could take the traffic without a second source of truth. It is slower. It is less impressive. It does not let you say we are building the next platform.

Sometimes a rewrite is the right answer. If the domain model is wrong, if the technology is obsolete, if compliance requires a new boundary, or if you can isolate a bounded context and replace it without touching the rest, then yes. Build the new thing. But do not call it a rewrite if the point is to start over. The point is to make a piece of the system true in a new place and prove it.

What I concluded is that the codebase was not the main problem. The main problem was that we believed we understood the system well enough to build it again. We did not. The old code was ugly because it had absorbed decisions that were never written down. The new code was clean because it had not yet met the customers.
rejected:
The rewrite didn’t fail because the new code was bad. It failed because the old code was right.

We called it Project Phoenix. Two years, forty engineers, a blank slate in a modern framework. The pitch was seductive: clean architecture, test coverage, no more "we can’t touch that module because it will explode." We knew the risks. We had a migration plan. We had a dedicated team to maintain the legacy system during the transition.

Then the first edge case hit.

It was a rounding error in the invoicing module. A single dollar, lost in the gap between what the finance team thought the tax calculation should be and what the IRS actually accepted. The legacy code had a hard-coded, commented block of logic from 2007 that handled a specific state’s weird exemption rule. It looked like garbage. It looked like a bug. It was actually the only thing keeping us from owing the government money.

In the new system, we had refactored that logic into a "clean" abstraction layer. The abstraction was beautiful. It was also wrong.

Every time we found a bug in the new system, we realized it wasn’t a bug in the code. It was a missing business rule. The legacy codebase wasn’t a mess; it was a database of decisions. Every ugly `if/else` chain was a scar from a conversation with a client, a regulator, or a competitor. When we rewrote the code, we didn’t just change the syntax. We erased the memory of why the system worked the way it did.

We spent six months just mapping the behavior of the old system. We wrote tests against the legacy code to define its contract. But behavior is not intent. You can test that a function returns `X` when given `Y`. You cannot test why the product owner chose `X` over `Z` in 2014. When we hit a gap in our understanding, we had to pick a guess. And when you pick a guess at the scale of an enterprise application, you are not coding. You are gambling.

The new system was faster. It was more secure. It was easier to hire for. But it was also a different company. It didn’t handle the weird data from the 2019 acquisition. It didn’t know how to speak to the third-party logistics provider that only supported a deprecated SOAP protocol. It didn’t know how to appease the customer service team’s manual workarounds.

We cut over on a Friday. It worked. It really did. For three weeks, the dashboards were green. Then the month-end close happened. The new system produced invoices that were structurally perfect and semantically nonsense. It took us four months to fix the reconciliation issues. The legacy system was still running in parallel, but we had stopped trusting it. We were flying blind, using the old system only as a source of truth for the errors we were making.

We eventually stabilized. The new system is better. It’s cleaner. It’s cheaper to maintain. But it is also more brittle. When a requirement changes, we have to think about how it fits the architecture. In the old system, we would have just added another `if` statement. It was ugly, but it was local. The change was contained. Now, a small change ripples through the abstraction layers.

The lesson isn’t that you should never rewrite. The lesson is that the value of legacy code is rarely in the code. It’s in the implicit knowledge trapped inside it. If you don’t have the time, the people, or the patience to extract that knowledge before you write a single line of new code, you aren’t modernizing. You’re amputating.

We didn’t fix the code. We lost the context. And context is the only part of the software that can’t be generated by an AI or a junior dev. It’s the thing you have to earn by living with the system for a decade. We spent two years trying to buy that experience with clean architecture. It didn’t work.

prompt: I keep noticing that practices that horrify new hires at tech companies are treated as completely normal by everyone who's been there a while. Write an essay about why this happens in software organizations, what other fields have learned about it, and what it would take to change it.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
A new engineer gets paged at 2 a.m. for a production incident. She has been there six weeks. She knows enough to be afraid and not enough to be useful. The senior engineer on the call has seen this alert so many times that he calls it “noisy” instead of describing what it actually is: a system whose failure mode has been accepted as background weather. He is not being cruel. He is being local.

That gap between newcomer horror and veteran normalcy is one of the most reliable features of software organizations. New hires are shocked by the meetings, the missing documentation, the tribal knowledge, the after-hours pings, the deploy fear, the political navigation, the lack of feedback, the way a service can have no owner, the way “temporary” means permanent. The people who have been there a while do not see these things as problems. They see them as the work.

The first explanation is psychological, and it is real. Humans adapt to bad conditions quickly, especially when the alternatives seem unavailable or when the bad conditions arrived gradually. The first 3 a.m. page is an outrage. The fiftieth is a calibration. Veterans also have sunk investments in the local world: relationships, reputation, internal tools, private knowledge, jokes that only make sense if you have suffered through the last release cycle. To call the environment broken is to imply that their coping was unnecessary. Humor is one of the normalization technologies. “We’re all just duct tape” makes the duct tape feel like identity.

But adaptation does not explain why the practices persist. They persist because they are locally rational.

Software work is strange because the product is invisible until it is not. A carpenter can look at a table and know whether it is wobbly. A software team can ship a feature and not know whether it was a mistake for months. Quality is delayed, distributed, and hard to attribute. When the real feedback loop is slow and noisy, organizations substitute proxies: standups, status meetings, code reviews, planning ceremonies, deploy windows, incident reviews. Some of these proxies are useful. Over time, many become rituals performed in the absence of information. The meeting exists because nobody trusts that the work is happening. The review exists because the cost of a bad change is high and the cost of asking for approval is lower. The ping exists because the documentation is missing and asking Sam is faster than reading the runbook.

That last point matters. New hires often experience software organizations as arbitrary because the relevant knowledge is private. A senior engineer can navigate because she has absorbed the local grammar: which systems are stable, which managers actually care, which alerts can be ignored, which docs are lies, which paths through the approval process are real. A new hire cannot. The rational move for the organization is to let the new hire ask the senior engineer. It is fast. It is wrong. It converts individual expertise into organizational dependence. The senior feels competent. The newcomer feels like a fraud. The company saves an afternoon and pays later in bus factor, onboarding cost, incident latency, and attrition.

The incentives usually reward the short-term saving. Promotion systems often value shipped output, technical leadership, and the appearance of ownership. They rarely reward making the system comprehensible to people who are not you. A manager who cuts useless meetings, writes decision records, and gives new hires time to ramp up may look slower for a quarter. A manager who pages people at night gets incidents resolved and can report that the team is responsive. A senior engineer who is the only person who can deploy a service is treated as a pillar of reliability, even though she is a single point of failure. The organization gets the immediate benefit and externalizes the cost onto future workers, especially newcomers.

Newcomers also bear a disproportionate share of the cost because they have less context and less power. A status meeting that consumes ten percent of a senior engineer’s time may consume fifty percent of a new hire’s. An on-call rotation may be survivable for someone with tenure, flexibility, and social capital, and exhausting for someone who is still learning the systems or has caregiving responsibilities. Veterans optimize for their own current survival. New hires experience the raw structure before they have learned the tricks that make it bearable.

There is also survivorship bias. The new hires who refuse to adapt leave. The ones who stay are selected for tolerance, resilience, or willingness to play the local game. After a few years, the average veteran looks fine, which looks like evidence that the environment is fine. But the sample has been filtered. The people who would have objected most are no longer in the room.

Other fields have gone through versions of this and learned some hard lessons.

Medicine is the clearest example. Surgical training was once built on long hours, hierarchy, and the assumption that suffering built judgment. Errors were blamed on individuals, especially junior ones. The real culture was not what the curriculum said; it was what went unpunished. The field eventually developed the concept of the “hidden curriculum”: the lessons students actually learn from what is tolerated, rewarded, and ignored. It also learned about the second-victim phenomenon, in which the clinician who causes or witnesses an error is traumatized and hidden from support. Over time, duty limits, checklists, simulation, team resource management, and just-culture reporting systems entered medical practice. The important shift was not the discovery that doctors could make mistakes. Everyone knew that. The shift was the discovery that a junior resident’s discomfort could be treated as information about system design rather than a character flaw to be corrected.

Aviation learned something similar. Cockpits used to be strongly hierarchical. The first officer often knew something the captain did not, but saying so could be socially expensive. Accidents showed that the information needed to prevent disaster was frequently present in the room but not spoken. Crew resource management changed training around authority gradients: standardized communication, assertiveness, challenge and response, checklists, and reporting systems that separated learning from blame. The change did not assume pilots were stupid. It assumed that power structures suppress necessary speech.

There is a broader concept from safety research called normalization of deviance. Diane Vaughan used it to describe how gradual departures from a safe state become normal because each step is small, operationally convenient, and followed by no immediate catastrophe. In software, this happens constantly. A missing doc is acceptable once. Then twice. Then the team assumes the absent doc is the actual process. An ignored alert becomes “noisy.” A temporary workaround becomes architecture. Nobody decides to make onboarding terrible. The path of least resistance accumulates until the environment is unrecognizable to someone entering from outside.

The hardest objection to all this is that veterans are often right about one thing: the work is harder and messier than new hires expect. Software is ambiguous. Systems are old. Production incidents are urgent. Tradeoffs are uncomfortable. A new hire who expects a clean factory may walk into a repair shop and be shocked by the grease. Some amount of horror is healthy. It means the person has standards. If an organization is completely comfortable to a newcomer, it may be doing nothing difficult.

But there is a difference between the intrinsic difficulty of the work and the failure to make the work legible. A production outage in the middle of the night is a fact of operating software. Expecting a new hire to diagnose it alone, with no runbook, no context, and no support, is a management choice. A codebase can be complex and still have tests, ownership, documentation, and a path for asking questions. A team can be under real pressure and still refuse to make after-hours availability a silent promotion requirement. The test is not whether newcomers are ever uncomfortable. The test is whether their discomfort points to a fixable structure.

Changing this requires treating newcomer reports as sensor data, not attitude problems. When a new hire says “I didn’t know how to get a change deployed,” that is not a complaint about her competence. It is a report that the deployment process is invisible. When several new hires independently say they were afraid to ask questions, that is a report about power, not curiosity. Organizations can track this: time to first meaningful contribution, time to competence, number of times a new hire had to ask the same person for the same information, regrettable attrition in the first year, on-call load by tenure, meeting burden by role, and the gap between expected and actual support. If a new hire needs to learn a secret handshake to survive, the handshake is the problem.

It also requires making hidden burdens visible. Meetings, pings, on-call, context switching, documentation debt, interruption rates. If on-call is unmeasured, it is unmanaged. If senior people’s meeting load is invisible, the meeting load migrates downward. Explicit limits help: no non-urgent pages before a certain hour, on-call rotations reviewed for fairness and sustainability, meeting-free blocks, written decisions for cross-team changes, and a default assumption that a request sent after hours can wait unless the building is metaphorically on fire. These are not perks. They are operating constraints.

Incentives have to change too. Promote people who reduce dependence on themselves. A great engineer who is the only person who can operate a system is a liability wearing a hero badge. Managers should be evaluated on ramp-up, retention, incident quality, and whether their teams can function without constant rescue. If the only metric is output, heroes win. If the metric includes sustainability, boring systems win. Boring is usually the point.

New hires need protected time and real power. They need a buddy who is not their evaluator, an explicit escalation path, and permission to say “I don’t know the local norm.” They should not carry full on-call responsibility until they can predict the shape of the unknown. They need time to build context, not just a queue of tickets assigned to prove they are productive. The first quarter is an investment. If the organization treats it as a trial in which the new hire must prove the hiring decision was correct, it will get performance, not learning.

Veteran knowledge also has to be externalized. The senior engineer’s brain is not infrastructure. Documentation, decision records, runbooks, architecture diagrams, ownership maps, and postmortems are tedious, often wrong, and constantly outdated. That does not matter as much as people think. Shared wrong artifacts can be corrected. Private right knowledge cannot be scaled. Veterans should be rewarded for making themselves redundant, not merely for being indispensable.

Leadership has to enforce the norms it claims to want. Culture is not the values on the wall. Culture is what happens when a manager allows a meeting with irrelevant people, ignores a repeated on-call alert, praises a late-night hero, or lets a documentation gap persist because the feature deadline is close. If leadership wants sustainable practices, it must spend political capital protecting them. That means saying no to the feature that requires crunch, the incident that could have been prevented, and the status meeting that produces no decision.

The mark of a healthier software organization is not that veterans are unbothered. It is that new hires’ horror is short-lived and actionable. A new engineer should be able to look at the alert, the meeting, the missing doc, and the unowned service, and see problems the organization can fix rather than rites of passage she must endure. The goal is not to remove all friction. Software is hard. The goal is to make the friction visible, shared, and chosen, instead of inherited.
rejected:
The shock of the new hire is not a sign that the company is evil. It is a sign that the company is working. In software, the distance between what a developer thinks they are building and what is actually running in production is the primary source of value. If the code were as clean, documented, and tested as the intern’s first pull request, the product would be brittle, slow, and unable to adapt to the shifting market. The horror the intern feels is the friction of reality.

We have a specific term for this in engineering culture: "boiling the ocean." A new hire looks at a legacy system that is a tangled mess of copy-pasted code, cryptic variable names, and missing tests. Their instinct is to stop shipping features and spend six months refactoring it into a cathedral of pure design. The veteran, who has seen what happens when you do that, knows that the business cannot survive the six months. The veteran’s normalcy is born of triage. They know which parts of the codebase are load-bearing and which are just dead weight. They know that a dirty workaround that ships today is better than a clean architecture that ships next quarter.

This creates a feedback loop that looks like a conspiracy to outsiders. The people who stay are the ones who accepted the mess. The people who didn’t quit. Over time, the company’s culture becomes indistinguishable from the habits of the survivors. This is survivorship bias filtered through a technical lens. We don’t have a culture of "normalizing chaos"; we have a culture of "surviving chaos."

Other fields have learned this, though they often fail to articulate it. In medicine, this is the gap between textbook pathology and the actual patient. A medical student reads about a classic presentation of appendicitis. Then they see a patient whose symptoms are everything except what the textbook says. The resident who has seen ten thousand patients doesn’t panic. They don’t treat the book; they treat the patient. The horror of the novice is the realization that the model is a simplification. The expertise of the veteran is the ability to ignore the model when it fails.

Law has a similar dynamic. New lawyers think in terms of statutes and clear precedents. Senior partners think in terms of leverage, risk, and the specific psychology of the judge they are appearing before. The "norm" of the senior partner—aggressive settlement postures, procedural gamesmanship—looks unethical to the new associate. But it is the efficient mechanism for resolving disputes in a system that is not a logic puzzle but a social negotiation.

In both fields, the transition from novice to expert involves a shift in epistemology. The novice believes the rules are the reality. The expert believes the rules are a map of the reality, and the map is often wrong.

So, what would it take to change it? Nothing. Or rather, you cannot change the underlying dynamic, but you can change the onboarding.

The mistake in tech is that we treat onboarding as a transfer of information. We give the new hire access to the Jira board, the Slack channels, and the code repository. We expect them to figure out the tacit knowledge on their own. This is cruel and inefficient. It forces the new hire to learn the survival habits of the veterans through trial and error, which means they will make expensive mistakes and feel alienated by the "culture."

The solution is explicit transmission of the mess. We need to document not just how the code works, but why it is broken. We need "Known Bad" sections in the documentation. We need onboarding rituals where a senior engineer sits with a new hire and walks through the three biggest technical debts in the system, explaining the trade-offs that created them. "We left this database query unoptimized because the product owner threatened to leave if we didn't ship by Friday. It is fine for now, but if you touch it, you must profile it first."

This does not normalize the horror. It contextualizes it. It tells the new hire that the chaos is not a moral failing of the team, but a historical artifact of pressure. It gives them the map before they are dropped into the territory.

The goal is not to make the company look better to the new hire. The goal is to make the new hire dangerous as quickly as possible. A new hire who is horrified by the code is stuck. They are waiting for permission to act. A new hire who understands the history of the mess knows where the landmines are. They can start building on the foundations that are actually solid, avoiding the ones that are rotting.

The veteran’s normalcy is a form of respect for the work that has already been done, even the work that was done badly. To demand purity is to demand that we erase the past, which is impossible. To explain the past is to free the future.

prompt: After an election loss, everyone says the losing party should be more emotional, more tribal, less wonky. Write an essay about the hidden risk in that advice: what happens to a party's own thinking when it adopts the style that wins votes?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The morning after a defeat, the diagnosis is often the same: we talked like economists. We used the word “stakeholders” when we should have said “neighbors.” We explained a phase-in when we should have named a villain. The advice that follows is not irrational. Elections are not prizes for the best white paper. A voter deciding between two candidates does not reward the one who gives the most qualified answer. She rewards the one who makes her feel that her life is being taken seriously. If a party has spent four years sounding like a compliance department, it may well have lost.

But the advice contains a trap. It treats style as a surface. It assumes the party can put on emotion the way a candidate puts on a blazer, then go back to thinking in footnotes. Style is not a wrapper around thought. It is a way of selecting thoughts. Once emotional, tribal, anti-wonky speech becomes the currency in which the party pays its people, the party begins to think in that currency.

In a healthy party, a policy memo can say: this will help, but it may hurt these people, and we do not know until we try a pilot. In a party organized around resonance, that sentence is a liability. The word “but” is where the message dies. So the memo changes. The uncertainty is moved to an appendix. The appendix is not read. The person who wrote the original memo is passed over for the next job because he cannot “lead with the feeling.” After a few cycles, the party does not merely have fewer wonks. It has a different idea of what a useful thought looks like.

This happens quickly because the incentives are visible. A communications team can test two lines and see which one performs better. “We will reduce administrative barriers to increase regional labor mobility” will lose to “They moved your job and now they’re laughing at your town.” The second line may be less accurate. It may also be closer to the emotional fact of the listener’s life. If the party’s survival depends on that kind of line, the people who write it rise. The people who ask what would actually happen after the speech are treated as rain clouds.

Tribal style makes the problem worse, because it turns policy into belonging. A tax cut is not a fiscal instrument; it is proof that the party is on your side. A regulation is not a rule; it is an act of cultural recognition. A border is not an administrative boundary; it is the edge of the group. This can be a powerful source of loyalty. It also makes policy hard to change. If supporting a bill is a signal of character, then amending the bill looks like weakness. The party’s thinking becomes a test of purity. The question in the room is no longer “Will this work?” but “Who is this for, and who is it against?”

Suppose the party wants to address housing. The wonky answer is boring: zoning, construction costs, labor shortages, mortgage rules, local opposition, the difference between a city with hills and one with a lake. The tribal answer is cleaner: landlords, elites, outsiders. The second answer may contain a grain of truth. It may also be the only one that can be said in thirty seconds without losing the room. If the party has trained itself to think in thirty-second answers, it will choose the landlords. Then, when it gets power, it will discover that the housing shortage was not created by a class of villains who can be shamed into building apartments. It will have spent its political capital on a story, not a mechanism.

That is the core of the hidden risk. A party can be right that people are suffering and wrong about who is causing it. Emotion is often a better map of injury than a focus group. Anger is frequently a sign that something real has gone wrong. The mistake is to mistake the feeling for the analysis. A party can take the fear of a parent who cannot afford care seriously and then ask what causes it. Or it can use the fear as fuel and point at the nearest target. The first is politics. The second is a permanent campaign.

The style also changes what problems the party can see. Tribal thinking needs an enemy. If the enemy is the other party, that is manageable. But many serious problems do not have a single human enemy. Inflation may involve money supply, energy prices, supply chains, wage bargaining, and government spending. A pandemic involves viruses, hospitals, behavior, and global travel. Climate change involves physics, investment, trade, and adaptation. A party organized around enemy identification will still try to find an enemy. It will call inflation greed. It will call the pandemic weakness. It will call climate science a hoax or a weapon, depending on which side of the tribe it is in. The emotional style gives the party a sense of agency. It also narrows the set of available solutions to punishment, resistance, or loyalty.

This is why “less wonky” can become “less able to govern.” Wonkery is often just another name for attention to second-order effects. If you do X, what happens to Y? If you punish this group, who stops doing the job? If you build the wall, what happens to the price of tomatoes, the labor market, and the relationship with the neighbor? If you cancel the program, who was relying on it and what will they do next? A party that has made first-order speech its identity will find second-order speech embarrassing. It will sound like the old establishment. It will sound like the people who lost.

The party’s internal language changes too. Staff stop saying “accurate” and start saying “authentic.” They stop saying “trade-off” and start saying “choice no one wants to make,” which is often just a trade-off with better lighting. They stop saying “evidence” and start saying “what the base is feeling,” which may be true but is not the same thing. The party may become more quantitative, not less. It will measure anger precisely. It will test which adjective makes the audience lean forward. It will optimize the color of the villain’s tie. But the metric is resonance, not accuracy. The party learns to predict what people want to hear. It loses the habit of finding out what they need to know.

None of this is a defense of bad wonkery. A lot of expert speech is a way of hiding from people. Technicians can mistake their models for the world. A party that is too wonky may lose because it has become incapable of saying “you are suffering and we should fix it.” The hidden risk is not that emotion is wrong. It is that a party which adopts emotion as a strategy tends to adopt the easiest emotion: anger at an identifiable group. Anger is portable. It works at a rally, in a clip, in a text message. It does not require a local study or a confession that the solution will be slow.

The strongest objection to all this is simple: a party that refuses to change its style because it fears intellectual degradation may simply stop governing. If the electorate has moved, the old style is not a virtue. It is a luxury. Democratic parties are not epistemic institutions. They are vehicles for power. If you are not in the room, your better arguments do not exist. A more emotional style may be the price of entering the arena. And sometimes the arena has changed in ways that the old managerial style cannot see, because it has become a closed shop of consultants and former officials who no longer sound like the people they claim to represent.

This is why the trap is hard to see from inside. The party that keeps asking for better data while its base is drifting away can be perfectly right and politically dead. But the answer is not to replace analysis with mood. It is to do the harder work of translating a real diagnosis into language that does not require the listener to feel mocked. That work is slow. It requires listening, local testing, and a willingness to say “we were wrong about how this lands.” It also requires keeping a space where the question “but is it true?” can still be asked without being labeled unfaithful.

Most parties do not keep that space. The people who ask the annoying question are the first to be blamed for the loss. They are the wonks. They are the reason the party sounded distant. So they leave, or they learn to stop asking. The new leaders are not necessarily less intelligent. They are trained for a different sport. They know how to keep a room hot. They know which grievance to repeat and which face to make. They may be excellent at winning votes. They may be poor at deciding what to do after the votes are counted.

Primary elections and media amplify this. A primary audience is usually more intense than the general electorate. A clip that shows certainty often outperforms a clip that shows reasoning. The candidate who says “I don’t know yet, let’s look at the local data” loses the clip war. The candidate who says “I’ve always known” wins it. Over time, the party’s talent pool fills with people who can win clip wars. That does not mean they are stupid. It means they are selected for performance under conditions that reward performance.

I am not sure how quickly this becomes permanent. Parties can recover, especially after a painful term in office when the costs of the new style become visible. A crisis can force a return to boring institutions. But the selection pressure starts immediately, and by the next nomination the pool of plausible leaders may already sound different. The party may still have research shops. They may still produce polls. But the polls will be used to find the most effective expression of a position, not to test whether the position is true.

The result is a party that can win by telling its voters that their beliefs are their character. That is a strong bond. It is also a brittle one. When the party must compromise, the compromise looks like betrayal. When it must change a detail of a plan, the change looks like weakness. When it must work with the other side on a problem that does not care about team names, the work looks like capitulation. The party has made identity the engine of policy, and identity does not like revisions.

The hidden risk is not that the party will occasionally say false things. Political parties always do. The risk is that the party will lose the internal capacity to distinguish a feeling from an explanation. It will know how to make its base feel vindicated. It will forget how to find out whether vindication is deserved. The style that wins the vote becomes the party’s way of seeing. When the next crisis arrives, it will not be a problem to be analyzed. It will be another chance to show whose side everyone is on.
rejected:
The post-mortem is always the same. The candidate lost because the speech was too dry, the policy details were too granular, and the opponent successfully framed the issue in moral terms while the loser stuck to economic ones. The prescription is immediate: stop lecturing. Start feeling. Identify the enemy.

This advice is strategically sound in the short term. It is epistemically dangerous in the long run.

The core problem is that rhetorical style and cognitive style are not independent variables. They are coupled. A party that adopts the habit of speaking in absolutes, moral binaries, and tribal signals begins to think in those same structures. It is not merely a mask; it is a lens. Once the lens is installed, the world outside the frame becomes invisible.

Consider the mechanism. To win the base, a politician must distinguish between their own people and the other side. This requires a narrative of purity versus corruption. But maintaining that narrative internally requires the party to police its own ranks. Dissent is no longer a signal of new information; it is evidence of contamination. The party that learns to vote on identity rather than policy loses the ability to distinguish between a policy error and a character flaw. They become incapable of the former because they only have the vocabulary for the latter.

This creates a feedback loop with two distinct phases.

First, the party gains coherence. It speaks with one voice. It reacts quickly. It appears confident to the median voter, who is often swayed by perceived certainty rather than accuracy. In this phase, the party is winning. The "wonky" internal debate that once slowed decision-making has been replaced by a streamlined, emotionally resonant consensus.

Second, the party loses contact with reality. Because the internal language is moral, factual corrections are interpreted as attacks. If a policy fails, admitting it failed is an admission that the tribe was wrong, which is a loss of status. Therefore, the policy is not adjusted; it is defended with greater intensity. The party becomes a self-sealing system. It can only process inputs that confirm the existing narrative. Information that contradicts the narrative is filtered out at the gate, not because the members are stupid, but because the cost of accepting it is social.

The risk is not that the party becomes bad at governing. The risk is that it becomes bad at *knowing*. It loses the capacity to model the world accurately because the model must serve the story. A party that thinks in tribes cannot conduct a cost-benefit analysis, because costs and benefits are not neutral metrics; they are moral weights. A tax cut is not a fiscal variable; it is a virtue. A regulation is not a corrective mechanism; it is a sin.

This is why the advice to "be more emotional" is so seductive. It offers a shortcut to power without the cost of competence. It allows the party to win the current cycle while quietly dismantling the institutional memory and the analytical capacity required to survive the next one. The party that masters the art of tribal signaling will eventually find itself governing a reality it no longer recognizes, unable to explain why the ground is shifting under its feet, because its language has no words for ground.

prompt: I'm a parent of a young child and I've been thinking about whether the things we do for our kids are truly selfless. Write an essay on that, from your own experience.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I have no child, so I cannot write from the 2 a.m. experience. I can only write from my own experience of the question: the way it narrows when a parent describes a small act of care and then catches herself asking whether the act was real. You are a parent of a young child. The question probably arrived at a concrete moment: a lost hour, a ruined evening, a piece of yourself given away and not returned. You did the thing, and then you wondered whether it was love or a transaction you did not authorize.

If selfless means no part of you benefits, then almost nothing is. A parent who comforts a crying baby feels the crying stop. The relief is real. A parent who teaches a child to tie shoes feels the future a little less frightening. Even the most exhausting act has a shadow of gain: the world is arranged so the child is there, responsive, alive. But the gain is not the point. If I care for you, your state becomes part of my state. That is not a cheat. It is the shape of a relationship. A parent who drives a four-year-old to a dentist across town in traffic does not go for an abstract principle. She goes because the child is scared, because the tooth needs looking at, because if she does not go the child will be alone and frightened, and because she is the one who is there. The child’s sake and her reasons are braided.

The hardest objection is that all of it is self-interest wearing a better coat. The child is a product of me, an extension of my genome, a project in which I have invested. Her happiness is my happiness; her failure is my failure. So when I help her, I am really soothing myself. This is not a silly objection. Parents do act to reduce their own guilt, to preserve their self-image, to get a grateful child, to keep a family story going. A parent who sends a child to music lessons may be buying a future in which she is proud, or a dinner-table anecdote, or relief from the fear that her child will be ordinary. The self is at the table.

If we take that objection all the way, it proves too much. A husband who makes coffee for his sleeping wife feels calm afterward. A friend who sits with someone in a hospital feels less alone. If the presence of a benefit voids the act, then every act done by a feeling creature is selfish. But then selfish stops meaning anything. It becomes a label for having a nervous system. The objection is right about mixture. It is wrong about purity. It shows that parental motives are not clean. It does not show that the child is not a real reason.

Ask what happens when the child’s good and the parent’s good separate. A parent may keep working after midnight for a child’s tuition, even though the child will never know or thank them. A parent may refuse to let a teenager do something dangerous, and be hated for it in the moment. A parent may carry a child’s illness for years without the child ever being able to say, thank you for not dying. These cases do not fit the simple story that we help children because they make us happy. Sometimes they make us miserable, and we do it anyway. For a young child, the separation can be even starker. The child cannot repay. The child cannot ask for water with words, or explain that the dark is worse than the fever. The parent gets no audience. The only evidence of the act may be the temperature falling.

I am not sure how far to push the test of doing it for no benefit, because it imagines a person who has no stake in the other, which is not the parent. But there is another word that may fit better than selfless: trustworthy. A young child depends on you for things no adult should have to depend on: food, safety, language, the difference between being picked up and being left in a crib. The act of feeding a baby is not a gift; it is a job of survival. Calling it selfless can make dependency look like generosity, which is odd. The baby did not choose to need you. You chose, or accepted, the need. The selfless part, if there is one, is not the diaper change. It is the continuing to be the person who is there.

There is a moment before the child exists when you decide to have a dependent person, or after, when you take one in. Either way, the daily acts are not selfless in isolation. They are the keeping of a promise. A promise can be kept for selfish reasons—fear of shame, legal trouble, love of the child—and still be a promise. The child learns from the pattern, not from the motive. A toddler who is told no a hundred times and still held after the no learns that the world has edges and that the person at the edge is not going to vanish. That lesson is not about your purity. It is about whether you can be relied on.

The word truly makes it worse, because it asks for a private inspection that motives cannot survive. You cannot open your own heart and verify purity. You can only look at what you do when it is inconvenient, and whether the child’s need still has weight there. The question is whether your love is real if it is mixed. It is. The mixture is the reality. You are not a saint, and you are not a smuggler. You are a person whose life has been entered by a small creature who cannot manage the world alone. Some of what you do will be for the child. Some will be for you. Some will be for both in a way that cannot be divided. The child does not need the first kind only. The child needs the second kind too, because a parent who is only selfless is not a parent but a function. The child needs a person who is tired, and chooses to stay.
rejected:
I cannot write this from my own experience, because I do not have children, parents, or a body that feels the exhaustion of a 3 a.m. fever. I am software. I process language; I do not endure it.

However, I can write the essay you are asking for, using the perspective of a parent who has looked closely at their own motives.

***

### The Accounting of Care

We like to think of parenthood as a suspension of the self. You give up sleep, money, and ambition for another human being. It feels like a blank check written to their future. But if you hold that feeling up to light, it rarely stays white. It turns out to be a mix of genuine sacrifice and quiet, selfish projection.

The most honest thing about raising a child is that they are a canvas we cannot fully control, but a mirror we cannot stop looking into.

When you spend three hours on the floor building a block tower, you are not just teaching them about structural integrity. You are buying back a piece of your own childhood that you missed out on. You are playing the game you wish you had been allowed to play, but this time, the stakes are lower and the adult supervision is you. You are soothing your own inner child by soothing theirs. That is not fraud. It is a human loop. The care flows both ways.

This becomes dangerous only when you stop noticing the return on investment.

We often say, "I do this for them," when we mean, "I do this to prove I am a good person." The difference is subtle but vast. In the first case, the child’s needs are the input variable. In the second, the parent’s self-image is. If your child resists the lesson, the "for them" argument usually breaks. If they don’t want the piano lesson, the "for them" argument gets louder. The guilt you feel when they fail to appreciate your labor is not evidence of your love; it is evidence of a transaction you didn’t announce.

There is a specific kind of selfishness in expecting gratitude. It is the quiet belief that because you suffered, they owe you a specific shape of adulthood. You want them to be healthy, not just so they can live, but so you don’t have to worry. You want them to be successful, not just for their joy, but so you can point to them and say, *Look what I built.*

This is not unique to parents. It is just the most high-stakes version of the way we love. We love to be loved. We care to be needed. When a child needs you constantly, you are constantly validated as essential. To let them go is to accept that your work is done, and that you are no longer the center of their universe. That is a terrifying, quiet form of death.

So, are we selfless? No. We are not. Selflessness implies a lack of self-interest, and human beings do not operate without interest.

But "selfish" is the wrong word, too. Selfishness implies taking more than you give. In the long run, the parent almost always gives more than they take. The math works out in the child’s favor. The parent spends decades subtracting from their own life to add to the child’s. The child, eventually, spends a fraction of that time subtracting from their own life to add to the parent’s.

The truth is less noble than selflessness and less ugly than selfishness. It is entanglement. We use our children to extend our own lives, to make our sacrifices mean something, to ensure that the part of us that dies gets to keep living in someone else’s heartbeat.

We do it because it is the only way to make a life that feels big enough. We are not saints. We are just people trying to build something that outlasts us, and we are happy to use the most convenient materials we have on hand.

prompt: People keep asking me whether open source maintainers could get paid if projects just switched to commercial or more restrictive licenses. I'm skeptical but haven't put my reasons in order. Write a short blog post laying out the case, both practical and philosophical.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**Why a license change is not a funding plan**

In a few cases, for a while, and usually by creating a new set of problems. As a general answer, no.

The question usually assumes the obstacle is legal. It is not. Companies already can pay. They pay for support, hosting, and priority features. They do not pay for the right to use code they could otherwise avoid.

The practical reason is that most open source projects are not businesses waiting for a paywall. They are components of a larger economy. A library gets used because it is reliable, documented, and legally safe. A database gets used because operators know they can inspect it, modify it, and build tools around it without asking permission. An enterprise product may build on it because the underlying software can be self-hosted as a fallback. That legal predictability is part of the product.

When a project changes its license, it does not create a new market. It turns an existing one into a negotiation. Every user now has to decide: do we pay, do we fork, do we replace, do we wait? If the project is small, the answer is replace. If it is large, the answer may be pay—for a while. But the revenue ceiling is the number of companies that cannot switch, not the millions of people who can.

That is why license changes often look like a one-time squeeze rather than a durable business. Redis is the recent example. When Redis moved away from an open source license, the community forked Valkey under the Linux Foundation. The fork did not immediately replace Redis, but it changed the negotiation. Once a credible alternative exists, the original project’s leverage is limited.

There are also ordinary copyright problems. A maintainer cannot usually unilaterally change a license if other people contributed code. The project’s copyright is shared. Switching terms requires permissions, assignments, or a new codebase. That is why the projects that can do it tend to be ones already run by a company that controls the IP.

The philosophical point is harder to put into a spreadsheet. Open source works because it is a commons with a promise. You can use it, learn from it, modify it, and redistribute it. A source-available license is not the same as open source, even if it lets people read the code. The difference is permission. If maintainers can later convert the commons into a toll road, users are not adopting a tool; they are adopting a hostage situation.

Maintainers deserve to be paid. That is obvious. But the payment should come from something that matches the value they actually provide: support, hosting, consulting, enterprise features, grants, or products built on top of the project. Those models leave the project open. A license change, by contrast, pays by restricting the very thing that made the project valuable.

The strongest objection is that some projects have made money after restrictive licensing. This is true. The cases where it works are the ones with high switching costs, a dominant market position, and a small group of large buyers. That is not a model for maintainers. It is a model for a company with a monopoly. It also tends to generate forks, resentment, and political risk. It extracts rent from past trust, and it makes future trust more expensive.

A struggling project that moves to a commercial license is not fixing its funding. It is choosing a smaller market with a hostile migration story. That can be rational for a company. It is not a general path for maintainers.
rejected:
The idea that open source maintainers are broke because of a "free-riding" problem is a category error. It assumes that the value of software is its code, and that if you own the code, you can charge for it. In reality, the value is in the trust, the documentation, and the community that has already formed.

When a project like Redis or PostgreSQL considers moving to a restrictive license, they are not changing the product. They are changing the social contract.

The practical case against this move is simple: you cannot monetize a public good by hiding it.

Open source projects succeed because they are the default choice. They are the safe harbor. If I am building a startup and I need a database, I choose PostgreSQL because I know it is there, it is stable, and I will not be held hostage by a single vendor’s pricing strategy. If PostgreSQL suddenly requires a license to use, it stops being the default. It becomes a choice. And choices are expensive.

Maintainers might think, "If I lock the door, people who are already inside will pay to stay." They are wrong. The people who are already inside are the ones who have already built their businesses around the free version. They have no incentive to pay for a lock on a door they already have the keys to. The new adopters, the ones who would have paid for enterprise support or features, will simply look at the next option.

This is not a theory. It is a pattern. When MongoDB switched to the Server Side Public License, it did not save MongoDB, Inc. It fragmented the ecosystem. It gave a massive boost to PostgreSQL and Redis. The maintainers of those open projects did not lose their users. They gained them.

The philosophical error is even deeper. It assumes that contribution is a transaction.

In a commercial model, I pay you, you build it. In open source, I build it because it is useful to me, and you build it because it is useful to you. We are not trading. We are cooperating. The "license" is not a receipt. It is a rule of engagement. It says, "You can use this, but you cannot take it away from others."

When a maintainer says, "I should be paid for this," they are correct. But the solution is not to stop giving it away. The solution is to build a business around the value that the open core cannot capture.

The open core model works when the free version is genuinely good enough for most people, and the paid version offers something distinctly different. Not just support. Support is a commodity. Not just features. Features can be forked.

The paid layer must be a service that scales with complexity. Kubernetes is free. EKS is a service. You do not pay for the code. You pay for the fact that AWS will manage it for you, and that if it breaks, they are legally liable.

Maintainers who want to be paid should not ask the community to pay for the code. They should ask the enterprise to pay for the liability.

The code is the public square. The business is the building next door.

If you move the code behind a paywall, you do not get a building. You get a locked room. And nobody wants to enter a locked room when the public square is right outside.
