The most honest external models are often the artifacts the system already uses: the schema, the event definitions, the deployment configuration, the load test. They are current because the system would break if they were not.

The practical implication is that software organizations should manage cognitive load as carefully as they manage compute. Protect long enough attention spans to load a real path. Give teams ownership that follows meaning, not just layer. Make interfaces boring, because every interesting detail in an interface is a detail another team must load. Review code not only for bugs but for whether it makes the next model easier or harder to build. When a change requires five people to explain five fragments, that is a design smell even if the code passes tests. When a new engineer can trace one real request from browser to database and back, and can say where their understanding stops, the organization has built something useful: a shared head, not a single person’s memory.
rejected:
When a programmer says they have a system "in their head," they are describing a specific cognitive state: a mental simulation of the code that runs fast enough to predict behavior without executing it. It is not memorization. No human can hold millions of lines of source code in working memory. It is a model. It is a graph of components, data flows, and invariants, compressed into abstractions that the brain can manipulate at the speed of thought.

This state is the difference between a coder and an engineer. A coder looks at an error message, searches for a pattern, and patches a symptom. An engineer with the system loaded anticipates the side effects of a change before writing the first character. They know that moving a database query to this function will break the caching layer three modules away because they hold the relationship between those modules in their mind.

Building this model is expensive. It requires deep, uninterrupted focus. Context switching is the primary enemy. If you are interrupted by a Slack message or a meeting while constructing a mental map of a complex distributed system, the map dissolves. Reconstructing it takes twenty to thirty minutes of deep work. Most modern software environments are hostile to this. Open office plans, daily standups, and instant messaging tools fragment the attention span required to build the model. A developer who spends six hours a day in meetings and interruptions cannot hold a large system in their head. They can only hold the file they are currently editing.

This has direct implications for how companies organize work. The unit of software work is not the line of code, nor even the feature, but the cognitive scope. A team can only efficiently work on a system if the system fits in the heads of the people working on it. When a codebase grows beyond what a single engineer can hold, you hit a wall. You can break the problem into smaller pieces, but only if the boundaries are clean. If the pieces are entangled, the engineers must spend their time synchronizing with each other to reconstruct the missing parts of the global model. This is why "big ball of mud" architectures are not just bad engineering; they are organizational inefficiencies. They force humans to act as the glue that the code lacks.

Companies that understand this optimize for cognitive locality. They prefer small, autonomous teams that own bounded contexts. They allow engineers to block out hours of uninterrupted time. They treat meetings as a cost, not a default. They accept that a small team working on a coherent slice of the system will outpace a large team working on a tangled whole, even if the large team has more bodies.

The mistake management often makes is treating programmers as interchangeable labor units that can be scaled linearly. You cannot scale a mental model by adding heads. You can only add more minds, each holding a different fragment, and then you pay the tax of communication to integrate those fragments. The most efficient organization is one that minimizes the distance between the code and the person who needs to understand it. It keeps the model loadable.

If you want to know if a company truly understands software, look at their calendar. If engineers are constantly context-switching, they are not thinking about the system. They are reacting to it. And a company whose engineers only react to the system is building a legacy in real-time, one broken assumption at a time.

prompt: I just finished reading a book about bee cognition and I can't stop wondering: are bees actually smart? Write a funny but serious review-style essay that works through what we know about bee behaviour and where the line between instinct and real thinking might lie.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**Review: The Bee as Small, Serious Mind**

The first sign that a book about bee cognition has done its job is that you stop seeing bees as punctuation. They are no longer tiny yellow commas landing on the sentence of your afternoon; they become small, furious colleagues with opinions about flowers. That is a useful feeling, because it forces you to abandon the comfortable idea that intelligence begins somewhere around the size of a rat’s brain. Bees do not fit that boundary. They are too clever for their bodies, which is either a miracle or an accounting error.

A honeybee’s brain is about the size of a pinhead and contains roughly 100,000 neurons. For scale, that is less than the number of neurons in a fruit fly’s visual system alone, and vastly less than a mouse. If you hold a bee up to the usual mammalian standard, it should be a flying reflex with wings. It is not. Bees navigate, remember, learn categories, communicate about distant places, and in some experiments appear to have a sense of number. The puzzle is not whether they are “really” smart; it is what counts as real.

Start with navigation, because that is where the case becomes hard to wave away. A foraging bee does not simply fly out and hope. It uses the sun as a compass, and on cloudy days it can read polarized light in the sky to estimate where the sun is. It uses landmarks. It uses smell. It can learn a route to a flower patch and remember it for days. If you move the landmarks, it does not merely crash into the world; it re-evaluates. That matters. A fixed instinct might say, “go left at the big rock.” A navigating animal says, “the big rock is supposed to be there; it is not; therefore my model of the world needs revision.” The bee’s model is not a map in the human sense—nothing so tidy—but it is a working representation. It has content, and the content can be wrong.

Then there is the waggle dance, which is the part of bee cognition that tends to make people reach for the word “language” a little too quickly. When a honeybee finds a good source of nectar, it returns to the dark comb and performs a dance: a straight run with a waggle phase, followed by loops back to the starting point. On the vertical comb, the angle of the waggle run relative to gravity encodes the angle of the food source relative to the sun. The duration of the waggle phase encodes distance. So a bee that found clover three hundred metres away, forty degrees left of the sun, does not simply announce “clover.” It draws a vector. Other bees watch or follow the dance, then fly out in roughly the right direction.

That is astonishing, but it is not human language. Bees do not have open-ended syntax. They cannot argue about the clover, invent a clover, or describe a hypothetical clover that might have been better if the sun had been elsewhere. The dance is more like an embodied advertisement: a directional recommendation with enthusiasm as amplitude. A good source produces a vigorous dance; a poor one produces a weak one, or none at all. That last point is important. The dance is instinctive in form, but not empty. A bee cannot dance about a flower it has not found. The template is inherited, but the data come from experience.

That distinction is where the line between instinct and thinking gets interesting, because “instinct” is often used as a magic word that means “not thinking.” But instinct is not the opposite of cognition. It is a prior. A bee is born with a brain already organized to solve certain problems: finding food, finding the way home, telling others where the food is. What it is not born with is the location of the clover. The colony has built a very good default operating system, but each forager still has to install local updates.

The learning is where the bees get troublesome. They can associate colours, odours, shapes, and places with reward. Train a bee to visit a blue card for sugar, and it will tend to prefer blue cards later. But it can do more than memorize a single card. It can generalize. Show it a new shade, a slightly different shape, a novel context, and it may still make the right bet. That is not a lookup table. That is categorization. In experiments, bees can be trained to prefer panels with small numbers of items over panels with large numbers—up to four, in the clearest cases—and then choose between numbers they have not seen before. Some studies even suggest they can learn the idea of “none,” which is a concept so abstract it feels like a bee-sized philosophical trick.

They are not doing arithmetic. Nobody should claim that a bee is sitting in a flower column and solving equations. What they appear to have is a quantity sense: a distinction between “a few” and “more than a few,” good enough to improve foraging decisions. That is still cognition. An animal that can extract a rule from repeated experiences, apply it to new stimuli, and adjust when the rule stops paying is not merely reacting. It is learning a pattern.

Then there are the puzzle experiments, which are where the internet likes to declare bees “geniuses” and scientists quietly sigh. In a lab, a bee can be taught to push a small disk aside to reach sugar. At first, that sounds like a rat in a box: animal bumps thing, sugar appears, animal bumps thing more. But the interesting version is not the first bump. The interesting version is the next puzzle, slightly different, where the bee has to figure out that the disk, not the wall, is the part that gives. If it goes for the disk with less random thrashing, something has been extracted from the previous experience. It has formed a representation of the task’s structure, however thin.

The same caution applies to all of this. Bees are small, their lives are short, and their cognition is built for flowers, not for human tests. A bee’s cleverness is not general intelligence in the way a chimpanzee’s or a crow’s is. It is compressed, sensory, and practical. Bees do not sit under a tree wondering what it means to be a bee. They do not have the metabolic luxury of an inner monologue. Their mind, if that is the right word, is a flight path.

And that is the hardest objection: maybe none of it is “real” thinking, just very elaborate instinct plus conditioning. A bee dances because bees dance. It chooses the blue card because it was rewarded. It pushes the disk because the disk happened to move before the sugar arrived. Why call that thinking?

Because the alternative cannot explain the flexibility. Pure instinct would not adjust when the landmark moves. Pure conditioning would not generalize from three dots to two dots against six. A fixed routine would not produce a dance whose angle changes depending on where the flower actually is. The content is not fixed. The bee’s behaviour changes with the world in ways that track the world’s facts. That is what thinking is for.

There is also the social dimension, which makes the whole thing stranger. A bee that has watched a dance can fly to a food source it has never visited. It is using another bee’s experience as evidence. The colony can regulate its temperature, allocate foragers, defend itself, and decide when to swarm in ways no single bee could manage alone. But one should not turn the hive into a giant brain too quickly. The colony is not a mind in the way a human is a mind. It is a system. The bees inside it are still individual animals, each with its own errors, preferences, and limited memory. The hive is smart the way a city is smart: through division of labour, feedback, and a lot of local decision-making that looks coordinated from above.

So where is the line between instinct and real thinking? There is no clean line, because the question assumes there is one. In bees, the line is a slope. At one end you have the inherited machinery: the dance pattern, the sun compass, the flower-loving visual system. At the other end you have the individual bee’s learned additions: this patch is good, that colour is risky, the disk is the handle, the sky is cloudy but the polarization says the sun is over the barn. The instinct provides the tools; the experience provides the information. Remove either and the bee performs badly.

That does not make bees wise. It does not make them self-aware, or moral, or capable of sitting in judgment on your life choices. They are not little philosophers. They are not little humans with wings. They are a different solution to the same problem: how to move through a changing world and extract energy from it without a big brain. Their cognition is not a smaller version of ours. It is a different shape, optimized for speed, economy, and flowers.

The honest answer, then, is that bees are smart in the sense that matters for an animal. They can learn, remember, generalize, communicate, and solve novel problems within the limits of their lives. They are not smart in the sense of being able to explain themselves. We will never know what it is like to be a bee, and they probably have no business to report. But the behaviour is too flexible, too informative, and too well matched to the environment to be dismissed as mere instinct.

So the next time a bee lands on your arm, do not make the usual mistake of treating it as a small accidental decoration. It is checking a situation. It has a compass, a memory, a preference, and a brain the size of a grain of rice. It is not pondering your soul. It is deciding what to do next. That is not nothing. In a creature that weighs less than a paperclip, that is a great deal.
rejected:
The honeybee is the size of a thumbnail. It weighs less than a paperclip. And yet, it has been sent into the sky, mapped a landscape, and returned to a hive of eight thousand sisters to perform a 90-second interpretive dance that conveys latitude, longitude, and the quality of the nectar source.

If you were a fly, you would call this luck. If you were a bee, you would call it Tuesday.

The question of bee intelligence is tricky because we tend to define "smart" by human metrics. We measure intelligence by how long an animal remembers a fact, how many variables it can juggle, or whether it can solve a puzzle box. By these standards, bees are modest. They have no cortex. They have a brain the size of a poppy seed, composed of roughly 950,000 neurons. That is a drop in the bucket compared to our 86 billion.

But if you define intelligence as the ability to navigate a chaotic world and survive, bees are terrifyingly competent.

Consider the waggle dance. It is not a random jitter; it is a vector. A bee juts its abdomen toward the sun’s position relative to gravity. The angle of the dance tells the audience where the food is. The duration of the waggle tells them how far. The enthusiasm of the shake tells them how good the sugar is.

This is not instinct in the way a spider spinning a web is instinct. Spiders do not have opinions about their webs. Bees do. They can update the map. If a flower patch dies, the bees stop dancing for it. If a new, better patch appears, the old dance is suppressed. The hive is running a real-time stock market of floral resources, and the ticker tape is a vibrating abdomen.

Then there is the matter of math. In 2011, a team at RMIT University in Melbourne taught four honeybees to perform arithmetic. They used sugar water and quinine (a bitter taste) to create positive and negative values. The bees learned that a yellow shape meant "add one" and a blue shape meant "subtract one."

They got it right 75% of the time.

That is not a high score. But it is not zero. It implies that the bee’s brain can hold a concept of quantity in working memory, apply a rule, and execute a motor response based on the result. They were not just reacting to the sugar; they were processing the symbol.

This leads to the hard part: the line between instinct and thought.

Instinct is a fixed program. It is fast, it is reliable, and it is dumb. A wasp builds a nest in a specific way. It does not try a different way. It does not wonder if the mud is too dry. It builds.

But bees improvise. If you put a bee in a lab and ask it to find food, it will use a strategy. If the strategy fails, it will try a different one. This is called flexible cognition. It suggests that the bee is not just running a script; it is making a decision.

Where is the line?

It might be in the difference between knowing a fact and knowing a situation. An ant knows that the trail leads to the crumb. A bee knows that the crumb is there *today*, but the wind is strong, so it should probably go to the lavender instead. That second thought—the adjustment based on a new variable—is where the magic happens. It is the spark that separates a machine from an animal.

Bees also seem to have something like empathy, or at least, social awareness. They recognize their sisters. They grieve for lost queens. They can detect fear in the pheromones of other bees and change their behavior accordingly. This is not a complex emotion. It is a chemical signal. But the response is nuanced. A bee that smells fear does not just flee; it assesses. It decides if the threat is to the hive or to itself.

This is the problem with calling bees "smart." The word implies a person. It implies a mind that looks back at itself and wonders. We do not know if bees do that. We do not know if they have inner monologues. We do not know if they dream of flowers.

What we do know is that they are efficient. They are social. They are adaptable. They have solved the problem of being small and fragile by being together. Their intelligence is not individual; it is collective. The hive is the brain. The bee is the neuron.

When you look at a bee buzzing around your garden, you are not looking at a tiny, dumb insect. You are looking at a node in a distributed network that has been running for millions of years, optimizing for energy, survival, and the propagation of its genome.

It is not human intelligence. It does not write poetry. It does not care about the meaning of life.

But it can do math. It can dance. It can change its mind.

And for a creature that fits on your finger, that is enough to make you want to step back and let it have the flower.

prompt: A magazine article says polyamory has a problem because black people are underrepresented in it. Write a response from someone in the poly community, thinking about why any group might be demographically skewed and what the framing does.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I read the article’s claim as a report card: polyamory, failing, reason: not enough Black people. The oddness is not that the writer cares about race. The oddness is that the sentence makes a racial population the test of a relationship practice’s success.

I am in the poly community, so I have a stake in this. I also don’t have a clean number, and I want to be plain about that. I don’t know how many Black people are polyamorous, because the label is self-applied and because people who maintain more than one relationship do not always organize their lives around the word. If “polyamory” means the people who show up to meetups, use the term in profiles, or appear in community directories, then the sample is already filtered by visibility, class, geography, and comfort with a particular kind of outness. If it means actual relationship patterns, the visible scene is a poor map. “Underrepresented” has to mean underrepresented relative to something: a city, a nation, an online platform, a neighborhood. A room in a wealthy suburb will look like a wealthy suburb. That is not automatically a moral failure, but it is not neutral either.

Any group is demographically shaped by the roads that lead to it. A climbing gym, a vegan co-op, a software meetup, a church, a mutual aid network: each one ends up looking like the people who can reach it. Access matters. Money matters. Safe housing matters. Language matters. Trust in institutions matters. If a practice spreads through online forums, college towns, progressive media, and private homes where people can talk without fear of family or employer consequences, it will not look like the whole population. It will look like the population with the most access to those channels. That does not mean the practice is bad. It means the visible form of the practice has traveled along certain lines.

But that explanation does not let a community off the hook. A demographic shape can be the residue of barriers. If Black people are underrepresented in a space because the space is in a place they do not feel safe in, costs money they cannot spare, assumes a communication style they were not rewarded for learning, or meets them with stereotypes the moment they arrive, then the underrepresentation is a trace of exclusion. The problem is not the number. The problem is what produced the number.

That is where the magazine’s framing gets shaky. “Polyamory has a problem because Black people are underrepresented in it” sounds like a concern, but it locates the problem in the absence rather than in the conditions. It turns Black people into the missing ingredient. Put them in, and the community becomes healthier, more legitimate, more modern. Without them, the community is incomplete. That is a strange thing to say about a group that has often been treated as morally suspect simply for existing in certain intimate arrangements. It implies that polyamory needs Black presence to prove that it is decent.

I think I understand the impulse behind the article. If you care about racial justice, an overwhelmingly white room can look like a moral failing, especially when the room is full of people who talk about consent, boundaries, and challenging norms. The mismatch is embarrassing. But the embarrassment is not the main issue. The main issue is whether Black people can enter, stay, and be believed without paying a special tax.

Representation is not the same thing as safety. A community can add a few Black members to its panels and feel better while leaving the underlying dynamics alone. It can celebrate diversity in the abstract while still treating Black anger as “too intense,” Black sex as “natural” or “spicy,” Black grief as a burden on the group, and Black relationship choices as a problem to be managed. Polyamory’s favorite tools are communication, honesty, and boundaries. Those tools do not automatically balance power. If a Black woman is in a triad with two white partners, the racial script does not vanish because everyone agreed to be transparent. Her feelings may be interpreted through old stereotypes. Her partners may be read as “evolved” while she is read as “exotic.” The structure can be consensual on paper and still feel unequal in practice.

The same is true for Black men, though the stereotypes are different. A Black man in a relationship with white women may be seen through a lens of predation or promiscuity, while the white partners are seen as open-minded. The community may say, “We don’t do racism here,” while nobody notices the racism happening in the micro-interactions. That is why a demographic audit is not enough. The question is not only who is in the room. It is who is trusted in the room, whose story is taken seriously in conflict, whose presence is treated as normal rather than illustrative.

There is also a cultural question the article seems to skip. Black intimate life has not been a simple mirror of mainstream marriage. It has been shaped by slavery, separation, migration, religious communities, extended family, economic survival, and constant surveillance. Some Black people may be deeply skeptical of a label that emerged from white progressive and therapeutic cultures. Some may find it useful. Some may have relationship patterns that overlap with polyamory without using the word. Some may be in churches where nonmonogamy is not a lifestyle option. Some may be queer and already outside the marriage script. Some may be parents for whom being open about multiple partners is a risk they cannot take. A demographic category cannot carry all of that. To say “Black people are underrepresented in polyamory” can flatten a lot of different lives into one absence.

I do not want to defend a white room by calling its whiteness natural. If poly spaces are hostile to Black people, that is a serious flaw. Polyamory claims to be about more honest relationships and more consensual structures. If it cannot handle its own racial dynamics, that claim rings hollow. The community should ask concrete questions: Are meetups accessible by transit? Are they cheap enough for people without disposable income? Do moderators actually intervene when someone is racially mocked? Do people of color have to explain themselves repeatedly? Are Black poly people treated as experts on race whether they want to be or not? Are relationships involving Black partners met with the same seriousness as other relationships? Are the community’s assumptions about privacy, family, and disclosure built around a particular class and racial experience?

Those questions matter more than the percentage.

The framing also does something subtle: it makes the community the victim of its own demographics. “Polyamory has a problem” suggests that the community is suffering because it is not representative enough. But if Black people are staying away, the suffering is not primarily the community’s missing diversity credential. The suffering is the lost possibility of connection, the avoided space, the repeated decision not to go where you will have to justify yourself. A magazine can turn that into a neat narrative about a movement’s failure to include, but the people on the outside may not be thinking about the movement’s image at all. They may be thinking about their own lives.

I also don’t think the answer is a quota. A quota can turn Black members into exhibits. “Look, we have representation now” is not the same as “we have changed the conditions that kept people away.” Inclusion should not mean that Black people are recruited to fix the room’s self-image. It should mean that the room stops being a place where whiteness is the default and everyone else is an addition.

There is a difference between a community being too white and a community being obsessed with its racial composition. The first is a fact about power and access. The second is a symptom of vanity. A group that is mostly white should not be proud of that, but it should be careful about how it complains about it. If the complaint is, “We are failing to reach Black people,” that can sound like a marketing problem. If the complaint is, “Black people report that they are not safe here,” that is a moral problem. The first invites strategy. The second demands accountability.

The hardest part of the article’s claim is that it is not entirely wrong to notice the skew. If a community says it is universal and then only one group shows up, something is off. But the notice has to be aimed correctly. The skew is evidence, not verdict. It points toward questions about access, safety, culture, and power. It does not by itself prove that polyamory is defective as a relationship form. It proves that the institutions carrying the form have a particular shape, and that shape may be exclusionary.

If I were responding to the magazine directly, I would say this: stop treating Black people as the measure of polyamory’s respectability. Polyamory does not need Black bodies to validate it. Black people do not need polyamory to be valid. The useful question is whether Black people who want to be in these spaces can be in them without being turned into a lesson in diversity. The less useful question is whether the scene has achieved the right demographic balance to look progressive in a magazine.

A relationship practice can be widespread and still be invisible in the institutions that claim to represent it. That gap is worth examining. But the examination should start with the people being kept out, not with the community’s discomfort at its own mirror.
rejected:
The premise is that a subculture is broken because it doesn’t look like the census. This is a category error.

Polyamory is not a public utility. It is a relationship structure that requires a specific amount of cultural capital to execute. You need disposable income to fund three houses, three cars, and three therapists. You need a career that allows for flexible hours or remote work, so you can coordinate calendars across time zones without getting fired. You need a baseline level of emotional literacy and a tolerance for ambiguity that is often taught in specific socioeconomic environments, not universal.

The demographic skew toward white, wealthy, and educated participants is not a sign of exclusion; it is a sign of cost. The barrier to entry is high. If you want to include more Black people, you don’t fix the ideology; you fix the economics. You lower the cost of maintaining complex networks. You stop requiring that every participant be a CEO or a freelance consultant.

The framing of "underrepresentation" implies that the community is currently a closed club that is actively kicking people out. The data doesn’t support that. It supports that the current model is expensive and that most people, regardless of race, are too poor or too time-poor to participate. By focusing on race, the article obscures the class issue. It lets the wealthy participants off the hook. They can point to their diversity initiatives and their inclusive language while ignoring the fact that their lifestyle is structurally out of reach for the majority of Black Americans.

If you want a diverse poly community, stop asking why people aren’t coming to your expensive, time-intensive table. Start asking why the table is so big.

prompt: In what situations does teaching technical topics with comics actually help, and is 'some people are visual learners' a good enough answer? Write a reflective blog post from the perspective of someone who makes programming zines.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
## What Comics Are Good For

I make little programming zines, the kind you staple in a bathroom and hand to someone who says, “I always thought APIs were magic.” A few weeks ago I made one about git merge conflicts. It is eight pages. Two of those pages are a comic: two versions of a file walk into a room, argue, and a third, uglier file is born. The other six pages are code, diffs, and commands.

When people finish it, they often say the comic helped. Then they add, “I guess I’m a visual learner.” I don’t buy that answer. It sounds like a preference, but the useful question is what the picture did that the prose couldn’t.

Comics help when the technical idea has a shape. Not just a fact or a rule, but a relationship: who talks to whom, what changes state, where the waiting happens, what breaks when the order changes. A network request is a sequence with delays and failures. A closure is a value that carries a small environment with it. A race condition is two events that are safe separately but unsafe interleaved. Those are easy to make into panels because the meaning is in the arrangement. If I draw a client, a server, and a packet moving between them, the reader gets a spatial model before the words arrive. The picture is not decoration. It is a compressed diagram with a narrative order.

This is where the visual-learner answer goes wrong. It treats the help as a property of the person, not the representation. “Some people are visual learners” does not tell me why a comic about DNS helps one reader and confuses another. It also quietly suggests that if you are not visual, a comic will not help you, which is nonsense. A comic is words and pictures. The words carry the precision. The pictures carry the structure. If the structure is the hard part, the comic can help almost anyone. If the hard part is exact syntax, edge cases, or formal proof, the comic can get in the way.

I have learned to separate three jobs that people lump together: making a topic approachable, making a model memorable, and making a skill executable. Comics are often good at the first two. They are not automatically good at the third. A comic can make HTTP feel less intimidating. It can give you a story about request, response, status code, retry. But it cannot replace the experience of reading a curl error, watching headers in DevTools, or debugging a redirect loop. If the zine ends with a cute mascot and no commands, the reader has a mood, not a method.

The best programming comics I have made are the ones where the image is doing work that code alone would make invisible. Take state machines. In code, a state machine is an enum, a switch, and some guards. It is hard to see the lifecycle. In a comic, the object can be a person at different stations: created, pending, active, cancelled. The panels show that some transitions are allowed and others are absurd. You can draw the illegal transition as a door that is bricked up. That is a concrete image for a constraint. It is not the implementation, but it is the thing the implementation is trying to enforce.

Concurrency is another case. A text description of a deadlock can be accurate and still hard to hold in your head: two threads each hold a lock and wait for the other. A comic can show two characters standing in a doorway, each holding the other’s key. The joke is almost unavoidable, but the joke is not the point. The point is that the waiting is mutual and structural, not accidental. Once the reader sees the shape, the code becomes a description of the shape rather than a spell to memorize.

But comics fail when the technical topic is mostly local detail. Regular expression syntax is a bad comic subject unless you are teaching the very first intuition that a pattern is a search with constraints. You can draw a little creature scanning a string and catching the words it wants, but the creature does not teach backreferences, non-capturing groups, or why your pattern fails on the twelfth test case. For that, you need the actual pattern, the actual string, and the actual error. The comic becomes a sugar coating that makes the reader overconfident. I have seen this with zines about regex: people love the pages where the dot is a wildcard and the asterisk is a greedy mouth, then get stuck when the real pattern has anchors and character classes. The mental model was too cute.

That is the hardest objection I keep coming back to: comics can teach a false model and make it feel obvious. In programming, false models are expensive. If a comic suggests that the browser “sends the request and then waits politely,” the reader may not think about DNS, TLS, connection reuse, or intermediate proxies. If it suggests that a database transaction is just a save button, the reader may not understand isolation levels. The comic’s strength—making something feel simple—can become its danger.

The fix is not to avoid comics. The fix is to make the boundary of the model visible. In the zine, I try to include a page called “What the cartoon leaves out.” It lists the simplifications: the network is not a tube, the server is not a person, the merge conflict is not a fight that can be settled by picking a side. The comic gets to be useful because it is not allowed to be the whole truth.

This is also why “visual learner” is not enough as an answer. Learning-styles talk has a comforting symmetry: visual, auditory, kinesthetic. But I don’t think the popular version of that idea explains much. A person who says they learn visually may actually benefit from diagrams because diagrams reduce working-memory load, or because they can compare alternatives side by side, or because the image gives them a place to attach a verbal explanation. A person who says they learn by doing may benefit from a comic if it motivates them to open the terminal. The medium is not the style. The medium is a set of constraints. Comics force sequencing. They force economy. They force you to choose one image per idea. That can be excellent pedagogy or terrible pedagogy depending on the idea.

I think comics are most useful at the boundary between ignorance and confusion. A beginner facing a new technical domain often has two problems at once: the content is hard, and the reader is anxious about being bad at it. A comic can lower the second problem without fully solving the first. The panels say you are allowed to be lost. The jokes say the experts are not solemn. The small page count says this will not eat your evening. That matters. I have handed zines to people who would not open a long article. Not because they are visual, but because the zine looks like a toy. They read it standing up. They laugh at a bad pun. Then they notice they have an image of the thing in their head. The image is not the knowledge, but it is a hook.

Where comics are less useful is when the learner already has a working model and needs to refine it. If you understand how garbage collection works at a high level and need to understand generational assumptions, a comic of little objects aging in rooms may be charming but too coarse. You need numbers, thresholds, allocation rates, and the specific behavior of the collector you are using. The comic can orient you, but it cannot replace the precision. At that stage, a diagram may be better than a comic: static, zoomable, less narrativized. A comic adds time and character. Sometimes the topic needs less story and more structure.

There is also a practical zine constraint: the page is small. A comic panel can hold a label, a code snippet, and a face. It cannot hold a long stack trace. So when I make a programming zine, I am always deciding what the comic is for. Is it the first page, meant to make the reader trust the zine? Is it a summary at the end, meant to turn a list of facts into a picture? Is it the central explanation, because the topic is inherently sequential? Those are different uses. A comic as frontispiece can be decorative and still useful, because it sets the tone. A comic as summary can be useful if it compresses. A comic as core explanation is useful only if the core is structural.

I have become suspicious of comics that only translate text into pictures. If you can remove the images and the words still make sense, the images may be redundant. If you can remove the words and the images still make sense, the images may be too vague. The best cases are in between: the words say what is true, the images show what it is like. For example, in a zine about DNS, the text can say that a domain name is resolved through a chain of servers. The comic can show a child asking, “Who is in charge of this name?” to one adult, then another, until reaching the house. The text prevents the comic from implying that DNS is a phone tree. The comic prevents the text from being a dry list.

Is “some people are visual learners” a good enough answer? No. It is a good enough conversation stopper, which is why it persists. It is also hard to test. If the comic works, the person must have been visual. If it fails, they must not have been. But it does not tell a maker what to make. If I ask, “Who is this for?” and the answer is “visual learners,” I have not learned whether the topic has a spatial structure, a sequence, a contrast, or a failure mode. I have only learned that the audience prefers a label. The better question is: what is the reader supposed to be able to see after this that they could not see before?

If the answer is a shape, a comic may help. If the answer is a procedure, a checklist or code may help. If the answer is a feeling of permission to try, a comic can help even if the technical content is thin. My current rule of thumb is this: use comics when the hard part is holding several things in relation. Use them when the reader needs a first model, not a final one. Use them when the topic has moving parts, boundaries, or embarrassment. Do not use them when the hard part is exact notation, dense edge cases, or performance numbers.

And never hide the simplification. A programming comic can be honest if it says, on the page, what it is not showing: the timeout, the retry, the exception, the version difference. Then the reader can use the picture to find the room, without mistaking the door drawing for the lock.
rejected:
The pitch is usually the same: code is hard, comics are easy, therefore comics make code easy.

This logic fails in practice. If I draw a cartoon of two computers shaking hands to explain TCP, I haven’t explained anything. I’ve just added color to an abstraction. For a junior developer, that visual is often *more* confusing than a text-based diagram because it implies a physicality that doesn’t exist. The internet isn’t a road; packets aren’t cars.

Where comics actually work is in the topology of systems, not the semantics of languages.

Consider dependency injection or middleware pipelines. These are inherently spatial. Who calls whom? Where does the data sit while it’s being transformed? A comic panel is a bounded container. It forces you to isolate a single state change. You draw the stack before the request hits. You draw the stack after the database query returns. The reader’s eye moves left to right, mirroring the flow of time. That spatial mapping is doing cognitive work that a paragraph of prose cannot.

This is where the "visual learner" myth gets in the way. The idea that people have fixed learning styles—some auditory, some visual—is pseudoscience. It’s a comforting lie that lets us skip the harder work of diagnosing *why* a concept is stuck.

It’s not that you are a "visual person." It’s that you are trying to understand a high-dimensional relationship between objects, and linear text is a terrible medium for representing n-dimensional graphs.

If I’m explaining how a garbage collector marks and sweeps memory, a comic helps because memory is a landscape. Objects are things sitting in a field. Some are reachable (connected to a root), some are not. The comic lets you see the disconnected objects visually before the sweep deletes them. The visual isn’t a preference; it’s a data structure.

But try that with syntax. Try explaining the difference between a `let` and a `const` with a comic. You can’t. The meaning is in the rules of the compiler, not the shape of the variable. A comic there is just decoration. It feels like learning because it’s novel, but it transfers to nothing.

I’ve found that the most effective technical comics are those that stop trying to be cute. They look like engineering diagrams with faces. They don’t anthropomorphize the CPU. They don’t give the API endpoint a mustache. They use the gutter between panels to represent state transitions that would be tedious to describe in text.

The test isn’t "do you like pictures?" The test is "is the concept topological?"

If the concept is a sequence of steps, use a numbered list. If the concept is a rule set, use a table. If the concept is a flow of state across components, use a comic.

We make zines with comics because we are lazy. We can draw a box labeled "User" and an arrow pointing to a box labeled "Server" in ten seconds. Writing a clear sentence that distinguishes the user’s browser context from the server’s execution context takes two minutes. The comic is the shortcut. It’s only useful when the shortcut still leads to the correct destination.

chosen:
**I Read a Sleep Medicine Textbook, and Now I Know Why Sleep Is a Horror Genre**

I am a medical trainee, and last week I made the mistake of reading a sleep medicine textbook for pleasure. I used to think sleep was the boring part of medicine: ask whether the patient is sleeping, tell them to sleep more, move on. The book made me understand that sleep is not a switch being turned off. It is a choreography. The brain has to let you lose consciousness, keep you breathing, cut off your muscles, block the outside world, edit memory, and then hand you back a body that can stand up. Each part can fail separately. The strangest sleep disorders are not usually about not sleeping. They are about the wrong systems being awake.

The first one that stuck with me is sleep paralysis. During REM sleep, the brainstem sends a “do not move” signal to the body. This is why you do not run after the rabbit you are chasing in your dream. In sleep paralysis, consciousness wakes before the muscle lock has lifted. You are aware, but you cannot turn over, call out, or open your mouth properly. You can move your eyes. You can twitch a finger. The rest of you is still asleep.

The textbook explains the scary part. The half-awake brain is still partly in dream mode, and it interprets the paralysis as threat. People report a presence in the room, a weight on the chest, a shadow by the door. The chest pressure is not a heart attack. The fear is real because the alarm system is real; the intruder usually is not. Episodes usually last seconds or minutes. They are common enough to be almost normal, especially with irregular sleep, stress, shift work, and sleep deprivation. They can also be a sign of narcolepsy. The treatment is mostly boring: regular sleep, less caffeine and alcohol, fewer all-nighters. But the image remains: waking up in a body that has not agreed to wake up.

Then there are the sleep terrors. These are not nightmares. A nightmare is a REM dream: there is a story, you wake, and you remember the monster. A sleep terror is a NREM event, usually out of deep slow-wave sleep. The person may sit up, scream, look around with a blank stare, and seem terrified, but the memory system has not come online. They do not know you are there. They do not remember it in the morning.

Sleep terrors are common in children and often fade, but they can persist into adulthood. They are associated with sleep deprivation, stress, sleep apnea, and other things that fragment sleep. The danger is not the terror itself; it is what the half-awake body does next. It can fall out of bed. It can walk. It can get into a car. The management is safety: remove sharp objects, lock doors, keep the bedroom clear, treat the sleep fragmentation. Telling a person in a terror to “calm down” is usually useless. They are not performing fear. They are in the middle of it, without the part of the brain that knows they are safe.

Confusional arousals are the quieter cousin. A person wakes from deep sleep and is awake in the way the eyes are open, but not awake in the way that matters. They may answer questions with the wrong words, look through you, or get up and do something complicated while still disoriented. This is the one that feels most like a horror movie because the person is present and absent at the same time.

The disorder I found most unsettling is REM sleep behavior disorder. In normal REM sleep, the muscle lock prevents you from acting out dreams. In REM behavior disorder, the lock fails. The patient punches, kicks, falls out of bed, or dives for an imagined object. The dreams are often vivid, and patients describe them as real. Because the actions are physical, the dream and the bedroom become one. A man may wake with a bruised hand because he fought a stranger in a dream. A woman may wake on the floor because she was running from something in a dream.

That is the part that should make people take it seriously. REM behavior disorder is not just a weird symptom. It is strongly linked to what neurologists call synucleinopathies: Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy. In many patients, it appears years before the motor or cognitive diagnosis. The textbook language was dry, but the implication is not. Someone may be acting out dreams for a decade before the disease announces itself in their gait. Treatment includes melatonin, sometimes clonazepam, and a bedroom that has been made safe. The bed should be low or padded. Weapons and sharp objects should not be in reach. The goal is not to stop the dreams; the body is already moving. The goal is to stop the room from becoming part of the injury.

Narcolepsy is the disorder where the brain loses the chemical that keeps wakefulness stable. In type 1 narcolepsy, there is a deficiency of hypocretin, also called orexin, a peptide made in the hypothalamus that helps maintain arousal. The result is sleep that can invade any moment. A person may fall asleep in a meeting, while eating, while standing. The sleep attacks are not laziness. They are the brain’s drive to sleep becoming impossible to postpone.

The most frightening feature is cataplexy. An emotion, often laughter, surprise, or anger, triggers a sudden loss of muscle tone. The knees buckle. The jaw drops. The head falls. The voice becomes slurred. The person remains conscious. That is the horror of it: the mind is fully there while the body temporarily forgets how to hold itself up. Cataplexy can last seconds or minutes, and it can be mistaken for fainting or a seizure, but the awareness is the clue. Narcolepsy also brings sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations, those strange experiences at the edge of sleep where the brain rehearses threat without the body. Diagnosis can involve a multiple sleep latency test and, in some cases, measuring hypocretin in cerebrospinal fluid. Treatment can restore some control: stimulants or wake-promoting agents for sleepiness, and other medicines for cataplexy and fragmented sleep. But the basic idea is creepy: the chemical that tells the body “we are here, stay here” is missing or not working.

Kleine–Levine syndrome is the one that felt least like medicine and most like a fever dream. It causes episodes of excessive sleep that can last days or weeks. A person may sleep fifteen to twenty hours a day, wake confused, eat large amounts of food, and show cognitive or behavioral changes: irritability, confusion, inappropriate behavior, sometimes hypersexuality. The episodes end. The person feels more like themselves, and then, later, it can happen again. It is rare, and it is more often described in adolescent males, but it is not limited to them. The cause is not fully understood; some episodes appear after viral illness. The scary part is not that the patient is asleep. The scary part is that the person who wakes up is not quite the person who went to bed.

Then there is fatal familial insomnia, and I will not romanticize it. It is a rare genetic prion disease. The problem is not ordinary difficulty falling asleep. The brain loses the normal architecture of sleep, and the insomnia becomes severe and progressive. It is accompanied by autonomic storms: sweating, fever, blood pressure swings, rapid heart rate. Hallucinations, movement problems, and cognitive decline follow. Death usually occurs within months to years. It is extraordinarily rare, and if you read this and think your bad sleep means you have it, you do not. But it is the clearest example of the point: sleep is not a luxury the body can simply do without. When the sleep system fails this badly, the body fails with it.

I would be dishonest if I skipped the common one. Obstructive sleep apnea is not strange. It is frightening because it is quiet. During sleep, the airway collapses, or the brain fails to send the breathing signal, and airflow stops. An apnea is generally defined as absent airflow for ten seconds or more. The body panics. Oxygen falls, carbon dioxide rises, the brain releases a jolt of arousal, and the person gasps or snorts back into sleep. They do not remember it. This can happen five, fifteen, fifty, or more times per hour. The usual threshold for abnormal breathing events is five per hour, but the damage is not only in the number. It is in the repeated alarms: blood pressure spikes, fragmented sleep, daytime sleepiness, accidents, heart disease, stroke, metabolic trouble. It is treatable. CPAP works by keeping the airway open. Weight loss, dental devices, surgery, and other options matter in selected patients. It is also a hidden amplifier for other sleep disorders: fragmented sleep makes terrors, parasomnias, and daytime impairment worse.

The hardest thing to balance is fear and proportion. Most people who experience a strange sleep event do not have a rare neurological disease. Occasional sleep paralysis is common. Most children who have terrors grow out of them. Most snorers do not have apnea, though many do. The textbook did not teach me to be afraid of sleep. It taught me that sleep is a set of active, fragile systems. The body has a muscle lock, a memory gate, a breathing monitor, a wakefulness chemical, and a door between dream and action. The disorders are what happen when one of those doors sticks.

So if the book has made you look at your bed differently, that is reasonable. But the useful response is not to lie awake cataloging failure modes. It is to notice what is actually happening: whether you are acting out dreams, whether you are falling asleep at dangerous moments, whether your partner hears apneas, whether you wake confused and dangerous, whether episodes of hypersomnia are changing your behavior. Sleep medicine is detective work, and the witness is often the person sleeping next to you.

# The Things That Happen When You Can’t Stay Awake

I just closed a 900-page sleep medicine textbook. My hands are shaking, not because I’m tired, but because I now know exactly what goes wrong when the brain fails to switch off.

We think of sleep as a pause button. It isn’t. It’s an active, violent biological process. When that process glitches, the body doesn’t just rest; it malfunctions.

Here are the three disorders that will ruin your perception of what a human being is.

### REM Sleep Behavior Disorder

In normal sleep, you enter REM (Rapid Eye Movement) stages where you dream. To prevent you from acting out your dreams, your brain paralyzes your skeletal muscles. You are locked in your own body, watching a movie that only you can see.

In REM Sleep Behavior Disorder, the lock breaks.

The patient is fully paralyzed, except for their limbs. They are dreaming, but the dream is vivid and often violent. They punch their bedsides. They strangle their partners. They leap out of windows.

The scary part isn’t the violence. It’s the eyes. When I read the case studies, the detail that stuck was the gaze. Patients often report that their eyes remain open and fixed on the ceiling or their partner. They are awake enough to see, but they are trapped in a dream where they are fighting for their life. They don’t know they are in their bedroom. They think they are in a jungle, or a bar, or a war zone.

This condition is also a prodrome to Parkinson’s and Lewy Body Dementia. It can appear decades before the motor symptoms start. So, a man waking up to punch his wife in the dark isn’t just having a bad night. His brain is likely dying in slow motion.

### Narcolepsy and Sleep Paralysis

Narcolepsy is often mistaken for extreme tiredness. It isn’t. It is a failure of the gatekeeper.

The brain cannot distinguish between being awake and being in REM sleep. So, it drops you into REM sleep while you are standing up.

This leads to two phenomena: cataplexy and sleep paralysis.

Cataplexy is a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion. You laugh too hard, and your knees buckle. You get angry, and your jaw drops. The mind is alert, screaming, but the body is gone. It is a functional stroke that lasts seconds.

Sleep paralysis is the flip side. You wake up, but the REM atonia hasn’t lifted. You are conscious, but you are a corpse.

The "demon" people describe during sleep paralysis is not a ghost. It is a hallucination. Because the brain is in REM state, it generates imagery. Because the body is paralyzed, the threat detection system is on high alert. The brain combines these two inputs: *I am threatened. I am immobile. I am in a dream state.* The result is a visual projection of a figure in the corner of the room.

It is not supernatural. It is neurochemistry misfiring in a dark room. But it feels like death.

### Fatal Familial Insomnia

If the first two are glitches, this is the end of the line.

Fatal Familial Insomnia is a prion disease. Prions are misfolded proteins that force other proteins to fold incorrectly. They are like a zipper that jams and pulls the rest of the fabric with it.

This disease targets the thalamus. The thalamus is the switchboard. It routes sensory information and regulates sleep-wake cycles. When the prions eat it, the switchboard burns out.

The patient loses the ability to sleep. Not the ability to fall asleep, but the biological architecture for sleep is destroyed.

They become awake for weeks. Then months.

The mind does not just get tired. It disintegrates. The patient experiences hallucinations, paranoia, and aphasia. They forget how to speak. They forget how to eat. They forget who they are.

The average survival from the onset of symptoms is 18 months. The cause of death is usually organ failure or infection from a completely awake, completely broken body.

### The Takeaway

We treat sleep as a luxury. We sacrifice it for work, for entertainment, for scrolling. We think that if we just push through, we’ll be fine.

The textbook taught me that sleep is not a pause. It is the maintenance crew. It clears the waste products from your neurons. It consolidates memory. It resets your emotional baseline.

When you deny it, you don’t just get a headache. You risk the lock breaking. You risk the gatekeeper failing. You risk the switchboard burning.

Go to bed. Not because you are tired. Because you are fragile.

prompt: We were all raised on 'you get out what you put in.' I'm increasingly convinced that's false and that rewards for performance are wildly nonlinear in most areas that matter. Write an essay on where these outsized returns come from and what an ambitious person should do about it.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The phrase “you get out what you put in” is a description of a workshop, not a career. In a workshop, an extra hour usually buys an extra unit: another chair leg sanded, another meal plated, another mile run. If you double the time, you roughly double the result, assuming the worker does not get too tired or the machine does not break. That logic is real, and it still governs a lot of life. But if by “areas that matter” we mean money, influence, reputation, impact, and power, then the workshop model is badly wrong. In those areas, a small difference in one variable can produce a huge difference in outcome, and a great deal of effort can produce almost nothing.

The premise needs one correction, though. The market is not usually rewarding “performance” directly. It is rewarding visible performance attached to leverage. A brilliant private opinion is worth less than a competent public one. A good piece of code in a private folder is worth less than mediocre code used by millions. A hard worker in a dead-end role is worth less, to the outside world, than a modest worker in a role with access to capital, customers, or attention. The nonlinear part comes from the fact that some outputs can be copied, scaled, or delegated almost for free, while others cannot.

The deepest source of outsized returns is non-rivalry. A conversation with one client is used up. A speech given to one room is gone. But a program can be installed on a million computers. A video can be watched by a million people without becoming worse. A book can be read by a million people. A financial position can control millions of dollars. A reputation can open a thousand doors. Once your work enters a medium that can be replicated at near-zero marginal cost, the relationship between effort and reward changes. You may spend a year building something, and then that something can serve one person or one million. A subscription service with one million users paying five dollars a month is sixty million dollars a year. The same service with fifty thousand users is three million. The engineering difference between those two cases may be small. The distribution difference is everything.

Software is the clearest example. Two engineers can have similar skill and work similar hours. One writes an internal tool used by five colleagues. The other writes a feature in a product used by tens of millions. The second person’s work is amplified by the machine. If the company succeeds, that person may also hold equity, so the payoff is not only a salary but a claim on a scalable asset. If the company fails, the payoff may be modest. The nonlinearity comes from the fact that the product can grow while the number of engineers does not need to grow in the same proportion.

Media works the same way, but through attention instead of users. A writer may spend a year on a manuscript. If it finds a small audience, it pays like a book. If it finds a large audience, it pays like a franchise. The quality may be comparable across cases; the distribution is not. A video can be seen by fifty people or five million. A tweet can die in a minute or be retweeted by a large account and become a career event. The reward function is not “hours written” or even “quality written.” It is “how many minds did this reach, and what did they do afterward?”

Capital is another form of leverage. An investor does not get paid by the hour. A venture fund may put money into twenty companies and have one company generate most of the fund’s profit. A founder may own a small percentage of a company that becomes large. A banker may arrange a deal that moves millions of dollars. In these roles, a person’s judgment is attached to resources much larger than their body. The same hour of thinking can control a thousand dollars or a billion dollars depending on position. That is why two people with similar intelligence and work ethic can end up with wildly different incomes: one is selling time, the other is allocating leverage.

The second source of nonlinearity is thresholds. Many rewards are not paid continuously. They arrive after a signal is crossed. A new lawyer is judged by credentials and appearances. After a few visible wins, clients start referring cases. A researcher needs first publications, a first grant, a first credible collaborator. After that, the next step is easier because the person is no longer unknown. A startup needs enough customers, revenue, or user growth to be taken seriously by investors, talent, and press. Before the threshold, it is just another idea. After it, the same idea is an opportunity.

This creates step functions instead of slopes. A developer with three polished public projects can get interviews. Twenty half-finished tutorials may not. A company with a hundred paying customers can raise money; ten may not. A scientist with one strong paper can get a postdoc; a notebook full of weak fragments cannot. The difference is not only quantity. It is legibility. Other people need a compact reason to trust you, and they usually will not reconstruct your full history. They will look for a threshold artifact: the degree, the hit, the citation, the customer logo, the viral post, the reference from someone already trusted.

That is why reputation compounds. Once you are known as the person who finishes hard things, new opportunities are interpreted through that fact. A missed deadline becomes a human error. A completed project becomes confirmation. Before you have the reputation, the same behavior is ambiguous. People give small chances to the unknown and large chances to the known. The unknown must pay a discount. The known gets credit. That discount and that credit are nonlinear because they change the size of the next opportunity, not just the evaluation of the current one.

The third source is position in a system. The same performance means different things in different places. A salesperson who closes one large deal may earn more than an engineer who writes elegant code if the company is starved for revenue. A junior person at a fund may have more influence over capital than a mid-level manager at another institution. A researcher at a well-funded lab may produce more because the lab has grad students, equipment, data, and collaborators, not because the researcher is magically better. The bottleneck matters. Rewards flow to those who control scarce constraints: money, customers, distribution, access, decision rights, or trust.

This is why “work harder” is often the wrong instruction. If the constraint is demand, more supply does not help. If the constraint is visibility, more private competence does not help. If the constraint is capital, better spreadsheets do not help. If the constraint is trust, more features do not help. Effort is only valuable in proportion to how close it is to the thing that is actually limiting the system. A waiter working extra hours may earn extra tips, but a founder working extra hours on the right customer problem may change the company’s trajectory. The hours look similar. The leverage is not.

The fourth source is luck, and this is the part people dislike. In power-law domains, random events matter. A meeting happens or does not happen. A reviewer likes a paper or not. A platform changes its algorithm. A market rises or falls. A rich person hears your name at dinner. A recruiter is looking for your exact skill that week. I am less sure about how much of any particular outlier’s success is due to raw luck than to preparation, because the evidence is full of post-hoc stories and survivorship bias. What I am sure of is the shape: in many important markets, a small random event can determine whether a good thing is noticed, funded, hired, or ignored.

But luck is not evenly effective. It can only hit what is exposed. A private genius has less surface area than a public one. A person with ten weak attempts has more chances than a person with one perfect secret. A person in a growing city, network, or industry has more collisions than a person in a stagnant one. You cannot choose the event, but you can choose the number of events you are eligible for. That is the practical part of luck: not predicting it, but making it possible.

The hardest objection to all this is that it sounds like an excuse for gambling. If rewards are nonlinear, maybe the smart move is to accept a reliable linear life and stop chasing tails. That objection has real force. Many people who chase outsized returns fail. Some are talented, some are prepared, and still they lose because the distribution is cruel. If you mortgage your stability for a lottery ticket, the variance can destroy you before the upside arrives. The nonlinear world is also unfair in a structural sense: people with capital, family networks, health, and geographic advantage can afford to wait for their option to pay off. People without that cushion cannot.

The response is not “ignore risk.” The response is to separate the base from the bet. A person can have a linear income that covers real costs and use the margin for convex work: writing, building, investing, publishing, contributing, pitching, learning a scarce skill. The downside is limited to the spare time and money put in. The upside is not capped by the hourly wage. This is less dramatic than quitting everything, but it is the version that survives contact with reality. Ambition without downside protection is just exposure.

What should an ambitious person do first? Diagnose the shape of the current payoff. If income rises almost exactly with hours, the role is linear. If there is a hard cap, the role is linear. If a small improvement changes almost nothing, the role may be linear even if the pay is high. That does not mean the role is bad. It may be the best available base. But it should not be mistaken for the whole game. The person should look for ways to attach part of their effort to outcomes: equity, commissions, ownership, residuals, project-based pay, promotions based on visible results, or responsibility for a scalable asset.

Second, build things that can outlast the hour. A task is gone when you finish it. An asset can keep working. Code is an asset. A dataset is an asset. A body of writing is an asset. A product is an asset. A community is an asset. A reputation is an asset, though it is made of events rather than files. Even small assets matter if they can be combined later. The point is not to become a “creator” in the vague social-media sense. The point is to make your marginal effort produce something that can be used, referenced, sold, or extended after you stop working on it.

Third, choose domains where one person’s work can be replicated or where judgment controls large resources. Software, media, finance, research, enterprise sales, publishing, and some areas of law or medicine have this property to different degrees. But leverage alone is not enough. A leveraged skill can be crowded. The better position is a scarce skill attached to leverage: technical writing for a difficult domain, sales for complex software, research that can attract funding, engineering for products with real distribution, investment judgment in an asset class you understand. Scarcity determines your price. Leverage determines your scale.

Fourth, get visible. Nonlinear rewards require that someone can notice you. Private competence is a poor substitute for public proof. Publish the project. Write down the lesson. Give the talk. Open-source the library. Post the case study. Ask for the introduction. Let people see the pattern of your work over time. Visibility is not vanity. It is the mechanism by which options arrive. A person who is unknown must be discovered from scratch. A person who is known can be recommended in one sentence. That one sentence is a threshold artifact.

But visibility must be backed by substance, because trust is the multiplier. Leverage is delegated to people believed to handle it. A person with a reputation for finishing, telling the truth, and making good calls gets bigger resources, better introductions, and more autonomy. This is often the hidden source of outsized returns. It is not one viral moment. It is the accumulated permission to act at scale. Investors give money to people they trust with money. Editors give platforms to people they trust with audiences. Companies give ownership to people they trust with outcomes. Friends give opportunities to people they trust not to waste them.

Fifth, take repeated asymmetric bets with limited downside. Write the article. Build the side project. Apply for the fund. Pitch the investor. Teach the course. Contribute to the organization. Run for the small office. Publish the research. The key is asymmetry: the cost of being wrong is bounded, while the cost of never trying is the lost option. Avoid bets where the downside is ruinous and the upside is merely good. A person who can lose their livelihood to chase a modest opportunity is not playing a nonlinear game; they are playing a dangerous one.

Sixth, work on the bottleneck, not on visible busywork. In a company, find what is limiting growth: sales, retention, hiring, product-market fit, capital, trust with customers. In a career, find what limits opportunities: reputation, a missing skill, network, decision rights, geographic or institutional position. Effort on non-bottlenecks feels productive because it is measurable. Effort on bottlenecks changes the system. The ambitious person should be uncomfortable with busywork, even flattering busywork, if it does not move the constraint.

There is a final caution. The nonlinear world concentrates rewards. Many people will do excellent work and get modest returns because they are in linear positions, lack distribution, or miss the threshold by a little. That is not a moral lesson about laziness. It is a fact about the shape of the game. The practical response is not to resent the shape, but to change the board. If you want a nonlinear life, you have to stop asking only how to add hours and start asking what kind of hour you are adding: an hour that disappears when the day ends, or an hour that attaches to a product, a reputation, a piece of capital, or a network that can keep working after you leave the room.
rejected:
The advice “you get out what you put in” is not just incomplete; it is actively misleading. It suggests a linear relationship between effort and outcome: if you work twice as hard, you earn twice as much. This model fits factory floors and data entry. It does not fit the modern economy, where a single individual can build a product used by millions, or where a single insight can generate billions in value.

In most high-leverage fields, returns are power-law distributions. A small percentage of actors capture the vast majority of the rewards. The median outcome is often poverty or mediocrity, while the top outcomes are astronomical. The question for an ambitious person is not how to work harder, but how to position themselves in the tail of the distribution.

Outsized returns come from three specific sources: leverage, compounding, and selection.

### Leverage

Effort is linear. One hour of work is one hour of work. Leverage allows that hour to produce results that scale without additional input. There are four types of leverage:

1.  **Labor:** Other people working for you. This is the oldest form of leverage. You build a company, hire employees, and their effort multiplies your output. However, labor is expensive, hard to manage, and scales slowly.
2.  **Capital:** Money working for you. You invest in assets, businesses, or markets. Capital scales infinitely but requires you to already have it. You cannot leverage what you do not possess.
3.  **Code:** Software that works while you sleep. A piece of code can be duplicated at near-zero marginal cost. If you write an application used by a million people, you have performed one hour of work that serves a million customers.
4.  **Media:** Content that reaches an audience without your physical presence. A video, a book, or an article can be consumed by millions. Like code, media has zero marginal cost of replication.

Code and media are the new forms of leverage because they are permissionless. You do not need a boss to give you a team (labor) or a bank to give you a loan (capital). You can build software or create content today. These are the only forms of leverage available to the individual who starts with nothing.

### Compounding

Linear growth adds a fixed amount over time. Exponential growth multiplies. The difference is not obvious in the early years. It takes about a decade for the gap to become visible.

Compounding applies to money, but it applies more powerfully to knowledge and reputation. If you learn a skill and then build on it, your learning curve accelerates. If you have a reputation for competence, your next opportunity comes easier than the last.

The mistake most people make is quitting before the curve bends. They see no results in the first two years, so they switch fields. But switching fields resets the compounding clock. To get outsized returns, you must stay in one domain long enough for your effort to begin feeding on itself.

### Selection

This is the most misunderstood factor. Most people believe that if they pick the right industry, they will automatically succeed. This is wrong.

Selection is not about choosing a winning horse. It is about choosing a game with a high payoff structure. In some games, the best player earns 10% more than the average player. In other games, the best player earns 10,000% more.

Consider two scenarios:
*   **Scenario A:** You are the best plumber in your city. You work incredibly hard. You charge high rates. Your income is capped by the number of hours you can physically work and the number of houses in your city.
*   **Scenario B:** You are an average founder of a software company. You build a product that solves a specific problem for large enterprises. If the product works, your income is not capped by your hours or your location. It is capped only by the size of the market.

In Scenario A, effort is the primary variable. In Scenario B, judgment and timing are the primary variables. An ambitious person should not just look for where they can work hardest; they should look for where the upside is unbounded. This means moving away from roles where your time is the bottleneck and toward roles where your judgment is the bottleneck.

### What to Do

If you accept that returns are nonlinear, your strategy changes. You are no longer trying to be "efficient." You are trying to get into the right distribution.

**1. Seek permissionless leverage.**
Stop asking for permission to have influence. If you have a skill, package it. Write it down. Code it up. Teach it. If you are a lawyer, write a guide on common mistakes. If you are an engineer, build an open-source library. If you are an artist, post your work online. These actions have zero marginal cost. They create assets that work for you while you sleep.
