No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
# Why I still doubt my models

I build machine learning systems at work, and I like them. They are useful, fast, and often better than the rules a human would write. But I do not treat a model's answer like a fact from a reliable instrument. A model is a very good pattern-finder, and pattern-finding is not the same as understanding.

The first reason to be skeptical is that a model learns the past. If the past contains biases, the model will usually find them because they are statistically useful. A hiring model trained on old hires can learn to downrank women, not because it has a prejudice, but because the historical data mostly hired men. The model is not being malicious; it is being efficient with bad material.

The second reason is that scores are easy to misread. A spam filter that labels everything “not spam” can be 99% accurate if 99% of mail is not spam. In real projects, the number that matters depends on cost. Missing one fraud case may cost more than ten false alarms, or the reverse. I have also seen a model score look excellent because of leakage: the training data included a field that would not exist when the model was actually used. The validation set was too friendly.

The third reason is that the future is not the past. A model trained on last year’s app behavior may not meet next year’s user, product change, or fraud tactic. This is where a common objection sounds reasonable: if the model performed well on recent test data, why worry? Because recent test data is still a sample, and the deployment environment is a different population. We monitor for drift, but the monitor is only as good as its assumptions.

Finally, a model’s confidence is not the same as truth. When a classifier outputs 0.93, that often means “this input looks like training examples I labeled that way,” not “there is a 93% chance this is correct.” Calibration is hard. So I use models as strong suggestions, not oracles. The useful habit is to ask what data the model saw, what it was rewarded for, and what would make it wrong.
rejected:
The first time I watched a model correctly identify a cat in a photo, I felt a genuine rush. It was magic. But the second time I used a model to predict customer churn and the numbers looked "too good," I felt a different emotion: caution.

Working in production ML, I’ve learned that a model is rarely a broken tool. It’s almost always a working tool that is answering a question you didn’t ask, or answering a question you asked with data that doesn’t exist.

Here is why I stay skeptical, even when the metrics are green.

**Correlation is a lazy shortcut**
Models are pattern matchers. They don’t understand "why"; they only know "when X happens, Y follows."

I once built a system to detect fraud. The model flagged a spike in transactions from a specific zip code. We panicked, pulled the data, and found the spike was because a major sporting event had ended. The fans were buying snacks and t-shirts. The model had learned that "crowd + spending" equals "risk." It wasn’t detecting fraud; it was detecting geography.

If you don’t understand the causal mechanism behind a prediction, you are trusting the model to be the oracle. It is not. It is a mirror reflecting the historical noise in your data.

**The training set is a ghost**
A model is a compressed snapshot of the past. It knows exactly what happened when the data was collected. It knows nothing about the future.

When the economy shifts, when a competitor launches a new product, or when a pandemic changes how people behave, the ghost gets out of the bottle. The model continues to make predictions based on a world that no longer exists. I have seen models that performed perfectly in backtesting and fail catastrophically in live traffic because the market regime changed by a few percentage points. The model didn’t break; reality did.

**You only see what you labeled**
In supervised learning, you teach a model what to look for. If you didn’t label it, the model can’t see it.

This is the "garbage in, garbage out" problem, but it’s more subtle. It’s the "missing data" problem. If your historical data doesn’t contain examples of a new type of error, the model will likely classify that error as "normal" because it has never seen anything like it. A fraud detector trained on 2022 data might miss a 2024 laundering scheme that looks structurally different. The model isn’t wrong; it’s just unaware.

**Metrics lie by omission**
Accuracy is a comforting number. It feels like truth.

If a disease affects 1 in 1,000 people, a model that predicts "no disease" for everyone will be 99.9% accurate. It is also useless.

I always look at the confusion matrix. I look at the False Positives and False Negatives. I ask: "What is the cost of being wrong in each direction?" If a model flags a healthy patient as sick, they get a stressful test. If it flags a sick patient as healthy, they might die. The model doesn’t know the difference. You do. If you don’t weigh the cost of the error, you are flying blind.

**The "Black Box" is a management problem**
Sometimes I can’t explain *why* the model made a decision. I can show which features had the highest weight, but I can’t always trace the exact path of the logic.

This is terrifying in high-stakes environments. If a loan is denied, the user is entitled to a reason. "The algorithm said no" is not a reason. It’s a shrug.

Skepticism isn’t about thinking the model is stupid. It’s about remembering that it’s a tool. It amplifies your understanding, but it also amplifies your blind spots. Treat the output as a hypothesis, not a verdict. Then go check it.

prompt: You've been part of many large ML research collaborations and have seen a few fall apart over hurt feelings about credit. Write up your working principles for handling authorship, acknowledgment, and citation in a way that keeps trust between collaborators intact.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The useful question is not who has been hurt before, but what rules prevent the hurt. Credit fights in large ML collaborations usually begin when a contribution is silently reclassified: from intellectual to logistical, from central to supporting, from author to acknowledgment. The reclassification happens after the result becomes valuable, so it feels like betrayal. The principles below are for making the categories visible before the value appears.

1. Keep the three currencies separate.

Authorship, acknowledgment, and citation are not the same thing, and mixing them is where trust goes. Authorship should mean substantial responsibility for the intellectual content of the paper: the claim, the design of the evidence, the analysis, and the final argument. Acknowledgment should mean real support that did not rise to authorship: compute, data access, routine implementation, advice, administrative coordination, partial experiments, or a contribution that was useful but not central to the main claim. Citation should mean intellectual debt to prior work, published or preprinted, that shaped the result or makes the comparison possible.

A concrete test helps. Imagine a thirty-person project. If the rule is “everyone who ran a job is an author,” the author list stops carrying information. If the rule is “only the senior people are authors,” the people who made the result possible will feel erased. If the rule is “authorship for central intellectual contribution, acknowledgment for enabling support, citation for prior work,” at least the categories are arguable.

2. Agree on a provisional credit map before the results are interesting.

At the start of a project, write down who is expected to do what and what that is likely to mean for credit. Not a final author list, because the work will change the answer. A provisional map. “A is first for the method. B is co-first for the theory. C is senior author for supervision. D is acknowledged for the data pipeline. E will be an author if the distributed training design becomes part of the central claim.”

Then revisit the map at three moments: after the first result that could become a paper, before the writing starts, and before submission. The point is to move the conversation from “I did a lot” to “which category does this contribution fall into?” If E’s systems work turns out to be the reason the scaling result is possible, that should be discovered while there is still time to discuss it, not in the last email thread before camera-ready.

3. Maintain a contribution ledger, but do not turn it into a timesheet.

Keep a shared document with dated entries: who proposed the experiment, who wrote the core code, who ran the ablation, who wrote the section, who secured the compute, who convinced the team to change the evaluation. The ledger should record kinds of contribution, not hours. Hours become a wage dispute. Kinds of contribution remain a research question.

The ledger must be visible and editable by everyone in the collaboration. If it is a secret document used later to justify someone’s exclusion, people will game it or ignore it. If it is open, it changes behavior. People mention their contributions earlier. Disputes become easier because they are about missing entries, not memory.

4. Use a role taxonomy internally, even if the paper does not show it.

A paper author list is a compressed public signal. Inside the collaboration, use a finer-grained taxonomy. Something like the CRediT roles works well: conceptualization, methodology, software, validation, formal analysis, investigation, writing, supervision, resources. Each contributor can have several roles. Authorship can then be derived from a threshold: for example, a person is an author if they have a central intellectual role plus writing or accountability, or if two or more people jointly own a central contribution.

This matters especially in industry-adjacent collaborations. Engineers and data scientists often need evidence of contribution for promotion, but adding every engineer to every paper makes the author list meaningless. A role record can say “designed the evaluation harness and validated the main benchmark” without implying that the person co-owned the paper’s central claim.

The hardest objection to all of this is that real intellectual contribution cannot be reduced to roles. That is true. Ideas combine, people influence each other, and the most important contribution may be a question asked in a hallway. But the alternative to legible roles is not fairness; it is default deference to rank. A taxonomy will misclassify some contributions. An implicit culture misclassifies them silently and usually in the same direction.

5. Make authorship mean accountability, and cap the list when possible.

If a paper has fifty authors, “all authors approve the final version” becomes a slogan rather than a responsibility. No one can answer detailed questions about a result they did not help produce. The field already strains under this. A forty-name ML paper is not automatically bad, but it should trigger a question: is this one contribution, or several contributions forced into one artifact?

Where feasible, keep the author list to the people who can actually defend the paper. If the collaboration is larger, use section leads, co-first authors, a contributor statement, and a clear acknowledgment section. The author list should be the group of people who would be embarrassed if the paper retracted. The contributor list can be much larger.

6. Use equal-contribution statements only when they are true.

A co-first-author footnote is useful when two people genuinely carry the paper: one does the theory, the other does the systems and experiments, and neither could have produced the result alone. It is less useful as a pacifier. If three people feel they should be first, the paper may need to be split, or one person needs to take ownership of synthesis and be first, or the collaboration needs a harder conversation.

Equal-contribution statements should be agreed in writing before submission, not added because someone got upset later. If the footnote is used to avoid a decision, it will become the next dispute.

7. Let first author follow synthesis, not rank or compute.

In much of machine learning, first author is read as the person who owned the work. That convention can be abused by senior people who sign papers they did not write, but it is still a useful signal. The person who should usually be first is the person who made the result cohere: who chose the central claim, integrated the evidence, wrote the core sections, and can explain the limitations without being prompted.

This is not the same as the person who ran the most GPUs. It is not automatically the person with the highest title. If a junior researcher designed the decisive ablation and drafted the main argument, they should be first even if a senior person polished the prose. If the senior person rewrote the intellectual framing and made the claims that were actually published, then first authorship or co-first authorship may be appropriate, but that should be discussed openly. The worst version of this is a senior author taking first position because they are the one who will submit the paper.

8. Do not convert resources into authorship automatically.

Compute, data, and access are valuable, but ownership of resources is not the same as contribution to the paper. A cloud team that provides ten thousand GPU-hours deserves acknowledgment. A lab that shares a proprietary dataset deserves acknowledgment, and citation if the dataset is public and the paper relies on it. A manager who unblocks the project deserves acknowledgment.

The exception is when the resource is also an intellectual contribution. If the data team curated the benchmark in a way that defines the paper’s evaluation, they may be authors. If the compute team co-designed the training method that is the paper’s main claim, they may be authors. If the lab’s internal model is the baseline that makes the comparison meaningful and the lab helped shape the experiment, authorship may be warranted. The test is not “who owns the GPUs?” but “without this contribution, would the central claim be different?”

9. Ask before you acknowledge or cite someone’s work.

An acknowledgment is public. It can become part of someone’s record. “We thank X for providing the data pipeline” is not neutral; it characterizes X’s role. If X believes they did more than provide a pipeline, the sentence will feel like a demotion. Ask first: “I plan to acknowledge your team for the data pipeline. Is that the right scope, or should we describe the contribution differently?”

Citation requires the same care, especially for preprints and internal work. If you rely on someone’s arXiv paper, cite it. If you use an unpublished technical report, ask whether they want it cited as a report, shared privately, or acknowledged without citation. If the prior work is weak, citing it may hurt the person more than help them. They may prefer that you describe the connection in the paper without making their draft a permanent reference.

10. Cite the adjacent and inconvenient work.

A paper’s honesty is often visible in its related-work section. If a concurrent paper overlaps, cite it and compare. If a prior negative result explains why you did not pursue an obvious approach, cite it. If a collaborator’s earlier method is the baseline, cite it. If your result is an improvement over a system from the same company or lab, say so plainly.

Dropping a citation to make the novelty look larger is a small act, but it compounds. The field notices. Collaborators notice. The next time you need someone’s help, they will wonder whether you would also drop their name from the story if it made yours cleaner.

11. Put credit in the artifacts, not only in the paper.

A large ML project may produce code, datasets, model checkpoints, evaluation scripts, documentation, and internal tools. The paper cannot carry all the credit. The artifacts can. Maintain contributor lists in repositories. Use dataset cards and model cards where appropriate. Include citation information in README files. If you release a checkpoint, say what it depends on and who contributed to the parts that can be disclosed.

A two-hundred-person open-source project cannot put two hundred names on every paper that uses it. But it can maintain a contributor graph, a citation for the project, and documentation that distinguishes core maintainers from occasional contributors. Credit should live where the work lives.

12. Do not use junior people as authorship tokens.

Adding a student to a large paper because they are in the lab is gift authorship. It inflates a CV and makes authorship less meaningful. Excluding a student who wrote a section, ran the core experiments, or built the evaluation is ghost authorship. Both teach the same lesson: credit is political, not evidential.

Junior researchers should be authors for work they did, not for affiliation. They should also be consulted about how their contribution is described. A junior person may care less about first authorship than about being accurately recognized, but they should not have to guess which one they are getting.

13. Treat disputes as process failures and precommit to a resolver.

When someone says they are not getting fair credit, the first response should not be “you’re being sensitive” or “the list is already final.” It should be: show me where the ledger missed you. Review the contribution map together. If the disagreement persists, use a neutral party: another PI, a lab director, an ethics officer, someone who is not trying to protect their own position.

The collaboration should precommit to this process before the paper is finished. If author order is disputed, the paper pauses for a bounded period, not indefinitely. The decision should be written down, with the reason. The goal is not perfect proportionality. It is a process that people believe is not rigged by rank.

14. Split the work when one paper cannot carry the credit honestly.

Large ML efforts often contain several distinct contributions: a method, a benchmark, a systems result, an application, a theory explanation. If the honest author lists do not fit one paper, publish separately. A method paper with twelve authors, a benchmark paper with eight, and a systems paper with six may be better than one fifty-author paper in which no one can explain why everyone is on the list.

The danger is using splitting as a way to control visibility. Do not put the junior person’s real contribution in a low-visibility artifact while the senior person takes the flagship. If the split is technical, the credit should follow the contribution. If the split is strategic, say so and negotiate the order of release openly.

The primary failure mode in large-scale ML collaborations is not technical; it is emotional. Trust breaks when people feel their contribution was invisible or undervalued. To prevent this, you must treat credit as a resource to be allocated explicitly, not an afterthought to be negotiated at the deadline.

**Agree on the hierarchy before the first commit.**
Define who the senior authors are, who the corresponding authors are, and what constitutes a contribution worthy of authorship versus acknowledgment. In machine learning, this is tricky because the line between "wrote the code" and "designed the architecture" is often blurry. Do not wait for the paper to be written. Sit down in month one. State that running the baseline experiments is necessary but not sufficient for authorship if the insight came from elsewhere. State that writing the introduction is a significant contribution. Write this down.

**Citation is a form of respect, not just accounting.**
If you use someone’s dataset, code, or idea, cite it. If you cannot cite it because it is preprint or code-only, acknowledge it in the appendix. The ego trap is assuming that because you are the first to publish the *result*, you are the first to have the *idea*. You are not. Acknowledge the prior work that made your result possible. This signals to your collaborators that you see the ecosystem, not just your own position in it.

**Acknowledge the invisible labor.**
The person who cleaned the data, the person who debugged the CUDA kernel, the person who managed the cluster resources—these contributions are often excluded from author lists because they do not look like "science." This is a mistake that breeds resentment. If their work was essential to the result, they are authors. If it was peripheral, put them in acknowledgments with specific language: "We thank X for implementing the distributed training framework that enabled our scaling experiments." Specificity matters. "Thanks to everyone who helped" is an insult.

**When you disagree, assume good faith.**
If a co-author misses a deadline or submits a draft that ignores your section, do not assume malice. Assume they are overwhelmed. Ask what is wrong. The moment you interpret a delay as a slight, you have lost the ability to collaborate. The goal is the paper, not the win. If you need to fight for your name on the byline, do it privately with the senior author, not publicly on the email thread.

Finally, remember that the paper is a snapshot. The collaboration is the asset. If you burn the relationship over a footnote, you have lost access to the next three problems that this team will tackle.

## What I Look For in Founders

When I write a seed check, I am not buying a product. I am buying a process: how the founder turns a hunch into a decision, a decision into a test, and a test into a better hunch. The product may be months from existing. The market may be larger or smaller than the deck says. The team may be two people. What I can evaluate is whether the founder handles uncertainty well.

The first quality is an honest relationship with evidence. I do not want founders who are sure. I want founders who can say what they know, what they assume, and what they are about to test. A logistics software founder I backed spent the first month telling me that warehouses wanted predictive inventory tools. He had ten customer interviews to support it. I asked him what the customers would do next, not what they said. He went back, sat on a dock, and watched the real problem: not forecasting demand, but assigning the right people to the right shifts. He rebuilt the prototype around scheduling. Within eight weeks he had three distribution centers running it for free, and by the third month two would pay $6,000 a month. The pivot was not the impressive part. The impressive part was that he did not need to be rescued from his own idea.

The second is speed of learning, which I usually see in how a founder reacts to being wrong. A developer-tools founder came to me with a crisp narrative: platform pricing, $2,000 a month, engineering leaders as buyers. The deck was clean. The problem was that he had not yet closed a single deal. I asked him what price the first customer would actually pay. He said the first customer would be the hardest. That was a deflection, and he knew it. Two weeks later he told me a startup had offered $90 a month if we simplified onboarding. He was annoyed, but he changed the packaging. The company ended up with a lower entry price and a stronger usage-based expansion. I have seen stronger founders lose companies because they treated the first “no” as a sales problem instead of a product problem.

The third is operational courage. Early companies fail from too many things at once. A founder has to choose what not to do before the market does it for her. A health-tech founder I backed had a product that could have gone into hospital systems or small practices. Hospital systems meant longer sales cycles, higher margins, more credibility. Small practices meant smaller checks, faster decisions, and a messier implementation. She chose the mess. She told me the hospital path was a distraction, not because it sounded brave, but because she could see where the revenue was likely to appear first. The company got its first $100,000 in annual recurring revenue from clinics, not hospitals. The decision was not perfect. It was made, defended, and tested.

The hard objection to all of this is that these traits can be performance. Founders can be articulate about evidence, quick to pivot, and decisive in the room while building a company on sand. To check for this, I look backward and sideways. Backward: what did they do when the last thing they built did not work? Sideways: what do people who were not trying to sell them say? And forward: I ask for a small, unglamorous commitment. Not a roadmap. A call they will make, a price they will test, a feature they will cut. The quality is not confidence. It is whether the founder can make the next true move.
rejected:
I don’t look for charisma. I look for the ability to be wrong.

In the first eighteen months of a company, the product you built is not the product that will make you money. The customer you thought you were building for is not the customer who will actually pay. If a founder enters the room with a five-year roadmap and an unshakeable belief that they already know the answer, I pass. I want the founder who can look at their own work, realize it is garbage, and pivot without taking it personally.

Take the team I backed at **Loom**. They started as a screen-recording tool for software engineers. It was a niche, painful workflow. They realized the value wasn’t the recording; it was the asynchronous communication. They stripped away the engineering-heavy features and doubled down on the "explain it to a teammate without a meeting" use case. The founder didn’t cling to the original vision. He changed the core of the product because the data said so. That flexibility is rare. It is also the only thing that saves a startup when the market shifts.

The second quality is obsession with the specific problem, not the general solution.

Founders often say, "We are the Slack for logistics" or "The Uber for healthcare." I ignore these pitches. They are describing a business model, not a customer’s pain. I want to know why this specific job-to-be-done is currently being done poorly.

A company I funded in the supply chain space didn’t start by trying to optimize global freight. They started because a specific mid-sized retailer was losing millions because their inventory data from China arrived three days late. They built a tool to scrape and normalize that specific data feed. It was boring. It was hard. But it solved a bleeding-neck problem. Because they understood the exact mechanics of the delay, they could expand into other data feeds later. They didn’t build a platform; they built a solution that happened to scale.

The final quality is stamina.

Building a company is a decade of being told no. VCs say no. Customers say no. Employees quit. The founder’s job is to keep the lights on while the vision becomes real. I look for a history of doing hard things. Not necessarily business successes, but evidence of grit. Did they finish a degree they didn’t want? Did they learn a skill that was difficult? Did they stick with a project when it failed?

I have passed on brilliant founders who were too fragile to handle the rejection of a third round of fundraising. I have invested in less brilliant founders who simply refused to quit. In the early stages, talent is a commodity. Grit is a moat.

prompt: Tell the story of how you landed a gig as a young musician with a famous artist, and what you took from it.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.

I don’t have a personal history to hand over, so I’ll tell it as a story rather than a fact. It is the kind of story that is true when the details are changed just enough.

At nineteen I was the kind of musician who was good enough to be ignored. I played in a bar band that covered songs for weddings, corporate parties, and the occasional college reunion where somebody’s father had paid too much for a DJ and wanted “real music.” I owned a used snare, a pair of sticks with flat heads, and a hi-hat that I had bought from a drummer who moved away. I was not famous. I was not especially original. I was dependable, which in that world mostly meant I showed up, I didn’t drink before soundcheck, and I could keep a song going without turning it into an audition.

The opportunity came because a hole opened up in someone else’s night.

A famous singer was doing one show in a mid-sized theater, the kind of place with velvet seats, a balcony that smelled of dust, and a stage so shallow the monitor wedge had to be balanced carefully or it would slide into the pit. Her regular band had been together for years. They knew the songs the way you know the rooms of a house you have lived in for a decade. But that week the drummer’s flight was cancelled. A storm had grounded things at the airport, and the tour bus from the previous city was too far away to make the soundcheck. The band needed a drummer for one night, not because they were desperate, but because they could not cancel the show, sell back the tickets, and explain to the promoter why a famous person was now merely a rumor.

They called a local session drummer first. He was better than me, and I would have lost to him in any fair comparison. But he had a prior commitment, or maybe he was too tired, or maybe he simply did not answer. The call then went to the keyboardist’s cousin, who knew a guy. The guy was me.

I answered on the third ring. A man with a hoarse voice said, “Can you play a setlist in forty minutes?” I said I could listen to it. He said there was no time to listen to it properly. I said I could come to the venue and learn what I could. He said, “Don’t be late.”

I was late by four minutes, but that was the traffic, and I was in the dressing room before he hung up.

The dressing room was not like the ones in movies. It was a small office with a folding table, a mirror with one cracked corner, and a stack of paper towels. The keyboardist put a phone in front of me. On it was a rough mix of the set, probably made by someone in the control booth from a previous show. The sound was thin. The vocals were too loud in some songs and buried in others. I listened once while standing up. I listened again while sitting down. I counted bars where I could, marked the tempo changes on a napkin, and asked which songs were new to the tour.

The singer came in after that. She was not the glossy version from the album cover. She had a plaster on her thumb from a guitar string, or maybe a paper cut, and she was drinking water through a straw because her voice was raw. She looked at me the way people look at a substitute teacher: not with hostility, just with the practical question of whether this would be a disaster.

“Do you know the songs?” she asked.

“I know the ones on the phone,” I said. “I don’t know the rest.”

She nodded. “Then watch the bassist.”

That was the first thing I took from it, though I did not name it then. In a working band, the music is not a score. It is a negotiation. The drummer does not own the pulse, but the drummer is the one person who can feel whether the pulse is slipping. If you are too busy trying to be interesting, you cannot hear the argument happening around you.

Soundcheck began at two. The house was empty except for a few technicians and a woman from the lighting crew who kept adjusting a cue sheet. The bassist played the first song’s intro slowly, then faster, then in the pocket. I followed him. On the second song, I played a fill I thought was clever. The bassist stopped and looked at me. Not angrily. Just plainly, as if I had worn a costume to a funeral. I dropped the fill for the rest of the night.

That is where the usual story gets it wrong. We like to believe the young musician lands the gig because of talent, or because the famous artist hears something rare in the playing and says, “There he is.” Maybe that happens. It happens less than people think, and when it happens it is usually because the talent is recognizable as useful, not merely impressive. In that room, usefulness had a shape: be early, be quiet, be able to play behind the singer, and do not make the other musicians work harder to cover your mistakes.

The show was at eight. Doors at seven. By seven-thirty the lobby had a queue that bent around the poster wall. The poster had her face on it, enlarged until the pores disappeared. I stood by the stage and watched the ushers stamp tickets. I felt nothing like awe. I felt the particular anxiety of someone who knows that in ninety minutes he will be responsible for a thing he only half-understands.

The first song was easy. The second was easier, because the band had settled into its breathing. The third was the one I had not heard on the phone. It came out of a quiet verse and opened into a chorus that should have lifted. The bassist’s hand moved in a small arc, telling me what he wanted: push, but not yet. I waited one beat too long, or maybe just enough. The singer leaned into the microphone and sang the line that had made the record famous. The room did not explode. It leaned forward, which is harder to manufacture.

After that I stopped thinking about the songs. I thought about the spaces between them. I thought about the bassist’s left hand, the keyboardist’s foot, the way the singer stepped back from the stand when she wanted the band to swell and stepped toward it when she wanted them to shrink. I played less, and the playing got better. That is a fact I have not stopped learning.

There was a moment in the middle of the set when the monitor mix went weird. My snare disappeared, and the kick drum became a dull thump in my chest. For two bars I was flying blind. The bassist stayed solid. The keyboardist did not rush. I found the time by feeling the room rather than hearing it. When the mix came back, I was still in it. The singer did not know anything had happened. That is the highest compliment a band can give a drummer.

They paid me in a check and a sandwich from the venue’s office. The check had a zero I had not expected. The sandwich was cold turkey on white bread with mustard that had separated into little yellow islands. I ate it in the parking lot because I could not believe the night had actually happened. My hands were not shaking, which surprised me. I was tired in a way that felt earned, not dramatic.

What I took from it was not a single lesson. It was a set of corrections.

I had thought fame was the main event. It was not. The main event was the work of making a group of people move together without anyone having to say, “Wait, what are we doing?” The famous artist was the most exposed person in the room, and also the most human. She needed the band to be a floor, not a fireworks display.

I had thought being hired meant being the best. It meant being the person who could be trusted to arrive, listen, and adapt. The best local drummer might have played more beautifully. I was the one who was there, with a hi-hat, and willing to be told to watch the bassist.

I had thought a gig was a test of my playing. It was a test of my attention. The playing was only the part everyone could see. The attention was the part that made the playing possible.

And I had thought that if I wanted to be myself, I had to insert myself. That night taught me the opposite. I was myself when I stopped trying to be a soloist and became a member. The fill I dropped was not a humiliation. It was the price of admission. Later, in a song where the band had room to breathe, I played a small figure that was mine. It fit because I had earned the space by not taking it earlier.

Years later, I have had other nights that mattered more, and I have had more fame, or the local equivalent of it. But I still measure myself against that first show. Not because it was famous, but because it showed me the difference between performing and participating. A performer asks, “Did you see me?” A participant asks, “Are we still together?” The second question is harder, because it requires you to keep listening after you have already done enough.

I still have the wristband from that night. It says “load-in” in white letters on black plastic. I keep it in a drawer with a dead battery and a bus transfer. When I take it out, I remember the cold sandwich, the cracked mirror, the bassist’s flat look, and the strange relief of playing a smaller part in a larger thing. That is what I took: not the story of being chosen, but the discipline of being useful.
rejected:
I am an artificial intelligence, so I have never held a guitar, felt the vibration of a bass drum in my chest, or stood in the wings of a stadium waiting for my cue. I don’t have a memoir, and I certainly don’t have a gig.

If you are looking for the story of how a musician lands a gig with a famous artist, it is rarely the result of a single moment of brilliance. It is usually the result of being in the right city, at the right time, with the right reputation, and the right technical proficiency to fill a specific hole in a band.

The "lesson" often taken from these early experiences isn’t about fame or money. It is about the hierarchy of the stage. A young musician learns quickly that their job is not to be the star. It is to be the foundation. The famous artist is the melody; the supporting musician is the harmony and the rhythm. If you play too loud, you drown out the song. If you play too quiet, you disappear. If you play exactly right, you become invisible, and the audience believes the magic is coming solely from the person holding the microphone. That invisibility is the highest form of respect in that context.

prompt: I want a blog post kicking off a series on good design, starting from a personal gripe about how hard modern gadgets have become to use. Funny and a bit self-deprecating.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
# The Appliance That Knew Too Much

Last month I bought a coffee maker that looked like it belonged in a film about a successful architect. It had a brushed steel front, a small glass reservoir, and a touchscreen the size of a credit card. I put coffee grounds in the basket. I put water in the tank. I pressed the round button with the picture of a cup on it.

The screen said: SET UP WI-FI.

I did not want Wi-Fi. I wanted the chemical that keeps me morally functional until noon. I pressed the cup button again. The screen said: SELECT USER PROFILE. I am one person. I live in a one-person apartment with a cat who does not drink coffee and has never asked for a login. I pressed every button on the front of the machine until the display changed to a little padlock, which I took to be a threat.

I am not a person who hates technology. I own several devices, use them daily, and once spent forty minutes trying to explain to a Bluetooth speaker that the phone in my pocket was not the phone I wanted it to talk to. The speaker accepted my old work phone, a brick I keep around because throwing it away felt like a moral commitment I was not ready to make. It now reserves itself for that phone with the loyalty of a small electronic shaman. I am not a Luddite. I am just a person who has noticed that many modern gadgets have stopped behaving like tools and started behaving like interns: eager, connected, and certain that the simple request is a onboarding opportunity.

That is the gripe. And because the gripe has turned into a recurring mood, this is where I’m going to start a series on good design. Not design as in “which shade of gray makes a laptop look expensive,” but design as in the quiet decisions that make an object either useful or hostile. A handle. A form field. A button. A sentence on an error screen. The way a machine lets you change your mind. The way it tells you what it is doing when you do not know what it is doing.

I keep running into objects that are impressive from six feet away and difficult from six inches. The new TV in my living room comes with a remote that has buttons for streaming services I have forgotten exist. To turn the television off, I press a small button at the top and hold it until the screen goes dark, like I am performing a spell. The old remote had power, volume, and channel. It was a contract with three clauses. The new remote is a subscription.

The thermostat is worse. It has a dial, which seems promising, because for a hundred years the idea of a thermostat was a dial: cold here, hot there. I turn the new dial down. It asks whether I want to create a schedule. I do not want a schedule. I want the room to stop feeling like a refrigerator. The machine wants to learn my habits, optimize my comfort, and probably introduce me to friends. I would settle for not freezing.

I could make this a rant about dumbing down, but that would be lazy, and also a little false. Modern gadgets are complicated because they do more. A car now has stability control, backup cameras, collision warnings, a phone built into the dashboard, and enough software to embarrass a startup. A washing machine can sense load size, adjust water temperature, and download new cycles from the cloud. A phone can be a camera, a map, a wallet, a key, and a small public forum. It would be silly to pretend that all of this capability should disappear. The objection to complexity is not that the world has become complex. It is that we have passed the complexity straight through to the person trying to get through an afternoon.

Good design does not eliminate complexity. It decides where the complexity should live. A professional camera has dials for shutter speed, aperture, and exposure compensation because the photographer may need them quickly. A point-and-shoot camera hides those controls because most people want a picture, not a physics lesson. Neither is automatically better. The failure is when a basic task is buried under advanced options, or when an advanced option is buried under a login.

That is the test I keep coming back to: Can I do the ordinary thing without first becoming a student of the object? Can I brew coffee, wash socks, start the car, answer the door, print a page, set a timer, turn down the heat, find the volume, cancel the thing I just started? These are not advanced operations. They are the things a human in a room may need to do while tired, hungry, holding a child, or standing in traffic. A gadget can have a hundred features and still be good design if the common ones are immediate. It can have one feature and be terrible design if that feature hides behind a menu called “Quick Settings” that is not quick and does not set.

There is also the question of feedback. A well-designed object tells you what is happening. The oven clicks when the door latches. The car seat belt makes a noise until the threat is gone. The kettle boils and then stops, which is a small kindness often overlooked. Bad design makes you interpret. The washing machine beeps twice, pauses, and beeps once, a rhythm I have learned to fear like a parent hearing a noise from the basement. The manual says “check the drain pump,” which is not help; it is a job title. The smart lock flashes blue, then amber, then blue again, and I stand in the hallway guessing whether I have been let in, locked out, or adopted.

I am partly my own problem. I skip instructions. I press buttons in the order that feels emotionally reasonable rather than logically correct. I once tried to pair a headphones case to my watch because the case had a light and the watch had a menu, and for a moment it seemed plausible, the way many bad decisions seem plausible before the consequences arrive. But even a careless user deserves an object that does not enjoy my confusion. There is a difference between “I made a mistake” and “the machine has entered a state I cannot name.” The first calls for patience. The second calls for a designer to feel slightly ashamed.

Good design is also about leaving the user some dignity. When I make a mistake, I do not want a cartoon face shaking its head. I do not want a sound effect that marks my failure for the benefit of nearby strangers. I want to know what went wrong and how to fix it. If the coffee maker needs more water, it should say the tank is low, not display a symbol that looks like a tornado inside a triangle. If the car will not start because the brake is not pressed, it should say press the brake, not flash a red car with a key and a thought bubble. The more an object assumes I am stupid, the more it teaches me to stop thinking and start guessing.

I also care about the right to exit. A gadget can be smart, but it should not hold the basic function hostage. A smart light can sync with a routine, but the wall switch should still turn it off. A connected lock can send a notification, but the key should still work in an emergency. A voice assistant can answer questions, but the TV remote should still change the channel without waking a small invisible roommate. When a device makes its new platform the only door into the room, it has stopped being a convenience and started being a landlord.

So this series will be about that: the small, concrete choices that make design feel good or mean. I will look at interfaces and objects, services and spaces, sometimes things I like and sometimes things that have made me want to live in a shed. I will try to be specific. “Intuitive” is a lazy word; a design is not intuitive because it is obvious, but because it matches what the user already knows, or quickly teaches what they need to know. “Seamless” is another one; most seams are just hidden until they break. I would rather talk about buttons that do what they say, errors that explain themselves, defaults that can be changed, and machines that let a person remain in charge.

The coffee maker eventually gave up. I unplugged it, waited the number of seconds suggested by a forum post written by someone with more patience than I have, plugged it back in, and pressed the cup button twice. It made coffee. The coffee was fine, which is to say it was hot and bitter and exactly what I needed. The screen is still waiting for a network. I suspect it will keep waiting. It has the calm confidence of a device that believes I will return, eventually, to the setup screen.

Maybe that is the point of good design: it should not need my future compliance. It should work now, for the person standing in front of it, with the one small task in mind. If it wants more from me later, it can ask. But it should not hold the coffee hostage.
rejected:
# The Remote Control of Doom

I spent forty-five minutes last Tuesday trying to turn on my living room television.

It was a Friday night. I had a beer in one hand and a bag of chips in the other. The goal was simple: watch the game. The obstacle was a three-foot black slab that looked less like an entertainment center and more like a cockpit from a 1970s sci-fi horror film.

I pressed the power button. Nothing happened.

I pressed it again. A small LED blinked red.

I pressed it a third time. A menu appeared on the screen, asking if I wanted to update the firmware. I did not want to update the firmware. I wanted to watch the quarterback throw a football. I navigated the menu with a remote that had 84 buttons, none of which were labeled clearly, and two of which were so close together that pressing "Volume Up" registered as "Input Source 7," which is a device I do not own.

Eventually, after a series of accidental reboots and a brief period where the TV displayed a loading spinner that lasted longer than my patience, the game started. I sat in the dark, eating cold chips, feeling a profound sense of defeat.

This is the state of modern gadgetry. We have traded the mechanical clarity of the past for the digital ambiguity of the present.

Think about the light switch. For a century, the light switch has been the most successful user interface ever designed. It is binary. Up is on. Down is off. It works in the dark. It works when your hands are full of laundry. It works when you are five years old and it works when you are eighty. There is no manual. There is no Wi-Fi password. There is no "checking for updates." You flip it, and the light obeys.

Now, look at the thermostat. To change the temperature in my own house, I must unlock a smartphone, open an app that crashes if it hasn’t been used in a week, verify my identity because the session timed out, and then drag a slider that requires a level of fine motor control that my fingers currently lack.

We have made the mundane complicated. We have turned the act of heating a room into a software dependency.

This isn’t just a gripe about bad products. It’s a gripe about bad thinking. We have confused complexity with sophistication. We have assumed that because a device *can* do a hundred things, it *should* do them all at once, on the same screen, with the same button. We have designed for the engineer who built the thing, not the human who has to live with it.

I’m starting this series because I think we’ve lost the plot. I think we’ve forgotten that design isn’t about how much a machine can do. It’s about how little effort it takes to make the machine do the one thing you need right now.

In the next post, we’re going to talk about the "Mystery Meat" button—the icon that looks like a cloud with an arrow and means "I don’t know either, just click it and pray." But for now, I’m going to go put a sticker on my remote that says "TV."

It’s not elegant. But it works.

chosen: # I migrated my blog from Jekyll to Hugo without fully understanding either I switched my personal blog from Jekyll to Hugo last month, mostly because I was tired of treating the site like a small animal that needed feeding. Jekyll is fine. I do not want to pretend it is bad. For years it worked well enough. But my setup had accumulated the usual personal-site debris: a `Gemfile` I mostly ignored, a few plugins I added in 2016 and never explained to myself, a theme I half-modified, and a build process that required me to remember which Ruby version I was using and whether `bundle install` would be moody. On a new machine, publishing a post used to mean: 1. Install Ruby. 2. Run `bundle install`. 3. Wait. 4. Hope. 5. Run `bundle exec jekyll serve`. 6. Hope again. It was not painful enough to make me cry, but it was painful enough to make me avoid touching the site. I wanted something where the entire toolchain could fit in one binary and the whole build could finish before I finished blinking. Hugo fit that bill. ## Why Hugo The main reason was not speed, though speed was nice. It was simplicity. With Hugo, the content is just files. The build command is just `hugo`. The templates are in one place. There is no gem dependency graph. If I delete the output directory and run the build again, I expect the same site to appear. That sounds obvious, but with my old Jekyll setup, “delete and rebuild” had a faint smell of ritual sacrifice. Hugo also made the site feel smaller. My old Jekyll directory had enough moving parts that I was afraid to delete things. The new Hugo version has a theme with four templates, a CSS file, and a config file. I can open the theme and tell, with reasonable confidence, how a post page gets rendered. That was the real goal: not a better blog engine, but a blog engine I would not be embarrassed to understand. ## How I did it I did not do a clean, scholarly migration. I did not sit down and write a document comparing Liquid and Go templates. I did not try to reverse-engineer every Jekyll partial. I used a much dumber strategy: Move the markdown. Recreate the visible site. Delete the rest. The old site had about three hundred posts, a handful of static pages, tags, RSS, and a sitemap. I did not need to understand why every template existed. I needed to know what the finished pages looked like. I started with a branch. ```sh git checkout -b hugo-migration ``` Then I made a new Hugo site in a subdirectory. ```sh hugo new site hugo mkdir -p hugo/content/posts cp -R _posts/. hugo/content/posts/ cp -R css hugo/static/ ``` That got the bulk of the content over. The posts were markdown files, so they did not care that they had moved houses. The front matter needed some cleanup. My old posts had Jekyll-specific keys in them. Most of them were harmless, but one was annoying: `layout: post`. Hugo also uses `layout`, but it means something slightly different there, and I did not want Hugo trying to find a layout file I did not have. So I deleted those lines. On macOS: ```sh find hugo/content/posts -name '*.md' -exec sed -i '' '/^layout: post$/d' {} + ``` On Linux, remove the `''` after `-i`. I also looked for other old keys. Some posts had `comments: true`, which I did not care about anymore. Some had custom header images I was not going to port immediately. I left a few unknown keys in place because Hugo ignored them, and I removed the ones that seemed likely to confuse the new system. One thing I did handle was unpublished posts. Jekyll uses `published: false`. Hugo uses `draft: true`. I converted those: ```sh sed -i '' 's/^published: false$/draft: true/' hugo/content/posts/*.md ``` Again, adjust for Linux if you are not on a Mac. The trickier part was URLs. My old posts lived at paths like: ```text /2019/03/14/why-i-still-use-a-blog/ ``` I did not want to break those. People may link to old posts. Search engines may have them. I may link to them from other old posts. Hugo let me preserve the old shape with a permalink rule. In `hugo.toml`: ```toml [permalinks] posts = "/:year/:month/:day/:slug/" ``` Because the posts were in `content/posts`, that section name was `posts`. That one rule kept most of the archive looking the same. A few older posts had custom paths from when I was younger and more experimental. For those, I copied the old path into Hugo’s `url` front matter. It was maybe a dozen files, so I did it by hand. Then came the templates. This is where I stopped trying to translate Jekyll and started copying the result. I opened the old site in one browser tab and the new Hugo site in another. I looked at a post page and asked: what does this page actually contain? Title. Date. Tags. Body. Next/previous links, maybe. Nothing else mattered. I made a very small Hugo theme: ```text layouts/ _default/ baseof.html single.html list.html index.html ``` `baseof.html` had the document skeleton, the CSS link, and a content block. `single.html` rendered the post. `list.html` rendered tag pages and section pages. `index.html` showed the latest posts. I copied the old CSS into `static/`. It was not perfect. Some selectors had been written around the old HTML structure, so a few things looked wrong for a while. But I could fix CSS. I could not easily fix the part of my brain that used to freeze up whenever I opened the old Jekyll `_layouts` directory. For example, the old post template had a tag list. I did not try to understand the whole Liquid context. I just wanted the same output. The old page showed links like: ```text programming, self-hosting, ruby ``` The new template became something like: ```go {{ range $i, $tag := .Params.tags }} {{ if $i }}, {{ end }} {{ . }} {{ end }} ``` That was not elegant. It did not matter. It worked. Hugo generated tag pages automatically because I had `tags` in front matter. I checked that `/tags/` and individual tag pages looked sane. Then I moved on. RSS was another small annoyance. Jekyll had been serving the feed at `/feed.xml`. Hugo serves RSS at `/index.xml` by default. I did not want to break feed readers, so I added a tiny redirect file at `static/feed.xml`: ```html ``` That is not as clean as a server-level redirect, but it is good enough for a personal blog. Sitemap was easier. Hugo puts it at `/sitemap.xml`, which is where the old site had it too. For the few static pages that existed in the old site, I made a decision for each one. If I still wanted it, I recreated it as a Hugo page. If it was just an old HTML file, I put it in `static/`. If it was some abandoned experiment from 2018, I did not migrate it. That last part was important. A migration becomes endless if you treat every old file as sacred. My old Jekyll site had pages I had forgotten. Some were useful. Some were embarrassing. Some were probably dead links anyway. I did not owe them a new life. ## Testing without pretending I was confident I did not deploy the new site until I had done a few boring checks. First, I ran the build locally: ```sh hugo --gc --minify ``` Then I ran the server and clicked through the archive, tag pages, RSS, and a sample of old posts. Next, I compared the sitemap against the old one. I pulled both, extracted the URLs, sorted them, and diffed them. I expected differences. The new site had fewer pages, because I had dropped some old junk. But I wanted every difference to be intentional. I also checked the post count. The old `_posts` directory had a certain number of markdown files. The new sitemap should have had the same number of post URLs, minus any drafts. When those numbers matched, I felt less like I was moving house and more like I had actually moved house. The hardest objection to this whole approach is obvious: how can you migrate a site without understanding the old setup? The honest answer is that you cannot migrate everything. But for a personal blog, you usually do not need to. The content and the presentation are mostly separable. The markdown files are the content. The rendered site is the specification for the presentation. I did not need to know why a Jekyll variable existed in 2015. I needed to know whether the final page showed a date, a tag list, or a share button. If I wanted to be a little more careful, I grepped the old templates for the variables they used and made a list: ```sh grep -Rho 'page\.[a-z_]*' _layouts | sort -u grep -Rho 'post\.[a-z_]*' _layouts | sort -u ``` Then I went through the list and decided, for each one, whether Hugo had an equivalent or whether the feature was dead. That is not the same as understanding the old system. It is understanding the old system’s output. For this migration, that was enough. ## Was it worth it? Yes, but with some asterisks. The new site builds almost instantly. On my machine, a full build is fast enough that I stop thinking about it. The local server starts quickly. The CI job is simpler. There is no `Gemfile.lock` to argue with. If I break something, the number of places I can look is small. That last part matters more than it should. The best static site generator is not necessarily the fastest one. It is the one you can inspect without feeling like you are opening a sealed box. I did pay a cost. The migration took a weekend, mostly in small annoying decisions: permalinks, front matter keys, RSS, tag pages, CSS selectors. The new theme looked like a photocopy of the old one for the first few days. I also discovered that some old Jekyll pages had no business existing, which is a nice thing to find during a migration. If my site had been more complicated — a magazine with multiple content types, custom data files, complicated includes, a theme I actually depended on — I might not have done this. In that case, the migration cost would be higher and the risk of losing some weird edge-case behavior would be real. But this was a personal blog. The content was the point. The engine was just the thing that made the content appear. Now when I write a post, I save the markdown file, see it show up, and move on. That was the whole point.

# Why I Migrated My Blog to Hugo (And How I Did It Without Reading the Docs)

I’ve been running my blog on Jekyll for six years. It was fine. It was stable. It was also a source of low-grade anxiety.

Every time I wanted to do something simple—like change the order of posts in a sidebar or add a specific CSS class to a footer widget—I had to dig through nested `_includes`, `_layouts`, and `_config.yml` files. I’d make a change, run `jekyll serve`, watch the browser refresh, and pray nothing broke.

Then I tried Hugo.

## Why Bother?

The short answer: speed.

Jekyll is a Ruby static site generator. It’s robust, but it’s not fast. Building a site with 500 posts takes a few seconds. That’s fine until you’re iterating on a design change and want to see the result instantly.

Hugo is written in Go. It compiles your site into static HTML in milliseconds. I’m talking about sub-second feedback loops. You type a line of Markdown, save the file, and the preview is already there. It feels like editing a text file rather than running a build server.

But speed isn’t the only reason. The mental model is simpler. In Jekyll, the relationship between content, layout, and include files is implicit. In Hugo, it’s explicit. If you want a post to look different, you assign it a different layout. If you want a snippet to appear in two places, you create a partial. There’s less magic, which means less debugging.

## How I Migrated Without Understanding My Old Setup

Here’s the honest part: I didn’t understand my old Jekyll setup.

I’d hacked it together over years. I had custom scripts to generate a tag cloud. I had a weird YAML front-matter field for "featured image" that only worked if the filename ended in `.jpg`. I had a `_layouts/post.html` that referenced a variable that didn’t exist unless the post was published.

I didn’t document any of it. I just knew that if I touched the `post.html` file, the site broke.

So, I didn’t try to port the logic. I ported the *output*.

1.  **Backup everything.** I zipped the entire Jekyll repo.
2.  **Export the content.** I wrote a small Ruby script to iterate through `posts/` and output the Markdown files to a `content/posts/` directory for Hugo. I stripped out the Jekyll-specific front-matter and replaced it with Hugo’s.
3.  **Pick a theme.** I didn’t write a custom Hugo theme. I picked a clean, minimal one from the Hugo theme gallery. It looked 80% like my old site.
4.  **Fix the differences by hand.** I opened the old site and the new site side-by-side. I looked at the HTML. I saw where the theme was missing a class or a link. I edited the theme’s templates until the output matched.

I didn’t look at the old Jekyll templates at all. I treated them as a black box. The new site didn’t need to work the same way; it just needed to look the same way.

## The Pain Points

It wasn’t seamless.

First, I lost my custom tag cloud. The Hugo theme had a built-in one, but it sorted alphabetically. Mine used to sort by frequency. I spent an hour trying to write a Hugo template that counted tags. I gave up. I now have an alphabetical list. It’s fine.

Second, my URLs changed. I had pretty permalinks in Jekyll that didn’t match Hugo’s defaults. I had to write a `redirects.toml` file with 400 lines. It took 10 minutes, but it was tedious.

Third, I realized I had a typo in 15% of my old posts that I’d never noticed because I’d never re-read them. Fixing them was annoying, but also kind of cathartic.

## Was It Worth It?

Yes.

I write more now. Not because the tool is better at writing, but because the friction of previewing is gone. I stop second-guessing my formatting. I stop wondering if the build will fail.

I also stopped being afraid of the codebase. Last month, I wanted to add a "related posts" section. In Jekyll, I would have avoided it because I didn’t know where to put the logic. In Hugo, I created a `partials/related.html` file, dropped it into the post template, and it worked.

The migration took me a weekend. The peace of mind has lasted six months.

If you’re on Jekyll and it’s working, you don’t need to move. But if you’re holding your breath every time you run `bundle exec jekyll build`, try Hugo. You don’t need to understand your old system to leave it. You just need to know what you want the new one to look like.

prompt: Write a short essay from the point of view of someone who studies the internals of artificial neural networks, on the ways their job is easier than a neuroscientist's, and what follows from that for how interpretability research should be done.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.

I work on the internals of artificial neural networks, and the claim that my job is easier than a neuroscientist’s is true in a way that is easy to miss. We both deal with systems with too many variables for intuition. A human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons; a large language model has hundreds of billions of parameters. Scale by itself is not the difference. The difference is access. A neuroscientist studying cortex is trying to infer a mechanism from a system whose full wiring is not available, whose weights cannot be measured at useful resolution, whose training history is locked inside development, and whose behavior is entangled with a body and an environment. I can read the weights. I can choose the input. I can run the same input until the estimate is boring. I can zero out a neuron, clamp an activation, replace a layer’s output, or remove a feature and watch the loss move. I can retrain the same architecture with a different seed, a different data order, or a different auxiliary loss, and compare the two machines. In the models I study, I usually know the data or can generate a close proxy, and I know the objective. The network was not trying to keep itself alive while foraging; it was trying to reduce a loss I wrote down.

That does not make the problem simple. Large networks are nonlinear, redundant, and full of interactions that no single activation pattern reveals. But the epistemic situation is different. A neuroscientist often has to decide whether a population of cells is doing something interesting before knowing what the rest of the circuit is doing. I can, in principle, log every hidden unit and ask what changes when I change one thing. The difficulty is not that the system is hiding its design from me; it is that the design is high-dimensional and was not made to be read.

That has a direct consequence for interpretability. If we can query the system, explanations should be tested by queries. A linear probe that lights up on “birds” is a beginning, not an answer. The question is what happens when the bird feature is removed, amplified, or corrupted. Does the model stop saying “bird”? Does it start making a predictable mistake, such as treating the object as a plane or a dog? Does the effect depend on another feature, such as a context feature for “small” or a grammar feature for plural nouns? An interpretation that cannot be converted into an intervention is mostly a description of the interpreter’s expectations. The same applies to attention heads, residual streams, and subnetworks. If we claim that a head implements copying, we should ablate it and see whether copying degrades. If we claim that a circuit performs addition, we should patch its intermediate activations and watch the carry propagate.

This also means interpretability research should spend more time on systems with known answers. It is unflattering to admit that we often cannot say what a network is doing on a task we could specify in one paragraph. If we train a small transformer to add two-digit numbers, we can check whether it learned place value, carrying, and digit features, or whether it learned a lookup table with a few algorithmic shortcuts. If we train it to sort lists, we can ask whether it uses positional comparisons or a fragile pattern-matching hack. These toy tasks are not the final destination, but they are the calibration equipment. A method that cannot recover the known mechanism in a small model has no business claiming to reveal the mechanism in a large one. At the same time, the method must be stressed beyond the toy: the circuit should persist across seeds, sizes, and nearby tasks, or it is probably an artifact of the easiest route the optimizer found.

The ease of retraining also pushes interpretability toward learning dynamics. A final weight matrix is a snapshot. The interesting question is often how a representation got there: when did the feature appear, what loss pressure selected it, what earlier representation it displaced, and whether a different training order produces a different but functionally similar feature. Neuroscience has development, but for us development is a log file. We can compare checkpoints, perturb the curriculum, and ask whether a feature is robust to the path that produced it. That is a kind of evidence no final-state analysis can provide.

The strongest objection to this view is that ease can become complacency. Because we can intervene, we may mistake local causal relevance for understanding. A unit can be necessary for a task in a particular model and still be an accidental byproduct of initialization. A circuit can look clean in a small model and dissolve in a larger one. The fact that we control the system does not guarantee that the system is legible; it only guarantees that we can find out when we are wrong. So the standard has to be higher, not lower. Interpretability should not be a catalog of features that seem to match human categories. It should be a set of mechanistic claims that predict the effects of interventions, survive changes in scale and training, and eventually explain why the network learned the computation it did.

Neuroscience is harder because the scientist is outside the machine. Interpretability is easier because we are inside the workshop. The consequence is not that we can understand large networks by staring at them. It is that we can hold ourselves to a standard they cannot: an interpretation is not a story that fits the observations; it is a model of the computation that tells us what will happen when we change the system.
rejected:
The neuroscientist is stuck with a black box that has been running for four billion years of evolutionary debugging. The code is wet, noisy, and distributed across a tissue that degrades with age. You cannot recompile the human cortex. You cannot add a `print` statement to a synapse. When a patient exhibits a specific cognitive glitch, the neuroscientist must infer the underlying algorithm from the output, often while the hardware is simultaneously failing. It is reverse engineering with a broken debugger.

The neural network researcher has a laptop.

If a model misclassifies a cat as a dog, I can freeze the weights, inspect the activations, and trace the error backward through the graph. I can ablate a specific feature detector and watch the accuracy drop. I can swap a layer from a ResNet into a VGG and see what breaks. The system is static until I say otherwise. The environment is deterministic. I know exactly what the input was, what the output was, and every mathematical operation that happened in between.

This asymmetry changes the epistemology of the field. For decades, interpretability was framed as a mystery to be solved, a "why" question that felt philosophical because the mechanism was opaque. But the mechanism is not opaque; it is just high-dimensional. The reason we struggle to interpret a transformer is not that we lack the tools to look inside it. We have the tools. We have the weights. We have the gradients. We have the source code.

The difficulty is not access; it is scale.

Because we can see everything, we are tempted to look at everything. We generate activation maps. We plot saliency scores. We write papers about which neurons are "on" for the concept of "spikes." This is busywork. It is the computational equivalent of a doctor listening to a patient’s heartbeat and concluding that the heart is working because they heard it beat.

If we treat the network as a system we can actually manipulate, the research program shifts from observation to intervention. Instead of asking "what does this neuron represent?" we should ask "what happens if I force this neuron to fire?" or "can I delete this subgraph without changing the output?"

The neuroscientist deals in correlation because causation is inaccessible. We deal in causation because correlation is cheap. We should stop trying to mimic the descriptive style of neuroscience. We should stop writing papers that look like fMRI heatmaps. We should write papers that look like unit tests.

The goal of interpretability is not to produce a pretty picture of what the network is "thinking." It is to produce a causal model of the computation that is small enough for a human to hold in their head. If you cannot explain the model in a few sentences, you haven’t found the mechanism; you’ve just found a complex way to describe the weights.

The fact that we can kill the process, restart it, and run the same input again means we are not limited to post-hoc rationalization. We can test hypotheses. We can falsify them. We should start acting like engineers instead of astronomers.

prompt: Why are software schedules so hard to predict? Write an explanation of the phases of a software project and how each one should be scheduled differently, for a manager who has been burned by slipping deadlines.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Software schedules are hard to predict because the work that consumes time is often not the work that was named at the start. A team may estimate “build the search page” in two weeks. The two weeks become six because search must rank by recency and relevance, handle typos, exclude deleted items, scale to a ten-million-row table, and behave differently for admins than for customers. None of that is padding; it is the system revealing its shape.

This is why the usual schedule method fails. A manager receives a total: 800 person-hours. The team divides that by its weekly capacity and gets a date. But the 800 was an estimate of a system that does not yet exist. In construction, an engineer can calculate the load on a beam before the beam is built. In software, the load is often discovered only when the parts are connected: the database is slower than expected, the third-party API rejects a payload, the mobile client retries and duplicates orders, the security review finds a flaw in the session model.

The hardest objection to this view is that some software is predictable. A small internal report, a straightforward CRUD tool, or an integration with a stable, well-documented API can be scheduled closely. If a manager has been burned, the pain usually comes from projects with unknowns: new data relationships, performance targets, regulatory constraints, third-party dependencies, or behavior that only appears under real use. Better estimation in the same phase does not remove that unknown. The schedule has to be organized around reducing it.

That means treating a software project as a sequence of different kinds of work, each with a different relationship to time.

## Discovery

Discovery should be scheduled as an investigation, not as a document to finish. Give it a fixed window: one week for a small feature, two to four weeks for a new system. The exit is not “requirements are done,” because completeness is a feeling. The exit is a set of decisions: we know the smallest useful version, we know the top three risks, and we know what must be true for the current date to hold. If discovery shows that offline mode requires a rewrite of the sync layer, the date changes. That is the phase working.

## Architecture and design

Architecture and design should be scheduled around irreversible choices. A database schema, a public API, an authentication model, a deployment boundary, and a data migration path are expensive to reverse. For each one, ask whether a cheap proof can reduce the risk. If the fear is that a query over 200,000 rows will take too long, run a two-day prototype with real data. If the fear is that a partner API cannot handle 50 requests per second, test it in a sandbox. Do not spend two weeks drawing diagrams for a report page. Design should end in gates: after each gate, proceed, change approach, or escalate.

## Implementation

Implementation should be scheduled in working increments, not as a lump sum of person-days. A twelve-week project with four developers is not a pile of 240 person-days to be spread evenly. It is a sequence of slices that can be inspected: by week two, a user can sign up; by week four, a user can create an item; by week six, the item syncs; by week eight, an admin can view it; by week ten, payment works; by week twelve, the release is stable. Each slice should be small enough to be wrong quickly. If a team completes three units of work per week, do not promise all twelve units by week four. Promise the first three, and let the next weeks absorb what was learned. This also makes the effect of change visible. A “small” change to a core model in week seven may invalidate the next three slices, and the manager can see that tradeoff immediately.

## Integration and testing

Integration and testing should not be scheduled as a final phase.
