Those who do write memoirs are selected for two traits: extreme experience and extreme articulacy. These traits are not evenly distributed across the population. They are concentrated at the poles. The writer is likely the person whose relationship collapsed spectacularly, or the person who reinvented their identity so thoroughly that the old self is a stranger. Both types of experience are dramatic. Both are legible as stories. The middle ground—the 80% of non-monogamous people who are mostly fine, mostly happy, and occasionally annoyed—is invisible because it is boring.

This creates a skewed data set for the reader. If you read three books by people in non-monogamous relationships, you are not reading a survey of the lifestyle. You are reading a compilation of the top 1% of intensity. If two of those books describe betrayal, jealousy, and psychological unraveling, the rational inference is that these are common features of the lifestyle. The irrational inference, driven by the sheer density of the evidence, is that the lifestyle *is* betrayal, jealousy, and unraveling.

This effect is exacerbated by the nature of the audience. People interested in reading about non-monogamy are often interested in the friction, not the routine. They want to know how it works when it breaks, or how it works when it defies social norms in spectacular ways. The market rewards the outlier. The author, seeking validation or an outlet for trauma, also rewards the outlier. The result is a feedback loop where the most visible representatives of a group are the ones who are currently suffering or currently rebelling.

Consider the parallel with celebrity. We form impressions of fame based on the behavior of people who are famous *and* currently in the news. We do not see the thousands of famous people who are quietly paying their taxes and keeping their marriages intact. We see the ones who are fighting, cheating, or breaking. We conclude that fame causes chaos. In reality, fame selects for visibility, and chaos selects for fame.

The same logic applies to any group where the act of belonging is itself a form of identity performance. For non-monogamists, the relationship structure is a core part of self-definition. For a memoirist, self-definition is the raw material. When the two overlap, the resulting narrative is intensely focused on the self and the structure’s impact on it. This focus is inherently reductive. It strips away the mundane context of jobs, family logistics, and minor irritations that make up the bulk of any relationship. What remains is the dramatic core: the conflict between the self and the structure.

Readers are not stupid. They are just dealing with a small, unrepresentative sample of high-signal data. A single novel is a strong signal. Three novels are an overwhelming signal. To counter this, the reader would need to access the null hypothesis: the millions of non-monogamous people who are not writing books. Because that data is silent, the loud voices dominate the mental model. The bad impression is not a prejudice; it is an inductive error based on the most available evidence.

prompt: It's 2010, VCs are starting to write smaller checks and a new breed of 'super-angels' has appeared. You fund very early startups. Write an essay predicting how startup funding is going to change over the next several years and why.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The check I wrote in 2006 was different from the one I am writing now. Then, a seed round was a $2 million equity round, with a board, a data room, and a legal process that could take two months. The company needed the money to hire, build, and maybe survive. Now, the first serious round is $300,000 or $500,000 on a convertible note, closed in three weeks, led by an angel who has already built two companies and knows the founders’ customers. A venture capital firm may follow with $1 million, but the angel has already decided whether the product works. That is not a temporary tightening of credit. It is the beginning of a longer change in how startup funding works.

The old funding ladder had a simple shape. Angels wrote small checks, usually under $100,000, to keep a team alive long enough to show investors a prototype. Venture capital firms wrote seed checks, usually $1 million to $3 million, to build the company and prove there was a business. Later venture rounds scaled the company. Each stage required more money, more formality, and more proof. The proof was often indirect: a pitch, a demo, a letter of intent, a famous founder, a hot market.

That ladder is compressing. The first real round is happening earlier and with less money. The later rounds are being redefined around the evidence that the early round produced. The reason is not that investors have suddenly become braver or more foolish. It is that the cost of testing a startup has fallen.

Cloud computing, smartphones, open source, payment systems, analytics, and application programming interfaces have made it possible for a small team to build and launch a product that reaches a global audience without the capital that would have been required a decade ago. In 2006, a consumer company needed a website, a marketing budget, and probably a distribution deal to learn whether people cared. Today, a team of four can ship an app to phones, watch the numbers, talk to users, change the product, and try again within weeks. The experiment is cheaper. The failure is smaller. The signal is also cleaner.

That last point matters more than the cheaper servers. Investors can now see whether a product is working before it has much revenue. They can look at retention, not just downloads. They can compare the first week’s users with the fourth week’s users. They can see whether people return, whether they invite others, whether they pay, whether support costs explode, whether the product works on different devices, whether growth slows when paid advertising stops. A company with a million downloads and poor retention is not a company; it is a marketing event. A company with 5,000 users, strong repeat use, and a path to revenue is more interesting. The data does not prove everything, but it changes the conversation. It moves due diligence from opinion toward measurement.

The super-angels have appeared because they are best positioned to use that measurement. The ones who matter are not wealthy amateurs writing checks to friends. They are serial entrepreneurs, operators, and early investors who have built companies, hired people, made product decisions, and felt the difference between a real market and a hopeful one. They can write $250,000 to $1 million without needing a limited partner vote. They can close in days. They can talk to users directly. They can say no without hurting a fund’s relationship with a platform. They can also say yes with enough conviction to change the company’s trajectory.

These investors will become more institutional, even if they do not call themselves venture capital. They will syndicate with one another. They will keep deal logs. They will track returns. They will develop theses, even informal ones: mobile commerce, developer tools, health data, enterprise software, global consumer markets. They will learn which metrics to trust and which to ignore. They will make mistakes, often expensive ones, but the best of them will compound knowledge the way venture firms do. The line between a serious angel and a seed fund will blur. In practice, it may disappear.

Venture capital firms will feel the pressure first. A fund raised at the top of the market cannot keep writing $2 million seed checks into a market where the best companies are being assembled with $500,000. If it wants access to the best deals, it must move down. But moving down is expensive. Seed investing requires more deals, faster decisions, more operational work, and a different relationship with founders. It also requires a different relationship with limited partners. A $400 million fund cannot run a seed portfolio without either becoming a generalist that does everything badly or splitting into smaller, more focused vehicles.

Expect more small early-stage funds, perhaps $30 million to $75 million, run by people who have built companies or have deep expertise in a particular market. Expect more sidecars and co-investment arrangements, where the main fund takes a smaller position and the partners or a separate vehicle take the early risk. Expect the most effective early-stage investors to look less like finance companies and more like operating partners with a capital allocation discipline. The old mid-size generalist, trying to be everywhere from seed to growth, will be squeezed.

The shape of the rounds will flatten. The first institutional-quality round may be $1 million to $2 million, not $5 million. The traditional Series A may become a smaller follow-on, or it may be skipped entirely if the angel round was strong. Companies will raise more often and in smaller amounts. The round will become less of a formal stage and more of a recurring event: an angel syndicate, a bridge, a seed fund, a venture follow-on, another bridge, then a large growth round when the company needs sales, international expansion, or heavy infrastructure.

The paperwork will simplify too. Convertible notes have already reduced the cost of early investing, but they are still debt in legal form and create awkward questions about maturity, interest, and conversion. The market will move toward cleaner instruments: simple convertible equity, with less legal friction and fewer traps. The goal is not to eliminate negotiation. The goal is to let a good founder and a good investor spend their time on the product and the market, not on the mechanics of the first check.

What gets funded will change as much as how it gets funded. The cheapest way to build a product has also made the cheapest way to make a bad product. More startups will be started, more will look plausible at first, and more will die after burning through a small round. The premium will move to distribution, data, and durable economics.

Mobile and social companies will dominate the conversation because they can acquire users through networks, devices, and behavior. But downloads are not a moat. The companies that matter will have retention, network effects, or a proprietary understanding of user behavior. A mobile game with viral spikes and no repeat play is a content business with high churn. A two-sided marketplace that becomes more useful as more people use it is a different animal. Investors will pay up for the second thing.

Data will become more important, not because founders suddenly become data scientists, but because the best products will be built from feedback loops. A company that can observe what users do, form a hypothesis, change the product, and measure the result has an advantage over one that relies on focus groups or founder taste. This is especially true in markets where behavior is complex: commerce, health, travel, work, finance, local services. The startup that learns fastest from real use will often beat the startup with the better deck.

Recurring revenue will remain a refuge. Consumer apps can be exciting and fragile. A business-to-business company with 40 customers, low churn, and predictable monthly revenue is easier to fund because the evidence is more stable. Investors will not ignore glamour, but they will price it. A company with high growth and negative unit economics will need to explain why the negatives will reverse. A company with modest growth and good margins will get a different kind of respect.

Founders will become a more formal market. Accelerators, repeat entrepreneurs, and the general professionalization of startup building have made the first idea less rare. A good prototype can be copied quickly. A good pitch can be imitated. The premium moves to execution: the ability to hire, to choose a market, to iterate, to sell, and to survive the unglamorous months after the initial excitement fades.

This will create a strange inequality. The best founders, especially those who have built and sold a company before, will have more choice than at any previous point. They can pick investors based on network, taste, operating experience, and follow-on capital. They can raise on their own schedule. They can ignore the firms that would have been honored a decade ago. The median founder, meanwhile, will face more competition for the same small pool of early checks. More applications, more demos, more metrics, more noise.

Some valuations will become silly. Capital will be wasted on teams that can make a good product but cannot build a business. Investors will overpay for celebrity, for a hot category, for a metric that looks strong for one quarter and then collapses. This is not a bug in the new system. It is the cost of learning at speed. The market will correct by getting more brutal about evidence. The next round will be where the fantasy dies.

The public markets will matter more than they have in recent years, but not in the way early investors usually hope. The absence of a strong public exit window has made venture capital the default endpoint for many companies. That cannot continue forever. Some of the large internet, mobile, and software companies being built now will eventually list. When they do, the money made by early investors and employees will reprice the private market. Founders will ask for more. Investors will pay more. Later rounds will get larger. But the seed investor’s return will still depend mostly on whether a later buyer or later fund appears, not on the IPO itself. The IPO is the ceiling, not the engine.

The hardest objection to all of this is that the change may be less structural than it looks. Venture capital is a conservative institution. Limited partners do not quickly change what they fund. Super-angels are often conflicted: they want control, they overinvest in friends, they make checks based on ego, and they create messy cap tables. VCs writing smaller checks may not be moving earlier; they may simply be scared. The next few years may bring a normalization, not a new system: angels stay angels, VCs return to comfortable seed sizes, and the mobile/social companies remain outliers rather than the center of gravity.

Some of that will happen. Many super-angels will fail. Many will become expensive hobbyists. Many venture firms will pretend to move down and actually write smaller Series A checks while keeping the same process. A lot of capital will go to companies that look good on a dashboard and fall apart in the real world. The new tools of early investing, metrics, speed, convertibles, syndicates, will be used badly.

But the underlying cost structure has changed, and that does not reverse. A small team can now produce evidence that used to require a much larger round. It can test a market globally, not locally. It can build on infrastructure that was previously available only to large companies. It can reach users through devices and networks that did not exist before. Investors can use that evidence. The ones who refuse to will be left outside the best companies. That is enough to change the market.

So the next several years will probably look like this: smaller first checks, led by angels or seed funds; faster closes; more follow-on rounds; more failure; more noise; more concentration in the best founders; more pressure on venture firms to specialize; and a slow return of public exits for the largest companies. The companies that make the returns will not be the ones that raised the most money earliest. They will be the ones that used the early money to find a real market, built a product that people kept using, and then raised again with evidence instead of hope.

The center of gravity will shift to the team of four or five that can ship, measure, learn, and repeat. The investor who can recognize that, fund it quickly, and stay out of the way will make the next power-law return. The rest will be debating whether the system has changed.
rejected:
The capital structure of the modern startup is fracturing. For fifteen years, the model was simple: seed money from a few large firms, a Series A to scale, and a Series B to dominate. That model assumed that raising $10 million in one round was the only way to survive. The 2008 crash killed that assumption.

Now, the gap between an idea and a business is being filled by smaller, faster checks. This isn’t just a recessionary hangover; it is a structural shift in how risk is priced.

### The Death of the "Mega-Seed"

In the boom years, VCs treated seed rounds as an investment in a person or a brand. They wrote $2 million checks because they wanted to own a piece of the next Facebook. Today, that capital is too expensive. If a founder asks for $5 million to "build a business," a venture capitalist will ask, "What does that buy you?"

The answer is usually nothing concrete. It buys time. It buys headcount. It buys office space. It does not buy proof.

So, the check size is shrinking. Instead of one $5 million round, you get three $1 million rounds. The investor is no longer betting on the founder’s charisma; they are betting on the product’s traction. Each round is a milestone. If you don’t hit the metric, you don’t get the next check. This turns the equity financing process into a continuous performance review.

### The Rise of the Super-Angel

As VCs pull back to later stages, a vacuum opens up at the bottom. This is where the "super-angel" enters. These are not hobbyists writing $25,000 checks. They are successful founders or operators writing $100,000 to $500,000.

Why are they doing this? Because the traditional VC process is too slow and too opaque. A super-angel can look at a code base or a user acquisition funnel in an afternoon. A VC needs a committee, a legal review, and a market analysis. The angel has information asymmetry. They know what it takes to build a product because they’ve done it. They can verify the founder’s competence without a board presentation.

This creates a new tier of professional early-stage capital. These angels are forming syndicates, not because they want to pool money for the sake of it, but because they want to co-invest with peers they trust. It’s a meritocracy of information. If you know the founder, you lead the round. If you don’t, you follow.

### The Data Feedback Loop

The most significant change, however, is in the feedback loop. In the past, a startup had to raise a round to get resources, build a product, and then try to prove it worked. Now, the tools for building and testing are cheap. A team of three can build a functional product and find 1,000 users in a month.

This means the "proof" happens before the money.

Investors are no longer funding hypotheses. They are funding validated traction. The barrier to entry for a startup is no longer capital; it’s execution. You can build the thing. You can find the users. The only thing you need money for is to grow faster than your competition.

This shifts the power dynamic. The founder doesn’t need the investor as much as the investor needs the founder. There are more good products than there are VCs willing to write small, fast checks. The investor’s job is no longer to provide air; it’s to provide oxygen to the companies that are already breathing.

### The Consequence

The result is a more efficient, less glamorous startup ecosystem.

There will be fewer "lottery ticket" investments. The VCs who are still writing $10 million seed checks are either wrong or they are playing a different game entirely. They are betting on brand and distribution, not product-market fit.

For the majority of founders, the path is now a series of small, verifiable steps. You raise a little. You prove a little. You raise more. You prove more.

This is harder. It requires more discipline. It rejects the "big bet" culture that defined Silicon Valley for the last decade. But it is more honest. It aligns capital with reality. The money follows the work, not the pitch.

prompt: Write an essay about deliberately pushing yourself into unfamiliar situations, and what happens to your sense of what's comfortable over time.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The first time you do something unfamiliar, your body usually answers before your opinions do. Your stomach tightens, your attention narrows, and the situation feels larger than the room. A cold shower is not just cold; it is an intrusion. A foreign city is not just unfamiliar streets; it is a place where you may be misunderstood. A difficult conversation is not just words; it is a risk to a relationship you have already arranged in your head. In all of these cases, comfort is not a vague preference. It is the condition of being inside what your nervous system can predict.

When you deliberately choose unfamiliar situations, you are asking that prediction to be wrong on purpose. You can choose the small version: sit with a group you do not know, ask a question in a meeting, take a class in a subject where everyone has background you lack. You can choose the large version: move, change work, end a pattern. The scale matters less than the fact that you enter with the intention to stay long enough to learn the difference between danger and novelty.

At first, the unfamiliar is mostly threat. The unknown has no handle. You do not know what will be expected of you, where the exit is, or whether your response will be read as courage or awkwardness. Public speaking is a clear case. The first speech feels total because everything is new at once: the room, the silence, the feeling of being watched, the possibility of forgetting the next line. The body has no file for it, so it treats the whole situation as emergency.

But if you do it again, the emergency breaks into parts. You discover that the fear is not evenly distributed. It is worst before you begin, worst in the first thirty seconds, worst when someone asks a question you did not expect. The rest becomes work. The room is still large, but it is no longer featureless. You know where the eyes go. You know that the silence after a sentence is not the same as the silence after a mistake. The nervous system does not stop caring, but it stops treating every variation as proof of annihilation.

That is the first change in your sense of what is comfortable. Comfort stops meaning the absence of demand and starts meaning the presence of handles. You are not necessarily calmer in the way people imagine. Your hands may still shake. Your mind may still race. But the situation has become navigable, and navigable is a different country from unknown. A person who has given five speeches is not five times braver than a person who has given none. They are someone whose body has learned where the edges are.

This expansion can be genuinely liberating. The person who has moved to a city where they knew no one often finds that making a life from scratch was harder than expected, but the old fear of being a stranger has lost some of its power. The person who has done difficult physical work learns that strain is not the same as injury. The person who has had several hard conversations learns that tension is not automatically betrayal. Small threats that once controlled the day stop controlling it. A raised voice no longer means war. A blank moment no longer means failure. An unfamiliar face no longer means judgment. The map gets bigger.

But the map does not simply get bigger. It changes texture. The things that become comfortable are not the things you started with. They are the things you can now survive. That sounds like progress, and it is, but it has a consequence: the baseline moves. A person who has lived in several places may find that staying in one place for years feels less like stability and more like slow disappearance. A person who has built a habit of learning new things may find that ordinary repetition feels thin. A person who has been through a lot may find that mild inconvenience is intolerable, not because they are weak, but because their body has been trained to expect more than mild.

This is where the practice can turn against itself. The goal was to stop being ruled by small fears. The result can be that you are now ruled by a need for intensity. You do not seek unfamiliar situations because they are worth knowing; you seek them because familiarity has started to feel like a kind of death. The new is not chosen for its content. It is chosen for the voltage. A new job, a new city, a new skill, a new conflict: each one works for a while, the way a strong flavor works when the palate has gone numb.

The hardest objection to deliberately pushing yourself into unfamiliarity is that it can be a very respectable form of avoidance. The unfamiliar is easy to identify. It has a name, a schedule, a visible endpoint. You can learn French, run a race, start a company, travel alone, take a hard class. The discomfort is real, and the output is real, and there is a story you can tell afterward. The familiar discomfort is harder to handle. It has no syllabus. It sits in the room with you: loneliness, boredom, resentment, the sense that a relationship is not working, the fear of getting older, the suspicion that you have made a mistake you do not want to name. If every uncomfortable feeling is answered with another experience, you can become very good at handling new environments and still unable to be still with one person.

Career changes make this easy to see. The first time someone leaves a familiar field for an unfamiliar one, the move may be an act of honesty. They are bad at the old work, or bored by it, or finally willing to test a different capacity. The second move can be growth. They have learned that they can rebuild competence, and that the identity they attached to the first job was narrower than they thought. By the third or fourth move, the pattern itself may have become the comfort. The unfamiliar situation is no longer the new work. The unfamiliar situation is the act of leaving again. The person is highly adaptable, and also possibly unable to let anything become home.

That does not mean the adaptation is fake. It is not. The skills are real. The confidence is real. The person can walk into a strange room and make it less strange. But if the only place they feel alive is the place where they are still figuring things out, they have not escaped discomfort. They have made discomfort their habitat.

There is another cost: without return, you cannot tell what has changed. Growth needs a fixed point. If you are always in a new place, a new role, a new set of people, you have no stable surface against which to notice your own development. You may be becoming wiser, or you may be becoming more restless. The two feel similar from the inside. Both involve a kind of momentum. Both make you feel less trapped than you did a year ago. The difference shows up only when you stop moving and ask what you actually want, not what you need next.

This is why the familiar is not the enemy of the unfamiliar. It is the place where the unfamiliar gets digested. A new experience does not become part of you while you are still reacting to it. It becomes part of you in the quiet afterward, when the adrenaline has left and you are doing ordinary things with a slightly altered body. You notice that you no longer flinch at the thing you used to fear. You notice that you can sit with a person whose opinions are annoying without planning your exit. You notice that you can rest without feeling guilty, or that you can want something and not immediately turn the wanting into a project. If you never return to the known, you never get to see what the new has done to you.

So the practice requires discrimination. Not every unfamiliar situation is worth entering. Some are just dangerous, degrading, or irrelevant. Some are uncomfortable because they are unsafe, and the correct response is to leave. Some are uncomfortable because they are hard, and the correct response is to stay. The distinction is not always obvious in the moment. That is part of the training. Over time, you get better at telling whether the alarm is telling you about a bear or about your own history. A person who has survived enough non-threatening conflicts learns not to treat every argument as a threat to survival. A person who has made enough honest mistakes learns not to treat every embarrassment as evidence of incompetence. The body becomes less literal.

But discrimination is not enough. You also need a center. A center is not the opposite of growth. It is the condition that makes growth possible. It can be a body you have learned to trust, a set of relationships where you are known, a place where the light comes in the same way, a practice that asks you to return. From that center, you can step into the unfamiliar without having to become the unfamiliar. You can leave and come back. You can take the new thing seriously and also keep your bearings.

Over time, if this is done well, your sense of what is comfortable becomes less fragile and less narrow. You can be in a strange room and not scan for the door. You can hear a hard thing and not immediately solve it, perform it, or escape it. You can be bored and not panic. You can be uncertain and not convert the uncertainty into a plan. The boundary between the familiar and the unfamiliar stops being a wall and starts being a membrane. Things pass through. You pass through. The inside changes, but it remains an inside.

If it is done poorly, the boundary becomes a treadmill. You keep crossing it because standing still feels like being buried. You are not afraid of the unfamiliar so much as you are afraid of what would be noticed if you stopped moving. The same behavior—seeking out what you do not know—can be enlargement or escape, and from the outside they often look alike. The difference shows up when the novelty has worn off. A person who has used unfamiliarity to enlarge themselves can sit in a familiar room and feel the enlargement there: less reactivity, more patience, a wider range of situations that do not require an explanation. A person who has used unfamiliarity to avoid themselves cannot sit in the same room without starting to plan the next departure.
rejected:
The first time you speak to a stranger at a bar, your heart hammers against your ribs. The second time, it’s a dull throb. By the tenth, it’s just a slightly elevated baseline. This is not courage; it is habituation.

We often mistake the expansion of our comfort zone for personal growth. We tell ourselves that becoming comfortable with discomfort is a sign of strength. But comfort is a ratchet. It only moves in one direction. Once you have successfully navigated an unfamiliar situation, your brain updates its map. The territory that was once dangerous becomes known. The unknown shrinks.

This creates a paradox. If the goal is to remain permanently unsettled, you cannot succeed. Every act of bravery ends in safety. You push the edge of the map out, and then you sit down on the new land. It feels solid. It feels like home.

The danger of this process is not failure, but complacency. People who have pushed themselves into unfamiliar situations once or twice often stop. They have tasted the adrenaline and achieved the result. They have a story to tell. But because the new territory now feels familiar, the internal alarm stops ringing. They begin to mistake their current level of competence for the ceiling of their potential.

To keep the discomfort alive, you have to accept that the thing that scared you last year is boring to you now. The solo trip to a foreign country that required weeks of preparation is now a routine. The public speaking engagement that caused insomnia is now a presentation.

This is why the pursuit of the unfamiliar is not a destination but a treadmill. You do not climb a mountain of difficulty and stay at the peak. You climb, you reach the top, and then the ground rises around you. You are no longer at the top. You are in the middle of a new, larger hill.

The sense of what is comfortable does not disappear; it inflates. It expands to fill whatever space you have conquered. And because it always fills, there is always a new edge to find. The only people who truly never face unfamiliar situations are those who stop moving.

prompt: I'm a seed investor with a decent track record and I've been looking back at which of my bets paid off. Write a blog post on what the best early-stage investments tend to have in common, and what that means for founders stressing about how popular their round is.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
## What My Best Seed Bets Had in Common

I have gone back through my seed portfolio more than once, trying to see why some checks mattered and others did not. The companies that paid off did not all look like the most obvious bets at the time. Some had small traction. Some were in categories I did not fully understand. A few were not even the most oversubscribed raises in their year. I am not claiming this is a formula; seed outcomes are noisy, and I am looking back from the biased vantage point of the bets that worked. What the better bets shared was less glamorous: a founder with a causal model, a product with a real wedge, a team that could operate, and metrics that were small but true.

The first thing is the founder’s theory. The best founders did not just have a pitch; they had a model of the world. They could tell me why a particular group of customers had a painful problem, why the existing way of doing it was broken, why now was the moment, and why their team was the one that could fix it. More important, they could tell me what would make them wrong. “If hospitals do not adopt this in six months, it is because of procurement, not product.” “If developers stop using this after the first project, the onboarding is the problem.” That kind of sentence is rare. It means the founder is thinking about the business as a set of testable claims, not a story.

The second thing is the wedge. The best early companies were not trying to be platforms. They were good at one job for one group of people. Maybe it was a weird workflow, a niche buyer, a specific pain that was expensive enough to solve. The traction that mattered was not a spike from a launch or a demo day. It was behavior: users who came back, referred someone, paid without being chased, or got visibly annoyed when the product broke. I have looked at enough early dashboards to know that a customer who would have called if the product disappeared is worth more than a hundred customers who are politely trying things.

The third thing is operational competence. At seed, the company is not just the product. It is the founder’s ability to sell, support, hire, manage cash, and keep the team from falling apart under uncertainty. The best teams were scrappy, but not in a chaotic way. They had shipped something hard before, even if it was in a different category. They knew what they did not know, and they were not embarrassed by it. A founder who can say, “We are bad at enterprise sales, so we are not pretending we can sell into the Fortune 500 yet,” is usually more investable than one who claims to be ready for every market.

The fourth thing is honesty about the numbers. The best bets did not all have beautiful metrics. Some had low retention in one segment and strong retention in another. Some had revenue that was lumpy. But the numbers were true. The founders could walk me through the cohort, the churn, the expansion, the cost of the next dollar. They did not ask me to trust the aggregate. They showed me where the product worked and where it did not. That is what early-stage investing is: paying for the right to be in the company while it finds the true version of itself.

That brings me to the question founders stress about: how popular the round is. A popular round is a signal, but it is a signal about attention. Attention is useful. It can bring talent, customer trust, partner intros, and a sense of momentum. If a company is hot, it often has some of the qualities above, because people are responding to something. But popularity is also easy to manufacture and easy to misread. It can measure the narrative, the timing, the investor brand, or the sector’s fashion more than the company’s odds. It is a lagging indicator of excitement, not a leading indicator of a durable business.

The hardest objection to that view is simple: popular rounds often produce winners because strong companies attract capital, and capital compounds. The best startups get the best engineers, the best sales hires, the best board advice, and the best introductions. They win because they are strong, and the strength is reinforced by the resources. I do not dispute that. What I dispute is treating popularity as the thing to optimize. A weak company can also raise a hot round when the story is fashionable. The difference is what the money buys. In the best cases, capital is used to reduce uncertainty: find the segment that retains, hire the first real salesperson, build the integration that makes the product indispensable, get the second opinion from a customer who matters. In the worst cases, capital is used to buy the appearance of growth: more logos, more headcount, more narrative, a faster burn, and a bigger next raise.

If your round is popular, the lesson is not to celebrate the crowd. It is to ask what the crowd is buying. If they are buying a market story, make sure the product can deliver it. If they are buying the founder, make sure the founder is not becoming the bottleneck. If they are buying momentum, make sure momentum is being converted into learning. A high valuation is useful, but it is not a strategy. It can let you move faster, but it can also make you sloppy. The most dangerous phase for a hot early company is after the raise, when the team starts raising the next round in its head and begins to build for the investors instead of the first hundred customers.

If your round is not popular, the lesson is not to assume you are broken. It is to use the silence as a diagnostic. A quiet raise can mean you are too early, your wedge is too narrow, your metrics are not yet real, your team is not clear, your ask is too high, or your market is smaller than you think. Some of those are fixable. Some are informative. The right questions are not “Why did Fund X pass?” but “Are customers choosing us despite us? Is the problem urgent enough that they change behavior? Are we good at one thing, or merely interesting? Can we get to the next stage without a miracle?” If the answer is that you are early, a smaller round can be a gift: less pressure, less burn, more time to find the true business. If the answer is that the problem is not painful enough, the quiet round saved you from scaling a mistake.

The raise is a financing event, not a business model. The cap table is a byproduct of harder questions: Is there a real pain? Is the product good enough that people keep using it? Is the team capable of the next two hard years? Is the market large enough to matter, and is there a path in? Those questions do not care how many institutions wanted in. They care whether a stranger with a painful problem would choose this product, and whether this team can keep making that choice true. A popular round can help. But it does not answer the question that determines whether the investment works.
rejected:
The most successful early-stage investments rarely look like the most popular ones. In fact, there is often an inverse correlation. When a round is oversubscribed, with fifty firms fighting for a ten-percent stake, the price has been bid up to reflect maximum confidence. That confidence is usually a lagging indicator of past performance, not a leading indicator of future growth.

The common thread in the winners is usually not the team’s charisma or the size of the market, but a specific structural advantage that is visible at the seed stage but not yet fully priced in. It is a technical moat, a proprietary dataset, or a distribution channel that competitors cannot replicate without breaking their existing business model. These advantages are quiet. They do not generate press releases. They do not invite viral loops. They generate compounding returns because they are hard to copy, not because they are exciting to talk about.

Foundators who obsess over the number of investors in their round are optimizing for the wrong metric. A crowded round signals that the asset is overvalued relative to its current capabilities. It also creates a fragile dynamic: if the next round is not immediately massive, the valuation correction is painful. The investors in a crowded round are all watching the same metrics, waiting for the same signals. When those signals are delayed, the exit velocity of the board is fast.

A smaller, concentrated round is a feature. It means the lead investor is taking a larger position because they understand a risk that the rest of the market is ignoring. It allows the founder to negotiate terms that reflect reality rather than hype. It provides a partner who is incentivized to help fix the specific structural weaknesses that exist, rather than a group of tourists who are there to ride the valuation.

The stress of an unpopular round is the cost of being early. The goal is not to be loved by the market in Year One. The goal is to build something that becomes impossible to ignore by Year Three. If you are building a durable advantage, you do not need the noise of a crowded round to validate your existence. You need the silence to get the work done.

prompt: I'm a psychiatrist and I just read a blog post arguing that my profession is negligent for not routinely testing depressed patients for environmental poisons like lead. A story about one doctor's patient who turned out to be lead-exposed is making the rounds. Write a thoughtful response from a practicing clinician's point of view: is it reasonable that we don't test more, or is the critic right?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The patient in the blog post is real, and the relief he felt is real. I do not want to wave that away. If a depressed patient has clinically significant lead exposure, and we remove the exposure and the depression improves, that is a case worth remembering. But the inference the post draws from that case—that depressed patients should be routinely tested for lead—is a different claim, and I do not think it survives contact with the clinic.

I take “routinely” to mean: every adult who presents with depression gets a blood lead level as part of the initial workup, regardless of history. That is not what I would do, and not because I think lead is unimportant. Lead is important enough that we should remove it from water, paint, soil, and workplaces. It is not important enough, in my judgment, to become a psychiatric screening test.

The first problem is that depression does not point to lead. Depression is one of the most common reasons adults seek medical care. It follows loss, trauma, chronic pain, sleep deprivation, alcohol, medications, thyroid disease, cancer, stroke, mania, and ordinary bad luck. It is also a nonspecific response to feeling badly in one’s body. Lead exposure, at levels high enough to produce clear neurotoxicity in adults, is much less common. In many developed settings, most adults have blood lead levels below 5 micrograms per deciliter, and only a small fraction have levels that would make a physician think seriously about lead as a cause of current symptoms. If you test a large group of depressed adults, you will find some elevated lead levels. You will also find that most of those people are depressed for the same reasons depressed people are usually depressed.

This is not a minor statistical point. A blood lead level is a measure of exposure, not a diagnosis of lead-caused depression. A level of 6 or 8 or 12 does not say, “This metal is making you sad.” It says, “There is some lead in your blood.” To attribute the depression to lead, you need more than that: a plausible exposure, a temporal relationship, symptoms that fit a toxic syndrome, exclusion of other causes, and ideally improvement after removal. Without those, a positive number is mostly a source of anxiety and follow-up visits.

The second problem is that the test does not have a clean positive. Public health reference values for lead are low, and there is no agreed level below which a person can be declared “not affected.” For children, the CDC reference value is 3.5 micrograms per deciliter, and the official position is that no safe level has been identified. If we bring that logic into adult psychiatry, we are in trouble. A patient with a blood lead level of 4 may be “above reference,” but what do we do? Chelation is not indicated for low-level exposure in an adult with depression, and it carries real risks: kidney injury, electrolyte disturbance, removal of essential metals, and in some cases worsening neurologic symptoms. The treatment for lead exposure is removing the source: old paint, contaminated water, occupational dust, a hobby, a traditional remedy, a workplace. If we cannot find a source, the number sits there, ambiguous and actionable in name only.

So the question becomes: in how many depressed patients will a blood lead level change management in a meaningful way? I have ordered lead levels, but usually the history was the test. A patient with fatigue, abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive complaints, and a job stripping paint. A young parent worried about a child in a pre-1978 house. A man with shooting-range exposure and progressive cognitive difficulty. In those cases, the test confirms a suspicion and helps focus the workup. In a patient whose depression began after a divorce, with normal neurologic examination and no exposure history, the pretest probability is so low that the result is unlikely to help.

That is the standard we already use for medical mimics of depression. We do not test every depressed patient for every reversible cause. We look for clues. We check thyroid function or B12 when the history, exam, age, diet, medications, or neurologic signs suggest it. We consider sleep apnea when there is snoring, daytime somnolence, resistant hypertension, or obesity. We consider steroids, alcohol, anticonceptives, antivirals, and other drugs. We consider cancer, chronic pain, stroke, dementia, mania, and psychosis. The reason is not that we distrust psychiatric diagnosis. The reason is that tests are useful when they answer a question the history has raised.

The critic is right about something, though. We could ask better questions. Psychiatric histories are often good at capturing stressors and poor at capturing environments. A patient may say, “I’ve been feeling off for a year,” and we may write “depression” without asking where they work, what they renovate, what they solder, whether they shoot clay pigeons, whether they use imported spices or traditional powders, whether their water comes from old service lines, whether their child plays on bare dirt near an old building, whether they have numbness in the hands or feet, whether their memory is failing in a way that worries them, whether they have had abdominal colic or unexplained anemia. Those questions are cheap. They do not require a lab panel. They require us to treat the body as part of the case.

I would be more willing to test for lead, or refer to occupational or environmental medicine, when the depression is embedded in a suggestive syndrome:

- Cognitive complaints, especially memory or concentration problems that feel different from the patient’s usual mood-related fog.
- Peripheral neuropathy, tremor, gait difficulty, weakness, or other neurologic signs.
- Abdominal pain, constipation, or unexplained anemia.
- Occupational or hobby exposure: construction, demolition, plumbing, battery work, shooting ranges, soldering, fishing weights, pottery glazes, stained glass, metal recycling, lead paint abatement without proper precautions.
- Housing exposure: old paint, recent renovation, peeling paint, children playing in dust or soil, lead service lines or old solder.
- Traditional or imported substances: certain cosmetics, powders, remedies, spices, or folk preparations that have been associated with lead.
- Treatment resistance or an atypical course, especially when the depression is accompanied by physical symptoms that do not fit a primary psychiatric picture.
- Children or adolescents with cognitive, behavioral, or learning problems in high-risk settings, where public-health testing may already be indicated for reasons other than depression.

That list is not universal screening. It is pattern recognition.

The broader category of “environmental poisons” makes the case for routine testing even weaker. If depression is the indication for lead testing, why not mercury, arsenic, manganese, pesticides, solvents, carbon monoxide, mycotoxins, PFAS, or whatever chemical is currently in the news? Many of these can cause neurologic or psychiatric symptoms, but usually in a more specific pattern: tremor, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, encephalopathy, abdominal illness, skin changes, occupational clustering, acute exposure. Depression alone is not that pattern. If we make mood the gateway to toxicology, the workup becomes unbounded and the results become uninterpretable.

The hardest version of the critic’s argument is this: maybe low-level lead is contributing to depression in enough people that we are missing a treatable cause because we are not looking. Some population studies have found associations between blood lead and depressive symptoms. Those studies deserve attention. But population-level association is not the same as individual diagnosis. If low lead exposure raises risk a little, the response is public health: reduce exposure everywhere. That is how we dealt with lead in gasoline and paint. We did not make every irritable child or depressed adult a case investigation. We removed the source from the environment. Testing is for diagnosis. Prevention is policy. We can support both without confusing them.

There is also a danger in the story itself. A single patient who improves after exposure removal feels like proof. It may be proof in that patient. But one case cannot tell us how often this happens, how many cases look like ordinary depression before the test, or how many patients with elevated lead levels would not have improved. Depression often improves with time, therapy, medication, sleep, exercise, social change, or the simple fact that the patient has finally been taken seriously. Without comparison, we cannot know what the lead did. We should be humble about that, not overconfident.

So is the profession negligent for not testing more? I would not put it that way. Negligence implies a standard that was known and ignored. The known standard is not “order every possible test.” The known standard is to take a history, examine the patient, recognize red flags, and follow them. If a depressed patient has obvious neurologic signs and a plausible exposure history, and the clinician never thinks of lead, that is poor medicine. If a patient with a typical depressive episode later turns out to have a mildly elevated blood lead level found by a curious physician, that is a different story. The first case supports better suspicion. The second does not justify a universal order set.

The critic and I are worried about the same failure: missing a reversible medical cause because we anchored on a psychiatric label. We differ on the remedy. The critic wants a test. I want a longer exposure history, a more careful neurologic exam, and a lower threshold for testing when the story fits. The patient in the blog post is a warning to be curious. It is not a blueprint for routine screening.
rejected:
The blog post is right about the diagnosis and wrong about the negligence. It confuses a specific, treatable etiology with a universal screening failure.

Lead poisoning is a real cause of depression. The literature is clear: chronic lead exposure alters neurotransmitter synthesis, particularly serotonin and dopamine, and induces neuroinflammation. A patient with "atypical" depression, cognitive slowing, or a history of working in battery recycling, plumbing, or renovation is a candidate for a blood lead level (BLL). If a clinician sees a young man with new-onset depression and a job stripping paint from a pre-1978 home, and they do not order a BLL, they have failed.

But "routinely" is the operative word that makes the argument collapse.

In the United States, the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend BLL screening for children under six, and for children in high-risk zip codes or with specific risk factors. For adults, the guidance is risk-based. The CDC does not recommend universal screening for adults because the prevalence of elevated lead levels in the general adult population is low, and the cost-benefit ratio of universal testing does not justify it.

Consider the math. The sensitivity of a standard depression questionnaire for lead-induced mood disturbance is low. Most depressed patients do not have lead toxicity. If you screened every adult presenting with depression for lead, you would be performing millions of tests to find a handful of cases. In a primary care or psychiatric setting, where the average visit is fifteen minutes, this is not just inefficient; it is impossible. It would require a separate workup, insurance authorization, and follow-up. It would push down access for the majority of patients who need counseling, medication management, or crisis intervention.

The critic’s error is a base rate fallacy dressed as a moral indictment. They take one anecdote—a patient who was missed—and generalize it to the entire profession. "Doctor X failed to test Patient Y" is a valid complaint. "Psychiatry is negligent for not testing everyone" is not. It is like arguing that internal medicine is negligent for not performing a cardiac catheterization on every patient with a headache. The headache might be a warning sign of a stroke, but the pre-test probability is too low to justify the procedure for everyone.

There is, however, a grain of truth in the criticism that deserves attention. Our intake forms are inadequate. We ask about family history, sleep, and trauma. We rarely ask about occupational history in a structured way. We do not ask where the patient lives, what their water source is, or if they participate in hobbies like shooting lead ammunition or working with stained glass. The tools exist to capture this data. The habit does not.

A reasonable standard of care is not universal testing. It is universal inquiry.

If we are to meet the critic halfway, the change should be procedural, not diagnostic. Intake forms should include a brief, targeted occupational and environmental history. Not a paragraph, but three questions:
1. What is your primary occupation, and does it involve dust, fumes, or heavy metals?
2. Do you live or spend significant time in a home built before 1978?
3. Do you have hobbies that involve lead, such as shooting, fishing with lead sinkers, or stained glass?

If the answer to any of these is yes, the threshold for ordering a BLL drops significantly. This is not negligence. It is pattern recognition.

The blog post wants us to be omniscient. It wants us to screen for every possible toxin, every rare genetic variant, every obscure metabolic quirk. That is not medicine. Medicine is triage. It is using the most likely causes to guide the workup. Lead is a real cause. It is a rare cause of *generalized* depression. We should test when the history suggests it. We should not test when it does not.

prompt: Every few weeks another magazine publishes an article attacking meritocracy, which sounds weird since the word seems to just mean the best people getting the jobs. I want an essay that works out whether these critics have a point and whether meritocracy is worth defending.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The confusion is real because the word has been drained of its original edge. “Meritocracy” was coined by Michael Young in 1958 as a satire, not a compliment. In his imagined future, an IQ test and school certificate assigned people to their proper stations, and the result was a society in which everyone got what he deserved and therefore had no grounds for complaint. The horror was not that smart people led; it was that the system made hierarchy look like arithmetic. When current magazines attack meritocracy, they are usually attacking that arithmetic: the belief that the existing distribution of jobs, pay and prestige is the visible residue of individual worth.

That belief is doing more work than the phrase “best people get the jobs” suggests. A job has requirements. A surgeon needs steady hands, anatomical knowledge, the ability to function under stress. A teacher needs the capacity to explain, organize a room, adapt to children. A manager needs to coordinate people and take responsibility for outcomes. These are not the same merit. A brilliant researcher may be a useless line manager; a charming salesperson may be a catastrophic finance director. “Best” is not a single number. It is a set of predictions: if we put this person here, will the work get done, and will others be helped or harmed? A society that takes those predictions seriously is not being meritocratic in the insulting sense; it is being responsible.

The critics’ first point is that the predictions are often bad, and we know it. Personnel research has found for decades that structured interviews, work samples and supervised trial periods predict job performance better than unstructured chats and impressive pedigrees. A law firm that promotes the partner who bills the most hours and brings in the most revenue is not measuring legal wisdom; it is measuring a particular commercial behavior, often reinforced by whom one went to school with. A hospital that promotes the physician with the most publications may be rewarding access to a well-funded lab, a famous mentor, and the time to write, not the quality of bedside care. The test is not evil. It is a proxy. The problem is that we stop calling it a proxy. We say the person has merit, when what we have observed is success in a particular set of signals.

The second point is harder: the signals are produced by family. College admissions make this visible because the machinery is public. In the United States, children from higher-income and more-educated families are far more likely to attend college, and far more likely to attend selective colleges, than children from poorer families. At elite institutions, legacy applicants have long been admitted at higher rates than non-legacy applicants with similar grades and test scores, a fact that is not a conspiracy but a policy choice. Private schooling, tutoring, extracurriculars that require travel and fees, and the quiet cultural fluency of the interview all mean that a teenager’s “merit” is often a family product. The child performs well because the family paid for the conditions of performance. When the employer later says it hired the best candidate, it has hired the downstream effect of an upstream advantage.

This is where the charge of social reproduction bites. A caste system says: you are low because you were born low. A market says: you are poor because you are not valuable. A meritocracy says: you are behind because you are not as talented or hardworking. The last is the most painful, because it turns inequality into a diagnosis. If failure is moral, the loser is implicated in his own defeat. That humiliation is not an accidental byproduct; it is part of the system’s stability. People accept bad odds when they believe the race is fair.

The mobility data show that the race is not obviously fair. In American intergenerational mobility studies, a child born in the top fifth of family income has roughly a one-in-five chance of reaching the top fifth as an adult, while a child born in the bottom fifth has a smaller chance, often estimated around one in ten or less. The United States is also less mobile than several wealthier countries. None of this proves that talent is irrelevant. It proves that the pipeline from talent to position is leaky, and that the leaks are sorted by class. A gifted child in an underfunded school, with sick parents and no car, does not simply fail to show her merit; she is not given the same chances to convert it into credentials.

At this point, the strongest objection to any defense of meritocracy appears. If institutions define merit, and institutions are shaped by the powerful, then to defend merit is to defend the powerful. The boss who says “we promote on merit” may be describing a process in which his own children’s friends get the visible assignments, the polished presentations, the invitations to lunches. The university that says it chooses the best students may be choosing the children who were prepared for its choices. If we always ask the institution to grade itself, we will get a report card with the grade already written on it. This objection cannot be answered by saying the system works most of the time. It requires a standard external to the institution: what is the job for?

That is why the defense of merit must be skeptical of merit. We have to separate three claims that are usually bundled together. First, this person can do the work. Second, this person earned the opportunity to learn the work. Third, this person is therefore a better person. Only the first is needed for competent administration. The second is a question of justice in preparation, not proof of worth. The third is the moral inflation that makes meritocracy poisonous. A doctor who saves lives is not morally superior to the home nurse who keeps those lives bearable; she is better qualified for a particular task. A startup founder who becomes rich may have read the market, taken risks, and been lucky in a way that has little to do with her character. Pay can reflect scarcity, leverage, and the revenue of the team, not a soul’s quality.

So what is worth defending? Not the claim that the hierarchy is just. It is not. Not the claim that everyone has an equal chance. They do not. Not the claim that the winners’ self-confidence is well founded. It is often a training effect: people who are told they are exceptional become better at performing exceptionality, and then mistake the feedback loop for nature. What is worth defending is the demand that serious work be assigned by evidence of relevant ability. That demand has a brutal practical content. If you choose a pilot by lottery, people die. If you choose a judge by patronage, the law becomes a branch of faction. If you choose a public health official by party loyalty during a pandemic, the metric of success becomes obedience rather than survival. The meritocratic principle is at its strongest when the consequences of error are concrete and when the selector has no private knowledge of the candidate’s character. Strangers must be sorted by something, and the something should be connected to the task.

But the principle must be kept humble. A test is a hypothesis, not a verdict. If a company finds that a selection test favors candidates from certain schools, it must ask whether the test measures future performance or prior privilege. If a promotion system rewards visibility, it must ask whether visibility is a job requirement or a byproduct of office proximity. If a profession finds that one group underrepresents itself at the top, the question is not how to make the group look more meritorious, but whether the meritorious traits have been defined too narrowly. The defense of competence becomes an instrument of critique when it forces the institution to show its work.

The critics, then, have a point, but it is easier to state than they often do. They are right that “merit” has become a word for whatever the existing elite happened to do well. They are right that the story of self-made ascent hides the scaffolding of family money, cultural preparation, and arbitrary advantage. They are right that the meritocratic insult—your failure is your fault—does real damage. They are wrong, or at least incomplete, if they conclude that selection by competence is therefore illegitimate. A society cannot run on the principle that no one is really better at the job; it can only run on the principle that claims to competence must be tested, corrected, and kept separate from moral rank. The best people do not get the jobs. The people with the relevant abilities, as far as we can measure them without being fooled by pedigree, should be trusted with the work, and the rest of us should remember that the measure is fallible. That is not a pretty ideology. It is the minimum condition for a civilization that asks strangers to operate on it, teach its children, regulate its money, and decide its disputes.
rejected:
The confusion stems from a linguistic sleight of hand. When people say “meritocracy” in the political sense, they rarely mean a system where the best people get the jobs. They mean a system where the best people are *recognized* as such, and where that recognition is treated as the sole justification for their power.

The critics are attacking the second definition, not the first. And they are right to do so, because the second definition is a lie.

Merit, in any complex field, is not a single scalar value. It is a vector. A brilliant surgeon who is sociopathic is not “more meritorious” than a competent one who is kind; they are different. A CEO who maximizes shareholder value at the cost of employee health is not objectively superior to one who balances profit with stability. But the meritocratic narrative requires us to flatten these distinctions into a single score. It demands that we look at a Harvard graduate and a community college dropout and say, without looking at the actual work, that the former possesses a higher essence of worth.

This flattening serves a specific function: it converts privilege into talent.

If the top jobs are filled by people who went to elite schools, who grew up with social connections, and who had the leisure to develop “soft skills” while their families were secure, the meritocratic story allows us to ignore those advantages. It tells us that the system is a race, and the winner crossed the line because they ran faster. It erases the head start. When a critique points this out—when it says, “You didn’t win because you were the best, you won because the track was tilted”—the defense is usually to say, “But I *was* the best.”

This is the core error. The meritocratic defender insists that the outcome proves the input. If you have the job, you must have had the merit. This is circular reasoning that protects the status quo from scrutiny. It makes inequality legible as personal failure rather than structural design.

However, this does not mean we should abandon the idea that competence matters. It means we need to stop using the word “meritocracy” to describe a social order, and start using it to describe a hiring process.

In a hiring process, merit is specific and testable. Can this engineer write code that scales? Can this teacher raise test scores? Can this manager keep their team from quitting? These are questions with answers. They are not questions about a person’s soul. They are questions about their utility in a specific role.

The danger of meritocracy-as-ideology is that it stops asking whether the role serves anyone other than the person holding it. It assumes that if the “best” people are in charge, the outcome will be good. History suggests otherwise. The most competent people in a room often optimize for the metrics they are given, regardless of whether those metrics align with human flourishing.

So, is it worth defending?

Defend the standard of competence. Hire people who can do the job. Fire people who cannot. Ensure that the criteria for “can do the job” are transparent and not just proxies for who went to the same school as the hiring manager.

Do not defend the belief that competence justifies inequality. Do not defend the idea that because someone is good at their job, they deserve a life of ease while others struggle. Those are two different claims, and conflating them is what makes the word so poisonous.

prompt: Investors say determination is the best predictor of startup success. Write an essay that tries to take determination apart: what is it made of, and which parts can a person actually develop?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The sentence is useful and misleading. It is useful because early-stage investing is mostly inference from small samples. When a founder says “we lost our biggest customer” and then describes the next three calls they will make, the investor sees something: a person who can keep a company alive through ordinary damage. It is misleading because “determination” is not one thing. It is a bundle of commitments, habits, interpretations, and social facts that can point in opposite directions.

A startup founder’s determination appears in many forms. One founder stays up late rebuilding the product. Another spends the week calling customers who stopped replying. Another cuts payroll and tells the team the truth. Another quits the original product and starts over around a smaller insight. All of these can be called determined, but only some of them are useful. The word often covers both perseverance and stubbornness, and the difference between those two can decide whether a company lives.

The first component is a chosen problem, not just an idea. A person can be determined to build a thing and not determined to solve a problem. The difference shows when the original product fails. If the founder says “the market is early,” that is commitment to the idea. If they say “let’s find the version of this pain that people will pay for,” that is commitment to the problem. The second is more developable because it can be specified: who has the pain, what do they do now, what would make them switch, and what would count as evidence that you are wrong.

The second component is an updating rule. Determination becomes dangerous when it is used to protect a story. Theranos is the obvious warning case. Elizabeth Holmes had determination, charisma, and a strong sense of mission, but she built a company around a claim the technology did not support. The company did not collapse because she lacked will. It collapsed because her will was attached to a false claim, and contrary evidence was treated as an obstruction rather than information. A more useful determination is the determination to keep testing. Before a launch, a founder can write down what result would make them change course. That turns determination from a mood into a decision procedure.

The third component is action under uncertainty. Many people can work hard when the path is clear. Determination is what remains when the next step is not. It shows in cold emails, demo days, procurement calls, support tickets, and the unglamorous work of making a small thing real. In 2008, the founders of Airbnb were short of money and designed political cereal boxes, raising about $30,000. The story is often told as grit. The more useful part is that they were willing to run a small, embarrassing, fast test to find out whether anyone would pay. They also kept changing the experience: better photos, better pricing, better host support. The cereal did not save them. The willingness to run unglamorous experiments did.

This part is the most trainable by repetition. The first ten requests are uncomfortable. The fifty-first is administrative. A person can build the muscle by choosing a project with real external feedback and finishing it, not by imagining hardship in the abstract. If the only evidence of your determination is that you once wanted to start something, the evidence is weak. If you have shipped a product, collected payment, handled a complaint, and made a hard tradeoff, you have data.

The fourth component is tolerance for low-grade rejection. Startups are not usually ended by one dramatic failure. They are worn down by small nos. A customer says maybe. A partner says not this quarter. A bank says no. A candidate ghost you after the second interview. Determination here is not heroic. It is the ability to treat a no as data and keep the pipeline moving. It can be developed by increasing volume and lowering the personal meaning of each response. But it depends on not tying your identity to every answer. If every rejection feels like a verdict on you, you will either stop asking or become brittle.

The fifth component is maintenance: sleep, cash, relationships. Determination is not immune to biology. A founder running on four hours of sleep and a two-week cash reserve will make bad decisions and call them conviction. They will mistake exhaustion for intensity and panic for urgency. The developable part is unglamorous: a runway, a schedule, a rule for when to raise, a reason to leave the office. Many people think they need more grit when they need more sleep or a better financial model. A determined founder who cannot think clearly is not an asset; they are a risk.

The sixth component is social commitment. Private will fluctuates. People continue when others depend on them or can see them stop. A co-founder, a small team, a board, customers who rely on the product: these create a container for determination. This is why the lone-founder myth is partly false. You can build the container even if you do not naturally feel relentless. Choose a co-founder who asks hard questions. Publish a roadmap. Take a board seat that requires metrics. Make a public commitment that would be embarrassing to break. Determination is often less a private flame than a set of obligations you have agreed to honor.

Some parts are less developable. Baseline anxiety, need for approval, chronic low energy, a temperament that turns feedback into humiliation: these vary and are hard to change by will. But startups are systems. A risk-averse founder can pair with an operator who pushes for speed. A solitary founder can hire a co-founder whose role is to challenge. A person who hates selling can build a product that attracts users and hire a founder who closes. The goal is not to become a different temperament, but to design a company where your weak points are covered and your durable points are used.

This matters because the investor’s claim is predictive, not causal. Determination may predict success because it is a marker of other things: the founder has finished hard projects, has a support network, can tolerate ambiguity, has chosen a problem they understand. It may also predict because investors need a simple story when the real variables—market timing, distribution, luck—are invisible. If you train only the visible part, you get more people who stay up late and defend bad assumptions. The causal ingredient is not the feeling of continuing. It is the pattern of continuing to take informative actions.

There is also a selection problem. The founders investors remember are the ones who persisted and won. The equally determined founders who persisted into a bad market are not on the keynote stage. That does not mean determination is useless. It means the lesson from survivors is narrower than it appears: persistence can keep a company alive long enough for a good thing to happen, but it cannot make a bad thing good.

The word also hides what success means. A startup that becomes a $2 million-a-year service business required a different persistence than one that becomes a public company. The first needs cash discipline and customer retention. The second needs a large market and a distribution edge. Determination can help in both, but it does different work. In the first, it is the refusal to let the books drift. In the second, it is the refusal to leave the table while the market is still forming.

So the practical question is not whether a person can feel more determined. It is whether they can make the next action cheaper: a clearer problem, a written test, a scheduled call, a co-founder who asks for the number, a cash buffer that removes panic. Those practices do not sound like character. They are what character is made of when it is examined.
rejected:
