system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
A dispute turns sour when one side stops testing a claim and starts auditing courage. The question is no longer whether a policy is wise or a norm is true, but whether the person opposing it is brave or merely safe. That shift changes the rules. If the issue is tax policy, one can look at receipts, projections, and incentives. If the issue is moral standing, the evidence becomes the person’s apparent risk. And apparent risk is easy to manufacture, hard to verify, and deeply tied to identity.

In political and cultural debate, bravery is usually not a trait. It is a social position. To be brave is to say something that costs you something inside a particular group. The same sentence can cost a junior lawyer at a progressive law firm and cost nothing at a conservative conference. It can cost a conservative professor at a research university and nothing at a community college whose students are angry about the same issue. Bravery is relative to a map of who disapproves, who can punish, and whose approval matters. When two people disagree about who the brave dissenter is, they often disagree about the map.

Both sides can feel like the underdog because social power is not one line running from left to right, or from establishment to rebellion. It is a set of local hierarchies that cross-cut each other. A progressive manager in a traditional company may be under pressure from the board, the customers, and the local press. A conservative administrator at a university may be under pressure from students, faculty groups, donors, and accreditation norms. A journalist at a metropolitan paper may feel boxed in by editors and advertisers, while a blogger outside the paper feels boxed in by algorithm and platform rules. Each person can point to real costs: lost promotions, hostile emails, professional isolation, legal threats, public shaming. The feeling is not always delusion. It is often a correct reading of one’s immediate environment.

The trouble begins when that local reading is treated as the whole truth. The person who is under pressure at work concludes that the whole culture is against them. The institution that is losing influence in one city concludes that it still controls the national conversation. Both mistakes feed the same story: we are the small, honest group standing against a vast, cowardly consensus. The small group is always real, because it is the group one is in. The vast consensus is also real, because it is the group one fears or resents. The debate sours because both sides are using the same emotional template with different names.

There is a second mechanism: the brave dissenter needs a penalty to be legible. If the cost is too small, the speech looks like opinion. If the cost is large, the speech looks like testimony. But the cost can be partly chosen. A person can post a contrarian view in the most hostile possible venue, demand the strongest possible concession, and then treat the resulting anger as proof of persecution. The audience may be cruel, but the speaker also selected the audience. I cannot tell from public behavior how much of that suffering is chosen and how much is imposed; the same post can be both. The conformist, meanwhile, can respond with mild moderation and still be called a collaborator, because the dissenter has defined any failure to execute the opposition as fear. The game has no exit. Pushback proves the threat; silence proves the conspiracy; compromise proves the weakness.

This is why “conformist” is such an effective insult. It does not say you are wrong. It says you are afraid. If you are afraid, your reasons are not reasons; they are the rationalizations of self-protection. The label also protects the accuser from having to engage. A conformist cannot be trusted to tell the truth, because their truth is bought with safety. The brave dissenter, by contrast, has already paid the price of honesty. Their suffering is taken as a down payment on credibility. That is a bad epistemic rule, but it feels good. We have all seen someone who is punished for a view and thought, at least for a moment, that the punishment made the view more true.

Cultural debates make this especially likely because the stakes are often about dignity, not just policy. In a fight over zoning or interest rates, one side can concede a practical point without feeling humiliated. In a fight over who is protected, who is silenced, or who benefits from the current order, concession can feel like admission that one’s group has been powerless. When #MeToo expanded, some said it was finally exposing abuse that institutions had shielded. Others said it had become a reputational weapon that could destroy careers before evidence was clear. Both sides were describing real experiences. The first could point to victims who had been ignored for years. The second could point to people whose lives were ruined by anonymous accusations. But the argument quickly became about which side was brave enough to name the real danger. To say “this process is going too far” was to be accused of defending predators. To say “this movement is still too timid” was to be accused of dismissing victims. The substance disappeared under the moral audit.

The same pattern shows up in debates over affirmative action, free speech, policing, gender, climate, and workplace culture. One side says a norm is being enforced by powerful institutions and that the cost falls on ordinary people who do not want to be punished for their beliefs. The other side says the norm is a minimum standard that has only just been recognized, and that the people complaining are the ones who benefited from the old arrangement. Each claim can be true in a particular case. A company that fires someone for a joke may be enforcing a norm that is too rigid. A worker who refuses to acknowledge harassment may be protecting a privilege they cannot see. The sourness comes from generalizing from the case. The dissenter wants their injury to prove the system is rotten. The conformist, as they see it, wants the system’s survival to prove the injury is imaginary.

Social media accelerates the process because it rewards clarity over calibration. A post that says “I think this policy has serious problems and I am prepared to lose some standing for saying so” is less attractive than a post that says “I am being targeted for telling the truth.” The second post creates a story. It names a persecutor, a victim, and a hidden truth. It also invites the reader to take a side in a moral drama. Moderation is hard to spread. “I am a little worried, but I do not feel under attack” is not a rallying cry. The brave dissenter script requires drama, and the platform supplies an audience that can turn a single uncomfortable conversation into a feeling of siege.

The hardest objection to this account is that it can sound like false equivalence. In many debates, one side really does have more institutional power. A newspaper editor, a university administrator, a platform moderator, or a corporate compliance officer can enforce norms in ways that an angry commenter cannot. If a professor is denied tenure for a view, the claim that they are just a conformist protecting their status is not a neutral correction; it can be a dismissal of actual sanctions. The same is true on the other side: if a worker is ignored or punished for raising safety or harassment concerns, saying they are merely following the new orthodoxy can minimize real coercion. The error is not in noticing power. It is in assuming that one’s local map of power is the whole field. The professor fired by one department may be part of a profession that still sets curricula and publishes books. The worker disciplined by one company may be part of a consumer class that is shaping markets and elections. Underdog status is real, but it is often partial and temporary.

That partiality is what makes the argument so hard to settle. To say “you are not the underdog” is to deny a person’s felt vulnerability. To say “you are the underdog” is to grant them a moral advantage they may not have earned by their argument. Both responses move the debate away from the issue. The issue might be whether a norm is true, useful, or justly applied. The status contest asks whether the person is strong enough to be believed. In that contest, evidence is secondary. A person who is punished becomes more credible, not less, because the punishment is treated as a kind of stress test. A person who is not punished becomes less credible, because they apparently had nothing to lose. The result is a debate in which the most exposed participants gain the most trust, even when exposure is a choice.

There is a less flattering reason the pattern persists: it is useful. Being the brave dissenter gives a person a coherent identity in a confusing social field. If you are merely wrong, you can revise. If you are a dissenter, your error is not error; it is prophecy ahead of its time. Being the conformist, in the opponent’s telling, does the same work for them. It turns a complex disagreement about institutions into a clean story about courage and cowardice. Both sides get to be the protagonists of the same narrative, with different names for the villain. The narrative is seductive because it answers a question that policy analysis cannot: why should I care if I am losing? The answer is that you are not losing; you are resisting.

The pattern would be easier to defuse if people were allowed to specify the scale of their claim. “I am under pressure in my office” is a different statement from “my side is under attack in the culture.” The first can be checked against local facts: who has authority, what the rules are, what has happened to similar cases. The second requires a national sociology that few people can actually see. Most people know their department, their feed, their city, their party. They do not know the distribution of power across the whole society. But the brave dissenter story demands that they do know it. It demands that the local injury be a sample of the whole. When the sample is accepted as the population, the debate stops being an argument and becomes a confession: do you see the persecution, or are you part of it?

That is the final reason the tone sours so fast. The question “who is the brave dissenter?” is not really asking about bravery. It is asking for recognition. It says, I am paying a cost; tell me it is real. The answer “you are the conformist” says, your cost is not what you think, or you are choosing it. Both claims are hard to hear because both touch the person’s standing. Once standing is the issue, every reply is taken as an attack or a defense, and every fact is sorted by which side it helps. The only move that might cool the argument is the least dramatic one: admitting that one can be vulnerable in one place and protected in another, that the map is incomplete, and that the truth of a claim does not depend on how much the speaker suffers for it. That admission is rarely satisfying. It leaves both sides less heroic. But it is the only version of the conversation that can survive contact with the fact that power is local, shifting, and often shared by people who are sure they are alone.
rejected:
The argument is never really about the specific policy. It is about the status of the speaker. When two people disagree, they are not just trading facts; they are negotiating who has the moral high ground. The charge of "conformity" is a weapon because it implies that the target is not thinking, but obeying. The charge of "dissidence" is a shield because it implies that the speaker is not merely wrong, but brave.

This dynamic turns sour quickly because the labels are mutually exclusive and self-referential. If you call your opponent a conformist, you are defining your own position as the deviation from the norm. If they call you a conformist, they are doing the same thing. There is no external metric to adjudicate who is actually going against the current. The current is whatever the other person says it is.

Both sides feel they are the underdog because the center of gravity in public discourse has shifted, but not in a way that is visible to everyone at once. A decade ago, the safe, mainstream position in many elite institutions was to support free markets, limited government, and traditional social norms. Today, the safe, mainstream position in those same institutions is often to support expansive government, identity-based protections, and progressive social restructuring.

A person who holds the old mainstream view now feels like a dissenter. They remember a time when their views were the default, not the exception. They see themselves speaking up against a new orthodoxy that has replaced the old one. They are not wrong that a shift has occurred. They are correct that they are now the minority in many professional and academic circles.

Conversely, a person who holds the new mainstream view feels like a dissenter because they were the minority when they formed their beliefs. They remember the ridicule, the marginalization, or the silence they faced. They have internalized a narrative of struggle. To accept that they are now the dominant voice in the room feels like a betrayal of their own history. They are not wrong that they were once underdogs. They are correct that their rise was hard-fought.

The tragedy is that both narratives are true, but they are true at different times. The person who was the underdog in 2010 may be the conformist in 2024. The person who was the conformist in 2010 may be the dissenter in 2024. But in the heat of the moment, neither side can grant the other the benefit of the doubt. To admit that you are now the mainstream is to admit that your moral authority is contingent on power, not principle. To admit that your opponent is now the mainstream is to admit that their arguments have won, not just that they have become loud.

So the argument curdles. It becomes a fight over who suffers more. If you can prove you are more marginalized, you own the debate. Facts become secondary to the demonstration of pain. The dissenter who is not actually dissident is seen as a hypocrite. The conformist who is actually a conformist is seen as a coward. And the cycle repeats, because the next shift in the center of gravity will create a new set of underdogs who will remember their struggle, and a new set of conformists who will deny their complicity.

## The Anecdote Is Not the Experiment

I am tired of reading “science” that starts with a scene: a woman in a lab, a toddler with a juice box, a CEO in a boardroom, a couple fighting over dishes. Then the author says, “And that, it turns out, is because…”

No. That’s because a story happened. A story is not a mechanism. A story is not even a result, unless it was observed, recorded, compared, and survived the boring question of what else could explain it.

But the form has become a conveyor belt. The evolutionary psychologist tells you why you tip at the restaurant, based on one waiter in one town. The neuroscientist tells you what the brain is “really doing” after interviewing three people and perhaps touching a scanner. The management book tells you what a penguin, a football team, and a failed startup have taught us about your spreadsheet. The column tells you that a child in a photograph has unlocked the future of learning.

Amusing? Yes. Scientific? No. It is storytelling with a lab coat draped over the shoulders.

What bothers me is not that these writers use stories. Of course they use stories. Humans need stories. What bothers me is that the anecdote is doing the evidentiary work. It is not a hook; it is the load-bearing wall. The reader is meant to feel that because the scene is vivid, the explanation is true. “Aha, that’s how it works.”

No. That’s how one person behaved once, or how one author remembers one person behaving once, in a context full of things the author has not measured.

The damage is quiet. It teaches people to mistake plausibility for proof. A good anecdote feels like insight. It makes uncertainty look lazy. It gives the public a version of science that is tidy, human, and immediately applicable, and it gives the writer a way to publish opinions by putting a quote at the beginning and a citation at the end.

And yes, I am guilty. I have started a paragraph with “I once knew a…” and let the story do more work than I would admit. I have chosen the memorable case over the uninteresting base rate. I have written a sentence that sounded like a finding because I found it satisfying to say. The difference between me and the worst of these books is not that I never do it. It is that, hopefully, I still know the difference between an illustration and a demonstration.

So keep the anecdotes. I like them. But put them where they belong: as examples, as color, as reminders that the data are made of people. Do not hand me one office argument and call it organizational behavior. Do not hand me one dinner party and call it social psychology.

If the story is the evidence, you do not have science. You have a parable with footnotes.
rejected:
The sentence structure is always the same.

First, a charming story. A dog who learned to walk the stairs. A CEO who meditates in a closet. A friend who quit her job to paint murals in Peru. You nod. You feel warm.

Then, the pivot.

"And this," the author writes, "is actually about neuroplasticity."

Or: "This mirrors the principles of behavioral economics."

Or: "It’s a perfect example of the Pareto distribution."

The anecdote is not a data point. It is a decoration. It exists to make the jargon palatable, to give the reader a mental hook so they don’t have to actually engage with the mechanism being described. The story does the heavy lifting of persuasion; the "science" is just a label slapped on the back of the box to make it feel rigorous.

I hate it because it is intellectually lazy. It assumes that if I laugh at the dog, I will accept the subsequent claim about synaptic pruning without checking if the sample size was three. It trades precision for vibes. It is the equivalent of wearing a lab coat to a cocktail party and calling it peer review.

The worst part is that I do it.

I just wrote a paragraph about a specific client’s failure to follow through on a deadline. I called it "confirmation bias." I felt clever. I felt precise. But I hadn’t measured their bias. I hadn’t isolated variables. I had just taken a human error, dressed it up in a buzzword, and moved on.

I am no better than the guy writing about the monk who meditated for ten years and then got hit by a car. I am just doing it in smaller doses, with less pretense, and hopefully fewer footnotes.

The fix is boring. State the observation. State the inference. Admit the gap between them. Don’t hide behind the dog.
