Another close friend was, in the first months, mostly irritating: too opinionated, too literal, too unwilling to smooth things over. I remember thinking, at least once, that they would be impossible to live near. A third was simply not my type in the way I understood type at the time—different age, different manners, different sense of what a normal evening should be. I did not pursue them. They remained available in a way I did not expect, and eventually I stopped finding them strange.

The pattern is not absolute. I have warm friends I recognized early. I have people I liked immediately and still like, without any dramatic revision. But the inner circle is weighted toward the misjudged. That is what puzzles me. If I am choosing friends, why do I keep choosing, after the fact, the people I initially passed over?

The easiest answer is coincidence. I have a small number of close friends, not a large dataset. Four or five people are not enough to support a theory. Memory also helps patterns along. I remember the friendships that surprised me because surprise is memorable. The friendships that developed smoothly may have been just as important, but they left no mark of contradiction, so they do not stand out when I look for a theme. It may be that I am not seeing a pattern in who becomes close to me; I may be seeing a pattern in which friendships I am willing to narrate.

That is a serious objection, and I cannot dismiss it. There is also a flattering version of the story: I am perceptive, I just need time. The charming people are performative; the difficult people are authentic. I learn to tell the difference. I do not fully believe that. It makes me too much of a connoisseur and the early years of a friendship too much like a tasting menu.

So I keep coming back to culture. Not culture in the grand sense of nations or traditions, but the small culture I was trained in: the family, the neighborhood, the school, the class of people whose emotional weather I learned first. In that culture, being easy was a virtue. If someone was agreeable, quick to laugh, unthreatening, I was taught to treat that as evidence of goodness. If someone was reserved, corrective, or absorbed in their own concerns, I was taught to treat that as evidence of distance. The problem is that ease is not the same thing as intimacy. A person can be very easy to be around and still leave you alone. A person can be hard to warm up to and then, once warmed, be strangely specific about you.

If that cultural training is part of the explanation, then the pattern is not really about my friends. It is about my first impressions. I may have a bias against people who do not mirror me quickly. They do not validate my jokes, adopt my opinions, or make me feel center-stage. I read that as coldness. But sometimes it is just a different tempo. Some people reserve their attention for what they consider real. Once they decide you are real, they give you a kind of seriousness that easy people rarely bother with.

But even this explanation is not clean. Some of the people I underestimated were not culturally misread; they were actually difficult, and I became close to them only after they proved they could be difficult without being cruel. That is character, not culture. One of them remembered a thing I had mentioned once, years earlier. Another stayed calm when I was incoherent with anger. Another could disagree with me and still let me be the kind of person who was wrong. Those are not signals I missed because of social training. They are facts about how they treated me. If the pattern is real, it may be that I need a little evidence of endurance before I can attach, and the people who provide it are often the ones I first found unapproachable.

There is also the possibility that the pattern depends on where I was when I met them. Several of these friendships began when I was tired, new, or not at my most likable. When I am functioning well, I can afford to be selective in a social way. When I am not, I notice different things. A person who seems stern during a period of my instability may later become a refuge, not despite the sternness but because of it. They did not add to the noise. That may explain why the misjudged people cluster in certain years of my life.

I don’t know the answer, and I don’t trust the explanations enough to close the case. I don’t know if I would see the same pattern if I listed the people I merely like, or the people I have outgrown, or the people who think they are close to me and I am not sure about. I don’t know if the answer would change how I behave at parties, or whether it would just give me a nicer way to explain why I am often wrong about people at first.

What I do know is that the question matters. If it is coincidence, I should stop looking for types and let friendships happen without a thesis. If it is culture, I should slow down before deciding that a serious person is cold, a blunt person is hostile, or a quiet person is uninterested. If it is just my own slow, stubborn way of attaching, then I should be less proud of my late recognitions and more careful with the people I brush off in the meantime.

For now I am leaving it open. The names that matter most to me were not the names I would have chosen at the beginning. I don’t know whether that is a gift, a bias, or a story I am telling myself to make the accidents look like taste. I only know that I am still trying to figure out which one it is.
rejected:
There is a list in my head. It is not a list of people I like, though I like them. It is a list of people who survived the culling.

The first friend I had in college was a guy who played the cello and wrote poetry about dirt. We bonded over the specific, crushing boredom of a Tuesday afternoon. The second was a woman who worked in a slaughterhouse and read Dostoevsky. We bonded over the smell of copper and the absurdity of suffering.

If you look at the common denominators, you might say I like interesting people. That is true, but it is not the whole truth. "Interesting" is a vague word that lets the brain off the hook. I want to know why these specific people, with these specific textures of life, kept showing up at the periphery of mine until we collided.

Is it choice? I tell myself it is. I am drawn to eccentricity. I avoid the smooth, the polished, the people who have optimized their lives into a frictionless surface. I seek out the rough edges. This is a defensible narrative. It makes me seem like a curator rather than a magnet.

But I am not sure I have that much control.

Consider the cultural argument. I grew up in a family that treated intelligence as a source of anxiety, not pride. We were not stupid, but we were not smart enough to be safe. We were always watching the weather. This creates a specific kind of hunger in a person: a hunger for people who are also watching the weather. I don’t want to be with someone who thinks the sun is always shining. I want to be with someone who knows how to pack an umbrella.

This is not a metaphor. I actually like people who are slightly paranoid. I like people who double-check the locks. I like people who have a plan for the plan. My closest friends are all people who have survived something they didn’t talk about. They don’t tell me what it was. They don’t need to. The fact that they are here, and they are alert, is enough.

This sounds like a pattern of trauma bonding. Maybe it is. Maybe I am just lonely in a specific way that only other lonely people can hear. If I am looking for a mirror, and I only find mirrors, is that a preference or a defect?

I don’t know.

I have tried to befriend people who are happy. Uncomplicated, sunny, people who think the sun is always shining. I like them. I can be with them. But they do not stick. They float away because there is no gravity between us. They do not need me to help them hold the world up. I do not need them to help me hold it up. We are just two objects drifting past each other in a void.

My closest friends are heavy. They pull on me. They have opinions about things that do not matter, and they are wrong about them, and they will not let it go. I hate it sometimes. I love it more.

The puzzle is this: I cannot tell if I am building a tribe of survivors, or if I am a survivor building a tribe. The difference matters. If I am building it, I have a choice. I can put down the hammer. I can go find someone who is not looking for a bunker.

If I am a survivor, then the pattern is just the shape of the hole I left in the world. People fit in. That’s all.

I don’t know which one I am. I know only that the people who stayed are the ones who made the staying feel like work. And I have never once wanted to stop working.

prompt: Why don't engineering and CS programs teach debugging as an actual skill? Write an essay about it, drawing on your own experience as a student and as a TA.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I cannot honestly write this from my own experience as a student or TA, because I do not have that experience. I can address the question by describing the patterns those roles tend to expose. I am not claiming to know the private reasons behind every syllabus; I am inferring from the structure of courses, assessments, and office hours.

Debugging is not one skill. It is a family of skills that appears whenever a person’s model of a system and the system’s actual behavior disagree. The statement “it doesn’t work” can mean the code does not compile, the program crashes, the output is wrong for one input, the program is too slow, the library changed, or the student has misunderstood the assignment. Each of those has a different first move. A program that teaches debugging as if it were a single topic usually ends up teaching either tool buttons or generic advice.

The student experience makes the gap clear. In an introductory course, a student may be able to write a loop on an exam and explain why it terminates. Then the same student runs the program, sees a sequence that is almost right, and freezes. The missing ability is not syntax. It is the ability to ask, “What should this variable be at this point, and what evidence would tell me whether my answer is right?” Without that, debugging becomes random mutation: add a print here, remove a line there, restart, hope.

The TA experience sharpens the point. In office hours, the most valuable question is often not “Have you tried a debugger?” but “What is the smallest input that fails?” A student may have spent an hour adding prints throughout a program. The prints are not useless, but they are scattered. The student has not yet learned to turn a large, confusing failure into a small, testable one. A TA with limited time may end up fixing the immediate bug, because that is faster. The course has thereby rewarded output over process.

Programs do not teach debugging as an actual skill partly because it does not sit neatly inside a course. Algorithms has a stable body of problems. Data structures has a stable set of tradeoffs. Operating systems has page tables, schedulers, and file systems. Debugging’s object is the gap between expectation and behavior, and that gap depends on the language, the compiler, the OS, the network, the hardware, and the student’s prior assumptions. There is no universal week-six lecture that covers all of it.

Assessment makes the problem worse. Many assignments are graded by whether the submitted program works. That is easy, but it teaches the wrong lesson. If the grade depends only on the final artifact, the student learns to make artifacts match examples. If the grade depends on a reproduction case, a hypothesis, a log, and a root-cause explanation, the student learns to investigate. The second is harder to grade, easier to game, and less comfortable for everyone involved.

Faculty incentives point the same way. A professor is usually responsible for a domain, not for the cross-cutting habit of finding errors. A compiler instructor can teach how to debug generated code. A web instructor can teach how to read the browser console. An embedded instructor can teach how to use a logic analyzer. Each is valuable, but none is the whole skill. If no course owns debugging, it becomes a set of incidental skills picked up, unevenly, by students who happen to get stuck in the right places.

Students also bring a theory of error that courses rarely challenge. In many educational settings, an error is a sign of failure. In debugging, an error is data. The student who hides the broken code, or who changes three things at once and cannot say what the change was supposed to test, is not merely careless. The student has not been trained to treat the machine as a witness and their own mental model as a hypothesis.

The hardest objection to teaching debugging directly is that it cannot be fully separated from the system being debugged. You cannot learn to debug a race condition by reading a list of debugging tips. You need to have written the code, seen the nondeterministic output, and learned what the logs can and cannot tell you. A course that debugs only toy examples may produce students who can say “bisect” but cannot decide what to bisect.

That objection is strong. It means a debugging course cannot replace domain expertise. But it does not mean nothing transferable can be taught. Engineers learn measurement, tolerance, calibration, and failure analysis before they can debug a particular turbine. Programmers can learn the equivalent moves: reproduce the failure, minimize the example, identify an invariant, instrument the boundary between what works and what fails, compare against a known-good case, and state the prediction before changing code. Those moves are boring enough to be general and useful enough to matter.

The concrete cases show why the skill has layers. In a C program, a crash may occur in a function that is innocent. The student who searches for the exact error message learns to patch symptoms. The student who rebuilds with a sanitizer learns that memory corruption can happen far from the place where it becomes visible. In a web application, a missing update may look like a logic bug but may really be an assumption about order: the code does not execute top to bottom; it executes when the event loop schedules it. A breakpoint is not a charm; it is a way to see the order. In an engineering simulation, a result that is “close” may be wrong because of units, floating-point tolerance, or an unstated boundary condition. The underlying move is still the same: find a quantity you can estimate by hand, compare it with the machine, and reduce the discrepancy.

Teaching debugging as an actual skill would not require a separate two-semester course. It would require making the invisible work visible inside existing courses. A problem set could ask for a debugging notebook: the initial symptom, the first hypothesis, the experiment, the result, the next hypothesis. A lab could include a planted bug and grade the path, not just the patch. An assignment could require a minimal reproduction, because the act of making the example small often forces the student to discover which variable matters. Code review could ask, “What did you expect, what did you see, and what did that difference tell you?” TAs could be trained to resist the impulse to fix the code before the student has formed a hypothesis.

That is why debugging often remains a rumor in engineering and CS programs. It is everywhere: in every failed test, every compiler warning, every stack trace, every “works on my machine.” But it is usually an ungraded byproduct of learning other things. It becomes an actual skill only when a program says, plainly, that the fix is not the point. The point is the evidence.
rejected:
The standard pedagogy for debugging in Computer Science and Engineering is a lie. We tell students that debugging is a matter of logic, that if they read the code carefully enough, the error will reveal itself like a ghost stepping into the light. We hand them a stack trace and expect them to see the mistake. We do not teach them how to hunt.

This failure stems from a confusion between understanding a system and operating on a broken one. A student who has just learned recursion understands how the call stack works. They can trace a recursive function on paper. But when the function segfaults at 3:00 AM, they do not know what to do. They stare at the code. They read it again. They change a variable name. They guess. This is not a lack of intelligence; it is a lack of tooling and a lack of a mental framework for observation.

Debugging is not reading. It is experimentation.

In physics, we do not ask a student to deduce the trajectory of a cannonball by reading Newton’s Second Law. We put them in front of a cannon. We give them a ruler. We let them measure. We teach them that the world is a black box that gives you feedback, and your job is to design a probe that extracts that feedback.

In CS, we strip away the feedback. We hide the runtime behavior behind the syntax. We treat the compiler error as the final word. But the most dangerous bugs are the ones that compile. They are the ones where the program runs, produces a number, and is wrong. For these, there is no error message. There is only silence.

I saw this as a Teaching Assistant. A student would come to office hours with a program that printed the wrong answer. They would show me the code. It was clean. It was idiomatic. It was exactly what I would have written. And it was wrong.

My first instinct was to read the code with them. We would point to a line. "Is this right?" "Yes." "Is this right?" "Yes." We would cycle through the logic until we were both exhausted and no closer to the truth. I was acting like a search engine. I was checking their work against my own.

The second instinct, the one I learned to force myself to use, was to stop reading. I would ask them to print the variables. Not all of them. Just the one they thought was the input. Then the one that was the output. Then the one in between.

We were no longer reading the code. We were measuring it.

This shift is the entire skill. The student’s mind is stuck in the *intended* state of the program. They are looking at the code and seeing the algorithm. They are not seeing the data. The data has mutated somewhere between the input and the output, and the code does not care. The code is just a set of instructions for moving bits. The bits have gone astray.

To find where, you must insert instrumentation. You must make the invisible visible.

We do not teach this because it feels like cheating. It feels like brute force. In a field that prizes elegance, printing `variable` to the console feels inelegant. It is messy. It clutters the code. But debugging is not about writing clean code. It is about finding the crack in the glass. You do not find the crack by looking at the glass. You find it by shining a light through it and seeing where the refraction bends.

There is also a cultural component. We train students to be builders. We give them a spec, and we ask for a product. We grade on the final output. If the program works, the grade is high. We do not grade the process. We do not ask, "How did you know to change that line?" We assume that if they got it right, they knew why.

This creates a generation of engineers who can build things that work in the happy path, but who freeze when the system behaves unexpectedly. They have been trained to trust their first reading. They have not been trained to distrust their own model of the system.

The model is always wrong. That is the point. The system is a complex, interacting mess of memory, timing, and state. Your mental model is a simplification. The bug is the difference between the two. You cannot find the difference by staring at the simplification. You must go out to the system and take a sample.

This is not a soft skill. It is not "critical thinking." It is a mechanical procedure.

1.  Reproduce the error. If you cannot make it happen on demand, you cannot fix it.
2.  Isolate the variable. Change one thing. If the error persists, that thing is not the cause. If the error disappears, that thing is in the causal chain.
3.  Instrument. Print the state. Log the time. Check the memory address.
4.  Compare. What does the code say should happen? What did the log say actually happened?
5.  Repeat.

We skip steps 3 and 4. We jump from 1 to 5. We try to fix the code without knowing what the code is doing.

As a student, I spent hours staring at a C pointer error. I knew pointers. I had read the chapter. I had solved the problems. But I was looking at the syntax, not the memory layout. I didn't know that I was reading from a stack address that had already been popped. I didn't know that until I printed the address and compared it to the stack frame size. I didn't know how to print the address. I didn't know how to compare it. I just knew it was wrong.

As a TA, I stopped trying to explain pointers to the student who was stuck. I asked them to print the address. They did. They looked at it. They printed the address of the next element. They saw they were off by four bytes. They found the bug in ten seconds.

The knowledge they lacked was not about pointers. It was about how to look.

We need to teach students that the computer is not a mind. It does not have intent. It does not have a "mistake." It has a state. Your job is to measure that state. The code is just the map; the runtime is the terrain. The map might be wrong. The terrain is always right.

If you want to learn to debug, stop reading your code. Start printing it.

prompt: Write a short essay arguing something counterintuitive about which startups are easier to get off the ground.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Startups are easier to get off the ground when they start as services. The conventional advice says build a scalable product, automate early, avoid being an agency. But those rules are about growth, not launch. The first problem is not whether the machine works; it is whether anyone has a painful enough problem that they will pay a stranger to fix it. A founder who can fix it by hand can ask that question immediately.

Suppose a founder wants to build software that reconciles expense reports for small construction companies. The product version takes months: login, bank feeds, rules, invoices, support. The service version takes a week: a spreadsheet, a weekly call, and a promise to send a clean report by Friday. If four companies pay $300 a month, the founder has $1,200 a month, a list of edge cases, and a sense of what the software should do. If no one pays, the founder has not wasted months building a product for a problem that may not exist. The service is not a placeholder; it is the experiment.

This is counterintuitive because a service feels like a failure to build. But the early customer is not buying technology. They are buying an outcome: invoices paid, leads answered, reports delivered. If the founder can deliver that outcome with a human, the core value proposition is testable. Zappos did a version of this when it began by photographing shoes in stores and shipping them after orders came in. Amazon started as an online bookstore, not a universal marketplace. The common move is not clever; it is to take the smallest real transaction and make it happen.

The strongest objection is that a service teaches you the wrong lesson. If your first customers stay because a founder answers their emails, fixes their data, and bends the rules, you may have built a custom agency, not a product. That can happen. The test is whether the service reveals repeated, describable steps. If every client needs a different workflow, you have found a business, not a startup. If the same three tasks keep eating the founder’s time, those tasks are the product. The service should hurt in a specific way: not “customers need love,” but “we keep doing the same invoice exception forty times a month.” That pain is a feature spec.

There are limits. A network is not a service; a marketplace with one side is not a market. A database, a compiler, a mobile game, a consumer social app, or a medical device may need the actual artifact before value exists. You cannot manually “be” a network effect or a microsecond latency. For those, the service argument fails. But many startups are not those things. They are workflows: sales, accounting, compliance, hiring, scheduling, fulfillment. In workflows, the easiest way to get off the ground is to become the person who does the work, charge for it, and automate only the part that is too expensive or too slow to keep doing by hand.

The uncomfortable conclusion is that many founders delay their first customer because they are trying to look like a company. A company can be a person with a bank account and a repeatable task. That is less impressive in a pitch deck, but it is much harder to mistake for a dream.
rejected:
The prevailing advice for new founders is to build the thing that solves the most painful, expensive, or complex problem. The logic is sound: large pain implies a large market, and a large market attracts capital. But this heuristic ignores the primary friction in the early stages of a startup: distribution.

Getting the first customer is not a problem of product quality; it is a problem of trust and attention. In a B2B enterprise context, the sales cycle is a gauntlet of procurement committees, security reviews, and budget cycles. You cannot hack your way into a Fortune 500 account with a Slack DM. You need a logo, a case study, and a sales team that has been doing this for years. This creates a paradox where the "biggest" opportunities are actually the hardest to launch because the barrier to entry is institutional weight, which new companies do not have.

Conversely, consumer businesses or simple B2C tools often face a lower barrier to entry because the decision-making unit is a single person. A user does not need to hold a meeting to decide if they want to use a new app. They need only a reason to care in the next ten seconds. This allows for speed. Speed is the only asset a startup has at the beginning. If you can iterate, fail, and pivot in a week, you can find a wedge. If you are stuck in a six-month enterprise sales cycle, you are frozen while the market moves.

This does not mean consumer products are easier to sustain. They have high churn, low margins, and brutal competition. But getting *off the ground*—finding product-market fit, validating the value proposition, and generating initial revenue—is fundamentally a game of velocity. B2C allows you to run the race. B2B forces you to walk it.

The counterintuitive truth is that the "small" problem is often the strategic entry point. Startups should look for problems where the buyer is the user, and the user is the payer. It is the only place where a two-person team can move faster than an incumbent with a thousand employees. Once you have a foothold, you can expand. But you cannot expand from zero.

prompt: It's early 2010, publishers are fighting Amazon over e-book pricing and delaying Kindle editions to protect hardcover sales. As a voracious reader who now buys almost everything on a Kindle, write a funny, pointed set of open letters to the parties involved.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**Open Letters from a Kindle**

**To the Publishers**

Dear Publishers,

I used to be the customer you wrote your quarterly reports about. I bought the hardcover, waited six months for the paperback, and once, in a fit of enthusiasm, bought the boxed set. Now I own a black slab thinner than one of your 800-page novels, and it holds more of them than my living room does.

You have decided that my next favorite book is not yet available because the hardcover still needs to be honored. I am not going to stand at the shelf. I am not going to buy a $25 object and leave it in a bag by the door. I am going to read the book that is available. If that means an older title, a foreign edition, or a file that technically should not be here, that is your choice.

You say you are protecting the book. You are protecting the margin. The book is not the binding. The book is the sentence that wakes me up at 4 a.m. If you make it harder to get that sentence to me, you have not saved the book. You have made me a pirate with a library card and a grudge.

**To Amazon**

Dear Amazon,

I do not love you. I love the thing you do: I want a book and it is there. I have become a one-book-a-night person, and some of those nights are 2 a.m. in a hospital waiting room, or the ten minutes before a train, or the moment after a bad argument when I need a stranger’s life more than my spouse’s opinion.

You are fighting the publishers over pricing and terms, and I understand. But if you win by making ebooks cost $12.99 and arrive late, you have won the war and lost the customer. I am not a loyalist. I am a reader with a glowing rectangle. If you make reading feel like a transaction instead of a reflex, I will find another transaction.

Also: stop selling me a device that turns my hand into a bookshelf and then acting surprised when I want the books in it.

**To the Authors**

Dear Authors,

I am reading you more than I ever did. I read you in the queue, in the bath, in the space between “I’ll be right there” and “where are you?” You have become less like objects I acquire and more like voices I keep on tap.

But I am also annoyed with you, because you are letting your publisher decide when I can have your latest sentence. You talk about the value of your work. The value of your work is that it reaches a person. If your agent signs a deal that says the Kindle edition comes out after the hardcover has had its moment, you have put a toll booth on the road to your own readers.

I will still read you. I am a voracious reader; that is my problem. But I will remember who stood between us.

**To the Hardcover**

Dear Hardcover,

You are handsome. You smell like a factory that is trying to smell like a forest. You rattle when you are new. You have weight, and therefore, you think, you have authority.

I do not hate you. I just cannot carry you to the dentist, and I do not have a wall for you. You were the book. Now you are the book’s packaging. If that offends you, consider that I still buy you when a book is worth keeping on a shelf and staring at. But when the publisher tells me I cannot have the Kindle edition until you have been honored, I have to say: I honored you by not buying you.

Rest easy. You are not dead. You are just no longer the default.
rejected:
**To the Big Five Publishers, Who Are Currently Holding My Books Hostage**

I have been reading since I was six years old. I have dog-eared pages until they fell out. I have carried three books in a bag to the beach and gotten sunburned because I was too busy finishing *The God of Small Things* to look at my own skin. I am, by every metric you use to segment your customer base, your ideal consumer.

And yet, you are delaying my books.

You have decided that because I now read on a glowing rectangle in my hand, my brain has been lobotomized and I am no longer capable of appreciating the *object* of the book. You believe that if I can buy a novel for $10 instead of $25, I will feel no attachment to it. You believe that the ritual of walking to the library, or the weight of a hardcover, is the only thing standing between me and indifference.

I can tell you that is not true.

I read more now than I have in my life. I read at 2 a.m. I read in the shower (waterproof case, obviously). I read on the toilet with a precision that would make a surgeon weep. The barrier to entry was never the price. The barrier to entry was the effort of finding the book, driving to the store, waiting in line, and hoping it wasn’t out of stock. You removed that friction, and I did not stop caring. I started caring about more books.

You are trying to protect the hardcover margin. Fine. I will buy the hardcover when I am in a bookstore and feel nostalgic for the smell of glue. But do not make me wait six months to read a book that is already written, already printed, and sitting in a warehouse in New Jersey. You are not protecting the sanctity of literature. You are protecting your Q3 earnings report.

Stop treating my patience as a resource you can mine.

***

**To Amazon, Who Are Trying to Buy My Soul for $9.99**

I love you. I am in love with you. I have never in my life had a more efficient romantic partner. You know what I want before I do. You deliver it overnight. You make me feel smart for having chosen the right book.

But you are also a vulture, and you know it.

You are using the publishers’ price-fixing conspiracy as a shield to justify your own margin erosion. You are smiling your plastic, toothy smile while you squeeze the author’s royalty down to a sliver. You are telling the world, "Look how much we are sacrificing for the customer!" while you quietly decide that a $15 book is a luxury good and a $9.99 book is a commodity.

The publishers want to sell me the book for $25. You want to sell me the book for $9.99 so you can buy my data and my loyalty and my entire digital life.

We are both being played.

The publishers think you are the enemy because you lowered the price. They are wrong. You are the enemy because you lowered the price *too much* to kill the middleman who actually cares about the words. The author of the book I am about to buy is getting paid less than the barista who made my coffee. And you are framing this as a victory for the people.

Don’t.

If you want my loyalty, raise the author’s cut. If you want to fight the publishers, fight for the creators, not just the customers. The customer is just the cash cow. The creators are the herd.

***

**To the Authors, Who Are Quietly Suffering**

I am not writing this to you. I am writing this to the room where you are currently sitting, watching your royalty reports.

You are the only ones in this triangle who actually made something. The publishers packaged it. Amazon distributed it. I consumed it. You wrote it.

The publishers are using your work to defend a business model that is dying. Amazon is using your work to buy a monopoly. And you are in the middle, getting squeezed.

Do not let them tell you that e-books are the enemy. E-books are not the enemy. The enemy is the idea that a book’s value is tied to the cost of the paper it is printed on. A story is a pattern of thought. It has no weight. It has no binding. It exists in the mind.

If the industry wants to die, let it die. But do not let it kill the distribution of ideas.

I will buy your book. I will buy it from you, if I have to. I will buy it from Amazon. I will buy it from the publisher. I will buy it in any format. But I need it to be available. I need it to be cheap enough that I can buy it without checking my bank account. I need it to be available *now*.

Do not let them hold your words hostage to save their balance sheets. We are waiting. We are reading. We are ready.

prompt: Someone who had worked for years as an architect just spent nine months fully immersed in our startup accelerator. I asked her what surprised her most about the startup world. Write a short essay built around her answers, with your own commentary on each, and end with whatever her outsider's view says about startup culture compared to the rest of the world.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
She had spent her career drawing buildings that would take years to construct and decades to wear. A school, a clinic, a municipal garage that someone’s teenager would dent on a Tuesday afternoon long after the project had vanished from every portfolio. So when I asked her what had surprised her most about nine months inside our accelerator, I expected her to say something about speed. Startups are faster, after all. Code gets written, deleted, rewritten. Meetings happen the day after decisions. Nobody waits eighteen months for a structural review.

She gave me three answers, and none of them were about speed.

“The first thing,” she said, “is that everything is a prototype, and everyone is proud of it.”

In architecture, a prototype is not the thing. It is the scale model on the table, the cardboard test of a corner, the small experiment that proves whether a space will feel closed or open. The model is not what people live in. In the startup world, the prototype is what people use. A rough interface goes to real customers. A half-built feature gets a name and a launch date. A workflow with no error handling is called a minimum viable product, which is a polite way of saying: this may not work, but we need to know.

That struck her as strange because in her old world, roughness was usually a confession. A jagged detail on a drawing meant someone had not finished thinking. In startup culture, roughness can be a method. If the product is ugly but people still use it, that tells you something. If they do not, you saved yourself months of polishing a mistake. The discipline is not making the thing good immediately; it is making the thing testable quickly. That is a real advantage, but it has a cost. Users of buildings do not get to give feedback while the load-bearing wall is still a sketch. They just stand in the room and feel whether it works. Startups can afford to learn in public because their errors are usually cheap and reversible. A bad app update can be rolled back. A bad staircase cannot.

Her second answer was less romantic.

“The second thing is that nobody knows what they are doing, and they say it like a virtue.”

She had expected expertise, or at least the appearance of it. In architecture, there is a reason for the appearance: a hospital wing has codes, contractors, vendors, fire systems, budgets, and patients who will actually walk through the doors. If the drawings are vague, the confusion becomes physical. Someone installs the wrong door. A corridor is too narrow for a stretcher. The building ends up with a scar that will be there for fifty years.

Startups operate in a different economy of ignorance. A founder may not know whether customers will pay for the product, whether the sales cycle will be two weeks or two quarters, whether the technology will scale, whether the co-founder will still be talking to her in six months. That ignorance is not incompetence. It is the material condition of the work. The company exists partly to reduce it. But the confidence she saw in the room was not always matched to the knowledge. People would speak as if the market had already chosen them, when in fact the market had barely noticed them.

The best founders I have seen handle this better than the worst. They treat uncertainty as a number to be lowered, not a personality trait. They know which questions are cheap to answer and which are expensive. They will spend a weekend testing a pricing page before arguing about the brand. They will not do the reverse. The worst ones mistake the energy of the search for the certainty of the answer. They talk their way out of the work that would tell them whether they are right.

Her third answer was the one I thought about most.

“The third thing is that the deck is the building.”

She meant the pitch deck. In architecture, the construction documents are where intent becomes obligation. They are thick, boring, and precise. They tell the contractor what to build, the inspector what to check, the client what she is getting. If the documents are weak, the building will be weak even if the idea was beautiful.

A pitch deck does a similar job, except the material it coordinates is belief. It tells investors what the company is for. It tells potential hires what kind of problem they are joining. It tells customers, before they have even tried the product, what the company thinks it is. It forces the founders to choose a story when the reality is still a mess of tabs, half-built features, and conflicting opinions. That is useful. A team that cannot explain itself in ten slides usually cannot explain itself in ten months.

But a deck can also make a weak idea look structurally sound. It can hide the missing foundation behind a confident roofline. I have seen teams raise money on a narrative that the product could not support, and then spend the next year trying to build reality up to the deck. The danger is not that startups use stories. Everything uses stories. The danger is forgetting that a story is not a test. It can move people, but it cannot tell you whether the thing works.

When I asked her what all of that said about startup culture compared to the rest of the world, she paused for a long time.

She said it was a world that had separated the process of finding out from the thing found. Most institutions are organized around durability. A courthouse is not supposed to be pivoted. A medicine is not supposed to discover it has the wrong side effects after it has been prescribed for a decade. A bridge is not supposed to say, give us feedback. Those worlds hide uncertainty behind standards, licenses, procedures, and the slow accumulation of responsibility. Startup culture does the opposite. It puts uncertainty in the room and calls it strategy.

That is why it can feel so alive and so flimsy at the same time. It is more honest than most organizations about not knowing, but less honest than it should be about the consequences of being wrong. The rest of the world wants to be right. Startups want to be able to change. The healthiest version of startup culture is not the one that moves fastest, but the one that knows which of its guesses are cheap and which are not.
rejected:
The architect’s first surprise was the silence of the feedback loop. In her former profession, a building takes three years to rise. If the foundation is wrong, you don’t know until the second floor is already poured. You cannot un-bury the pipes. The cost of a mistake is amortized over decades. In the accelerator, the feedback loop was measured in hours. A feature shipped on Tuesday was dead by Thursday. She found this disorienting, not because the pace was fast, but because the permanence of failure was absent. In architecture, a flaw is a monument. In software, it is just a commit log.

My commentary here is that the architect missed the point of the iteration. The speed wasn’t the surprise; the irrelevance of the past was. She was used to carrying the weight of history. A startup carries no weight. The company is defined entirely by its current velocity. If you stop moving, you don’t just stagnate; you cease to exist. The architect was trying to build a structure. The startup was trying to stay alive.

Her second observation was about the hierarchy of expertise. She noted that the person with the most knowledge was rarely the person with the most authority. In her firm, the senior partner spoke last, but he spoke first in the room’s memory. His word settled the debate. In the accelerator, the engineer who could refactor the codebase in an afternoon held more sway than the founder with the MBA. The architect was unsettled by the lack of tenure. In architecture, you earn the right to be ignored. In the startup, you earn the right to be heard only while you are useful.

This is where the culture diverges from the rest of the world. Most professions are based on the accumulation of status. You learn, you wait, you lead. Startups are based on the accumulation of options. The engineer with the refactor has a higher option value than the founder with the pedigree. The architect’s discomfort came from trying to apply the logic of a cathedral to a campfire.

The final thing she said was that nobody was trying to build a legacy. They were trying to build a bridge. Not a monument to be looked at, but a structure to be crossed. Once you’re across, you leave it behind.

The outsider’s view is that startup culture is not a different kind of work. It is work stripped of the desire to be remembered. It is the purest form of functionalism, but it is also the most lonely. You can build a thing that saves millions of lives, and if it works, it becomes invisible. The architect missed that. She was looking for the plaque on the wall. There is no wall. There is only the next crossing.

prompt: I've noticed words like 'lie' and 'abuse' getting stretched to cover more and more. Write a post arguing about whether it matters when we broaden the meaning of a word like that.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**When “abuse” stops meaning something**

When a word starts covering everything, it often stops covering anything. I do not mean that in a dictionary sense. Dictionaries record use; they do not police it. I mean it in the sense that matters when people are trying to decide what to do. “Lie” and “abuse” are not decorative words. They are tools for judgment. They tell us that something has crossed a line, that trust has been broken, that a relationship has become dangerous, that a sanction may be appropriate. If we make those words apply to almost anything, we do not merely change definitions. We change the map we use to navigate other people’s lives.

The pressure to broaden them is real and often legitimate. For a long time, “abuse” could mean a broken arm, a burned hand, a visible mark. That was useful for proving a crime in court, but it was a poor name for a life in which a partner controls the money, isolates a person from friends, humiliates them in front of children, or makes ordinary decisions feel terrifying. If we had insisted on the old meaning, we would have left a large area of harm unspoken. The same is true of “lie.” A person can avoid saying the false sentence and still destroy confidence: answer a direct question with a technically true nonanswer, emphasize one fact to hide another, present a prediction as a certainty when it is not. If “lie” only covered flat, deliberate falsehood, it would miss a lot of deception.

But there is a difference between extending a word to cases it should have covered and inflating it until the center disappears. The difference shows up in gradation. A useful moral word usually has a neighborhood: milder forms, serious forms, extreme forms. “Lie” can be a small concealment, a cover-up, a sworn falsehood. “Abuse” can be harsh treatment, sustained domination, an attempt to make a person distrust their own experience. When we collapse those differences, we lose the ability to say what is worst.

Suppose a parent yells at a child after a bad day. That may be unkind, inconsistent, or even harmful. Suppose another parent makes a child believe that their own memory is false, that they are to blame for every crisis, and that leaving is impossible. The second case is worse, obviously. But if both are simply “abuse,” the word has told us less, not more. It has registered that something bad happened, but not that one relationship contains a mechanism of control. The same with lying: a researcher rounds a number carelessly; an executive knows a product causes injury and says it is safe. Calling both “lies” is not precision. It is a way of avoiding the harder questions of intent, power, and damage.

The hardest objection to this worry is obvious: moral progress often begins when someone refuses to accept the narrow meaning of a word. “That is not abuse, there are no bruises” has been a defense. “That is not a lie, it was an opinion” has been a defense. If we become too quick to police language, we can end up giving the powerful a technicality. The person who says “my boss abused me” because he publicly humiliated her and made the workplace unsafe is not being dramatic. The person who says “the company lied” because it knew what its emissions data meant and presented it in a misleading way is not being pedantic. In many cases, the broadened word is the first honest word available.

So the answer is not “use the old meaning.” The answer is that broadening has to be anchored. A good expansion names a real harm that was previously hard to see. It also keeps a standard that can be disputed. It asks: Was there a violation? Was there a power imbalance? Was there a pattern? Was there an attempt to control, deceive, or silence? If the answer is yes, the word may fit. If the answer is merely “I felt bad,” the word may be too heavy. Not because the feeling is invalid, but because “abuse” is not a word for feelings alone. It is a word for what someone did to you, or allowed to happen to you, in a way that corrupted a relationship or a duty.

I cannot prove that the average private conversation has changed as much as public argument does. What is visible online is a different problem: a transcript without tone, a screenshot without history, a single sentence without the relationship around it can look like evidence of abuse. The word becomes a verdict before the facts are in. That does not mean the person using it is wrong. It means the category is being used faster than understanding can catch up.

Institutions feel this quickly. If every boundary dispute is “abuse,” a manager cannot tell a difficult conversation from a campaign of intimidation. If every false statement is a “lie,” a newspaper cannot distinguish error from corruption. If every omission is a “lie,” a court cannot decide what counts as deception. The result is not that people stop feeling hurt. It is that the word stops helping us decide what to do.

A lie is not just a false statement. It is a false statement made with a betrayal of the expectation of truth. That expectation varies. A joke is not a lie because both parties know the game. A seller’s puffery is not exactly a lie, though it can become illegal when it crosses into material deception. A politician’s slogan may be false, misleading, or a lie depending on what the speaker knows and what he intends the audience to believe. If we flatten those distinctions, we make political language easier to dismiss. When everything is a lie, the discovery of a real one becomes less remarkable.

Abuse is often about a pattern, not an incident. A single cruel act can be terrible, but the word usually points to a climate: fear, obligation, guilt, isolation, repetition. That is why people sometimes say they did not recognize it as abuse until later. The word captures a shape. If we apply it to any unpleasant shape, we lose the shape that matters.

It matters because moral language is a budget. We have finite attention, finite anger, finite willingness to intervene. If we spend the strongest words on the weakest offenses, the strongest offenses get a weaker reception. That does not mean the weaker offenses are unimportant. It means we need a wider vocabulary: discourtesy, betrayal, manipulation, negligence, cruelty, domination, deception, error, malice. We need to say what kind of bad thing happened, not just that it was bad. Broaden “lie” and “abuse” when they have been too narrow. But do not let them become words for everything that goes wrong. A word that can be used for anything is a word that cannot be trusted to point to the worst.
rejected:
We are currently engaged in a quiet linguistic inflation that is far more dangerous than any hyperinflation of currency. Words like "lie," "abuse," and "violence" are expanding their territory until they cover almost everything. A slight exaggeration is now a lie. A disappointing boundary is now abuse. A disagreement that makes you feel unsafe is now violence.

This isn’t just a semantic nitpick. It is a crisis of information.

The value of a word is determined by its friction. A word is a tool for sorting the world into categories so we can act on them. If I say, "He is lying to you," I am telling you that he is deliberately constructing a falsehood to manipulate you. That triggers a specific response: distrust, investigation, potential termination of the relationship. If I say, "He is being abusive," I am telling you that he is using power to harm you, which triggers a different response: safety planning, legal action, physical removal.

When we stretch these words to cover low-intensity behaviors, we lose the ability to distinguish between a jerk and a predator.

Consider the word "lie." Historically, a lie required intent. If you guessed the weather wrong, you didn’t lie. If you estimated your arrival time poorly, you didn’t lie. But in the current digital discourse, any statement that is later proven technically inaccurate is often branded a lie. This conflates error with malice. When we label every error as a lie, we stop investigating *why* someone is wrong. Are they lazy? Misinformed? Or are they actually committing fraud? The distinction matters for the remedy. You educate the lazy; you prosecute the fraudster.

"Abuse" is even more problematic because it has migrated from the physical and sexual into the emotional and professional. In the past, "abuse" implied a power imbalance and a pattern of control. Now, it is often used to describe any instance of rudeness or disagreement. If your manager criticizes your work, you are not being abused; you are being evaluated. If a friend cancels plans, they are not abusing you; they are flaking.

The danger here is twofold.

First, it desensitizes us to actual abuse. If every minor social friction is labeled abuse, the word loses its weight. A victim of domestic violence is speaking the same language as someone who is annoyed by a rude comment. The listener, overwhelmed by the volume of "abuse" reports, may treat the severe case with the same casual dismissal as the mild one. We drown the signal in the noise.

Second, it removes agency from the speaker. To call something "abuse" is to declare that you are powerless against it. It frames you as a victim of a force rather than a participant in a conflict. If a colleague is difficult, calling it "abuse" absolves you of the work of managing that relationship. You cannot "manage" abuse; you can only escape it. But you can manage a difficult colleague. By broadening the term, we create a culture where people expect the world to be removed from their path rather than learning how to navigate it.

This inflation is not accidental. It is strategic. Broadening the definition of harmful acts allows people to assign maximal moral condemnation to minimal infractions. It is a way to win arguments without evidence. "You are lying" is a stronger accusation than "you are mistaken." "You are abusing me" is a stronger accusation than "you are being inconsiderate."

We are losing the language we need to describe the world accurately. We have a shortage of words for the middle ground: the rude, the careless, the selfish, the incompetent. We are forced to use the language of war crimes to describe a bad Tuesday.

If we keep stretching these words, they will eventually mean nothing. And when "lie" means "disagreement" and "abuse" means "disappointment," we will have no words left to describe the things that actually threaten us.

prompt: Everyone says you can't travel once you have a baby. I think that's wrong. Write a persuasive blog post for new parents.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
## You Can Travel With a Baby. You Just Can’t Do the Old Trip.

The warning usually arrives in the first year, offered with a smile. “You won’t get to travel once you have a baby.” It sounds like a fact, but it is not. It is a comparison to the wrong kind of travel.

Before the baby, travel could mean a last-minute flight, a hotel you checked into at midnight, a museum that swallowed the afternoon, a meal that started late and ended later, a day when nobody had to be fed at exactly the right time or put down in a safe sleep space. That trip may be impossible now. But a two-night stay at your sister’s, a drive to a town you have never seen, a flight home to your parents when the house has started to feel like a room: those are still travel. They are just travel with a small person in the center of the plan.

The myth works because it protects a version of travel that belonged to your former schedule. It says the old life is gone, not that a new one is available.

Think about what travel actually does. It changes the air you breathe, the sounds you hear, the distance between your bed and the nearest familiar face. It interrupts the loop. With a baby, the loop is powerful: kitchen floor, stroller route, nap, feed, repeat. A trip does not have to include a famous landmark in order to break that loop. It only has to put your body somewhere else for long enough to remember that the world is wider than the hallway.

A concrete example helps. A family with an eight-month-old drives four hours to grandparents’ house. They leave at seven, baby naps in the car seat, one parent drives, the other watches the rearview mirror and pretends the gas station sandwich is a meal. They arrive at eleven. Baby naps in the crib while the parents shower, sleep for two hours, and walk outside without a destination. On Sunday they leave after lunch. There is no gallery, no wine bar, no spontaneous detour to a village. There is still the fact that they left, crossed some distance, slept in another bed, and came back with the edges of the week softened. That counts.

The strongest objection is not romantic. It is practical. Babies get sick. Ears hurt on planes. Unfamiliar water, sand, bugs, and germs are real. When you are running on four hours of sleep, a minor problem can become a major one because you have less patience, less bandwidth, and less trust in your own judgment. That is true. The answer is not to stay home forever. The answer is to match the trip to the baby’s age, your actual reserves, and the level of medical support around you.

For most healthy full-term babies, a few hours in a car or a short domestic flight is usually manageable. But “usually” is doing important work. If the baby was premature, has breathing or feeding problems, is very young, or the trip is long, remote, or to a place with limited pediatric care, the calculus changes. Ask the pediatrician when there is a medical question. Do not treat a well-meaning relative as the authority on infant safety.

The point is not that every trip is equally wise. It is that “you can’t travel” is too broad. A weekend in the next state is not the same category as a three-country tour. A flight to see family is not the same category as a beach week in a town where the nearest hospital is an hour away and the tap water is not something you want an infant near. Travel with a baby becomes a risk-management problem, not a moral test.

There is also the packing. The old travel skill was spontaneity. The new one is redundancy. A weekend away requires diapers, wipes, formula or pumping supplies, a stroller, a car seat or travel crib, changes of clothes for every hour the baby is awake, a bag for leaks, a bag for sleep, and a plan for what you will do when the baby is awake and the parents are not. If your suitcase looks like a medical kit, that is not proof that travel is absurd. It is proof that you are carrying a small person’s survival.

You will also miss things. You will feed in an airport bathroom. You will leave a hotel room at six because the baby is awake and the parents’ plan is dead. You will stand in a restaurant while the baby bounces in a seat, eating pureed peas with the focus of a soldier. You will come home from a beautiful place and feel only tired. None of that means the trip failed. It means the terms changed.

The baby, for their part, is not thinking about the itinerary. They are thinking about rhythm: hunger, sleep, temperature, whether the person holding them is calm enough to regulate them. A baby can adapt to a new room, a new smell, a new stretch of road, as long as the caregivers can keep the basic needs met. In that sense, the fragile part of the trip is often not the infant but the adults. A well-rested parent in a strange town is usually better company for a baby than an exhausted one at home.

This is also not a claim that every family can or should travel often. Money, work, caregiving support, disability, mental health, and the sheer cost of infant supplies all matter. If travel is not possible right now, that is a constraint, not a character flaw. The problem with the saying “you can’t travel once you have a baby” is that it turns a temporary limitation into a permanent identity. It tells new parents that their lives have narrowed when, more often, the shape of the life has just changed.

Start small. A day trip that returns before bedtime. A night at a relative’s. A short drive to a park you have never visited. A flight when the baby is older and you have help at home. Keep the radius small until it grows. The goal is not to prove that baby can handle Paris. The goal is to keep the world from shrinking to the size of your sleep schedule.

The old trip is gone. Grieve that if you need to. But do not let the memory of it stand in the doorway while you stand there with a diaper bag, waiting for permission that was never really the issue. Get in the car. Choose a place close enough that you can handle a bad night. Go.
rejected:
The first few months are a war. You are sleep-deprived, your body is a wreck, and your primary function is keeping a small human alive. If you try to book a flight to Kyoto during this phase, you will fail. You will be miserable, the baby will be miserable, and you will believe the naysayers are right.

But the naysayers are describing the first six months. They are not describing the next eighteen years.

The advice to "wait until the kids are older" is a trap. It implies that parenting is a linear progression toward a destination where you can finally relax and explore. It suggests that the baby phase is a temporary infection that will clear up, leaving you with a clean slate and free time. That is not how it works. The kids will be teenagers who hate you. They will be adults who have their own lives. There is no golden era of "easy travel" waiting for you. The only window where a child is small enough to be carried and old enough to be interested in the world is right now.

Traveling with an infant is not a luxury. It is a logistical puzzle that changes your brain.

When you are at home, your world is the house. The kitchen is the center of the universe. When you travel, your world expands to the city, the airport, the train station. Your baby sees this. They hear different languages. They feel different vibrations. They learn that the world is bigger than the nursery.

The practical arguments against traveling with a baby are real, but they are manageable.

*   **The stroller:** You need one that folds with one hand. If you are in a crowded train station in Tokyo or a narrow street in Rome, you will not have two free hands. Buy the good one. It is an investment in your sanity.
*   **The diapers:** You need a wet bag. You need a change table, or a place to set things down. You need to pack more than you think.
*   **The schedule:** You cannot control the baby’s sleep. You must abandon the itinerary. If the baby naps, you stay. If the baby wakes, you move. The rigid plan is the enemy. Flexibility is the strategy.

The biggest lie is that you are doing it for the baby. You are not. Infants do not care about the Colosseum. They care about the texture of the brick and the sound of the pigeons. They are traveling because they are alive.

You are doing it for yourself.

You are doing it to prove to yourself that you are still a person with a body, a mind, and a desire to see new things. You are doing it to break the monotony of the domestic loop. When you step off a plane in a new country, you are not just a parent. You are a traveler. That identity does not disappear when you hold a baby. It just gets louder.

There will be days where you are exhausted, the baby is crying, and you are standing in a foreign airport with a broken stroller wheel. You will want to go home. You will want to quit.

Do not.

The memory of that moment will fade. The memory of the light hitting the water in a city you never thought you’d see will stay.

The people who say you can’t travel are protecting their own comfort. They are saying, "It is easier if you stay home." They are right. It is easier.

But easy is not the point. The point is to build a life that includes the world. Start now, while the baby is small enough to fit in your pocket, and while you are still young enough to carry the bag.

prompt: Why do so many people (and writers, and artists) start out wild and interesting and then slowly become repetitive and safe? Write a blog post on staying creative over decades, and what it costs.

No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
## After the Wild Years

The first novel is often the strangest. The author has no backlist, no brand, no audience large enough to be disappointed. The publisher takes a chance because the manuscript is cheap and one sequence is strong. The book is uneven, maybe too long, maybe too private. It has edges. Then the second book comes out and is better made, and therefore less surprising. The third is a sequel in everything but title. By the fifth, the writer has a voice, a subject, a face on the cover, and a set of expectations that begins to function like a contract.

This pattern shows up in music, painting, design, film, food, almost anywhere people make things in public. The early work is wild because it has not yet been priced. No one knows what kind of artist you are, so you can try several kinds before the market pins one to your name. Your mistakes are invisible. Your audience is small. Your income is low enough that you cannot afford to think about the next customer. You make the thing that is in front of you.

Then something works. A record sells, a show gets reviewed, a book gets optioned, a style gets imitated. If the first record sold five thousand copies, a strange second album is a manageable gamble. If it sold five hundred thousand, the label will ask for the chorus that worked. If the gallery sold small paintings to a roomful of collectors, a sculpture may be too large for the next conversation. The work that found you now has to keep finding you. The people who bought it expect a related thing. The people who sold it want a related thing. The people who talk about you have built a sentence in which you are a noun: the noir novelist, the lo-fi guitarist, the painter of domestic interiors, the chef who cooks only with fire. To be anything else is to ask them to revise the sentence, and people do not like to revise sentences.

The artist internalizes this. At first the pressure is external: the label wants a second album, the gallery wants more of the same series, the editor asks for the book that will make the first one make sense. Later the pressure becomes a habit of thought. You know what you can do. You know what looks like you. You know which risks are interesting and which are merely expensive. The method that got you through the hard years starts to feel like taste. You make the recognizable thing because it is efficient, because it is good, because it is what you love, or because if you stop making it you will have to find out who you are without the help of your own reputation.

That last motive is the one that matters. Repetition is not always safety. Sometimes it is mastery. A musician who plays the same changes for thirty years may know them better than anyone alive. A painter who returns to the same landscape may see in it what a tourist could not. A writer who keeps returning to a family, a place, or a moral question may be doing slow work that novelty would ruin. The mistake is to treat “new” as the only sign of life. Maturity often looks like narrowing. The hard thing is not to repeat; the hard thing is to know whether the repetition is coming from your present perception or from your past success.

This is why the early-wild/late-safe story is too simple. Much early wildness is just untrained energy. The artist is imitating people they have not yet fully absorbed. The form is loose because the hand is weak. The book is strange because the author does not yet know how to make a door open. Later, the doors open. The sentences are cleaner. The composition is more confident. What critics call safety may be control. Some artists become more interesting later, not despite their discipline but because of it, because they can now break a rule knowingly instead of accidentally.

So the question is not how to stay wild. It is how to stay in contact with what you are actually seeing. That is a smaller and more annoying goal. It does not require a breakthrough every five years. It does require that you not turn your own history into a filter so strong that everything new has to pass through it. It requires that you notice when you are making a work for the person who praised your last one, or for the person you were at twenty-five, rather than for the thing in front of you.

Staying creative over decades is mostly a system, not a mood. It means making work on days when the market has already told you what you should be. It means keeping a practice that is not dependent on being discovered: the sketchbook, the practice room, the garden, the workshop, the notebook, the long walk, the bad drafts. It means using constraints to force movement: write only in letters, paint with one color, compose for an instrument you cannot play, make a film in one take, cook only with what is in the drawer. Constraints are not the opposite of freedom; they are the only way to keep choosing when taste has become a reflex.

It also means making work that will not sell, or will not fit, or will not be understood by the people who understand you. Every serious career needs a second line: the piece that is too small, too personal, too ugly, too difficult, too quiet. It may never be shown. It may be the thing that keeps the public work from becoming a product. Without it, the artist becomes a supplier. With it, the artist remains a person who happens to make things.

The cost is not romantic. It is not a noble struggle with the muse. It is a series of losses you agree to keep taking.

You lose the ease of being known. If you are known for one thing, changing means asking your audience to meet you again as a stranger. They may not come. The people who liked the first album often do not want the sixth. The critics who built your reputation may treat your new work as a betrayal, because it disrupts the file they have on you. You will have to start over with people who have not yet decided what you are.

You lose income, or the possibility of income. The safe work is safe partly because it is priced. The strange work has no price until someone is willing to take a chance on it, and chances get harder to get as you get older. If you are lucky, you have enough saved, or enough loyal, or enough outside money to survive a fallow period. If you are not, the bills will teach you a very conservative style.

You lose a story about yourself. The breakthrough narrative is comforting. It says you were found, you arrived, you are this kind of person. To keep making work that changes is to refuse that story. You have to live without a clean arc. You have to accept that your best-known work may be the least interesting thing you will ever make, and that your most important work may be a draft no one sees.

You lose the right to be only good at one thing. If you want to remain perceptually alive, you will have to be bad at new things. You will have to take the class, learn the software, study the period, read the science, talk to people whose work you do not like, sit in rooms where you are the least skilled person present. This is humiliating in a way that early ambition never was, because early you could blame ignorance. Later you have a record.

You lose certainty. The safe path gives you a prediction: make the thing, get the review, sell the ticket, repeat. The other path gives you only feedback. A show may be empty. A manuscript may be rejected for being “confusing.” A project may take three years and produce one usable page. You have to be able to continue after that without turning the experience into proof that you should have stayed in your lane.

There is also a physical cost. Creativity over decades is not just an identity project; it is a body project. The body that could work all night and recover by noon will not do that at fifty. The eyes change. The memory changes. The tolerance for boredom and pain changes. Staying creative means adapting the work to the animal you still have, which often means making smaller, slower, more disciplined work. It means protecting sleep, attention, and relationships, because those are the infrastructure, not the enemies, of the life.

The hardest objection to all this is that the price may be too high. A coherent body of work can be more valuable than a series of shocks. An artist who stays with one idea can say something an artist who chases the next idea never can. A writer who returns to the same town, a musician who deepens a groove, a painter who refines a palette may achieve a kind of truth that requires patience, not novelty. If you insist on being new, you can become a person with no depth, only surface. The answer is not to glorify reinvention. The answer is to make the repetition chosen.

A chosen repetition is different from a trapped one. In a chosen repetition, the artist could stop, but does not, because the material still has rooms in it. In a trapped repetition, the artist cannot stop because stopping would mean admitting that the work was a job, a brand, a way to avoid the next unknown. One feels like digging. The other feels like polishing the same stone until your hands bleed.

There is no test that works in every case, but there is a useful question: Could the previous version of me have made this? If the answer is yes, and you made it anyway, you are probably manufacturing. If the answer is no, because you had to learn something, suffer something, notice something, or become less confident about your old methods, then the work may be alive. The later work does not have to be wild. It has to be earned by a present that the past did not predict.

That is what staying creative costs: the willingness to be paid by the thing itself, not by the continuity of your fame. It costs making the next true thing even if it is smaller than the last. It costs letting the audience that knew you go. It costs being a beginner in a body that has a résumé. It costs accepting that the wild years were not a permanent state but a period when the stakes were low enough to try.

Decades later, the interesting question is not whether you are still surprising people. It is whether you are still making the work that only the person you have become could make. If you are, you have paid. If you are not, you have been conserving a specimen.
rejected:
The first decade of a creative life is often a fever dream. You don’t know what you’re doing, so you try everything. You write in the dark, paint with your hands, or sing off-key because the fear of failure is outweighed by the terror of being boring. You are new. The world is new. Your constraints are low because you haven’t yet learned how to build the cages that protect you from judgment.

Then, you get good. And getting good is where the danger starts.

Proficiency is a sedative. When you know exactly how to write a three-act structure, or how to mix a vocal track so it sits perfectly in the pocket, or how to craft a punchline that lands every time, you stop experimenting. You start optimizing. You chase the high that worked last time. You become an engineer of your own success, and engineering requires blueprints. Blueprints require repetition.

The shift from "wild" to "safe" is rarely a moral failing. It is a survival mechanism. Creativity is high-risk. It invites rejection, confusion, and financial instability. Repetition is low-risk. It invites comfort, recognition, and revenue. The human brain is wired to conserve energy and avoid pain. Why would you risk the unknown when you have a reliable formula for the known?

Writers feel this most acutely in the middle of their careers. The debut novel was a mess of talent and terror. The second was a lesson in craft. The third through the tenth are often attempts to recapture the debut’s electricity using the second book’s structure.
