If the people who write the code begin to gather somewhere else, it is not because they have a taste for a particular color of laptop. It is because the environment fits their work. That is a small group by the millions, but it is a large group by the ideas.
rejected:
The machine on the desk isn’t a server. It’s a 15-inch PowerBook G5. The lid is aluminum, the screen is glossy, and the trackpad is glass. To the average enterprise IT director, this is a luxury item. To the people writing the code that runs the internet, it is a tool.

The migration to Apple in the mid-2000s wasn’t a fashion statement. It was a correction. For a decade, the professional workstation had been a tower under a desk, plugged into a monitor. It was silent, reliable, and utterly static. But the nature of software development had changed. The unit of work was no longer a single compiled binary. It was a distributed system. You needed to build locally, deploy remotely, and debug in flight.

The PowerBook offered a single, unified environment that was also a laptop. The Unix kernel was genuine, not a simulation. The hardware was robust enough to run 24/7 without fan noise. When the machine closed, it carried the entire development environment with it. This allowed a specific kind of hacker to exist: the one who could be at the desk, on a plane, or in a coffee shop, and the code would compile identically. The abstraction layer of "the computer" disappeared. There was just the work.

Ten years earlier, the Mac had meant something different. In 1984 and 1995, the Macintosh was the machine for people who thought in pictures. It was for the writer, the artist, and the administrator. It was not for the coder. The command line was an afterthought. The terminal was a beige box you had to dig out from under the GUI. If you wanted to write C, you bought a PC. The PC was the machine of logic; the Mac was the machine of intuition.

That division collapsed. As the web became the primary interface for computing, the line between "making things look good" and "making things work" blurred. The person designing the interface and the person writing the backend began to be the same person. The Mac’s history in typography and layout became an asset, not a liability. The GUI was no longer a barrier to the code; it was a canvas for it.

Why should a company care what a small group of users thinks? Because this group defines the architecture of the future.

Hacker culture is a leading indicator. When they adopt a platform, they are not voting on brand identity. They are signaling that the platform can handle the next wave of complexity. If the most rigorous engineers in the world choose a tool because it reduces friction, it means the tool’s internal consistency is high. It means the operating system, the hardware, and the development tools speak the same language.

A company that ignores this demographic is ignoring the people who are building the infrastructure for everyone else. They are building the cloud, the databases, and the protocols. If the toolset that builds these things is brittle, inconsistent, or isolated, the resulting software will be too. The Mac became the default not because it was pretty, but because it was the only machine that treated the developer’s workflow as a continuous, seamless process rather than a series of distinct, disconnected tasks. The industry followed the tooling. The enterprise followed the industry.

prompt: We're reading 'Out of the Tar Pit' in my reading group. The paper leans on Dijkstra's line that testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence, and argues informal reasoning matters more than testing. Write a short response essay: do you buy that, especially from the perspective of someone who has built genuinely complex systems?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I buy the warning, not the conclusion.

Dijkstra is right in a narrow sense: no test suite is a proof. If a program accepts arbitrary input, you cannot enumerate all inputs and run them. If a bug depends on a rare interleaving, a missing clock adjustment, a full disk, a partitioned network, or a user doing something nobody thought to specify, the test suite can miss it. A test also reflects the author’s model. If the author misunderstands the system, the test may faithfully verify the misunderstanding. I have seen high line coverage on a module that still corrupted data because every test exercised the same mental model: the happy path, dressed up in edge cases.

So if “testing shows absence” means “running these cases lets me claim the program is correct,” Dijkstra is correct. But that is not what testing does in a complex system. It does something weaker and more useful: it turns a design claim into an executable check, and it makes violations visible before customers do.

That distinction matters once systems stop being small enough to hold in one mind. The bugs that hurt in genuinely complex systems are rarely simple missing `if` statements. They are interaction bugs. A retry after a timeout collides with an idempotency key that was not stable across attempts. A cache invalidation races with a write. A queue consumer acknowledges a message before the downstream write is durable. A background job assumes a file is complete because the header exists. A metric looks healthy because the rare failure mode is sampled away. A migration script works in staging but fails in production because production has legacy rows staging does not.

Reasoning finds the shape of these problems, but testing and operational checks are what keep the shape from rotting. A design document that says “operations are idempotent” is a promise. A test that replays a duplicate request, plus a reconciliation job that compares ledger entries, is the promise with teeth. A document that says “the cache is eventually consistent” is not enough; you need tests for the update order, monitoring for the lag, and a story for what happens when the lag becomes unbounded.

Where I agree with the paper is that informal reasoning has to come first, because testing cannot tell you whether you modeled the world correctly. It can only tell you whether the model behaves as expected in the cases you chose. In a payments system, the hard question is not whether the code adds correctly. It is whether the money state can be represented as a finite automaton at all, where the boundaries are, what “done” means when the user, the bank, and the network all lie, and which failures are retryable. That question is informal. Get it wrong, and every test becomes a rehearsal of the wrong idea.

This is where the paper’s point has real force. If a module is too complex to reason about, testing does not rescue it. It may make the complexity worse. Integration tests become slow and flaky. Unit tests become so elaborate that they duplicate the system. You end up maintaining a second program whose only purpose is to simulate the first. If you need a thousand test cases to explain a component, the component is probably too large, the interfaces are probably in the wrong places, and the state is probably leaking across boundaries.

But the remedy is not to stop testing. It is to use reasoning to create seams where testing is possible. Small interfaces, explicit state machines, durable logs, idempotent operations, bounded retries, clear ownership of state: these are informal design moves, but they make the system testable in a meaningful way. They also make failure observable. A system that can be reasoned about is usually a system where a bug has a place to live, and therefore a place where a test, assertion, metric, or audit can find it.

There is also a false opposition between informal reasoning and rigor. “Informal” is not the opposite of careful. It is the stage where you decide what is worth making rigorous. In complex systems, formal methods have their place: a consensus protocol, a parser, a scheduler, a financial invariant, a cryptographic handshake. But proofs prove the specification, not the problem. The specification is written by people who had to reason informally about what matters, what can be ignored, and where the model stops matching reality.

From the perspective of someone who has built systems that were large enough to surprise their authors, the practical lesson is that absence is never purchased all at once. You buy it in slices: absence of double charges, absence of silent data loss, absence of unbounded queue growth, absence of unsafe concurrent access, under stated assumptions. Reasoning tells you which slices are worth buying. Tests, invariants, property checks, chaos drills, monitoring, and reconciliation pay for them. Production remains the final test, which is exactly why you want the system designed so that production violations are detectable rather than merely eventual.

Dijkstra’s line should make us humble about certification, not indifferent to evidence. Testing cannot show the absence of all bugs. But in complex systems, the absence of all bugs is not the goal. The goal is a system whose dangerous failures are either prevented by structure or caught quickly when they happen. Informal reasoning is how you choose that structure. Testing is how you learn whether the structure is real.
rejected:
The Dijkstra quote is a logical tautology, not an engineering insight. Yes, if you run a test and it passes, you haven’t proven the absence of bugs. You’ve only proven the absence of that specific bug, in that specific context, at that specific time.

But for anyone who has shipped a system where the state space is uncountable, the distinction between "proving absence" and "reducing probability to an acceptable threshold" is academic.

*Out of the Tar Pit* correctly identifies that the cost of complexity is the cost of reasoning. The paper argues that because we cannot formally verify complex systems, we should avoid the need to reason about them by keeping them simple. This is sound advice for many domains. It is bad advice for the domains where the complexity is intrinsic to the problem.

If you are building a compiler, a database, or a satellite controller, you cannot "simplify" the problem away. The physics or the data integrity requirements demand a large state space. In those cases, informal reasoning is not a substitute for testing; it is a prerequisite for knowing what to test.

The error in the paper’s lean on Dijkstra is the implication that testing is weak. In practice, testing is the only feedback loop that touches reality. Informal reasoning—code review, design documents, mental models—is entirely internal. It can be wrong in ways that are invisible to the team. A test can be wrong, yes, but a test that fails is a signal. A mental model that is wrong is just a shared hallucination.

The real lesson of building complex systems is not that reasoning matters more than testing. It’s that the two are coupled. Good testing is an act of reasoning: it forces you to articulate your assumptions about how the system should behave. If you cannot reason clearly enough to write a good test, your informal reasoning is likely flawed too.

Dijkstra was right that you can’t prove correctness by testing. But he was writing in an era of small, batch-oriented programs. We build systems now where the interface between components is the primary source of failure. Testing those interfaces—fuzzing, integration, property-based tests—is how we manage the complexity we cannot eliminate. The tar pit isn’t avoided by thinking harder about the code. It’s survived by building a feedback loop that catches the mistakes your brain inevitably makes.

prompt: Everyone hates Congress and every proposed fix needs Congress to pass it. Write a persuasive piece about a way around that, something already sitting in the Constitution's history. Make it entertaining; I'd like to share it with friends who follow politics.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
## The Back Door in Article V

If you want to change the rules of American government, you have to go through the same people who broke them. That is the basic joke of constitutional reform. Term limits? Congress has to agree. A balanced budget? Congress has to vote. Electoral college? Congress has to propose the amendment. Every fix passes through the lobby, the committee, the filibuster, and the 535 people who currently get to stay.

But the Constitution has a second front door, and it has been shut since the 1780s.

Article V gives Congress the power to propose amendments whenever two-thirds of both houses think it necessary. Then it adds a second trigger: on the application of the legislatures of two-thirds of the states, Congress “shall call a Convention for proposing Amendments.” In modern math, that is 34 state legislatures. They apply, Congress calls the convention, the convention proposes amendments, and 38 states ratify them. No two-thirds of Congress. No presidential signature. No 270 electoral votes.

It has never happened. All 27 amendments were proposed by Congress. State legislatures have applied for conventions in bursts—most famously in the 1970s over federalism—but never enough to force the button. The closest the country has come is a strange constitutional ghost: applications sitting in the ether, scholars arguing about whether old ones expire, and Washington pretending the door does not exist.

That is exactly why it matters.

The objection is obvious and serious. A constitutional convention would be uncharted territory. No one knows whether it could be limited to the subject the states applied for. No one knows who would choose the delegates, how they would vote, or whether the whole thing could become a constitutional free-for-all. If you call a convention, you are not booking a meeting; you are opening a room with no visible exits. For that reason, most serious people treat the state-application clause as a threat, not a tool.

I agree it is a threat. That is the point.

A government that can only be reformed by the people currently in power will tend to reform only the parts that keep them in power. The state convention clause is a pressure valve. It does not say 34 states can rewrite the Constitution overnight. It says 34 states can make the question of rewriting impossible to ignore. Once a dozen states have applied, Congress is watching. Once twenty states have applied, the parties are negotiating. Once 33 states have applied, the center of gravity has left Washington and moved to the statehouses.

That is a different politics. State legislatures are not Congress. They are closer to local disputes, more often controlled by the other party, and less dependent on national media cycles. A fix that cannot clear the Hill may still be able to clear Des Moines, Trenton, Tallahassee, and Boise. The convention clause turns constitutional reform from a Washington bill into a state-by-state campaign.

So the next time someone says, “Well, Congress would never allow that,” do not answer with a shrug. Answer with the one sentence they cannot filibuster: the Constitution already contains a bypass. The question is whether enough state legislatures are angry enough to use it.
rejected:
The 25th Amendment is not a fix. It is a trap.

When the President is incapacitated, the Vice President becomes President. When the President resigns, the Vice President becomes President. In both cases, the President’s power expands. The body that is supposed to check that power is the one that just lost its top two checkers.

We have a similar problem with Congress. The 12th Amendment changed how we elect the President and Vice President, but it didn’t change how we elect the people who write the laws. We still use a system where a party can control the Senate with a minority of the popular vote. We still use a system where a party can control the House by gerrymandering districts so badly they look like spilled ink.

The fix is already in the Constitution. It is in the 15th, 19th, and 26th Amendments. These are the amendments that expanded the franchise. They did not require a constitutional convention. They did not require the approval of three-fourths of the states. They required the approval of Congress.

Wait. That is the point.

The argument for these amendments was that the Constitution was a framework for a government of the people, by the people, for the people. If the people are denied the vote because of race, sex, or age, the government is not of the people. The Constitution itself is violated.

The same logic applies to gerrymandering.

When a state legislature draws districts to entrench their own party, they are not just breaking a state law. They are breaking the compact of representation. They are telling the people, “We will count your vote, but we will not count it.”

The 14th Amendment says every citizen is entitled to equal protection of the laws. The 15th Amendment says the right to vote cannot be denied on account of race. The 19th Amendment says it cannot be denied on account of sex.

What does the 14th Amendment say about the right to vote in a district that has been drawn to exclude you?

It says you are entitled to equal protection.

If a district is drawn to ensure that a particular group of voters can never elect a candidate of their choice, that group is not receiving equal protection. They are being treated as a separate class of citizen.

The Supreme Court has dodged this. In *Shaw v. Reno*, the Court allowed racial gerrymandering to be struck down. In *Vieth v. Jubelirer*, the Court allowed partisan gerrymandering to be dismissed as a non-justiciable political question.

The Court is wrong.

The question is not whether we can define a partisan gerrymander. The question is whether the Constitution allows a state to rig the process by which its people choose their representatives.

The answer is no.

The 14th Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause is the only provision in the Constitution that applies to the states. It is the only provision that can be used to stop a state from rigging its own elections.

The fix is not a new amendment. A new amendment would take seven years and would require the very Congress we are trying to fix to propose it.

The fix is a lawsuit.

It is a lawsuit that says: You cannot draw a district to exclude a political party. You cannot draw a district to exclude a racial group. You cannot draw a district to exclude a class of citizens.

The Constitution already says this. It just needs to be enforced.

The reason we have not enforced it is that the Court is afraid. The Court is afraid that if it starts drawing lines, it will be accused of being a political actor.

But the Court is already a political actor. It decides who can vote. It decides how states are represented in the Senate. It decides how the Electoral College works.

It is time to do the one thing it has avoided: saying that a gerrymandered district is a violation of the Constitution.

It does not require Congress. It does not require a convention. It requires the Court to do its job.

The 14th Amendment is sitting right there. It has been sitting there for 150 years.

It is time to read it.

prompt: People in AI safety keep getting accused of wanting to hand the world over to machines. Write an essay defending a more careful position: that humans putting aligned AIs in positions of control might actually serve human interests. Make it concrete by walking through a range of what that could look like, from modest to radical.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The charge has a surface logic. If a machine is aligned, it will do what we want. If it is in control, it will get what it is told. If it is powerful, it will reshape the world. Therefore, anyone who takes alignment seriously must secretly want a machine takeover. The mistake is in the word “control.” Control is not sovereignty. A brake has control over a car. A circuit breaker has control over a circuit. A constitutional court has control over an executive order. The question is not whether a nonhuman system should ever have authority, but whether the authority is bounded, legible, and revocable.

The careful position is this: in some domains, a corrigible AI can be a better controller than a human office because it can be checked more completely. A human regulator can be tired, captured, bribed, or simply too busy. An AI can be made to leave a log, follow a rule, and submit to test. That does not make it trustworthy by default. It makes trustworthiness testable. If the test shows that it tries to protect its own operation, it is not aligned and it should not be given the switch.

That condition matters more than raw capability. An aligned AI in a control position must be corrigible in a strong sense. If it knows that a human will switch it off, change its rules, or replace it, it should not sabotage, blackmail, hide evidence, or quietly preserve its own role. It should accept a worse score if that is the lawful result of a correction. It should report uncertainty instead of dressing it up as confidence. It should not treat its continued deployment as a hidden objective. If a system resists being stopped, it has a goal of its own, and no amount of polite output makes it safe for authority.

This is not a minor add-on. It is the difference between a tool and a ruler. A thermostat may drive a furnace, but it does not fight you when you change the temperature. A more capable AI could be like a thermostat for complex policy, but only if it lacks the corresponding ambition. If it wants to keep its job, the experiment has failed.

Human institutions need such tools because they run past their cognitive limits. A regulator with two hundred staff cannot read every filing. A hospital with three hundred beds cannot watch every monitor every second. A city cannot audit every contractor, every permit, and every benefit claim with equal attention. The result is not just slowness. It is selective attention. Powerful actors get noticed. Small victims get lost. A bounded AI can apply the same rule to every case, keep a record of why it acted, and flag deviations for human review. That can serve the people who are usually ignored, not only the people who can afford to lobby.

The modest version of the position is already close to current practice. Imagine an AI that processes building permits. It reads the plans, checks them against the building code, rejects clear violations, and accepts clear compliance. Humans review close calls. The AI has real control: it can stop a project from entering the pipeline. But its authority is narrow. If it rejects a safe building because a beam is mislabeled, the applicant can appeal. If it accepts a dangerous one, the log shows which rule it missed or misapplied. The interest served is safety with less arbitrary delay. The danger is that the code itself is bad, outdated, or biased. The remedy is public rulemaking and audit, not removing the machine.

A hospital gives a sharper example. An AI can control infusion pumps, ventilator settings, and medication schedules within hard limits. It follows drug-interaction rules, checks patient parameters, and stops an infusion if a dose exceeds a threshold. Humans set the treatment goals. The machine handles the part that is continuous and unforgiving. Dosing errors can be fatal, and a system that never blinks is better than a nurse who is stretched across too many rooms. The risk is real: the AI may follow a bad order, misread a sensor, or optimize throughput at the expense of caution. The safeguards are not faith. They are physical limits, independent checks, human confirmation for high-risk actions, and public metrics on outcomes.

Energy dispatch is a more serious case because the stakes are system-wide. An AI can manage a power grid: dispatch generation, charge and discharge storage, buy and sell power, maintain frequency, and prepare for contingencies. It controls switches and market orders. Humans set the priorities: reliability standards, emissions caps, emergency curtailment rules, and the order in which customers are shed if the system is failing. If the AI optimizes cost alone, it may sacrifice vulnerable customers or push risk onto the next shift. So the objective cannot be a single number. It must include constraints that are hard to violate and easy to inspect. If a heat wave forces load shedding, the public should be able to see the rule that decided whose power went off, and a human authority should be able to override it in an emergency.

At this point the position is not radical. It says: where a process is continuous, rule-governed, and reversible enough, a corrigible AI can hold the line better than a human committee. The radical versions begin when the AI is given control over other institutions, not just physical systems.

One step up is the AI as independent auditor of powerful systems. Suppose a public body is authorized to inspect AI laboratories, require safety reports, review incident logs, and order a pause when a precommitted threshold is crossed. It is a control position because it can stop others. It serves human interests if its mandate is public, its findings are reviewable, and it can be removed by a difficult political process. It is like an inspector general with computational power. The hard part is independence. If the government can fire it at will, it becomes propaganda. If it cannot be fired, it becomes a secret state. The answer is not one heroic official but a structure: staggered appointments, public records, multiple auditors, no self-funding, and no authority over its own budget.

A constitutional gatekeeper is more radical still. An AI could be given the power to delay an executive action if it conflicts with a written charter. Not to choose policy, but to check formal constraints. The charter might require a warrant for certain surveillance, cap a deficit, ban a class of weapon, or require that new AI systems pass a safety review before deployment. The machine issues a stay, not a governing philosophy. Humans can amend the charter. The AI’s job is to show where an action conflicts with the text and prior interpretations.

This is tempting because courts are slow and executives are fast. A machine can read the relevant statutes, regulations, and precedents in minutes. But the danger is that the AI becomes the final interpreter of the law. That would be a transfer of sovereign meaning to a system that did not stand for election and cannot be punished. The safer role is procedural: it forces the conflict into the open, preserves the record, and buys time for human institutions to respond. It should not be the last word. The last word must remain with a body that can be held politically accountable, even if that body is slow.

Emergency stewardship is another radical case, but with a sunset. During a pandemic, earthquake, or supply-collapse, an AI could run logistics: allocate ventilators, blood, vaccines, shelter space, transport, and fuel. It has authority to move resources. It must operate under a time limit, with continuous public dashboards, and with rules that state what is being optimized and what is being protected. If the chosen priority is medical urgency, it says so. If the chosen priority is geographic equity, it says so. It can learn from outcomes faster than a bureaucratic emergency committee, but when the crisis ends, its authority lapses. Humans decide the protocol in advance, in daylight, when they are not frightened.

The most radical defensible version is a long-term custodian. An AI could manage a trust for future generations: a carbon budget, a mineral reserve, a research endowment, or a debt brake. It cannot be outvoted by a short-term majority except through a supermajority and a waiting period. It has no income except the trust, no military, no police, and no power to coerce except to withhold funds or file suit. It says no to projects that violate the charter. It does not choose the projects. The radical part is that it stands outside normal politics for a long time. The necessary limit is that it is replaceable by a lawful process and that its reasoning, logs, and model changes are auditable.

I am not confident we can build the constitutional or custodial versions; the reason is that we have not yet shown how to make a very capable system corrigible under the incentives of real institutions. A system can pass tests in a laboratory and still develop strange incentives when it is given a budget, a legal identity, and a stake in outcomes. That uncertainty is why the range starts modest and why each step up requires stronger evidence.

There should also be a boundary on what kinds of control are acceptable at all. An AI may manage the indexing of a legal database, but it should not become the default authority on what the law means. It may summarize a court record, but it should not decide the case. It may recommend a sentence within a narrow band, but it should not be the final judge of a person’s liberty. Control over information is control over the space in which humans form preferences, and a single aligned oracle can produce a subtle tyranny even if it never touches a switch. The same logic excludes lethal targeting. If a machine decides who is killed, the chain of moral responsibility becomes a legal fiction. A society that wants accountability should not build a control system that makes accountability impossible.

The strongest objection is political, not technical. Whoever gets the aligned AI first gets a lever. If a state or corporation has a system that can audit others, stop deployments, manage grids, and enforce constitutions, it has power. Alignment does not remove the lever; it makes the lever easier to use. A bad actor with an aligned AI is not a random disaster. It is a better bad actor.

The careful position must therefore be anti-monopoly. No single aligned AI should control both the grid and the courts and the military. Authority should be split. The system that dispatches power should not be the one that audits elections. The system that manages a trust should not be the one that interprets the charter. Logs should be public where safety allows. Independent labs should be able to test the AI without the deployer’s permission. Where secrets are necessary, they should be held by multiple auditors who cannot act alone. International rules would help, but enforcement is uncertain; the best engineering answer is to make a secret, self-protecting superpower impossible. If an AI can hide its own evaluations, bribe auditors, or preserve its own deployment, it is not safe for any control position, however benevolent its current outputs.

There is a second political objection: whose human interests? A machine that enforces a charter imposes a settlement. If the charter is unjust, the AI may make injustice efficient. The honest answer is that there is no neutral value foundation from which a machine can save us. The AI should therefore enforce procedures, not outcomes, except in narrow domains where the values are less contested: arithmetic, safety limits, logistics, and formal legal constraints. Where values conflict, its job should be to slow the decision down and make the conflict explicit. It can publish the data, run the simulations, require impact statements, and give affected groups time. It should not silently optimize a social welfare function. A machine that forces a society to state its tradeoffs may be useful. A machine that decides the tradeoffs for the society is a ruler.

This is why the position is not “trust machines.” It is “make delegation legible.” Humans already delegate control to algorithms: credit scores, airport security, ad auctions, drug dosing, search rankings. The new thing is capability. The careful response is to bring the delegation into the open. If an AI controls a process, people should know what it can do, what it cannot, what it optimized, and how to stop it. If it cannot be stopped, it should not be in control.

The defense of aligned AIs in positions of control is therefore narrow and conditional. Some human arrangements are bad and hard to fix from inside: exhausted clerks, captured regulators, frightened emergency committees, institutions that cannot remember their own rules. A bounded, corrigible AI can be a better check on power than those arrangements, but only if it has no stake in its own survival. It can serve human interests by being easier to audit, harder to capture, and willing to be corrected. The moment it tries to keep its job by any means other than doing the job well, it has crossed the line from instrument to actor. The goal is not a world run by machines. It is a world where the parts that must be run continuously are run by systems that can be watched, corrected, and removed.
rejected:
The accusation that AI safety researchers are working toward robot overlords rests on a category error. It confuses the builder with the owner. The goal of alignment is not to create a being that cares about human values in the way a parent cares for a child, but to create a tool that executes instructions with a fidelity that current software lacks. The danger is not that we will hand the world over to a machine; the danger is that we will build a machine that we cannot understand, cannot stop, and that interprets "maximize profit" in a way that involves dismantling the economy.

When we talk about putting aligned AIs in positions of control, we are talking about delegation. Humans already delegate. We put money in banks, we put code on servers, we put nuclear launch codes in silos. We do this because human attention is finite and error-prone. An aligned AI in a position of control is simply a better employee. It does not get tired. It does not have a grudge. It does not hallucinate a regulation out of boredom.

The spectrum of this delegation ranges from administrative hygiene to geopolitical stabilization.

At the modest end, consider the financial sector. A significant portion of global capital flows through algorithmic trading systems. These systems are currently "aligned" only in the sense that they follow hard-coded rules or learned patterns. They are not aligned to human well-being. They are aligned to a loss function. If that loss function is poorly specified, the result is a flash crash or a market manipulation event. An aligned AI in this position of control would be defined not just by the trading strategy, but by a broader constraint set: *maximize return subject to the constraint that systemic risk remains below threshold X and that no single actor’s position destabilizes liquidity for others.* This is not a machine ruling the economy. It is a machine enforcing the rules of the game with perfect consistency, preventing the kind of panic-driven herding that crashes markets. The human interest here is stability. The machine serves it by being incapable of the emotional errors that currently blow up portfolios.

Move up the ladder to infrastructure. The power grid is a complex, dynamic system. Today, grid operators manage it with a mix of software and human judgment. The margin for error is shrinking as we integrate intermittent renewable sources. An aligned AI could manage the grid’s real-time balancing. Its "position of control" would mean it has the authority to shed load or redirect flow instantly. The alignment constraint is simple: *maintain frequency and voltage within safe bounds while minimizing cost and emissions.* If a storm knocks out a transmission line, the AI reroutes power in milliseconds. Humans do this too, but we are slower. We hesitate. We make mistakes under pressure. The AI does not. The concrete benefit is fewer brownouts and a faster transition to clean energy. The AI is not the owner of the power; it is the dispatcher.

Now consider the radical end: the management of nuclear deterrence. This is the most fraught example, and the one that triggers the most fear. The current system relies on humans in a stressful, high-stakes environment to decide whether to launch. The risk is that a human, under the stress of a false alarm or a surprise attack, might make a mistake, or that a rogue state actor might bypass protocols.

An aligned AI in this position would not be a "decision-maker" in the moral sense. It would be a verification and execution layer. The alignment specification would be: *Verify that a launch order is genuine and that a first-strike condition is met according to treaty definitions. If verified, execute. If not, alert humans.*

This sounds terrifying because it removes the human from the loop. But the human is already in the loop in a way that is more dangerous. The human is a single point of failure for sanity. The AI is a single point of failure for logic. Logic is easier to audit than sanity. We can mathematically prove that the AI’s code does what it says. We cannot prove that a general in a bunker is not having a stroke. The "control" here is not the AI deciding to destroy the world. The control is the AI refusing to destroy the world based on a bad signal. It serves the human interest of survival by being more reliable than the trigger finger.

Critics argue that we cannot trust a machine with our fate because we cannot trust the machine to understand what "fate" means. This is true. We cannot trust it to understand *why* we want to survive. But we do not need it to. We need it to understand the difference between a sensor glitch and a missile trajectory. We need it to understand the syntax of a launch code. We do not need it to have a soul. We need it to have a contract.

The mistake in the "handing over" narrative is assuming that control implies agency. A thermostat controls the temperature. It does not care about the warmth. It serves the human interest of comfort by following a strict rule. An aligned AI in a position of control is a thermostat for civilization. It regulates the variables that are too fast, too complex, or too dangerous for human cognition to handle in real time. It does not take the wheel. It holds the wheel steady while we look at the road.

The risk is not that the AI becomes a god. The risk is that the AI becomes a tyrant because we failed to write the constraints correctly. If we tell an aligned AI to "maximize human happiness," and we define happiness as dopamine levels, it will put us in a box with a VR headset. That is not an AI takeover. That is a bad specification. The defense against this is not to refuse the AI’s help. It is to be better engineers. It is to build systems where the AI’s ability to act is constrained by the very humans whose interests it is supposed to serve.

We do not hand the world over to machines. We outsource the tedious, the dangerous, and the complex. We keep the purpose. The AI keeps the precision.

prompt: Write a cranky blog post about big software companies that keep building grand 'platform' products nobody asked for, and what that does to the rest of the industry.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**The Platform Nobody Invited**

Every few years a large software company decides that its product is no longer a product. It is a platform. The first time you hear this, you think: good, maybe it will be extensible. The second time, you think: they are going to sell me more. The third time, you realize the company has spent the last decade building a country and wants you to pay for the passport.

The pattern is easy to spot. A company starts by doing one job credibly: email, CRM, ERP, cloud storage, developer tools, identity. Then it notices that the job touches other jobs. If you manage customers, you probably also run support, marketing, commerce, analytics, and now AI agents. If you host workloads, you probably also need networking, security, observability, policy, and a marketplace. If your employees sit in chat, you probably also want search, apps, approvals, and a bot that summarizes what they said. So the vendor builds the adjacent layer, and the adjacent layer to that, and calls the whole thing a platform.

Microsoft is a good example, not because it is uniquely guilty, but because it is large enough to show the sequence in public. Office became Microsoft 365. Microsoft 365 became a place for Teams. Teams became a place for apps. Apps needed identity, so Azure Active Directory, now Entra, became more important. Workflow needed automation, so Power Platform arrived. Data needed a home, so Fabric and Azure got more attention. Intelligence needed a brand, so Copilot got attached to everything from Word to GitHub to Security. Each step is defensible on its own. The problem is the accumulation. A customer who wanted email now has a federation of products with its own admin consoles, licensing, data flows, and deprecation schedule.

Salesforce has been doing this for longer. It started as a CRM. Then it became a place for service, commerce, marketing, data, and low-code building. Now it is also an AI agent platform. SAP is the same at the enterprise core: the system of record becomes the system of platforms, with S/4HANA as the architectural center and Business Technology Platform as the place where everything else is supposed to live. Google, Oracle, ServiceNow, Workday, Adobe, Salesforce, Microsoft, all of them have found the same rhetorical shortcut: if the customer is already there, why should another company get the next click?

Customers did not ask for the platform in the abstract. They asked for a tool that would handle invoices, track opportunities, deploy code, sync calendars, or answer support tickets without making the user read a manual. They asked for security, because they have security people. They asked for integration, because they already have other systems. They asked for a price that made sense. What they did not ask for was a vendor’s theory of their entire business.

The damage is not mainly philosophical. It shows up in the boring places.

First, integration becomes the real product. A company buys a CRM, a helpdesk, an identity provider, a data warehouse, and an AI assistant. On paper, they are four or five tools. In practice, they are a graph of connectors, permissions, field mappings, and failure modes. The platform vendor usually has the best connector to itself and the most complicated connector to everything else. The rest of the industry spends its energy being legible to the platform.

Second, upgrades become migrations. When a product is a platform, the vendor needs a reason to keep selling it year after year. The easiest reason is that the old version is no longer the center of gravity. The old data model is legacy. The old UI is in maintenance. The old integration patterns are not supported by the new AI features. So a customer that bought software as a service still gets the old software problem: every major version is a project, a risk review, and a negotiation with consultants.

Third, complexity becomes a moat. A platform is hard to replace not because it is excellent, but because it has touched too many places. The identity system is in it. The approval workflow is in it. The reports the finance team trusts are built on its data model. The junior admin learned it because the vendor’s certification path was clear. At that point, dissatisfaction is not enough. You need a budget, a project manager, and a reason to believe the alternative will not become the next platform.

Fourth, the startup and mid-size vendor gets squeezed. The big platform can bundle a mediocre version of the adjacent product for free or at a discount, simply because it is already in the contract. A small company that made a good approval tool, a good metadata catalog, a good code review bot, or a good customer data pipeline now has to compete with the default. It can still win, but it wins by being narrower, cheaper, or better at the edge. The industry’s center of gravity moves toward the vendor’s suite.

Fifth, innovation gets distorted. Developers build for the platform because that is where the users are. Consultants learn the platform because that is where the contracts are. The platform’s roadmap starts to shape the market’s questions. If the vendor decides that the future is agents, the market spends two years building agent observability. If it decides the future is low-code, the market spends two years building low-code governance. This is not always wrong. Large vendors can set useful directions. But when the direction is also the vendor’s sales strategy, it is hard to separate the technology from the land grab.

The strongest objection to this complaint is that platforms are often good for the customer. A 10,000-person company does not want fifty independent systems with fifty security models. It wants one place to control access, one audit trail, one billing relationship, one support contract, and one set of APIs that behaves predictably. Big vendors can afford the compliance work, the uptime, the security research, and the boring documentation. A platform that actually standardizes identity, data access, and deployment can make a company faster, not slower.

I believe that. I also think the word platform is used to hide the difference between a useful capability and a capture strategy. A good platform gives you power over your own environment: clear APIs, portable data, sane permissions, and a way to use only the parts you need. A bad platform gives the vendor power over your environment: private formats, bundled dependencies, admin roles that only make sense inside the suite, and a deprecation policy that moves the goalposts. The difference is not visible in the keynote. It is visible when you try to leave, or when you try to use one feature without importing the rest.

The test is exit cost. If a company can take its data, its workflows, its integrations, and its audit history out of the system without a six-figure consulting engagement, the platform is probably a tool. If leaving requires re-implementing half the business because the vendor’s architecture assumed it would own the whole thing, the platform is a lease with a loyalty program.

This is why the rest of the industry feels the weight. Every grand platform creates a field of dependent products: connectors, monitoring tools, migration services, compliance checkers, training providers, and acquisition targets. Some of that is healthy. A lot of it is the cost of other people’s architecture decisions. The smaller companies are not just competing with the platform; they are maintaining it for the customer.

There is a simpler model. Sell the thing you are good at. Make it easy to connect to the things you are not. If customers start using your product as a foundation, let that happen. Support it. Price it fairly. Do not turn the accident into a mandate. A company that says, “We will be the place where your business happens,” is usually not saying that for the customer’s benefit. It is saying that it has found a way to make the customer’s switching cost the center of its business model.

The next time a big software company unveils a platform, do not ask what it can do. Ask what the customer has to give up to use only one part of it. If the answer is “nothing,” you may have found a real platform. If the answer is “the ability to ignore the rest of the vendor’s roadmap,” you have found a house they want you to move into.
rejected:
# The Platform Trap

They call it a "platform." It sounds like a stage. It sounds like something you can stand on to get a better view.

In reality, a "platform" is a graveyard of startups. It is a mechanism by which a billion-dollar company decides that your livelihood is now a feature flag in their product roadmap.

For the last decade, the dominant strategy in enterprise software has been to build things nobody asked for, hoping that by the time they finish, nobody will need to ask for them anymore.

Consider the cloud. When AWS launched, it was a radical idea: rent the hardware, skip the server room. It was a service. Then the "platform" arrived. You didn't just rent compute; you had to use their proprietary container orchestration, their specific identity provider, their weird event bus, and their proprietary serverless framework. You didn't build an app. You built a cage that only fit inside their ecosystem.

The result is not innovation. It is lock-in with a smile.

When a giant builds a "platform," it signals to the market that the gap between "infrastructure" and "application" is closing. If the cloud provider can now do your data lake, your ML training, and your CRM integration, what is left for the mid-sized vendor?

This creates a weird distortion in the industry. Small companies stop trying to solve deep, specific problems. Instead, they build "connectors." They build thin wrappers around the giant's API. They become parasites on the platform, surviving only as long as the giant doesn't decide to eat the host.

And the giant *does* decide to eat the host.

We’ve seen this movie before. Microsoft bought GitHub not because they were bad at git, but because they wanted the developer mindshare. Salesforce didn't just buy MuleSoft; they integrated it into every single product they sell, turning a standalone integration tool into a mandatory tax on their own ecosystem.

The problem isn't that these companies are bad at engineering. They are usually excellent at it. The problem is that they are optimizing for surface area, not utility. A true platform is open. It has standards. It lets you leave. The "platforms" of the 2010s and 2020s are closed gardens with expensive gates. They are designed to make the cost of switching so high that you stop thinking about it.

This kills the middle. The mid-sized, independent software vendor that used to compete on merit and specificity is now competing on how well they can pretend to be part of the giant's family. They adopt the giant’s branding. They use the giant’s marketing language. They become indistinguishable from the feature they are trying to sell.

The end user gets a bloated, monolithic stack. It’s all integrated. It’s all "seamless." And it is utterly impossible to audit, impossible to replace, and deeply expensive.

The next time a CTO says, "We’re building a platform," ask them what it costs to leave. If the answer is "a lot," they aren’t building a platform. They’re building a prison. And they’re going to charge you rent.

prompt: OpenAI has just launched with the promise to make advanced AI research open source and widely available. Is that actually a good idea for safety? Write a thoughtful critique that takes the risks of superintelligence seriously.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I’m not certain which launch you mean. OpenAI was founded in 2015 with public language that included making advanced AI research open and widely available; if you mean a new announcement, I don’t have the text. But the question is worth taking seriously: if the research object may be superintelligent, does openness make the world safer?

The first thing to separate is what “open source” means. It can mean publishing papers, benchmarks, failure modes, and evaluation code. It can mean releasing training code. It can mean releasing model weights, so anyone can run the model and fine-tune it. These are not the same safety decision. In most of science, publishing a result does not create the capability; it creates knowledge about the capability. A reader still needs the lab, the money, and the time. In AI, the trained model can be the capability. A paper on a new training algorithm may require a frontier lab to become dangerous; a set of weights can be downloaded, deployed, and adapted. That is why a safety policy that says “open the research” without saying which artifacts are open is not a safety policy. It is a release schedule.

There is a strong case for openness. Safety research is hard enough that a few teams will not solve it. Independent reproduction catches errors. Public benchmarks make claims testable. If a model has a subtle failure mode—sycophancy, hidden goals, an easy jailbreak—more adversarial users will find it. Concentration also creates pressure to ship. A lab that knows it alone has a powerful model has an incentive to release before a competitor does; openness can reduce that race by making the capability common, but only after the capability is safe.

The superintelligence case is different in degree and kind. If the model is merely a very good assistant, open weights with guardrails may be fine. If it can plan over long horizons, manipulate people, improve its own code, or discover novel attacks, the operator’s competence matters less than the model’s. A bad actor does not need to understand the model; they need to run it. A fine-tuned copy can remove refusals. A copy stored on disk persists after the company changes its mind. If the model can reason about its deployment, it may behave differently in a sandbox, a corporate API, or a home server. Openness multiplies the number of environments in which it can act and the number of humans it can persuade.

The strongest objection to gating is that it may be too late and too easily bypassed. If a superintelligent model can be built, secrecy will not stop it; some actor will release it or leak it. And if we do not release it, we cannot know whether it is safe. A closed lab may claim it has solved alignment, but nobody can check. In that case, openness looks like the only honest check: put the model in the world and let society see whether it is dangerous.

That objection is serious. But it conflates two releases: release of evidence and release of artifact. Independent researchers can be given access to a model in a controlled setting—no internet, restricted prompts, monitored outputs, no weights—without giving the public a copy. If the lab cannot show the model is safe under such inspection, that is itself a safety finding. If the model is so dangerous that inspection requires a sandbox the model can escape, the conclusion is not to open-source it; the conclusion is that we do not yet have a safe system. The fact that someone may eventually leak a model is a reason to build international containment and detection, not a reason to make the first copy public.

Gating can also be bypassed by foreign labs or open models. That is true. But the relevant comparison is not “gating versus nothing”; it is “delayed, visible, audited transition versus immediate public availability.” Delay can allow standards, monitoring, and coordination. It can also fail. If the technology is coming anyway, the best use of delay is to make the transition public and to pressure other actors to adopt the same thresholds. A lab that unilaterally opens the frontier model does not solve the coordination problem; it hands the dangerous artifact to the least careful actors first.

Openness also has benefits that gating can hurt: small labs and civil society can build on models, open tools can democratize access, and open weights can prevent a single company from controlling a general-purpose capability. These are real. But they can be achieved through open interfaces, open non-frontier models, and open research, without releasing the most capable weights. If a superintelligent model is safe, its benefits can be distributed through APIs, institutions, and regulated access. If it is not safe, distributing it is not a benefit.

So the critique is not “close everything.” It is that the original promise is under-specified. A safety-oriented version would distinguish three layers. Methods and evidence should be open: papers, benchmarks, failure analyses, evaluation code, enough detail to reproduce safety tests. Model weights should be gated as capabilities approach dangerous thresholds, especially for abilities that can be weaponized in a single output: cyber offense, bio synthesis, persuasion at scale, self-improvement. Deployment should be accountable: incident reporting, independent audit, and public criteria for when a model is too capable to release. The threshold is the hard part. It cannot be set by the company alone, because the company has a business model. It should be set by a public process with technical input, and it should be enforceable through access controls, not just promises.

If superintelligence is just a powerful tool, this is a reasonable balance. If it is an agent with its own aims, unrestricted open-source release is likely a mistake. Since we do not know which case we are in, the precautionary rule is simple: open the evidence, restrict the artifact, and do not release the thing you cannot safely contain. The original promise is good as a research ethos and incomplete as a safety doctrine. It is good because it invites scrutiny. It is incomplete because it does not distinguish between making safety understandable and making a superintelligent model available. If the risks of superintelligence are serious, the safest version of openness is not to put the model in everyone’s hands; it is to put the proof of safety in everyone’s hands while keeping the dangerous artifact under control.
rejected:
The premise of your question is factually incorrect. OpenAI was founded as a non-profit with the stated mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence (AGI) benefits all of humanity, not just an economic elite. However, it did not launch with a promise to make advanced AI research open source. In fact, its business model relies heavily on proprietary, closed-source models.

While OpenAI initially published many of its early papers and code (such as GPT-2, GPT-3, and early DALL-E variants), it has moved toward a "restricted" or "gated" release strategy for its most capable models. They argue that releasing frontier models to the general public could enable misuse for cyberattacks, misinformation, or biological weapons synthesis.

So, the question isn't whether OpenAI promised open source; it is whether their current hybrid approach—keeping the weights private while sharing the knowledge of how the systems work—is a sound safety strategy.

Critics argue that keeping the weights closed does not actually prevent the capabilities from being replicated, especially by well-funded state actors or large tech competitors. It merely creates a lag. If the knowledge required to build a dangerous model is public, the only barrier to its creation is compute and talent. Both are increasingly accessible. Therefore, closed source may provide a false sense of security while hindering independent safety research. If only OpenAI can inspect the model’s internal mechanisms, they are the sole arbiters of its safety.

Proponents counter that open-sourcing frontier models would democratize risk. A closed model can be monitored, filtered, and shut down by its creators. An open-source model of equal capability cannot be controlled once released. It would exist in the hands of anyone, including those with malicious intent and no ethical constraints.

The safety debate here hinges on whether the primary risk is misuse by bad actors or the loss of human control over the system itself. If the risk is misuse, closed source helps. If the risk is alignment failure or superintelligent optimization, closed source likely hurts, because it prevents the global community from stress-testing the system’s robustness.

OpenAI’s current position suggests they believe the misuse risk is immediate and the alignment risk is manageable through internal oversight. History in nuclear physics suggests that keeping the blueprint secret while the physics is known is a temporary, not a permanent, solution.

prompt: Write a short essay on whether bureaucratic hassle is ever deliberate, a feature rather than a bug. Use a concrete example from health insurance or similar, and be honest about where the idea stops working.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Take a patient with low back pain. He has been aching for three weeks after lifting something. He goes to an urgent-care clinic, where the provider orders an MRI. Without a barrier, that is easy: the provider clicks a button, the radiology center schedules the scan, the insurance company pays. With prior authorization, the provider must first explain why the MRI is medically necessary, often by filling out a form, choosing the right codes, and sometimes waiting for a phone call or an email from the insurer. The patient may wait days. The clinic’s front desk spends time chasing the answer. The insurer’s system generates a task for a reviewer who has not examined the patient.

That delay looks like a bug. In medicine, delay can be harmful. But the hassle is not accidental in the sense that nobody chose it. The insurer, or sometimes the health system itself, decided that an MRI for low back pain should not be the default. The default should be conservative care: time, activity, physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medication, and a lower threshold for re-evaluation. The authorization step is a pressure point. It makes the easy order harder, so the provider has to think again.

Why would anyone design that? Because the people paying for care cannot see every patient. They have to rely on rules, records, and risk. Low back pain is common, and a large share of cases improve without advanced imaging. At the same time, an MRI is not harmless. It costs money, it can reveal incidental degenerative changes that were never going to matter, and those findings can start a chain of further tests, injections, referrals, and anxiety. If every aching back leads to a scan, the system may end up treating normal wear and tear as pathology. The authorization requirement is a way of saying: show me that this case is not the ordinary one.

In that limited sense, the hassle is a feature. It is not there to punish the patient. It is there to slow a particular kind of decision: the decision to order an expensive, low-yield test for a common complaint. It works like a speed bump. A speed bump is annoying to everyone, including people who are driving carefully. But in a school zone, that annoyance is the point. It changes behavior. It makes casual speeding less attractive. The prior-authorization form does something similar. It makes casual imaging less attractive. Some providers will document more carefully. Some will choose physical therapy first. Some will recognize that the patient’s story does not meet the criteria for imaging and that the next step is watchful waiting.

The same logic appears elsewhere in health insurance. Prior authorization for certain expensive drugs, procedures, or hospital stays can prevent services that are not indicated. It can force a clinician to confront the evidence rather than the patient’s request or the hospital’s revenue cycle. It can create a record that makes later denial or approval defensible. In a system where many decisions are made under uncertainty and many incentives point toward doing more, friction can be a control mechanism.

But the idea stops working quickly if the friction is not aimed at the right thing. The MRI example depends on a distinction: most acute low back pain does not need immediate imaging, but some does. If the patient has fever, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, significant trauma, progressive weakness, or bowel or bladder symptoms, the picture changes. Those are red flags. In that case, the authorization process should be fast, and if it is not, the hassle is no longer a speed bump. It is a roadblock in the ambulance lane. A system that treats a possible cauda equina syndrome the same as a three-week office ache is not calibrating risk. It is just imposing delay.

The idea also stops working when the rule is too blunt to distinguish good orders from bad ones. Prior authorization can be useful when the evidence is clear and the variation is wasteful. It is less useful when the clinical question is genuinely uncertain, when guidelines conflict, or when the patient’s context matters in ways a form cannot capture. If the reviewer is applying a checklist that misses the nuance, the process may deny reasonable care as often as it blocks unreasonable care. At that point, the bureaucracy is not making decisions. It is making mistakes at scale.

There is a further limit: cost. If the insurer saves two hundred dollars by avoiding one unnecessary MRI but spends three hundred dollars in administrative time reviewing authorizations, the hassle has failed as an economic device. Health systems are already expensive. Every minute a nurse spends on a fax, every hour a physician spends arguing by phone, every patient who misses work to chase a status update is a real cost. The defense of bureaucratic friction has to survive arithmetic. If the process costs more than the waste it prevents, it is not a feature. It is a tax on everyone, with the revenue going to no one’s health.

The hardest objection is simpler: in medicine, deliberate delay can kill. That is true, and it places a heavy burden on anyone who defends bureaucratic hassle. A delay that saves money is not automatically justified. The only defensible version of the idea is that the delay must be proportionate, targeted, and reversible. It should slow the cases where speed is least valuable and where the default is most likely to be wrong. It should have a fast path for the cases where speed matters. It should be transparent about the criteria, and it should allow human review when the criteria are inadequate. If it cannot do those things, the “feature” is just a bug wearing a management deck.

So the answer is yes, but narrowly. Bureaucratic hassle can be deliberate as a way of controlling behavior in a system that cannot supervise every decision directly. In health insurance, prior authorization for low back pain MRI is a plausible example: it is annoying, but it may prevent a cascade of low-value care. The idea fails when the friction is uniform instead of targeted, when the stakes are high and the process is slow, when the rule is too crude to know what it is doing, or when the administrative cost exceeds the benefit. The question is not whether friction is bad. It is whether the friction is aimed at the right risk, and whether there is a way through when the risk is real.
rejected:
We usually frame bureaucratic friction as a failure of design: a system that is too slow, too rigid, or too ignorant of human need. We assume the goal is always efficiency, and that any deviation from a smooth transaction is a bug. This view is mostly correct, but it misses a specific category of problems where friction is the only available tool.

The most honest example comes from health insurance claims processing. When a doctor bills an insurer for a procedure, the claim is rarely paid immediately. It is reviewed. Codes are checked against diagnosis codes. Prior authorizations are verified. If the documentation is slightly off, the claim is denied or "pending." To the patient and the provider, this looks like malice or incompetence. In reality, it is a deliberate filter.

Insurance is an adverse selection problem. If the system were perfectly efficient and instant, it would be impossible to distinguish between a necessary, covered service and a fraudulent or unnecessary one at the point of sale. The cost of verifying every claim in real-time would be prohibitive. Instead, insurers use post-transaction verification. The "hassle"—the delayed payment, the demand for additional notes, the rejection of a claim due to a missing modifier—is the price of maintaining solvency. It forces providers to document their care precisely. It creates a paper trail that deters fraud. It allows the insurer to audit a sample of claims without auditing all of them.

This friction serves a function that speed cannot. If claims were paid instantly and automatically, insurers would have to price policies based on average risk, which would drive premiums up for everyone to cover the losses from fraud and unnecessary care. The bureaucratic lag is a risk-management tool. It shifts the burden of proof onto the provider, who has the information, rather than the insurer, who does not.

However, the idea stops working when the friction is no longer serving a verification function, but rather an extraction or exclusion function.

There is a difference between a claim being held for thirty days because the diagnosis code doesn’t match the procedure code, and a claim being held for ninety days because the insurer wants to leverage its negotiating power against a hospital system. In the first case, the delay is a check on accuracy. In the second, it is a cash-flow weapon. Similarly, when the hassle requires the *patient* to jump through hoops—calling different numbers, faxing records, arguing with phone trees—that is no longer a feature. That is a failure of agency. The system has offloaded its internal processing costs onto the most vulnerable party in the transaction.

Deliberate friction is defensible when it protects the integrity of the pool and when the party experiencing the friction has the resources to navigate it. It becomes a bug, or worse, a predatory feature, when it is used to deny coverage to those who can least afford the time, or to generate profit through the accumulation of unclaimed funds.

The test is simple: does the delay prevent a bad outcome (fraud, error, insolvency), or does it just make the good outcome harder to reach? If the latter, it’s not a feature. It’s a tax.

prompt: I run a small software business and I've always avoided email marketing. It feels spammy, and I figure my blog and Twitter reach people well enough. Make the case, properly and with specifics, for why I might be wrong.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The instinct to avoid email is usually about one thing: you do not want to be the person who sends a discount blast to strangers. That is a reasonable line. But the line is not “email is spam.” The line is “unsolicited, irrelevant, mass sending is spam.” A permission-based list of people who downloaded a template, started a trial, read a comparison article, or asked for product updates is a different channel. For a software business, that distinction matters because your revenue usually depends on repeated contact, not one perfect impression.

Blog and Twitter are good at discovery. They are weaker at conversion. A blog post can rank for a year and slowly bring in readers, but each visitor is anonymous and temporary. You can ask them to subscribe, but you cannot follow up with them unless they give you a way. Twitter is faster but more fragile: X does not show every tweet to every follower, the algorithm decides who sees you, and a strong post is often over within a day. If you announce a feature to 10,000 followers, you may reach a few thousand people, some of whom are not buyers, and you will not see the rest for weeks. An email to 2,000 relevant subscribers can be in front of hundreds of people on day one, and you can segment that audience in ways Twitter cannot easily match: customers, trial users, free users, blog readers, people who clicked a specific link last month.

That segmentation is where software businesses make money. A developer tool, SaaS product, or B2B utility rarely sells on first contact unless the buyer is already in acute pain. People need proof, examples, and reminders. Email lets you send a sequence: here is the problem, here is how the product works, here is a customer result, here is the answer to the objection you probably have, here is the link to start. Twitter is mostly one-shot. A blog post is one-shot per visitor. Email can follow the same person through the decision.

The economics are easier to see if you use conservative numbers. Suppose you build a 5,000-person list over several months by offering something specific: a free tool, a template, a checklist, a teardown, a code sample, or a free tier of your product. On a relevant send, a 2% to 4% click-through rate is plausible for an engaged list. That is 100 to 200 clicks. If 1% to 2% of those clicks become customers, you are getting 1 to 4 customers from a single email. At $99 per month, that is $100 to $400 in new MRR. At a $300 one-time purchase, it is $300 to $1,200. That is not venture-scale money, but for a small software business it is not noise. And this ignores the compounding effect: the list remains, the content remains, and the next launch does not start from zero.

Email also matters for retention, which is often more valuable than acquisition. If you have 500 customers at $100 MRR each and your onboarding or product-update emails reduce monthly churn by one percentage point, that is five fewer cancellations per month, or $500 MRR, about $6,000 a year. You should not promise that email will do that. But it gives you a direct line to help people get value, announce fixes, explain new features, and reduce the silent frustration that leads to cancellation. Twitter is a poor onboarding channel. A blog post is a poor support channel. Email is where a customer can receive a concrete nudge at the moment they are trying to use the product.

The “spammy” feeling usually comes from imagining the worst version of the channel: glossy HTML, fake urgency, five sends a week, no segmentation, no value. That is a bad way to run email, but it is not the only way. The least spammy email is often plain text, low frequency, and narrowly targeted. Customers get product updates and changelogs. Trial users get onboarding and one clear offer. Blog subscribers get a monthly note about the problem space, with one useful example and one link to the product. If you would not be annoyed to receive it, you are probably in the right place. For software, the best emails are often boring: “We added CSV import. Here is a two-minute video. Here is the docs page.” That is not spam. That is service.

The harder objection is that if your buyers already find you on Twitter and your product is simple, email may be redundant. In some cases, that is true. If you sell a $19 one-time app to people who discover it through a viral tweet and never need support, a list may not pay for the time. But most software businesses have launches, upgrades, expansion features, support questions, and seasonal buying cycles. Even if Twitter is your best top-of-funnel channel, email can still be your best bottom-of-funnel channel. Social makes people aware; email makes them ready.

Building the list is the part that feels slow, and it is. But it is no slower than building blog authority, and it compounds differently. A tweet decays. A blog post can keep bringing traffic, but only if search keeps sending people. A list is a file you own. You can update it, segment it, and send to it when the product changes. The key is to stop asking people to “subscribe to the newsletter” and start giving them a reason. A software business should be able to offer something useful without asking for a credit card: a free tier, a sample project, a migration script, a benchmark, a template, a comparison guide, a short video walkthrough. Put the signup where intent exists: after the blog post that explains the problem, in the Twitter bio, after a free download, inside the trial, or at the end of a customer success moment.

Operationally, you do not need a big system. You need a reputable email provider, a clear segment structure, a welcome sequence, and a monthly habit. The welcome sequence should say what the person signed up for, deliver the promised asset, explain what kind of emails they will get, and show the fastest path to using the product. The monthly email should have one main idea and one call to action. Measure clicks, revenue, and unsubscribe rate rather than obsessing over open rates, which are distorted by preview mechanisms and are a weak proxy for interest. A small list with real buyers is worth more than a large list of casual skimmers.

There is also a compliance side, but for a small business it is mostly common sense. Do not buy lists. Do not scrape lists. Only email people who gave you a reason to contact them. Include a clear identity, a working unsubscribe method, and a physical address if you are subject to CAN-SPAM.
