The point is not a handout. It is to make the claim on growth visible. If automation raises output, the fund’s assets should rise, and the dividend should rise with them. Citizens would have a direct financial interest in the economy working, not only in their own wage.

The open problems are severe.

First, scale. To pay a dividend that matters, the fund needs a large asset base. If the average payout is $2,000 a year, a country with 250 million adults needs $500 billion a year. At a 4% payout ratio, that is a $12.5 trillion fund. A one-time tax on top wealth may not get there without being confiscatory, politically explosive, or triggering asset migration. An ongoing capital tax might work, but only if it is broad, simple, and hard to avoid.

Second, what counts as national growth. If the fund buys global index funds, it is easier to run and may be more stable, but it gives citizens a stake in world growth, not the domestic economy. If it invests heavily at home, it becomes an industrial policy machine. It will be pulled by politicians toward favored regions, favored industries, and favored friends. Alaska’s Permanent Fund works partly because the asset is a single resource with a relatively clear cash flow. A whole economy is messier.

Third, governance. A fund with universal payouts is a political target. It can be raided to cover deficits, overpaid to buy votes, or underpaid to save the treasury. If the payout becomes a legal entitlement, the state loses the ability to adjust when growth slows. If it is discretionary, people will not feel ownership.

Fourth, distortion. A tax on capital gains, exits, or corporate value can change investment behavior. Companies may delay exits, shift value into compensation structures, incorporate abroad, or price the tax into returns. A one-time levy is easier to understand but harder to make fair, because wealth is not the same as income and valuations are contestable.

Fifth, legitimacy. If ordinary people receive a check but cannot see what the fund owns, how it is invested, or why the payout changed, it will feel like a transfer. The “stake” part has to be real: transparent holdings, independent trustees, public reporting, and some citizen accountability, even if not direct voting on every investment.

I am not sure the exact tax design is solvable. I am more sure that the current setup is unstable: a small number of people own the capital that is becoming more important, while most people have only a wage claim on an economy that is increasingly automating the wage claim. A citizen fund would not fix that by itself. It would not address skills, healthcare, housing, or the social meaning of work. But it would change one thing: the upside of growth would stop being invisible to the people who do not own the machines.
rejected:
I spent the last decade helping founders build machines that do the work of three people with the precision of one. I’ve watched labor’s share of national income shrink while capital’s share expands. The standard defense is that this is just efficiency. But efficiency without distribution isn’t a market; it’s a enclosure.

We are currently in a situation where the people who do the work have the least claim on the fruits of that work. Automation doesn’t just displace jobs; it displaces the mechanism by which people participate in wealth creation. If you aren’t an owner, and you aren’t highly specialized enough to command a premium wage, you are outside the system.

Here is a policy idea that has been floating around my head: a universal capital endowment, funded not by taxes on labor, but by a tax on automated productivity gains.

Let’s be clear about what this is not. It is not a universal basic income. A UBI is a transfer of existing wealth. This is a mechanism to create new ownership. Every citizen would receive a non-transferable equity stake in a national pool of corporate capital. You cannot sell it. You cannot leverage it. But you receive the dividends, and you have a vote in how the capital is deployed, subject to guardrails that prevent political capture.

The logic is that as automation raises returns on capital, the state should socialize the upside of that efficiency. It aligns the interests of the worker with the shareholder. When the robot works, the citizen gets paid.

The open problems are severe.

First, valuation. How do you measure "automated productivity gains" without letting companies define their own baseline? If a firm argues that its profits came from better management rather than software, it escapes the tax. The administrative burden of auditing this distinction would be immense. We would need a regulatory agency with the technical sophistication of the SEC but the mandate of the IRS.

Second, governance. If every citizen has a vote on how this capital is deployed, you have handed the economy to a referendum. Markets move faster than legislatures. A national holding company might become a slow, risk-averse entity that picks only safe, incremental investments, stifling the very innovation it was meant to capture. Alternatively, it could become a vehicle for rent-seeking, with politicians directing capital to their donors.

Third, the political economy of the status quo. The current class of asset owners does not want their returns socialized. They will lobby to define "automation" narrowly, to exclude financial engineering, and to carve out exemptions for their specific industries. The politics of implementation will be worse than the economics of design.

Finally, there is the risk of moral hazard. If people feel they have a permanent, passive claim on the future, does that dampen the incentive to take entrepreneurial risks? Or does it provide the safety net that allows for more risky behavior? We don’t know.

I’m not sure this is the right policy. I’m not sure it’s even possible. But the alternative—accepting that the people who built the machines have no claim on the output of those machines—is a choice. And I don’t think it’s a sustainable one.

prompt: A 19-year-old guitarist from Alabama emailed me wanting to become a session musician. He's eyeing an expensive music school in Hollywood but is scared of decades of debt. Write the reply you'd send him, with real advice on how to actually get there.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Subject: Re: Session musician

Thanks for writing. I’ll be blunt because the money is at stake: do not sign up for the expensive Hollywood school on a loan yet. If the program will put you at $80,000, $100,000, or $150,000 in debt, you are buying a gamble, not a job. Session work pays when people trust you. A diploma does not create that trust. It only creates a payment schedule.

I’m not saying school is useless. I’m saying the school you’re looking at has to earn its cost. Ask them for the names of graduates who are working as session musicians in the local market. Call three of them. Ask what they earned in the first two years and whether the school helped them get the first paid session. If the school can’t do that, or if the graduates say it mostly taught you to be more expensive, walk away.

Here is the path I’d take if I were 19, in Alabama, and trying to become a session guitarist.

1. Pick the market, not the postcard.

Los Angeles is the most famous session town, but it is also the most expensive place to be unknown. Rent and food can add $25,000 or more a year to the cost of going there. If you move to LA with no savings, no job, and no local reputation, the city will teach you to survive, not to play sessions.

Look at other session markets first. Nashville has a deep country and pop-country session world. Atlanta has a large recording, R&B, gospel, and film/TV market, and it is usually cheaper than LA. If your guitar style fits those scenes, you can build a real reputation there and then move to LA with a track record instead of a credit card.

If you are certain you want LA, do not go there to “find out.” Go there with a reason for someone to answer your phone: a studio assistant job, a day job, a booked session, or a specific network of people who know your work.

2. Build the instrument for sessions, not for your hero worship.

A session guitarist is not hired to be the most exciting player in the room. You are hired to make the record sound right quickly. That means time, tone, reading, ear, and restraint.

You need to be able to take a lead sheet or chord chart, hear a reference track, and play the right part without making a scene. If you can only play by tab and by memory, you will be limited. Start learning standard notation and chord symbols now. You do not need to become a conservatory theorist, but you need to be able to read a page and follow a click.

Your daily practice should be boring enough that you want to quit. That is how you know it is working.

A useful split:

- One hour on time and feel: play simple chord changes with a metronome at slow tempos, then faster. Play straight, swing, half-time, and different genres. If you can play a simple blues comping part at 60 bpm and it still feels alive, you are doing it.
- One hour on ear training and transcription: pick one part from a record and learn it without looking at the tab. Not the whole song at first. Just the guitar part, or the comping, or the fill. Then write it down.
- One hour on reading and charts: take a simple lead sheet and play it with a click. Add dynamics. Play it softer, harder, cleaner, dirtier. Make the same chart serve three different songs.
- One hour on repertoire and style: learn the actual language of the music you want to play. If you want country sessions, learn how country rhythm guitar works. If you want pop, learn how to double, texture, and leave space. If you want film, learn how to play a cue that supports an edit.

If you are fast but you cannot play a simple chord change in time, fix the time first. Speed is not a session skill. Accuracy is.

Also learn to play less. The solo is the last thing you are hired for. If a producer says “less,” play less. If a take is not helping the song, mute the amp and listen. A good session player can make a bad take sound better by not overplaying.

3. Make proof you can work.

You need a small home setup that lets you record and send files cleanly. You do not need a $5,000 guitar. You need a reliable guitar, a good cable, a tuner, an audio interface, a decent microphone, and a DAW. Pro Tools is common in professional studios, so learn it if you can. Logic is fine if you can deliver what is asked.

Make a 90-second reel. No three-minute intro. No “my name is…” Show four or five short clips: pop rhythm, rock lead, country comping, R&B, film texture. Each one should be short, clean, and obviously useful. The listener should think, “I could put that on a record,” not “Wow, he can bend.”

Get on local records. Find artists in your area who need a guitarist for an EP, a demo, a worship service, a student film, or a commercial. Charge a modest fee, or trade for a good recording and a credit if they cannot pay much. The point is not fame. The point is a track you can show and a person who will vouch for you.

Do remote work too. Platforms like SoundBetter and Fiverr can be a race to the bottom, but they can also give you early reviews and cash while you build a local base. Do not stay there forever. Use them to learn how to deliver files on time: labeled correctly, aligned to the click, mixed at a sane level.

4. Get hired locally before you chase the big market.

The first paid session is usually small. A local band’s record. A producer’s demo. A church. A podcast jingle. A student film. Do not wait for the big one. The first one teaches you how the transaction works: how to quote, how to show up, how to handle revisions, how to invoice, how to be easy.

Reliability is a musical skill. Being on time, knowing the chart, and not arguing about your solo are part of the sound. In sessions, people do not book only the best player. They book the player they do not have to worry about.

Join a band even if it is not your style. Sessions are ensemble work. You need to know how to listen to a drummer, follow a bass player, and adjust when the arrangement changes in the room.

Find a working musician who already does the kind of sessions you want. Pay for lessons if you have to. A working player who knows how a session runs is more useful than a classroom that only talks about music.

5. Build the target-city network from where you are.

You do not have to be in LA to start building a reason to be in LA.

Make a list of 50 people in the city you want: engineers, producers, songwriters, studio owners, music supervisors, working guitarists, session booking agents. Send short, specific notes. Not “I’m a hard worker and I dream of LA.” Something like: “I’m a guitarist from Alabama working on remote sessions and local records. I can play country comping, pop rhythm, and simple leads. Here is a 90-second reel. If you have 15 minutes, I’d like to ask how you get hired in town.”

Do ten of these a week. Do not attach a 20-minute demo. Do not beg. Do not follow up five times in one day. Be professional enough that a “no” still leaves a good impression.

If you want LA specifically, the best entry point is often a studio assistant job, not a student job. Assistantships are not rich, but they put you inside the room where the work happens. You learn how studios run, how players are treated, how sessions are booked, and how the money moves. But you need to line one up before moving. Rent in LA will not wait for you to figure it out.

6. Protect the money.

If the school costs $60,000 in tuition and you add living costs, you are easily looking at a seven-figure decision over time, not a six-figure one. A $100,000 loan at 7 percent costs about $1,160 a month over 10 years, or about $775 a month over 20 years. If your first real income is $35,000 or $45,000, that payment eats rent, gear, and the ability to take small jobs while you build.

Do not move on debt to chase a reputation. Save six to 12 months of expenses first. Work a day job while you build your music base. Teaching can help, but it is not a shortcut; it trades practice time for money. Use it carefully.

If a school is serious about you, it should help with the money. Scholarships, assistantships, grants, or a clear local job pipeline change the equation. If the answer is “just take the loan and work hard,” that is the answer.

The hardest objection to all of this is probably: “But if I’m not in LA, I can’t get LA sessions.” That is true. But moving to LA without a base is the most expensive way to learn that. You can build a remote base, a local base, and a savings base first. When you move, you are not a stranger with a guitar. You are a player with a reel, a job or a path to one, and people who know your work.

Here is a realistic timeline.

In 12 months: you can play a simple lead sheet with a click, you can transcribe a basic part by ear, you have recorded at least five usable tracks, and you have had 50 meaningful conversations with working musicians, producers, or engineers.

In 18 months: you have your first paid session or a regular gig that pays like one. It may be small. That is fine.

In 24 months: if you still want the bigger city, you have six months of savings and a specific reason to go there. If you do not have those two things, you are not ready to move. You are ready to keep building.

Send me three clips: one where you comp, one where you play a simple lead, and one where you follow a chart. Tell me what you have saved and which city you are actually considering. Then we can talk about whether the school is worth it.
rejected:
Don’t go to Hollywood.

The "expensive music school" model is a trap. It assumes that access to A-list producers is the bottleneck in your career. It isn’t. The bottleneck is your ability to play what is asked, on time, in a specific style, without ego. You can learn that in Alabama. The only thing Hollywood offers that your local studio doesn’t is a headstart on your credit score.

Session work is a trade, not a performance art. A pop producer doesn’t need a virtuoso who can shred; they need a player who can nail a specific chord voicing, stay in the pocket, and not argue about the arrangement. If you spend four years and $50,000 learning to sound like a jazz icon, you will have wasted time. You need to learn to sound like whatever the record needs.

Here is how you actually get there:

1.  **Get a job in the studio.** Not a music school. Find the best local recording studio in your state. Walk in. Don’t ask for a gig. Ask if they need someone to clean, load gear, run errands, or sit in the control room and take notes. You are paying tuition with labor. In six months, you will know how a tracking session actually works, what engineers hate, and how the money flows.
2.  **Build a portfolio of "correct" sounds, not "cool" sounds.** Record yourself playing in five distinct styles: 80s pop, hip-hop, country, indie rock, and orchestral. Do not post them as "my music." Post them as "my session demos." If a producer hears your "creative" take on a standard drum loop, they will think you are difficult. If they hear you replicate the exact timbre and timing of a famous track, they will think you are employable.
3.  **Learn the language of the room.** Learn Pro Tools. Learn Ableton. Understand what a comp is, what a quantize is, and why a producer says "let's leave it." When you speak the language of the engineer, you stop being a liability and start being a tool.
4.  **Network with engineers, not artists.** Artists are fickle. Engineers are the gatekeepers. If the engineer trusts your hands and your attitude, they will call you when the artist brings in a demo that needs tracking. Build that trust locally first. Once you have a reputation for being reliable, you can move.

You are 19. You have the advantage of time and low overhead. Use it to accumulate work experience, not degrees. The debt will be with you for decades; the skills you learn from a local engineer will be with you for your career.

prompt: Write an essay about the word "racism". People use it to mean very different things, and I suspect that muddle is part of why political arguments get so nasty. Open with some puzzling hypothetical cases if that helps, and take your time getting to a view about what we should do differently.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Suppose a bank denies a loan to a Black applicant because the officer says, in the privacy of his mind, that he does not want that kind of person in the neighborhood. Suppose another bank denies a loan to an applicant from a census tract with a low median income, a tract that is mostly Black because of decisions made forty years ago. The second bank uses a formula. It claims to be colorblind. Now suppose a white resident says, “I am not racist; I have Black friends,” while voting against a plan that would integrate a school two miles from his house. And suppose a Black man says, “White people cannot be trusted.” Are all four racist? The answer depends on whether you are checking a heart, an act, a machine, or a social position. That is where the trouble begins.

The word racism is not a mistake. It did necessary work. It grew up around a real evil: the idea that human beings come in natural ranks, and that some ranks deserve to rule. Slavery, colonial exclusion, segregation, and scientific ranking all fed on that idea. To call a practice racist was to say that it was not merely unfair, but that it treated race as a moral fact. The word’s strength was its simplicity. Its danger is the same simplicity.

In current use, racism can mean a belief, an act, a structure, or a position. A belief: this group is inferior, lazy, dangerous, or less entitled to respect. An act: I will not hire, house, teach, or protect you because of your race. A structure: a set of rules produces different outcomes for racial groups, and the people who control the rules leave it that way. A position: you belong to the group that has, on the whole, used race to dominate others. These are connected. Beliefs can justify acts, acts can build structures, structures can protect positions. But they are not the same claim, and they do not fall or stand together.

Political arguments get nasty because the word lets a speaker move among those claims without saying so. If I say “you are racist” and you answer “I don’t hate Black people,” I can say I meant your vote, not your heart. If you answer “the disparity is economic,” I can say I meant the system, not the budget line. Each reply is true, and neither answers the question that was actually asked. The charge also lands on identity. To be called racist is not to be called wrong; it is to be sorted into a kind of person. Once that happens, the person being accused has a strong incentive to deny everything, and the accuser has a strong incentive to treat the denial as proof of bad faith. The policy becomes a side issue.

The hardest objection to untangling the word is that the muddle has a politics. If we insist that racism requires a racist heart, we give a pass to institutions that were built by racism and still operate in racial patterns. A credit score, a school boundary, a police stop, a hiring test may be neutral in the moment and poisonous in the aggregate. To call the result “bias” or “inefficiency” is to drain it of its history. The people who suffer the outcome are not the people who define the word. So any proposal that sounds like “let’s stop calling systems racist” deserves suspicion.

That objection is right, and it shows where the fix should go. We should not stop calling institutions racist. We should make the claim specific enough to be tested. A bank is racist if it sorts customers by race. It is also racist, in a defensible sense, if it uses a proxy that it knows functions as a racial sort and refuses to correct it. A school district is racist if it maintains boundaries that reproduce segregation after being told what those boundaries do. This is not the same as saying every statistical difference is racism. Race is a social category, and many inequalities attach to it for complex reasons. But when a known racial pattern is left in place by people who could change it, the word racism is not an insult. It is a description of what the institution is for.

The position sense needs different handling. It is true that race is not only a set of individual opinions; it is a distribution of power. A white person in a country with a history of white supremacy occupies a different social position from a Black person, whether or not they hold hateful views. That fact matters. But if “you are racist” means only “you are in that position,” the statement is no longer an accusation that can be answered. It is a coordinate. It may be true, but it tells the person little they can do except change their ancestry. For argument, we need claims that involve agency: you benefit from this arrangement, you defend it, you stay silent when it is challenged, you vote to keep it. Those claims can be true or false, and they point toward action.

So the practical change is not to retire the word but to stop using it bare in serious disagreement. When someone says “that is racist,” ask which sense is at work: a belief, an act, an institution, or a position. And when you make the charge, say which one. “I think you are prejudiced” is a claim about your mind. “I think your act discriminates” is a claim about your conduct. “I think this institution is racist” is a claim about rules, outcomes, and maintenance. “You have the social position of the dominant group” is a claim about location, not character. The first two can be complicated by good intentions; the third can be true even when everyone in the room is personally decent; the fourth can be true even when the person is fighting the system. Keeping them separate does not weaken the charge. It makes the charge harder to dodge and easier to prove.

Go back to the cases. The officer who does not want Black people in the neighborhood is racist in belief and act. The formula may be colorblind on paper, but if the bank knows it re-creates old exclusion and leaves it running, the bank is racist in structure. The resident with Black friends may have no hatred in his heart, yet his vote against integration can still be a racist act if its effect is to keep schools separate by race. The Black man who says white people cannot be trusted is expressing a prejudice, perhaps one formed by real treatment, but it is not the same kind of claim as the power-backed hierarchy that has shaped the other three. If we can say that much, the argument can begin. The word racism will still carry weight. It should. The point is to make the weight land on something that can be examined, changed, or refuted, instead of on a person’s whole self.
rejected:
Consider a man who buys a house in a neighborhood where he is the only person of color. He is polite, pays his taxes, and fixes his gutters. But every time he walks to the mailbox, he feels the eyes of the neighbors. He feels a specific, cold weight in his chest. A week later, a woman from that same neighborhood moves into a predominantly white suburb. She is greeted with warm smiles and offers of lemonade. She feels welcomed.

If the first man says he experienced racism, and the second says she did not, are they using the same word?

On the surface, it seems obvious that the first man was treated differently. But was he treated *because* of his race? The neighbors might not have cared about his skin color. They might simply be insular, suspicious of change, or bad at small talk. If the second woman had moved in, they might have been just as cold. If so, the first man was the victim of general human indifference, not racism. Yet, to him, the difference in treatment was inextricably linked to his visibility as an outsider. To say “it wasn’t racism” feels like a gaslighting tactic, minimizing his lived reality.

Now consider the opposite case. A hiring manager rejects a candidate with a resume that lists a degree from a prestigious university. The manager is Black. The candidate is also Black. The manager thinks, “I went to that school, and I’m tired of seeing it on resumes. It feels performative.” He rejects the candidate. No one can point to a slur, a segregated facility, or a denied service. But the rejection was based on a cultural marker that is deeply coded by race. Is this racism? It is certainly prejudice. But if “racism” is defined strictly as prejudice plus power, or as systemic institutional bias, this individual act of bias might not qualify. Yet to the rejected candidate, it feels indistinguishable from any other form of racial exclusion.

The muddle arises because the word “racism” has become a container for three distinct phenomena that people conflate.

First, there is **individual malice**. This is the bigot. He hates a group of people for their biological traits and acts on that hatred. This is the oldest definition. It is clear, morally unambiguous, and relatively easy to identify. When this happens, the problem is solved by naming the act and punishing the actor.

Second, there is **systemic disparity**. This is the observation that groups with different racial traits occupy different positions in society. Black Americans have lower median wealth than white Americans. They are incarcerated at higher rates. They live in neighborhoods with less lead paint. These are facts. But are these facts “racism”? Not in the sense of individual malice. No single person is necessarily acting out of hatred. The disparity is the result of historical policies, legal structures, and economic forces that have compounded over generations. Calling the *outcome* “racism” conflates the cause (history, policy, inertia) with the effect (inequality). It is like calling a flooded basement “water.” The water is there, but the word doesn’t tell you if the roof is leaking or the foundation is cracked.

Third, there is **social friction**. This is the uncomfortable space where people of different backgrounds interact and fail to understand each other’s cues. A white person makes a joke that lands as casual banter but lands as a microaggression on a Black listener. A Black person interprets a white person’s silence as hostility, when it is actually social anxiety. These interactions are messy, subjective, and often asymmetrical. They are not necessarily acts of malice, nor are they necessarily systemic failures. They are the grinding gears of a society that has not yet figured out how to be a diverse one.

The political nastiness comes from using the single word “racism” to cover all three.

When a politician points to a crime statistic and calls it “racism,” they are using the word to mean **systemic disparity**. They are arguing that the structure is broken. When a civil rights group uses the word, they are often pointing to **systemic disparity** to demand policy changes, or to **individual malice** to demand accountability.

But when a conservative commentator hears “racism,” they are usually listening for **individual malice**. They are looking for the bigot. If they don’t see a bigot, they reject the premise. So, if a Black man says, “The criminal justice system is racist,” he is describing a structural reality: police practices, sentencing guidelines, and community composition all interact to produce disparate outcomes. If a white man hears this and thinks, “I am not a racist, I don’t hate Black people, therefore the claim is false,” they are not having a debate. They are speaking different languages. The first man is talking about the machine; the second man is talking about the operator.

The confusion deepens because the word carries a moral weight that is disproportionate to the diagnostic precision it offers. “Racism” is a moral verdict. It implies guilt. It implies a hierarchy of victimization. It is a word that, once deployed, ends conversation rather than starting it. To accuse someone of racism is to say they are on the wrong side of history. To deny it is to say they are not. There is little room in the middle for nuance.

We should stop using the word for everything.

If you are describing a specific act of hatred, use the word. If a man spits on a stranger because of their skin, call it racism. It is precise, it is true, and it is actionable.

If you are describing a pattern of inequality that results from policy, stop using the word. Say what the policy is. Say that the redlining of the 1930s led to the wealth gap of today. Say that mandatory minimum sentences affect populations differently based on who is stopped. These are descriptions of cause and effect. They are harder to dismiss than the label “racism,” because they require the listener to look at the data, not the motive. You can argue about the data. You cannot argue about the moral character of a word.

If you are describing the awkwardness of a specific interaction, call it a misunderstanding. Call it a failure of empathy. Call it friction. “Racism” is too heavy a word for a missed cue in a conversation. It turns every social stumble into a moral trial.

The goal is not to sanitize language. The goal is to make language work. If we want to fix the system, we need to name the system. If we want to punish the bigot, we need to name the bigot. If we want to navigate a diverse society, we need to name the friction.

When we collapse these three things into one word, we allow the most defensible position to win. The person who says, “I’m not racist, I have Black friends,” has successfully deflected a conversation about historical policy, policing, or even their own clumsy behavior. They have moved the debate from the public square of facts to the private sanctuary of their own intentions. And because intentions are always pure in the eyes of the person holding them, the debate ends in a stalemate.

We don’t need to agree on who is the "real" victim or who is the "true" racist. We need to agree on what is actually happening. The machine is broken. The operators are mixed. The gears are grinding. Fix the machine. Train the operators. Lubricate the gears. Don’t just stand around shouting "racism" at the smoke.

chosen:
If modernist poetry has made you feel like you are being asked to admire a locked room from the outside, *Kora in Hell* is the odd comfort. If you know Williams from the red wheelbarrow, this is earlier and stranger. It is not a collection of poems. It is a small 1920 prose book, subtitled *A Discourse on Music*. You can open it without a key because the sentences are in prose. The trouble is that Williams uses prose the way a drummer uses a snare: the words are there, but the point is the hit. It reads like a doctor’s fever chart for a patient named Rhythm.

The book is a manifesto, a rant, and a tune-up all at once. Williams is trying to explain what the new American poem should sound like, and he keeps getting distracted by the fact that the old poem sounds like a dead language. To him, meter is not a neutral tool. It is an inheritance, a habit, a way of making the present speak in a costume. He wants poetry to have the phrase, not the foot; the breath, not the rule; the street, not the drawing room. The result is a book that talks about rhythm while trying to become one.

How was it written? In the manner of a man who had a day job, a strong opinion, and no patience for ceremony. Williams was a physician, and the prose has that diagnostic snap: no, not that; yes, this; again, but faster. It is full of fragments, dashes, false starts, and sudden declarations. That is not a flaw to be corrected. It is the argument. If he insists that the new verse should be made of phrases, he writes in phrases. If he believes the old forms are stiff, the sentences stiffen only to be broken. Read a page and you will see a mind that has decided to stop polishing and start playing.

This is where the book can be funny, if you are willing to laugh at its confidence. Williams is not a subtle explainer. He is a converter. He will tell you what a poem is not, as if negation were a genre. He will pile up musical terms, American terms, urgent terms, and then land on a point that seems obvious only after he has shouted it. There is a lot of posturing. There are passages where the energy outruns the idea, where the man is clearly more excited about the new thing than the reader is yet. I have put the book down for this. I have picked it up because the next page started to sound like a band finding a tempo.

That tempo is the real subject. The title sounds like a Gothic novel, a little character study of someone in damnation, but the book is not about hell in any way that will comfort a theology student. I do not think the title is a riddle you have to solve before entering. The name is a door with a strange sign on it. Behind it is a room full of music: jazz, the new American idiom, the idea that a poem can be built from the way a phrase lands rather than the way a foot marches. Williams is not saying poetry should be nonsense. He is saying it should be alive in the mouth, and that the mouth is American, and that America has a new music, so why keep marching in iambic pentameter like a man in a funeral parade?

Do you need a literary critic? No. You need a little context, and the context fits in a sentence: Williams is trying to make American poetry sound like American speech and American music, and he is impatient with the old forms. A critic can add the genealogy—Pound, Europe, the postwar mood, the desire to make it new—but the book does not depend on the genealogy. It depends on your ear. If you read it slowly, treating every fragment as a clue, it becomes a puzzle. If you read it at its own speed, it becomes a character. The best method is to read a page, then another, then stop when it gets tedious, then come back when you are annoyed. The annoyance is useful. It means you are listening.

I would not recommend it as a first exposure to modernist poetry if what you want is a single beautiful poem to sit in your pocket. It is not that. It is a book about the making of poems, and its own making is part of the show. But it is a better first exposure than most anthologies, because it names the problem instead of hiding in it. Modernist poetry often asks you to trust a surface. *Kora in Hell* asks you to trust a rhythm. That is not the same thing, and it is much less frightening. Buy the cheap edition. Read it in an afternoon. If you finish it wondering whether the man was brilliant or merely loud, you have read it correctly.
rejected:
You do not need a literary critic to read *Kora in Hell*. In fact, a literary critic would probably ruin it by telling you that the book is a "deconstruction of the Romantic ego" or a "manifesto for American Imagism." That is boring. The book is not a puzzle. It is a mood.

*Kora in Hell* (1920) is a collection of 43 poems. They are short. Most are under ten lines. Some are three lines. They are written in a style Williams called "variable line," which sounds technical but is just the rhythm of someone talking fast because they are excited. The lines start at different points on the page, creating jagged, uneven blocks of text. It looks like a receipt that got torn in half. It looks like a thought that refuses to sit still.

The poems are not about deep, tragic things. They are about a woman walking, a red wheelbarrow, a slice of lemon, the feeling of being awake when you should be asleep. The subject matter is so mundane that your first instinct will be to roll your eyes. "Oh, you wrote a poem about a piece of fruit. How original." But that is the point. Williams is trying to prove that if you look at a lemon closely enough, without adding any metaphors about the sun or the soul or death, the lemon is already interesting. He is stripping away the 19th-century habit of dressing up ordinary things in fancy clothes.

The "hell" in the title refers to the poet’s own mental state. Williams was a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey. He was depressed, restless, and convinced that American poetry was dying because it was copying European masters. He wrote these poems to save himself from that depression. The energy in the book is manic. It is the literary equivalent of a person pacing around a kitchen at 2 a.m. saying, "Look at this! Look at this! Isn't it weird that this exists?"

There is a risk in reading it, though. Because the poems are so short and so plain, they can feel like fragments. You might read "The Red Wheelbarrow" and think, "Okay, so? I’ve seen wheelbarrows." If you stop there, you are missing the point. You are not supposed to analyze the wheelbarrow. You are supposed to see it. The poem is a spotlight. It shines on a red wheelbarrow in the rain and says, *This is the only thing in the world right now.*

You do not need to know who Kora was (a muse name borrowed from Greek mythology) or what Imagism is. You just need to be willing to let a poem be small. If you expect a narrative arc, a moral lesson, or a reference to Shakespeare, you will be annoyed. If you are willing to stare at a few words for ten seconds and feel the texture of them, you will find the book funny, urgent, and surprisingly fresh. It reads like a text message from a brilliant, slightly unhinged friend who has just noticed something beautiful in the yard and is too excited to wait for you to get up.

prompt: Write a short, punchy blog post defending nitpicking: why it's worth correcting small exaggerations and falsehoods even when they're on your own side's talking points, and when it isn't. Include caveats.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**In Defense of Nitpicking**

The most useful correction often starts with “Yes—and also not quite.”

When your side says “the data prove it,” and the data only suggest it, correcting that is not pedantry. It is maintenance. A movement that lies a little teaches everyone that its truths are negotiable. A policy debate that rounds by a billion can become a debate about a different policy. A campaign that says “everyone agrees” when a minority agrees has made the minority invisible.

Small falsehoods are not small because they are small. They are small only until they become the version people repeat. “Almost all” becomes “all.” “Most years” becomes “always.” “It was worse then” becomes “progress is impossible.” Once the inflated claim is the baseline, the honest claim sounds like a defense.

This matters most when the exaggeration is on your side. Allies can be sloppy because they expect you to cover for them. If you don’t correct the cover story, you own it. Not morally, maybe, but practically: the public will remember the claim, not the footnote.

But nitpicking has a failure mode. The worst kind treats language as the only thing that matters. You can be exact about a statistic while missing that the person is frightened. You can win a word and lose the room. You can make your side look bloodless, more concerned with sounding right than doing good.

So the test is not “Is this technically false?” It is: “Does the inaccuracy change what someone would do, believe, or feel?”

If a friend says, “This law is a disaster,” and the law is actually a mixed bag with one serious problem, correct it. The mixed bag is more true and more useful.

If a supporter says, “The other side doesn’t care about people,” maybe don’t. That may be a feeling, not a census. If it’s clearly hyperbole, let it be hyperbole. If the forum is a comment section, maybe don’t. If the person is trying to be heard, maybe don’t. If the correction will be read as a loyalty test, maybe don’t. If the real issue is power and you are polishing adjectives, don’t.

And if the exaggeration is load-bearing—if the whole argument depends on “always” or “everyone”—then it isn’t a nitpick. It’s the point. Challenge it plainly.

The good nitpick is quiet about itself. It does not say “actually” with a smile full of knives. It says: “I want to say the same thing, but I don’t want to say it too fast.”

That is the version worth keeping.
rejected:
The most common objection to nitpicking is that it’s a distraction. You are trying to fix the decimal point while the building burns. This is true, but only when the fire is real.

Most of the time, the building is not on fire. The debate is about a policy that affects 4% of the population, not 40%. The statistic is off by a factor of three. The quote is missing the context that changes its meaning.

When we let those errors slide because they support our side, we are not being strategic. We are being dishonest. We are borrowing credibility from the truth to pay for a lie. And the debt comes due.

There are two costs to unchecked exaggeration. The first is external. The opposition notices. They don’t need to attack the core of your argument; they just need to point to the inflated number. Now the entire conversation is about your integrity, not your policy. You have handed them the microphone.

The second cost is internal. If you allow your allies to exaggerate, you are training them to value victory over accuracy. Next time, the exaggeration will be larger. The next time, the falsehood will be central. You cannot build a movement on a foundation of sand and expect it to hold when the wind blows.

Correcting small falsehoods is an act of respect for the audience. It tells them: *I believe you are smart enough to handle the actual truth. I am not trying to manipulate you.*

But there is a limit.

If the correction is pedantic to the point of obscuring the main point, you are not a truth-teller. You are a troll. If the “exaggeration” is a standard rhetorical flourish—“prices are skyrocketing” when they are up 15%—correcting it is a waste of everyone’s time. The spirit of the statement is clear.

The test is relevance. Does the error change the conclusion? If the data says the problem is a leak and you say it is a flood, you must correct it. If the data says it is a leak and you say it is a significant problem, you are free to let it slide.

Nitpicking is not about being right. It is about being useful. If the truth is stronger than the lie, say the truth. If the truth is weaker, you have a bigger problem than a nitpick.

prompt: I keep seeing a particular kind of bad argument in debates where someone who says 'we should do some of Y too' gets treated as though they claim 'only Y matters.' Can you write a short blog post naming and explaining this pattern, with several examples and some sympathy for why it happens?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**The “Only Y Matters” Strawman**

There is a common move in policy debates that goes like this:

Person A says, “We should do more of Y.”  
Person B replies, “So you think only Y matters?”

Person A did not say that. Person A said that Y is currently underweighted, or that it has been ignored too long, or that the present mix of priorities is badly skewed. Person B has turned that into a claim of exclusivity: if Y gets any room, everything else must vanish.

The pattern shows up everywhere.

Someone says, “We should spend more on public transit.” The reply is, “You want to ban cars and end the economy.” Someone says, “We should put more money into AI interpretability.” The reply is, “You want to stop building AI.” Someone says, “We should enforce existing labor laws more consistently.” The reply is, “You want to destroy small businesses.” Someone says, “Vaccines are important, but ventilation matters too.” The reply is, “You think vaccines don’t work.”

In each case, the original point was about relative priority. The response treats it as a zero-sum demand: either Y gets everything, or Y gets nothing.

This is not always done in bad faith. There are understandable reasons it happens.

First, debates reward clear positions. “I want a better mix” is harder to dramatize than “they want to sacrifice everything else.” A person who says “we should also do Y” is making a comparative claim, and comparative claims are less satisfying to argue against. It is easier to build a caricature: the transit person hates cars, the safety person hates progress, the enforcement person hates enterprise.

Second, there is a fear of concession. If one side admits that the other side’s concern has some weight, the next question is how much weight. That can feel dangerous. If you are defending the current arrangement, even a modest shift can look like a foothold. So the rationalizing move is to treat any demand for change as a demand for replacement.

Third, the person making the original point may not be precise enough. “We should do some of Y too” is often too thin to defend. It does not say how much Y, what gets displaced, or whether Y is a complement or a substitute. If someone says “we need more testing” without saying whether that means taking money from treatment, hiring from another department, or finding new revenue, the listener is invited to assume the worst.

But inviting a bad inference is not the same as making the bad inference correct.

The real question is never whether Y matters at all. In most serious debates, everyone already agrees that Y matters. The question is how much Y matters relative to the other things on the table. If someone says, “We should raise Y’s priority,” the honest reply is not, “You’re a Y maximalist.” The honest reply is: “How much higher? What are you willing to give up? And is that tradeoff worth it?”

That is a harder conversation, but it is the actual one.
rejected:
The straw man of the "Only"

In online debates, a specific distortion appears with such regularity that it has its own grammar. One participant argues for a compromise position. They say, "We should increase funding for schools, but we also need to invest in infrastructure." The opponent responds, "So you think schools are the only thing that matters?"

This is the **Exclusive Inference Fallacy**. It takes a call for *more* of something and treats it as a dismissal of everything else.

### The Pattern

The structure is simple:

1.  **Claim A:** "We should prioritize X."
2.  **Claim B (by opponent):** "Therefore, you believe Y, Z, and W are irrelevant."

The error lies in the word "prioritize." To prioritize is to rank, not to eliminate. If you are building a house, you lay the foundation before you paint the walls. You are not claiming that paint doesn't exist. You are claiming that without the foundation, the paint has no surface to adhere to.

The opponent, however, hears the ranking as a banishment. They assume that because X is at the top of the list, the rest of the list is empty.

### Examples

**The Medical Triage**
A doctor in a war zone says, "We must treat the patients with internal bleeding first."
The critic says, "So you are saying the patients with broken arms are worthless?"
The doctor is managing resources under scarcity. The critic is demanding equal distribution of finite attention. These are not the same conversation.

**The Environmental Debate**
An economist says, "We must price carbon to incentivize change."
The activist says, "So you think the environment is just another market commodity?"
Pricing carbon is a tool for reducing emissions. It is not a philosophical stance on the intrinsic value of trees. The activist has moved from a policy mechanism to an ontological insult.

**The Tech Ethics**
A developer says, "We need to audit our AI models for bias before release."
The critic says, "So you think profit is the only goal?"
Auditing is a risk mitigation strategy. It is how you keep the business alive long enough to have any goals at all. The critic mistakes a safety check for a mission statement.

### Why It Happens

This fallacy is not usually born of stupidity. It is born of **emotional salience**.

When someone says, "We should do X," they are often reacting to a specific pain point. The person opposing them often feels a different pain point. The opponent of "prioritize schools" is often terrified that their specific concern—say, healthcare or housing—will be ignored in the budget fight.

They do not actually believe the original speaker thinks healthcare is unimportant. They believe the original speaker *doesn't care* about healthcare. These are different claims. The first is about the speaker's mental model; the second is about the speaker's empathy.

The Exclusive Inference Fallacy allows the opponent to attack the easier target: the speaker's alleged lack of empathy. It is more satisfying to call someone heartless than to engage with their argument for resource allocation. It turns a complex logistical problem into a moral character test.

### The Cost

The cost of this pattern is that it makes nuance impossible. If saying "we should do A first" is interpreted as "we should never do B," then the only safe thing to say is a flat, undifferentiated list of all possible good things.

"We must do schools, and healthcare, and roads, and bridges, and arts, and space exploration, all simultaneously, with equal weight."

This is not a policy. It is a litany. It satisfies no one because it commits to nothing. It allows everyone to walk away feeling that their specific cause has been acknowledged, while leaving the actual work of prioritization undone.

The fallacy protects the status quo by making any move forward look like a betrayal of everything else. It is a very effective shield, but it is made of straw.

chosen:
## The Busiest People Have the Clearest Priorities

A man in a clinic chair told me he couldn’t do the program. He had a job, a kid, no car, no money. I believed him. Then he pulled out his phone and showed me a text: a friend offering him twenty bucks if he would pick something up from a shop across town. He said, “I can do that tomorrow.”

Tomorrow he did not come to session. Tomorrow he went to the shop.

I don’t tell this to be cruel. I tell it because it keeps happening. People who cannot find fifteen minutes for a promise, a parent, a treatment plan, a bill, a relationship that is slowly dying will find three hours for the thing they love. The father who misses the recital but checks the fantasy football league every night. The woman who can’t manage the bus fare to her appointment but can manage the fare to the bar, the phone, the person, the machine.

We call this a time problem. It is not. Time is the least interesting part.

Money is usually clearer. A person may be broke in a real way: rent is high, wages are low, the system is stacked. But if the same person can produce $20 for a drug, $50 for a ticket, $100 for a gift to someone they want to impress, the scarcity is not total. It is selective. The wallet is doing what the calendar does. It is revealing what the person has already decided matters.

The hard objection is obvious: depression, trauma, chaos, poverty, disability, bad luck. These things can make obligations genuinely impossible. I do not think every missed appointment is a moral choice. But in the pattern I’m describing, the missed thing is not just hard. It is specific. It is the promise that would require them to be reliable, sober, present, accountable, or loving in a way that feels like a cost. The thing they love is not necessarily easier. It may be risky, expensive, and bad for them. But it is a place where they feel wanted, skilled, free, or like themselves.

That is the key. Obligations often ask a person to be responsible. The thing they love often lets them be themselves.

Responsibility is a strange demand. It says, “Show up for someone else’s world, before you feel ready, before you enjoy it, before you are sure it will go well.” For people who have been punished for needing, failed by institutions, or spent years being used, responsibility can feel like a trap. The thing they love, even if it is destructive, can feel like a home. It does not ask them to be mature. It asks them to be there, and it rewards them for it. A game rewards you. A substance rewards you. A certain person rewards you with the feeling that you matter. A habit rewards you with the feeling that you are still in control of something.

Addiction makes this sharper because it does not just compete with the good life. It becomes the good life, at least for the next hour. The next dose, the next hand, the next contact, the next hit is not a small item on the schedule. It is the center of gravity. Everything else becomes background noise. When the brain has decided that one thing is urgent, the rest of life starts to look like chores.

This is why shaming the “too busy” person usually fails. If I say, “You just don’t care,” I am right about the behavior and useless about the cause. The person may care in the abstract. They may know the obligation is good. They may even say they want to do it. But wanting is not the same as being moved. A person can know that treatment is important and still reach for the thing that makes the present moment bearable.

The useful question is not, “Why can’t they find time?” It is, “What is the thing they love actually giving them?” And, “What would have to be true for the obligation to feel less like a debt and more like a life?”

A promise that is only a demand will lose. It will lose to the phone, the bottle, the game, the person, the fantasy, the next easy relief. But if the obligation can become something the person wants to be part of—something where they are respected, where the cost is fair, where they can be honest about what they can do—then the calendar changes without a single lecture about priorities.

People do not run out of time. They run out of reasons to be the kind of person who keeps the promise. The thing they love is the place where they still feel like they have a reason to be themselves. Recovery, or a relationship, or a life, only starts when the other place begins to offer something like that too.
rejected:
The patient had a stack of overdue bills on the counter. They weren’t hiding them. He had brought them in, fanned out like a bad poker hand, and asked me to help him prioritize.

He paid for meth every day. He paid for it before rent, before the car payment, before the phone bill that got him disconnected. When I asked why he didn’t just stop, he shrugged. It wasn’t a lack of willpower. It was a difference in currency.

We talk about motivation as if it’s a muscle that gets tired. It isn’t. Motivation is a signal of value. If someone is "too busy" for their family, their job, or their health, they aren’t lazy. They are allocating resources to a higher-priority objective.

The brain doesn’t distinguish between a craving for a drug and a craving for a new car, a specific person, or a career. It just looks at the expected reward and the cost of effort. If the drug offers a reliable, immediate, and intense hit of dopamine, it wins the auction. The rent is distant. The shame is abstract. The high is now.

This is why trying to shame a person into change usually fails. You are asking them to devalue their most precious asset. You are asking them to look at the thing that makes them feel alive and say, "No, actually, that’s a waste of time." They won’t do it unless you offer a competitor.

The reason the addict finds time for the needle is that the needle is the thing they love. It’s the only thing in their life that provides a clear, immediate feedback loop. The rest of their life is a series of delayed, uncertain, and often punishing feedback loops.

To change the behavior, you have to change the value proposition. You don’t need to fix their schedule. You need to make the alternative more valuable than the addiction. That is a much harder, slower, and less clinical task than cutting off the supply. But it’s the only one that works.

**Cuddling Is Not a Warm-Up**

The first time I asked a partner to cuddle, plainly and without preamble, they went quiet. Not offended, exactly, but uncertain, as if I had changed the genre of the evening. I am asexual, and I am polyamorous. A lot of what I want from relationships is physical closeness that is not sex: being on a couch with someone, a hand on the small of my back, the weight of a body across my lap. I have learned to ask for it carefully, which means I have learned to ask for it rarely. That feels wrong.

Cuddling matters because it is one of the few ways a relationship can accumulate evidence. A grand gesture is memorable, but it is also expensive and therefore scarce. Cuddling is cheap. It can happen after dinner, during a bad episode, while watching something neither of us is interested in. Each time, someone is making a small decision: I will be soft with you, I will not use this proximity to escalate, I am available for a minute longer. Over months, that becomes a kind of knowledge. You know that a person can be near you without wanting something from you. You know your own body is allowed to relax in front of them. That is not a small thing.

In a culture that treats touch as a ladder toward sex, non-sexual closeness has no stable category. A hug is either friendly or not. Holding hands is either innocent or foreplay. Cuddling is either a prelude or a consolation prize for people who can’t manage the real thing. For an asexual person, that framework is not just incomplete; it is a dead end. If sex is the summit, then I am stuck in the foothills, and everyone assumes I am climbing. But the foothills are where I live. I need a vocabulary that says: this is not a substitute. This is not a lesser form of intimacy because it is missing the most famous part. This is the part I was looking for.

Polyamory makes the problem sharper because it multiplies the bodies involved. I do not expect one person to be all of my touch needs, and I do not want them to be. One partner may be good for long, silent cuddles. Another may be good for quick hugs and a hand in the pocket while we walk. Another may prefer close conversation with no physical contact at all. None of these arrangements is less committed than the others. But they require a level of specificity that monogamous scripts rarely reward. “I love you” is not enough. “I like being touched” is not enough. You have to say: I need ten minutes on the couch before I can do my evening. I need someone to sleep near me. I need a hand on my shoulder when I’m anxious, not a solution. I need you to ask before you pull me in.

That sounds logistical, and it is. But logistics are what make love possible when desire is not automatic.

Can whole communities make cuddling normal? I think they can, but only up to a point, and only if “normal” is defined carefully. A community makes a behavior normal when enough people can do it without being treated as an exception. If I ask for a cuddle and the response is curiosity or simple consent, the behavior is available. If the response is laughter, pity, or a long explanation of why I must be lonely, the behavior is available only at the cost of my dignity. Communities change that cost. A friend group with a comfortable couch and a history of people sitting close together is not the same as a friend group where anyone who initiates touch is immediately interpreted as making a move. The difference is not the furniture. It is the script.

Asexual and queer communities are especially well placed to do this, because they are already working on a different set of possibilities. We already have to explain that romance does not require sex. We already have to invent forms of relationship that the default narrative does not name. Cuddling fits naturally into that work. A “cuddle relationship” is not a failed sexual relationship; it is a relationship whose center is non-sexual physical closeness. A community that takes that seriously gives asexual people something rare: a model in which our bodies are not problems to be managed, but participants in intimacy.

But here is the objection I keep coming back to. If a community makes cuddling normal, can it also make it expected? The two are easy to confuse. Some people do not like being touched. Some people have trauma histories that make closeness dangerous. Some people have chronic pain, sensory differences, cultural backgrounds, or simply a temperament that finds unsolicited affection intrusive. A community that celebrates cuddling can quietly become a place where people who do not cuddle are seen as cold, broken, or unsocial. That would be bad. It would replace one pressure with another: the pressure to want sex, with the pressure to want touch.

So the goal is not universal participation. It is universal respect for the ask. Cuddling becomes normal when a person can say “yes” without being read as available for more, and when another person can say “no” without being read as rejecting the relationship. It is normal when a man in his forties can ask for a hug and not be mocked. It is normal when a teenager can pull away and not be punished. It is normal when “I’m not up for touch tonight” is as boring and acceptable as “I’m not hungry tonight.” That is a much lower bar than making everyone a cuddler, and a much higher one than leaving every person to negotiate touch from scratch in a world that assumes sex is the point.

Communities can build the lower bar in concrete ways. They can model asking: “Can I sit close?” “Do you want a hug?” “I’m going to put my feet on your legs; tell me if that’s annoying.” They can make refusal uneventful. They can create spaces where touch is explicitly optional—cuddle parties, if they are run with strict consent, are one example, though they are not the only one. They can stop treating public non-sexual affection as suspicious. They can let couples hold hands in a park without turning it into a story. In polyamorous contexts, they can encourage agreements that name non-sexual touch directly: who is expected to provide it, how often, what forms count, what happens when needs change.

I do not think a community can make bodies want what they do not want. It cannot make a person who flinches from touch feel safe simply by declaring touch wholesome. It cannot make a person who needs distance feel held simply by surrounding them with people who are hugging. The body is not a policy problem. What communities can do is reduce the social cost of saying what the body needs. If asking for closeness is expensive—because it might be sexualized, infantilized, or dismissed—people will not ask. They will go home and sit on their own couch, and the absence will look like contentment.

What I want, in the end, is not a world where everyone cuddles. I want a world where I can say “sit with me” and people understand that I am not being coy. I want non-sexual closeness to be a recognized currency of love, not a leftover from a love that failed. I want my partners to know that a hand on my back can be a complete sentence. If communities can make that ordinary, even in small rooms and small groups, they will have done something that no amount of theory can: they will have made it possible to be near another person and mean nothing more than that.
rejected:
The first thing people get wrong about asexuality is the idea that it is a lack. They look at your life and see a hole where the heat should be. They think you are cold. They are wrong. You are not cold. You are just tuned to a different frequency.

For me, that frequency is contact. Not the kind that leads to a finish line. Not the kind that requires performance, stamina, or the awkward negotiation of who is on top. I mean the kind where you lie down next to someone, and their body becomes a piece of furniture you can lean on. A heavy blanket. A wall that breathes.

Cuddling is not a prelude. It is the destination.

When two bodies align, the nervous system does something remarkable. It stops scanning for threats. The cortisol drops. The oxytocin rises. You feel safe in a way that words cannot manufacture. Words are abstract. They live in the air. Physical presence is concrete. It has weight, temperature, and texture. When someone rests their head on your shoulder, they are telling you, *I am here. I am not going to leave. You are not alone in this room.*

That is a profound thing to offer another human being. In a culture that treats intimacy as a transaction—a currency to be earned through sexual performance—cuddling is a radical act of generosity. It says that your body is valuable simply because it is yours. It does not need to do anything to be held.

But there is a friction here. The friction is that we have no infrastructure for non-sexual touch.

Think about how we are taught to touch. We shake hands. We hug briefly at parties, usually with the shoulders, rarely with the face. We kiss on the cheek in some cultures, but even that is fleeting. Beyond that, the only socially sanctioned reason to press your body against another person’s is sex. If you want to lie down next to your friend and stay that way for three hours, you are either in a romantic relationship or you are making them very uncomfortable.

This leaves a lot of people isolated. Not just asexuals. Think about the widower who misses the weight of his wife. Think about the college student who lives alone and misses the ambient warmth of a shared bed. Think about the elderly person in a care home who has not been touched with affection in months. We are all starving for something that is not food.

Can a community make this normal? I think it can, but only if it stops trying to mimic the sexual model and starts building its own.

The answer isn't to create "cuddling clubs" that feel like awkward dance parties. The answer is to decouple touch from romance. It requires a shift in how we view the bedroom and the couch. It requires friends who are comfortable saying, *I don't want to have sex with you, but I want to watch a movie with you and I want to be close.*

It requires language. We don't have good words for this. "Cuddle" is infantilizing. "Snuggle" is for babies. "Lap dog" is degrading. We need a vocabulary that treats non-sexual physical intimacy as an adult, serious, and vital form of connection.

Right now, the norm is solitary. We live in apartments. We sit across from each other in offices. We scroll our phones in parallel on the bus. We have engineered the physical presence of other humans out of our daily lives. We have made isolation the default state and intimacy the exception.

If we want to change that, we have to make the default more porous. We have to normalize the fact that humans are mammals, and mammals need to be near other mammals. We need to build spaces—physical and social—where the default expectation is proximity, not performance.

It will be messy. People will get the wrong idea. People will be awkward. People will have different boundaries and different levels of comfort. That is fine. The goal isn't to force everyone to cuddle. The goal is to make sure that when someone *does* want to cuddle, they have a place to do it without apology.

I am not looking for a partner to complete me. I am looking for a person to be near. And I think that is a reasonable thing to want.

prompt: Your team has a messy, fragile codebase that began life as a prototype, and people are itching to throw it out and start over. Tell the story of an alternative: how a careful cleanup went, with the pros and cons.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The rewrite proposal made sense on paper. The current system had begun as a two-week prototype: one database, one admin user, a cron job that did four unrelated things. It now carried most of the company’s revenue, a patchwork of integrations, and a pricing model that only two engineers could explain by memory. The new system would be clean, typed, and designed around the product we said we wanted to build. What the proposal did not price in was the fact that the messy system already knew things about customers, edge cases, and historical behavior that no one had written down.

We did not choose cleanup because we were sentimental about the code. We chose it because a full rewrite would have meant freezing the product for long enough that competitors could walk through the front door. We gave ourselves a narrower goal: make the old system comprehensible enough to decide whether it was salvageable. For one quarter, feature work slowed, and the team spent its time learning what the system actually did.

The first step was boring. We picked the most common production requests and traced them through the code, then wrote a plain description of each path. We found a discount that only applied when a gift card was present, a permission check that depended on the order of two database queries, and a webhook retry that could create duplicate invoices if the network timed out. These were not theoretical risks; they had been handled by support for years. We started adding tests around the parts that changed often and broke often: order totals, refunds, permissions, retries. The tests were ugly. One was named after a legacy discount code. We did not care. A test that recorded what the system did was worth more than a diagram of what it should do.

At the same time, we looked for dead weight. We turned on request logging for a week, compared the routes and jobs that actually ran against the modules in the repository, and deleted what no live path touched. That removed a substantial amount of code, but the bigger effect was psychological. When people could see which parts mattered, they stopped being afraid of every file. The codebase went from a dense forest to a map with some burned-out clearings.

The real turning point was not a refactor. It was a boundary. We decided that new business logic could no longer be added to the old views and models. It had to go through a small set of services with named inputs and outputs. At first this made work slower. A feature that used to be one controller edit became a service call, a data mapper, and a test. We accepted that cost for two sprints. After that, the old code stopped growing, and the team stopped feeling like it was bailing water with a cup. New work had a place to live, and old work could be cleaned without being rewritten in one heroic pass.

The pricing module was the best example. It had grown into a thousand-line model file with branches for every special customer from the early years. We moved the logic out one rule at a time. First the annual discount, then the nonprofit rate, then the rounding behavior that finance had once approved in an email. Each step was small: extract a method, add a test from a production example, delete the old branch. When the last branch moved, the old model was a thin adapter, and the new service had a README, explicit inputs, and no direct access to the database. The code was longer in places, but a new engineer could read a function and say what it meant without asking someone who had left the company.

We also renamed things, but only where the names were lying. “Customer” meant a person, a company, and a billing account in different places. “Active” meant subscribed, enabled, not suspended, and not deleted. We did not attempt a global naming cleanup. We renamed the boundary objects and left the rest alone until they caused pain.

We measured the effect in ways that could be checked. We tracked how long a normal change took from branch to production, how often it caused an incident, and how many people needed to be in the room to explain a module. After four months, a pricing change took a day instead of a week. Not because the engineers were faster, but because the change touched one service instead of five files and a migration. Incidents from that area dropped from almost weekly to rare. The on-call engineer could look at a log line and name the component responsible. That may sound small, but it changed how the team worked under pressure.

The strongest objection to all of this was not that the code was ugly. It was that the prototype may have made the wrong architectural assumptions. If the core shape was wrong, cleanup would be polishing a bridge built over the wrong river. We tested that fear by taking the next hard requirement—supporting multiple currencies and a partner network—and asking where it would land in the current system. If the answer was “everywhere,” we would plan a rewrite. The answer was narrower: the ledger needed a tenant field, partner identity needed its own table, and the old invoicing path needed a flag. That was unpleasant but finite. If the requirement had been to become a multi-region platform with a different consistency model, I would not have argued for cleanup. Some debt is structural, and pretending otherwise is how teams waste a year.

The pros of the careful route were mostly things that did not happen. There was no nine-month rewrite, no second prototype, no period where the product stood still while the team proved it could build the simple version again. Customers kept getting value. The company kept its revenue. The team learned the system by touching it safely instead of guessing at it from the outside. A new engineer could fix a bug in her second week instead of spending a month asking for help. The codebase became a place where work could be done without fear, which is a strange thing to want from software until you have been on call for it.

The cons were also real. Cleanup did not produce a launch. It produced fewer surprises, and that is hard to sell in a meeting. For two months, velocity looked worse because the team was paying for earlier shortcuts. The old code still contained assumptions about single-tenant data, and some of them would always be there. The boundary we built could become a wall: the old side would be left to rot if nobody owned it. We had to assign ownership and keep deleting, not just isolating. The plan also required management to tolerate a quarter of unglamorous work. If a deadline arrived and the team was forced to skip the tests, the debt came back with interest.

The alternative to throwing the code out was not pretending it was fine. It was doing enough work to find out what it was worth, then paying the debt in pieces small enough to survive contact with reality. The prototype had earned its keep by getting the product to market. The cleanup had to earn its keep by making the next decision possible.
rejected:
The urge to rewrite is seductive because it solves the immediate pain of navigating spaghetti code. It promises a blank slate where every variable has a purpose and every function does what its name says. But a rewrite is not a refactor. It is a bet that you can reproduce the system’s behavior in a new language or architecture while it is still running in production. The old system contains years of edge-case handling, workarounds for upstream bugs, and implicit business rules that were never documented. When you start over, you build the system you *think* you have, not the one you actually do.

The alternative is a slow, disciplined dismantling of the mess. It begins not with code, but with tests. You cannot change what you cannot verify.
