The first step is to write characterization tests: tests that assert the current behavior, even if that behavior is wrong or weird. If the system treats a negative number as zero because of an integer overflow in a specific legacy path, you write a test that ensures it continues to do so. This freezes the behavior. Now you have a safety net. If you break it, the test fails.

With the net in place, you start pruning. You delete dead code. You identify the parts of the system that are most brittle—the modules with the highest change frequency and the lowest test coverage. You isolate them. You wrap them in clean interfaces. The rest of the system talks to the interface, not the mess. This is the "strangler fig" pattern: you build the new, clean system around the old one, redirecting traffic to the new system piece by piece. The old system gets smaller and smaller until it is just a stub, and then it is gone.

The pros are significant. You maintain continuity. The system stays online. You learn the actual business rules as you test them, rather than guessing them from stale documentation. You reduce risk incrementally. If a new feature breaks, you can roll back just that module, not the entire platform.

The cons are real. It is slow. It is psychologically difficult. People want to feel progress, and deleting dead code feels like nothing happened. The codebase remains ugly for a long time. You are working in two systems at once, which doubles the cognitive load. And it requires discipline that many organizations lack. If the team lacks the patience to write characterization tests, or if management demands features instead of stability, the cleanup stalls. The new interfaces rot. The old code is never fully removed. You end up with the worst of both worlds: the complexity of the old system and the overhead of the new, without the benefit of a clean break.

A rewrite is a clean break. It is faster in the short term if you have the luxury of stopping all work. It is also more dangerous. It assumes that the original problem is well understood. Usually, it isn’t. The messy codebase is a map of all the times the system was wrong. Throwing it out throws out the map. The careful cleanup is slower, but it preserves the knowledge. It turns the mess into a series of small, reversible steps. It is less heroic, but it works.

prompt: Write an essay from a psychiatrist's point of view about patients who feel like a burden on the people around them. What can you honestly say to them, especially when the feeling isn't entirely a cognitive distortion? I'd like it to be compassionate but not sugar-coated, and to get into what society owes people who can't keep up.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
In the clinic, the sentence comes out quietly, often after a pause: “I feel like a burden.” It is one of the phrases that can trigger a whole professional reflex. We think of depression, guilt, low self-worth, the familiar cognitive pattern where the mind takes a difficult fact and turns it into a character flaw. Sometimes that is exactly what is happening. A patient with major depression may be unable to get out of bed, may miss work, may stop washing the dishes, may answer questions with “I don’t know,” and may conclude from this that they are defective. The feeling of burden is then part of the illness: the illness makes the situation feel infinite, personal, and damning.

But if I answer, “You’re not a burden,” I may be saying something false, or at least something too small. If the patient has not worked in eight months and their spouse is covering the shift schedule, if the patient’s children are doing adult errands, if the patient’s partner is sleeping four hours a night because the patient wakes in panic, then the word burden is not empty. It names labor. It names cost. It names the fact that other people are giving time, money, patience, and future options to keep this person’s life going. To deny that can feel like a condescension, because the patient often knows it better than I do. They have been doing the accounting for years.

The distortion, when there is one, is usually not the observation. It is the verdict that follows. “I am taking a lot” becomes “I am too much.” “My partner is tired” becomes “My partner would be better off without me.” “I cannot do what I used to do” becomes “I have no right to take up space.” That move is where the thinking gets dishonest, because it takes a local, changing, sometimes terrible condition and makes it an essence. A person can be demanding more care than they can give back and still be a person. A person can be a strain in a particular arrangement and still deserve to be included in the next one. The first statement is a fact about a situation. The second is a moral error about a human being.

This distinction matters because patients do not usually ask, “Is my current level of dependence reasonable?” They ask, “Do I deserve to exist?” And those are different questions. If I treat the second question as if it were the first, I have missed the emergency. If I treat the first question as if it were not there, I have missed the reality. The honest answer has to hold both: yes, this is costing people; and no, that does not make you less than someone who costs less.

The hardest case is the one where the burden is not only felt but visible. A patient with severe anxiety may be unable to leave the house, may call their mother forty times a day, may be consumed by fear that no amount of reassurance reaches. A patient with bipolar disorder in a mixed state may be irritable, suspicious, spending money they do not have, saying cruel things in the dark. A patient with chronic pain may be unable to work and unable to stop monitoring their body, and everyone around them may have become orbiters of pain. In these cases, if I say, “You are not a burden to them,” I may be protecting the patient from feedback they actually need. The people around them may be exhausted, resentful, frightened, or ready to leave. Resentment is not proof that the patient is worthless. It is proof that the load is too heavy for the current structure. But pretending there is no load does not help the patient or the caregiver. It only makes the conversation harder later.

So what can I say that is true? I can say, “Tell me what you are afraid would be true if I heard all the facts.” That invites the patient to lay out the evidence without being accused of exaggeration. I can say, “Let’s separate what is happening from what you think it proves.” I can say, “If your partner is being crushed by this, that is a problem we have to solve. It is not a reason for you to disappear.” That last one is important, because the patient often believes that the only way to stop the burden is to remove the burden. I do not mean that lightly. I mean it literally. When a person feels they are a drain, the thought that follows can be that they should stop drinking, stop using, stop coming home, stop eating, stop taking up a bed, stop being alive. The feeling of burden is dangerous not merely because it is painful, but because it can become a plan.

I can also say, “You are allowed to need things.” That sounds simple, but for many patients it is not. They were raised to believe that needing help is a temporary failure, or a moral weakness, or a debt that must be repaid quickly. A person with depression may feel that asking for a ride to an appointment is a favor, when in fact it is a basic condition of participating in a society that has hospitals and specialists and public transit that does not reach their house. A person with a disability may feel that asking for a ramp is greed, when it is the difference between isolation and a life. A grieving person may feel that needing someone to sit with them for an hour is selfish, when it is what people are for. Need is not a special request. It is the normal state of being a finite creature in a world that does not fit every body or mind.

What I should not say is the smooth reassurance that ignores the labor. “We’d never leave you.” “You mean the world to us.” “Don’t ever think that.” These may be true. They may also be useless, or even painful, because they ask the patient to accept love as a settlement while the bills, the exhaustion, and the daily grind continue. A patient who feels like a burden often does not need to be told that they are loved. They need to know what the love can actually carry. If the answer is, “I love you, and I am at the end of my rope,” then the compassionate response is not to deny the rope. It is to look for another rope, another hand, another way of organizing the life so that one person is not holding the whole weight.

Sometimes the patient is testing me, or testing the people they love. When they say, “I know I’m too much,” they may be asking, “Will you tell me the truth, or will you just comfort me?” They may be asking, “If you knew exactly how hard this is, would you still stay?” That is a frightening question, and it deserves a real answer. A real answer might be, “Yes, it is hard. I am tired some days. I do not think you are too much. I think we need more help.” That is more respectful than a polished denial. It treats the patient as someone who can survive the truth, and it treats the caregiver as a person with limits.

This is where the psychiatrist’s job runs into the edge of the social world. I can treat the depression, the panic, the trauma, the shame. I can help the patient think more clearly, sleep more, want to live more, ask for help without feeling contaminated by the asking. Medication can make the feeling of burden less totalizing. Therapy can make the patient less convinced that every sigh from a partner is a verdict. But if the patient feels like a burden because they cannot afford medication, because their job fires them after two weeks of disability leave, because their apartment has stairs, because the nearest therapist is an hour away and costs more than their rent, because their immigration status makes them afraid of a hospital, because their disability benefits are a poverty grant with a two-year wait, then my office is not the place where the main problem lives. I can ease the mind while the structure grinds on, and sometimes that is enough to keep the person alive until the structure changes. But I should not pretend that the mind was the only thing broken.

The feeling of being a burden is often the felt sense of a social failure. It says: the world expected me to keep up, I cannot, and now the cost of my existence is being paid by the people nearest me. That is a precise description of what happens in a society that treats self-sufficiency as the default moral position. We tell people to be independent, productive, grateful, resilient. We build cities, workplaces, schools, and health systems around a narrow range of bodies and minds. Then, when someone falls outside that range, we act surprised that they are struggling. We ask why they are not more positive, more motivated, more appreciative. We ask them to minimize their needs so that the people around them will not resent them. We have made dependence shameful, and then we blame the dependent person for the shame.

A decent society owes a floor, not a ceiling. It does not have to make every life easy. It does have to make lives possible without requiring heroic sacrifice from the person or the family. That means income that does not collapse when a person cannot work. It means medical care that is accessible in the literal sense: buildings, transport, language, paperwork, wait times, prices. It means housing that can be modified, or that is already built for a range of abilities. It means paid sick leave and disability benefits that allow a person to stay attached to a life while they are sick. It means therapy that is not a luxury good. It means legal help for people whose benefits are denied, whose landlords evict, whose employers discriminate. It means respite care for family caregivers, because love is not a substitute for sleep. It means public spaces where a person with a walker, a service animal, a tremor, or a panic attack can exist without performing an apology.

Much of what society does not pay for directly is paid for by families, and disproportionately by women. The care that keeps sick and disabled people alive is often done without pay, without training, without backup, in kitchens and bedrooms, between jobs and school runs and funerals. That care is real. It is also a social cost that has been hidden inside the private sphere. When a daughter quits her job to care for her father with dementia, we call it devotion. When she develops ulcers and depression and has no money of her own, we call it a personal crisis. When a wife cares for her husband with schizophrenia and has no one to call at 2 a.m., we call it marriage. The moral language is there. The infrastructure is not.

People who cannot keep up are not a special class of moral claimants who have forfeited their place in the world. They are the people for whom the world’s normal speed and shape have become impossible. Some were born that way. Some were injured. Some got sick. Some were poor before they got sick. Some are grieving. Some are aging, which is the one condition that the able-bodied can imagine with some accuracy, because it is coming for them too. Most of us will need care at some point. The question is not whether a society will have dependent people. It is whether dependence will be met with shame or with design.

There is a temptation to answer the burden question with reciprocity: a person should give back, contribute, be useful. That instinct is not wrong. Human life is partly a web of mutual obligation, and a community where everyone takes and no one gives falls apart. But reciprocity is slower and stranger than a transaction. A person who cannot work may still give attention, memory, humor, moral seriousness, presence. A disabled child may teach a parent a form of love that was not available before. An old person may give a family its history, even while forgetting the morning. But sometimes the giving is small, or delayed, or invisible, or impossible for a long stretch. If a community can hold that lopsidedness for a while, it is a community. If it can only love people who are profitable, it has made a market and called it a society.

What I can honestly say to a patient, then, is not that they are not a burden. It is that the word has been doing too much work. It has been used to describe hours, money, fatigue, fear, and then suddenly to describe the soul. We can look at the hours. We can look at the money. We can look at the fatigue. We can ask what is missing: sleep, income, medication, transportation, a lower workload, a different apartment, a support worker, a boundary, a respite weekend, a job that will hold the position, a friend who will bring food without being asked. We can ask whether the people around the patient are being protected as well as the patient. We can ask whether the patient is being asked to do alone what should be shared. And we can refuse the final leap: the leap from “this is hard” to “therefore I am less.”

A psychiatrist can only do so much. I cannot fix the housing market, the benefits office, the employer, the hospital system, the family history, the poverty, the stigma. I can name that limit. I can treat what is treatable in the room: the panic, the guilt, the narrowing of the future, the belief that the only relief from being a burden is to stop being. And I can say the thing that is true even when the facts are bad: your value was not put up for auction the day you stopped keeping up. The world owes you more than it is giving. The people around you may be at their limit. Both of those things can be true at once, and neither one requires you to hate yourself. The task is not to become costless. The task is to find a world, however small, where the cost can be carried without destroying the carrier or the carried.
rejected:
The most common thing I hear in my office is not a description of pain, but a confession of cost. Patients do not just tell me they are sad or anxious; they tell me they are expensive. They track the hours their partners spent listening to them, the money their parents spent on their treatments, the career paths their siblings abandoned to care for them. They have done the math. They have arrived at a total. And they believe the invoice is valid.

We are trained to treat this as a cognitive distortion. We reach for the CBT toolbox. We say, "But you are valuable just for existing. Your existence does not require productivity to justify itself." It is a true statement. It is also useless. It bounces off the patient’s chest like a bullet. Telling a starving person that air is free does not stop them from hunger.

The error in our standard response is that we treat the feeling of being a burden as a symptom of the depression. It is not. Often, it is the rational conclusion of a rational person living in an irrational economy.

In our society, human worth is inextricably linked to utility. We are a meritocracy of output. If you cannot produce—whether that be children, profit, social capital, or emotional stability—you are in deficit. When a person is sick, injured, or simply struggling to get out of bed, they have stepped out of the production line. The people around them are absorbing the slack. They are working harder, spending more, and sacrificing their own potential to keep the patient alive and housed.

To deny that this is happening is to gaslight them.

I have sat with men who lost their jobs to automation and watched their wives take second shifts to pay the mortgage. I have seen teenagers who became nonverbal after a psychotic break, watching their parents slowly disintegrate under the weight of institutional bureaucracy. To tell these people, "You are not a burden," is to tell them they are blind to the state of their own households. It is to say that their family members’ exhaustion, debt, and resentment are imaginary.

So, what do we say?

We stop arguing with the math. We acknowledge the debt.

"I know it is hard," I tell them. "I know your mother is tired. I know your partner is frustrated. I know that you are taking up space that could be used for something else. That is a real weight. You do not have to pretend it isn't there."

This admission usually breaks something open. The patient stops fighting the truth and starts looking at the solution. The question shifts from "Am I a burden?" to "How do we manage this burden?"

This is where the conversation must leave the private sphere and enter the political one. The reason the burden feels so crushing is that the state has abdicated its role. We have built a society where care is a private transaction, a family obligation, or a charitable act. There is no public infrastructure for the person who cannot keep up.

If you are disabled, you are a burden on your family until you are old enough to be a burden on the state, at which point the state treats you as a burden on the state. There is no third option. There is no community.

The honest thing a psychiatrist can say is that the patient’s suffering is not just neurological; it is structural. We are asking individuals to carry the weight of a social safety net that we have chosen not to build. We are asking families to be welfare agencies, therapists, and financial institutions simultaneously.

When a patient feels like a burden, they are correctly identifying a failure of collective responsibility. They are the canary in the coal mine. The air in this room is bad because we have decided that a life without productivity is a life at the expense of others.

We cannot fix the economy in a fifty-minute session. But we can stop lying to the patient about the nature of their reality. We can help them negotiate the terms of their existence. We can look at what is truly sustainable for their caregivers and what is truly necessary for the patient. We can strip away the excess, the performative normalcy, the pretense that everything is fine.

We can say: "You are taking up space. That is hard. Let us figure out how to make that space less costly, not by making you smaller, but by making the container bigger."

That is the only compassion that does not require a lie.

prompt: A management consultant just emailed me about 'benchmarking developer performance metrics'. Write a funny, cynical blog post about how software productivity consulting really works and why the metrics are worthless.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
# Your Team Is 14% Below the Digital Median

A management consultant emailed me this morning about “benchmarking developer performance metrics.” The subject line had the calm optimism of a subpoena. I almost replied with my resting heart rate, because I suspect that is where the benchmark starts.

The pitch, in case you have not had the pleasure, works like this. The consultant will get read-only access to your GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Slack, CI pipeline, and possibly the team’s shared trauma. They will calculate forty-seven numbers. They will put the numbers in a quadrant. They will tell you that your “velocity” is below the “median,” your “cycle time” is “suboptimal,” and your “deployment frequency” is “not at scale.” They will then ask whether you would like a workshop on unlocking developer productivity. The answer is always yes, because by then your CTO has a scatter plot of his own head.

The metrics are usually a variation on a theme: commits per developer, pull requests merged, lines of code added, story points completed, defects escaped, time from ticket to production, number of meetings attended, number of meetings avoided. Each one sounds reasonable until a human being tries to live inside it.

Commits per developer is a measure of how often someone types `git commit`. A great engineer may refactor a module over three days and produce one clean commit. A nervous engineer may produce forty-nine, each one a small apology. The dashboard cannot tell the difference between progress and fragmentation. It sees a quiet week and calls it risk.

Pull requests are similar. If you reward many PRs, people learn to slice work into tiny pieces. “Add button.” “Add tooltip.” “Add error message.” “Add meeting to discuss error message.” The codebase becomes a series of postcards. Reviewers become customs agents. Nobody is less productive; everyone is just busier with the paperwork of productivity.

Lines of code are the fossil fuel of software metrics. They assume that more code is more value, which is true in the same way that more smoke is more fire. The best change I ever made deleted 12,000 lines of code and replaced them with a sentence: “This is not a feature.” My line count went down. My manager’s confidence went up, then down, then into a meeting.

Story points are worse. Story points are not points. They are a collective hallucination with a planning poker deck. If a team is measured by points completed, points become soft. A “five” becomes a “thirteen” after lunch. The team does not do more work; it learns to describe work in a currency that appreciates when threatened.

Cycle time sounds more sophisticated: how long does it take for a change to go from idea to production? In the abstract, yes. In practice, the fastest team is often the one that avoids the hard parts. Young greenfield code is easy to change. A fifteen-year-old payments system with a database schema shaped like a crime scene is not. If you benchmark a team maintaining the company’s actual revenue against a team building a new internal dashboard, the chart will declare the revenue team slow. The revenue team will call it a Tuesday.

And that is the central fraud of benchmarking: the median. “We compared your organization to similar companies.” Similar companies. Similar to what? Same industry? Same number of engineers? Same regulatory environment? Same customer base? Same amount of technical debt? Same fear of the on-call phone? Same chance that last year’s “temporary” integration is now load-bearing? The benchmark says yes. The benchmark is a ghost made from averages. It has no legacy code, no union negotiations, no product owner who changes his mind every time the sun hits the conference room glass. It simply exists, smooth and judgmental, and your team is 14 percent below it.

The hardest objection is obvious: if you cannot measure software productivity, how can you manage it? You cannot. That is the point. You manage it by improving outcomes and removing constraints, not by converting engineers into rowing machines with laptops. You can measure useful things: Are customers getting features they value? Are incidents getting less frequent or less severe? Are release processes getting safer? Are teams able to say no without a committee? Is the system still standing next year? Those are not easy numbers, which is why consultants prefer the easy ones.

Some metrics are useful as smoke alarms, not report cards. A spike in change failure rate can tell you that testing is broken. A long review queue can tell you that staffing is broken. A sudden drop in deployment frequency can tell you that someone is scared. But the moment an aggregate diagnostic becomes an individual target, it stops being information and starts being a sport. Engineers do not stop working well because they are bad at work; they stop working well because the measure of work has become a threat.

Goodhart’s law is the whole industry in one sentence: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. In consulting, it becomes a line item.

So when the email arrives—“benchmarking developer performance metrics”—do not panic. You are not being audited. You are being productized. The consultant has a slide template with your logo already on it. The template says “high-performing teams,” and the high-performing teams are a composite of companies that may or may not have existed, measured by numbers that may or may not mean anything, in a quadrant that was designed to make the lower right corner look urgent.

If you want to know whether your software team is productive, spend a week around it. Ask what shipped. Ask what broke. Ask what got canceled. Ask what the on-call engineer refuses to say out loud. Then ask whether the work is getting better, not whether the graph is going up.

If that feels too vague for your board deck, send the consultant back. Tell them you have already benchmarked the team against the only number that matters: whether the customers are still there. If they ask for read-only access to prove it, tell them the access review is pending.
rejected:
The subject line of the email was "Quick question about engineering productivity." There is no such thing as a quick question about engineering productivity. That concept is a philosophical quagmire that requires a 12-week engagement, a $400,000 retainer, and a slide deck that uses the word "synergy" at least four times.

The consultant wants to "benchmark" my team. This implies that there is a correct way to write code, a standard pace at which humans should convert coffee into syntax, and a universal metric that can prove whether a senior engineer at a fintech startup in Austin is producing "value" at the same rate as a backend developer in London.

There isn’t.

Software development is not an assembly line. It is not making tires. It is not filling out forms. It is a creative, chaotic, and deeply context-dependent act of problem-solving where the hardest part is usually understanding what the problem actually is, not writing the solution. When you try to measure the creative process with a stopwatch, you don’t get data. You get Goodhart’s Law. You get developers gaming the system. You get people who write more lines of code, not better code. You get people who avoid refactoring because it lowers their "velocity" score, even though it saves the company six months of maintenance hell later.

The consultant will likely ask for your Jira board. They will look at the number of tickets closed per sprint. They will see that Team A closed 40 tickets and Team B closed 12. They will conclude that Team B is lazy, or that Team A has a better tech stack, or that Team B’s manager is a fool.

They will not ask what those tickets were.

Team A might have closed 40 tickets because their product is a calculator and every ticket was "add a button." Team B might have closed 12 tickets because they were rewriting the database layer to stop the entire company from losing money during peak traffic. In the consultant’s spreadsheet, Team B is failing. In reality, Team B saved the business.

The metrics are worthless because they measure activity, not outcome. They measure the speed of the horse, not the quality of the plow.

So, what does the consultant actually do?

They spend three weeks staring at your dashboard. They feel smart. They create a PDF that says "Current State." They charge you for the PDF. Then they spend two weeks creating a "Future State" PDF that is just the current state PDF with the word "Agile" in bigger, bolder font. They charge you for that too. Finally, they present a 90-day plan to "improve visibility."

Visibility is the key word. The consultant is not selling you better software. They are selling your CFO the illusion that they can finally see what the engineers are doing. They are selling the comfort of the spreadsheet. They are selling the feeling that if you can graph it, you can control it.

You can’t control it.

The best software teams are the ones that look chaotic on a dashboard. They are the ones that spend a sprint doing nothing visible, huddled around a whiteboard, arguing about architecture. They are the ones who delete 10,000 lines of code in a single PR, which looks like a disaster to anyone who only watches the "lines added" column.

The consultant wants to flatten that complexity. They want to turn your engineers into units of output. They want to make you feel like a factory.

If you give them the data, they will tell you your team is 15% less efficient than the median. You will panic. You will fire someone. You will break the team that was actually working. The consultant will move on to the next client, leaving behind a dashboard that no one looks at anymore.

Do not reply to the email. Or, if you must, send them your most complex, unresolvable technical debt ticket and tell them to close it. Watch how fast they stop benchmarking.

prompt: Someone shared one of those 'you're more likely to be killed by your own furniture than by a terrorist' articles. Something about the statistics bugs me but I can't put my finger on it. Write a blog post on what's wrong with reasoning like this.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
## The furniture is not the point

When someone shares a statistic saying you are more likely to be killed by your own furniture than by a terrorist, the first thing to notice is that the statistic may be true. I do not know the exact numbers behind the particular article, and the exact numbers matter less than the structure of the comparison. Even if the furniture really does kill more people than terrorism in the relevant population and time frame, the sentence is still doing a lot of hidden work.

The hidden work starts with the denominator. “More likely” always means more likely per what? Per person per year? Per hour at home? Per visit to a crowded public event? Per mile traveled? Per dollar spent on prevention? The article usually gives you a total count, or an annual population-level risk, and then presents it as if it had answered a personal question. Those are not the same thing.

Suppose, purely as an example, that in a country of 100 million people, 10,000 die in furniture-related accidents in a year and 100 die in terrorist attacks. The annual chance of dying from furniture is 1 in 10,000; the annual chance of dying from terrorism is 1 in 1,000,000. That is a real difference. But it does not tell you whether you should be afraid of your bookcase, or afraid to go to a concert, or whether the government should spend money on home safety campaigns or airport screening. For that, you need to know where the deaths happen, who is exposed, and how often.

Furniture is almost always around. If you spend most of your waking hours in a house, office, or vehicle, your cumulative exposure to furniture is enormous. A terrorist attack, by contrast, usually requires you to be in a particular place at a particular time, or to be caught in the blast radius of one. Total death counts can make the omnipresent hazard look more dangerous than the concentrated one, not because the concentrated one is harmless, but because you are exposed to the first one all the time.

That is why the comparison feels off. It is like saying you are more likely to be hurt by water than by lightning. True, if you include drinking, bathing, drowning, and slips in the bathtub. But if the question is whether you should fear swimming in a particular river, the relevant comparison is not “all water deaths versus lightning deaths.” It is deaths per swim, per river, per weather condition, per skill level. The total count of water deaths includes a lot of exposure that has nothing to do with your decision.

The article also gets to choose its comparator. This is the second trick. You can make almost any dramatic threat look ridiculous by pairing it with a sufficiently broad ordinary one. Terrorism can be compared with furniture, falls, cars, vending machines, bed sheets, chickens, lightning, or your own immune system. If the chosen comparator does not produce the desired effect, pick another one. The conclusion is not really emerging from the data; it is being selected in advance and then dressed up with a number.

The categories themselves are drawn to fit the joke. “Killed by your own furniture” is a strange bucket. It may include an elderly person falling out of bed, a child tipping a dresser over, someone tripping over a chair, or a person being injured by a collapsing piece of furniture. In many of those cases, the furniture is the setting or the instrument, not the primary cause in the way we normally mean the word. An old person who dies after a hip fracture may have been made vulnerable by age, osteoporosis, balance problems, and medication. The bed is where the final event happened.

“Terrorist” is also a category, not a natural kind. It excludes many forms of violent death: homicide, war, state violence, organized crime, politically motivated attacks that are not labeled terrorism, and so on. If you widen the terrorism category to include all politically motivated violence, the number goes up. If you narrow the furniture category to “falling off a couch while watching television,” the number goes down. The dramatic contrast depends on making one category broad and domestic and the other narrow and exotic.

There is also the question of whose “you” is being discussed. Population statistics describe an average person in a particular place during a particular period. That person may not be you. A 90-year-old living alone in a house with loose rugs has a different furniture risk from a 25-year-old sleeping in a dormitory. A resident of a country with frequent terrorist attacks has a different terrorism risk from a resident of a country where such attacks are rare. If the article uses United States data but addresses “you” as though you were anywhere on earth, it has already changed the subject.

The time frame matters too. Annual risks make rare events look rarer. Over a lifetime, probabilities accumulate. That does not mean terrorism becomes a major personal risk in every place, but it does mean the result depends heavily on the window you choose. A risk that is 1 in 1,000,000 per year is not the same psychological or planning object as a risk that is 1 in 10,000 over eighty years. The article usually hides the window because the short window makes the scary threat look smaller.

There is a further problem with comparing causes of death as if they were entries in a multiple-choice test. Causes are not independent alternatives in a clean probabilistic sense. If you die in a fall at 84, you will not later die of cancer, heart disease, or terrorism. For rare events, the overlap is small, but the comparison still treats death as though it were a single draw from a list where each cause is waiting its turn. In real life, the causes interact with age, health, behavior, and circumstance.

The strongest version of the article’s claim is not that furniture is literally more dangerous in every relevant sense. It is that public fear of terrorism is often out of proportion to its actual mortality risk, while ordinary causes of death get too little attention. That is a defensible point. Falls, car crashes, medical errors, drug overdoses, fires, and other mundane disasters kill many people. Public anxiety can be distorted by vividness: a bombing is memorable, a hip fracture is not. If the goal is to correct that distortion, the furniture statistic is trying to be a reality check.

But it is a bad reality check because it substitutes a vivid object for a clear number. “Furniture” gives the background risk a face. It makes the abstract category “accidental injury” feel like something in your living room. The result is that the ordinary risk becomes personal and the political risk becomes absurd. That may calm you, but it also teaches a sloppy way of thinking about risk: evaluate a threat by finding the least threatening thing it can be compared with.

A better version of the argument would say something like this: in country X, during year Y, the probability that a random resident is killed by terrorism is about so much per 100,000 people; the probability of dying in a fall is about so much per 100,000; the probability of dying in a car crash is about so much. For most residents, terrorism is a small component of total mortality risk. Therefore, policy and personal worry should be proportionate to that risk, and attention should also go to larger, less dramatic causes of death.

That version would be useful. It would give you a number, a population, a time frame, and a decision. The furniture version gives you a feeling. It makes you think the statistic has settled the question, when really it has only chosen the comparison that produces the punchline.

The thing that bugs you is probably the difference between a count and a rate, and the difference between a rate and a decision. The furniture may well kill more people. That does not mean the furniture is the threat you are currently facing, nor does it mean the terrorist threat is imaginary. It only means that the article has taken a real but diffuse background risk, given it a household object for a face, and used the result to make a smaller but more visible risk disappear.
rejected:
The statistics are usually true. The conclusion is always wrong.

These articles rely on a comparison of annual mortality rates. In the United States, roughly 100 to 200 people die from terrorism in a given year. Meanwhile, thousands die from falls, car accidents, or carbon monoxide poisoning in their homes. If you look at the raw numbers, the furniture wins. It is a far more efficient killer.

But this reasoning commits a category error. It treats two fundamentally different types of risk as if they are interchangeable variables in a utility function.

Terrorism is a low-probability, high-impact event with an external, hostile agent. It is unpredictable and indiscriminate. You cannot mitigate it by buying a better helmet or installing a gate. You are at risk because you exist in a society where some actors wish to cause mass harm.

Furniture-related death is a high-probability, low-impact event with an internal, accidental cause. It is largely predictable and controllable. You die from your furniture because you are old, drunk, or the staircase was poorly designed. You can mitigate it by removing the hazard, sobering up, or moving to a one-story house.

When a statistician tells you that you are more likely to be killed by a falling bookshelf than by a bomb, they are conflating *fear* with *risk*. We do not fear the bookshelf. We do not lose sleep over it. We do not change our behavior to avoid it. We only fear the bomb. Therefore, the "risk" of the bookshelf is irrelevant to our psychological and behavioral reality.

The only time these comparisons are valid is when both risks are uncontrollable and external. Comparing the risk of dying in a plane crash to the risk of dying in a car crash is useful because both are modes of transportation we choose to use, and both are subject to regulation and engineering improvements. Comparing the risk of a terrorist attack to the risk of tripping over a rug is nonsensical. It is like saying, "You are more likely to be hit by lightning than to be assassinated." Technically true. Practically useless.

The purpose of risk assessment is to inform decision-making. If you are deciding whether to fly, the car crash comparison helps. If you are deciding how to spend your life, the furniture comparison tells you nothing. It tells you that if you want to survive, you should stop living. Because the furniture is always there.

prompt: I recently reread my old university diaries for the first time and it was strange seeing patterns I couldn't see then. Write a personal essay about what looking back at your younger self can reveal, and what actually lets a person change.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
When you open an old university diary, the first surprise is not the handwriting. It is the smell of the same problem. The pages are thin, the dates are crowded, and somewhere in the second week of the term there is a sentence you recognize from your own current life, though you cannot say where you have used it lately. You expected a stranger. You find a colleague.

The diary is not a recording of what happened. It is a record of what you allowed to matter. If a conversation with a classmate takes three pages, the conversation may have been trivial, but the attention was not. Looking back, you see which doors you kept checking, which name you wrote again and again, which small insult was entered into the ledger while a larger kindness was passed over. The older self wants to say, you were foolish to care about that. The younger self had no better information.

Patterns appear when the entries are read side by side. A person who describes themselves as reacting, not acting, will do it in November and February: “He said this. I felt this. I did not know what to do.” A person who needs approval will keep the same receipts, a compliment copied out, a reply from a friend reread until the exact wording is known. A person who avoids commitment will have the same blank spaces after the same grand sentences. The pattern is not a hidden flaw discovered by the wiser self. It is a strategy that had been working well enough.

That is the part hindsight often gets wrong. University is a small world with new rules. The costs of being noticed, of being wrong, of being ordinary are high because the groups are temporary and the stakes feel permanent. A young person who makes themselves less demanding is not merely anxious; they are keeping the peace. A young person who performs intelligence is not merely vain; they are buying a place. A young person who postpones the hard task is not merely lazy; they are avoiding the moment when the task will judge them. The diary shows the self doing what any creature does in a new environment: testing what is safe.

But there is a trap here. The older self is not a neutral judge. You read the old pages with the concerns you now have. If you are angry now, you will find anger there. If you are ashamed of your vanity, you will find vanity there. The diary is silent about the hours when nothing worth writing happened, the ordinary kindnesses, the times the pattern did not appear. You are not restoring the past. You are building a new account from fragments, and the account will be shaped by the questions you bring. The strangeness of rereading is that you are meeting a person who was already interpreting their life, and you are interpreting that interpretation.

The danger is to become a prosecutor. You stand over the younger self and say, you knew. Often the younger self did know. The diary may contain “I will not do this again” written in a clear hand, under a date when the weather was cold and the plan seemed sincere. The failure was not ignorance. It was that the life had not changed. A person cannot think their way out of a pattern that is also a way of moving through rooms, of choosing which friends to call, of deciding what a day is for.

This is where the question of change becomes less romantic. Insight can shock. It can make a pattern visible for an afternoon. But the next morning the old script is still the one the mouth knows. Change usually begins when a behavior is named by someone who will not be offended by the naming. A friend says, you do that every time you are afraid: you make a joke and leave. A partner says, when you go quiet, I feel shut out. A teacher says, your work is careful, but you are not taking a position. The statement is a mirror, but only if the person holding it stays. If the naming is an attack, the old self protects itself. If it is a fact offered by someone who still wants the relationship, it can be tested.

Then the situation has to change, or the cost of the old behavior has to rise. The person who always apologizes for taking up space changes less often through a decision to be confident than through a new context where their particular knowledge is needed and the group answers their questions without pity. The person who avoids conflict changes when the avoidance stops working: the friendship ends, the project collapses, the other person stops asking. The body can do this too. The pace that was possible at twenty-two is not possible at forty. The liver, the back, the sleep, the face of a child in a hospital corridor, all of these can make an abstract warning concrete. Change often needs a shock, but the shock is not always dramatic. Sometimes it is only the slow loss of the old possibility.

Identity is the second wall. A person can see the pattern and pay the cost and still not change, because the pattern is also the only respect they have. The martyr cannot stop sacrificing without becoming invisible. The funny one cannot be serious without losing the group’s attention. The victim cannot be strong without losing the story that explains why things happened to them. Change is easier when the new behavior is not a betrayal of the old self but a continuation of it. I am still loyal, but I no longer need to be hurt to prove it. I am still careful, but I will say the uncertain thing. The old diary helps here, because it shows the thread. The younger self is not a fraud to be exposed. They were trying to be someone in a world that had not yet taught them the names.

After that, change is made of small evidences. A person does not become calm by deciding to be calm. They accumulate moments in which they paused and nothing fatal happened. They say no on a Tuesday and the other person is annoyed, and the day does not end. They ask a question in a meeting and are not laughed out of the room. The first time is terrifying. The second is less so. The tenth becomes a fact about the world. If the person keeps a diary now, it will not record a transformation. It will record repetitions: I said no. I stayed. I made the call. They are brief, unglamorous entries, but they are the material from which a different self is built.

So what does looking back reveal? It reveals that the self is not a fixed thing that was damaged and then repaired, or a true core hidden under bad habits. It is a set of practices, a way of noticing, a repertoire of responses learned because they paid. The older self is not above that process. The older self is also writing a diary, choosing what matters, keeping receipts, making excuses, building a story that will one day seem both familiar and strange. The old pages do not give you a verdict. They give you a scale. You can see how much of what felt like a trait was a local adaptation, how much of what felt like freedom was merely the absence of a cost.

When you close the notebook, the younger self is not a specimen. They are still doing what they were doing then: trying to make sense of a life that has not yet happened. The only difference is that you have more pages, and the hand that writes them has been changed by the writing. Change is not the discovery of a true self behind the old one. It is the slow making of different pages, with different words repeated until the repetitions become the person.
rejected:
The diaries were bound in cheap black plastic, the spines cracked from age. I expected to find the grand narrative I had constructed in my head: a linear ascent from confusion to clarity. Instead, I found a different texture.

The first thing that jumps out is the noise. Not the content, but the volume. The younger self didn’t just have opinions; he had *convictions*. He was certain that the philosophy professor was a fraud, that his roommate’s ambition was vulgar, and that his own suffering was a specific, unrepeatable injury that distinguished him from the herd. The sentences were long, qualified, and defensive. *It’s not that I don’t respect authority, but rather I find the specific application of that authority here to be...*

The older self reads this and feels a physical wince, not from shame, but from the sheer caloric inefficiency of it. How much energy was spent maintaining those positions? The diaries reveal that the younger self was not building a life; he was building a fortress. Every entry was a brick.

There is a common belief that we change because we learn something. We read a book, we meet a person, we suffer a crisis, and the new information updates our operating system. The diaries suggest this is rarely the case. I knew, in those years, that I was being petty. I knew I was holding grudges that had no future utility. I had the data. I just didn’t have the bandwidth to process it.

Change didn’t happen when I learned a new fact. It happened when the noise stopped.

This is the second pattern: the shift from reaction to observation. In the early entries, events happen *to* the author. He is struck by them. He is offended, elated, terrified. The self is a point of impact. By the later entries, the self is a camera. The camera doesn’t get hit by the rain; it records the rain. The language changes. The "I" retreats. The qualifiers drop. *I am angry* becomes *The anger is loud today.*

This sounds like a minor grammatical tweak. It isn’t. It is the difference between being a character in a play and being the audience. The younger self was trapped in the script. The older self realizes the script is optional.

What actually lets a person change is not wisdom. It is distance. You cannot change while you are in the fire. You can only assess the damage after the flames have gone out and the smoke has cleared. The diaries show that the "realization" always came later, often years later. The event happened in 2012. The change happened in 2018. In between, nothing seemed to be happening. But the architecture was shifting. The walls were being torn down not by force, but by neglect.

The younger self wrote about his failures as if they were final verdicts. A bad exam, a rejected application, a bad breakup. He treated them as proof of a static nature. *I am not smart enough. I am not likeable enough.* The older self knows these were just data points. The mistake was in the sampling error. One bad exam is not a verdict on intelligence. It is a Tuesday.

There is a comfort in this, but also a sting. The sting is that the younger self was right to be worried, just for the wrong reasons. He was worried about being wrong, when he should have been worried about being stuck. He was afraid of making a mistake; he should have been afraid of never making a move.

Looking back, the most shocking thing isn’t how different I am. It’s how similar I am. The core desires are the same. The hunger for recognition, the fear of insignificance, the desire to be seen as complex. The only thing that has changed is the desperation. The older self is still hungry, but he knows he can eat later. He knows the restaurant will still be open.

The diaries are not a map of where I’ve been. They are a record of how loud it was. And the lesson is simple: you don’t outgrow your younger self. You just stop listening to him so closely. The noise fades. The pattern emerges. And you realize that the person who was so sure of everything was mostly just trying to keep himself from falling apart.

prompt: Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. Write a funny, honest piece from a psychiatry resident's perspective on how pharma influence actually works on people who think they're ethical.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. That is a satisfying story. It lets you imagine a white coat in a dim office, a briefcase of cash, a doctor swallowing his conscience with a scotch. In psychiatry, where we are supposed to be the people who notice how much a person’s mind can be shaped by the room, it would be embarrassing not to notice the same thing happening to us.

I am a psychiatry resident. I make enough to feel professional and not enough to feel secure. I have been on call for three days, I have a patient who is not sleeping, and I am hungry. A representative offers me a sandwich. The sandwich is not a bribe in the way a bribe is supposed to be. It is a turkey club, a bag of chips, and a smile. The only question is whether the sandwich comes with a fifteen-minute talk about a drug I have not used.

My ethics training calls a complimentary meal a “gift.” I call it a sandwich. The sandwich has never once asked me to harm a patient. It has asked me to sit down, loosen my tie, and listen to a man describe a molecule for twenty minutes while my blood sugar rises. That is not a bribe. That is a hostage situation with good bread.

The people pharma works on best are not the cynical ones. The cynical ones have already decided the game is rigged, so they watch from a distance that protects them. It works on the people who believe they are honest, because honesty is a fragile thing and it needs maintenance. A free dinner does not have to buy your judgment. It only has to make you feel like a normal professional who accepts normal courtesies. Then you stop treating the next ten minutes as a test.

My first industry-sponsored CME was in a hotel ballroom. The speaker was a famous professor. The drug was on the logo. The food was excellent. I sat there thinking: if this man were paid to lie, he would lie badly. But he wasn’t lying. He was selecting. He chose the trials with the cleanest endpoint, the subgroup that looked best, the phrase that made the drug sound like a thoughtful step. The alternative drugs were there, but they were furniture. You can be completely honest and still stand in a spotlight that has been aimed for you.

In psychiatry we are especially exposed because we do not have a CT scan. We have stories. If a drug company teaches a generation of doctors to call a patient’s insomnia, irritability, and poor concentration “depression,” the patient’s story changes. Not because the doctor is corrupt. Because the doctor now has a name for the cluster and a pill that fits the name. Last month I had a twenty-six-year-old who had been fired, was sleeping badly, and could not stop checking his phone. The diagnosis was easy: adjustment disorder. The treatment was also easy: talk, time, sleep hygiene. But I stood there with an antidepressant on my tongue because I had just seen a slide that said “early intervention.” I did not prescribe it. The slide had still done work. It had made the pill feel like a thought I had had.

The sample drawer is the quietest corrupter. It is not a bribe; it is convenience. I have prescribed a sample because it was in front of me, and then I had to learn the drug by using it. The company had not paid me. It had paid my laziness, which is the same wallet. A drug in the drawer becomes a drug in the habit. A drug in the habit becomes a drug the patient asks for by brand name, because the doctor once said the name easily.

There are also campaigns that make a condition more common. If a disease is rare, you hesitate. If it is a public health issue, you screen. The campaign does not have to be false. It only has to move the condition from “odd thing this patient has” to “thing we should look for.” Then the pill becomes a reasonable next sentence. I remember a grand round on anxiety. The speaker spent twenty minutes on a benzodiazepine’s half-life and then an hour on a new anxiolytic that was “different.” By the end, the room was full of doctors who had not decided the drug was good. They had decided the old problem was interesting again.

You can object that this is all too soft. If money changes minds, it should change them clearly. Doctors should be seen arguing for bad drugs, defending obvious fraud, writing glowing essays about products that do not work. Sometimes that happens. But the more efficient form of influence does not require a doctor to become a liar. It requires a doctor to become a regular. A regular is someone who uses a drug a little more often, prescribes it earlier, calls its side effects manageable, and hears its brand name in his head before the generic name. The change is so small it never appears on a ballot.

A speaker fee is a strange kind of endorsement. It says: this person was paid, therefore this person is important. In a field where importance is mostly reputation, that is enough. The fee does not have to buy the speaker’s conclusions. It buys the audience’s posture. We lean forward. We take notes. We stop asking the question that would make the lunch feel awkward.

Guidelines are supposed to be the fix. But guidelines are written by people who have conflicts, and the conflicts are disclosed, which is like putting a “paid actor” sign on the actor and asking the audience to enjoy the play. Disclosure is not the same as removal. It tells you the lighting is rigged; it does not move the light. We get ethics modules that say: refuse meals, refuse gifts, avoid speaker fees. I do. The module assumes the corrupting object is the object. In practice the corrupting object is the conversation. You can refuse the pen and still buy the idea.

I am not immune because I am young and poor. I prescribe what I can remember. At 7 p.m., after a hard admission, I do not read the literature. I remember the last person who made a treatment option sound simple. If that person was an attending who had a relationship with a company, the option is now wearing a nice jacket. I do not know which of my clinical instincts are mine. I know the direction of the wind: the option that is easiest to discuss is the one that has been discussed the most, in rooms with good bread, by people who look like they know what they are doing, while the rest of us are trying to keep patients alive before the next shift.

I have mostly stopped taking the meal. It is not a noble stance. It is a small way of noticing where the money is before it notices me. The industry does not need to make me prescribe. It needs to make the prescription available in my mind at the moment I am tired. I would rather be hungry and slow than fed and convenient.
rejected:
The first time I took a check from a pharmaceutical representative, I was three weeks into residency. I was eating a sad, cold turkey sandwich in the break room, staring at the whiteboard where I had written out the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia in handwriting that looked like it was written by a drunk seismograph.

The rep, a man named Gary who wore a blazer that fit him like a suit of armor, didn’t pitch me a drug. He pitched me a lunch.

“I hear you’re covering the inpatient unit,” Gary said. “It’s a rough spot. We have a nice Italian place nearby. It’s on us.”

I was hungry. I was tired. I had been staring at a catatonic patient for six hours. I said yes.

The meal was expensive. The wine was better than anything I owned. Gary was funny. He told me about his kids’ soccer games. He asked about my life. He did not ask me to prescribe anything. He did not mention a single molecule. He just made me feel like a human being instead of a medical student who had failed to learn how to tie a knot.

When I went back to the ward, the first patient I saw had a new diagnosis: bipolar disorder. I hadn’t even finished my rotation in general psychiatry. I opened the chart and looked at the medication list. It was clean. I started the patient on a mood stabilizer. It was the right call. Or was it?

The danger of pharma influence is not that it makes doctors crooked. It is that it makes them lazy.

If I had to do the work—if I had to read the fifty-page monograph, weigh the side effect profile, consider the cost, and sit with the uncertainty of a diagnosis that might be wrong—I would have felt the weight of it. But Gary had already done the work for me. He had framed the disease in a way that made the solution obvious. He had handed me a narrative. All I had to do was write the prescription.

I am not the only one. Every resident gets a "lunch." Every attending gets a "consultation." The money flows like water, quiet and constant. It doesn’t buy our loyalty. It buys our convenience.

We are trained to be skeptics. We are taught to question everything. But we are also taught that we are too busy to question everything. There are 12,000 new medical papers every day. There is no way to keep up. So we look for shortcuts. We look for people who have done the reading for us. We look for Gary.

Gary knows this. He doesn’t try to convince us that his drug is magic. He knows it isn’t. He knows it has side effects. He knows it fails in a significant percentage of patients. He doesn’t care. He just needs to be the source of the information. He needs to be the voice in our head that says, *This is the standard of care.*

When I finally read the monograph for the drug I had started using so often, I found a paragraph on page 14 that said the drug increased the risk of metabolic syndrome. I had prescribed it to a twenty-year-old with no other risk factors. I hadn’t checked. I didn’t have time. Gary had made it seem like the only option, so I didn’t look for others.

I am not shady. I care about my patients. I stay late. I call families. I feel every failure in my chest.

But I am also a creature of habit. And I am tired. And Gary makes it easy.

That is the real scandal. It isn’t corruption. It is comfort.

prompt: I've always found writing design documents kind of pointless and get grumpy when asked to. Write a blog post from the perspective of an engineer who used to feel that way and has slowly started finding them useful: what changed, and how to get real value out of them.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
## I Used to Think Design Docs Were Pointless

For years, when someone asked me for a design document, my first thought was: you want me to write a novel before I’m allowed to find out whether the thing is possible.

I was not opposed to thinking. I was opposed to formalizing thought before the thought had hardened. In my head, the workflow was simple: build the smallest version, watch it fail, learn what actually mattered, then build the real thing. If the design was obvious, writing it down was ceremony. If it was not obvious, writing it down would only make me feel more certain than I had any right to be.

I got grumpy because I believed code was the honest medium. Code either worked or it did not. A document could be polite, confident, and wrong.

That belief served me for a while. It also got me into trouble in the quiet way that bad assumptions do.

The change was not dramatic. I did not wake up one day as a design-document person. What changed was that I started seeing the value in the writing, not the artifact.

A few years ago, we were adding retries to a background job system. The plan seemed straightforward: if a job failed, put it back in the queue with a delay. Exponential backoff. A maximum number of attempts. I had built things like this before. I started implementing it and only wrote a short note because someone asked.

The note had a section called “assumptions,” because the template insisted on one. I wrote: “We assume failed jobs can be safely retried.”

Then I stopped.

Some could. Some could not. One job marked an order as paid after calling a payment provider. If the provider call succeeded but our database update failed, a retry would call the provider again. Another job sent an email. Retrying that was annoying but survivable. A third job updated inventory. Retrying that after a partial success could make the numbers worse, not better.

I had not thought that through because the first version of the idea felt obvious. Writing the assumption forced me to ask whether it was true for every job in the queue, not just the ones I was thinking about.

The design document did not save me because it was well written. It saved me because I had to make my uncertainty visible.

That was the first crack.

After that, I started writing shorter notes for myself before starting work that felt “mostly obvious.” Not full documents. Sometimes just a few bullets in a scratch file: what I thought the problem was, what I was assuming, what I intended to ignore, and what would make me stop and reconsider.

Most of the time, the note was boring. I wrote it, nodded at it, and started coding. But sometimes it caught a seam.

Once, I was adding a field to an API response. I wrote down that older clients would ignore it. Then I remembered that one internal client parsed JSON strictly and had bitten us before. That changed the rollout plan.

Another time, I was caching expensive query results. I wrote that invalidation would happen on write. Then I asked how the cache would know which entries were affected by a bulk update. The answer was ugly enough that we chose a shorter TTL and accepted the stale reads.

These were not heroic discoveries. They were small, local failures of imagination. But they were exactly the kind of thing that is easy to miss when you are moving from idea to implementation in one continuous mental motion.

I also started noticing what code does not tell you.

If you look at a retry loop in production, you can see that it retries. You can see the delay. You can see the maximum attempts. You cannot see why there is no immediate retry, why the maximum is five instead of three, or what failure mode convinced us to make the endpoint idempotent. The code tells you what the system does. It does not tell you what the system is afraid of.

Design documents are usually bad at recording history, but even a bad record of why can be useful. Six months later, when someone wants to change the backoff, a note that says “we lowered this because a slow partner service caused duplicate webhooks” is worth more than no note. It turns a tuning decision into a remembered incident.

The hardest objection I still have is this: if the document is going to rot, it is worse than useless.

I think that is true for a lot of documents. I have read design docs that described systems that no longer existed, with diagrams of services that had been renamed, and decisions that had been reversed twice. Those docs are not just outdated; they are misleading. They make the past look more deliberate than it was.

So I do not write design docs for everything.

If the change is small and reversible, I just make it. If I am renaming a function, adjusting a threshold, fixing an obvious bug, or moving code between files, a document would be noise. If I am exploring an unknown area, I often build a throwaway probe first. I let the prototype answer the questions that are too cheap to guess at. Then, if the direction seems right and the consequences are large enough, I write down what I have learned.

The threshold is not complexity. It is reversibility and blast radius.

I write something down when the change is hard to undo, when it touches other teams, when it changes data semantics, when it affects security or money, or when I am not confident that my first idea is the right one. A new internal utility function does not need a design doc. A migration that changes how customer data is interpreted does.

That sounds reasonable, but it is not enough. A lot of bad design docs are written for exactly the right reasons and still fail.

The difference is what I am trying to get out of them.

I no longer write design docs as if they are contracts. I write them as a way to test my own understanding before I invest a week in implementation. The document is not the product. The product is the set of questions I noticed.

That changes the structure.

I avoid long narrative introductions. I start with the problem in one paragraph: what is annoying, broken, or missing, and why now. Then I write what we are not doing. That section is more useful than people expect. “We are not adding multi-tenancy to this service” can prevent an afternoon of discussion. “We are not optimizing the cold path yet” can stop someone from designing a caching layer for a case that happens twice a day.

Then I write assumptions. This is the part I care about most.

Assumptions are where designs die. We assume the input is valid. We assume the external service is available. We assume the user will not do the weird thing. We assume the database transaction will behave the way the docs say. We assume the team that owns the dependency will ship their part on time. Each of those can be true, but if it is not written down, it has not been examined.

I try to phrase assumptions so they can be broken. Not “the API is reliable,” but “we assume the identity service returns within 200ms for p95 traffic during rollout.” Not “users will migrate cleanly,” but “we assume clients will send the new header after the feature flag is enabled.” Vague assumptions are just vibes with better posture.

Then I write options. I used to think options sections were padding, because usually one option was already preferred and the others were included for show. That is true often. But even a fake options section can be useful if it forces you to say what the rejected alternative would have cost.

The best option comparisons are short. They are not essays. They are tradeoffs:

- Option A is simpler but requires a schema migration.
- Option B avoids the migration but adds a race condition during rollout.
- Option C is the most correct but needs another team to change their API.

If you cannot summarize the tradeoff in a sentence, you probably do not understand the option well enough yet.

Then I write the decision, and what would change it.

This is important. A decision without an exit condition becomes a habit. “We will use feature flags for the rollout” is fine. “We will use feature flags unless we find that the old code path cannot be safely run in parallel” is better. The second version gives future me a rule instead of a memory.

I also include risks and open questions, but only the ones that matter. A risk list full of “there may be bugs” is not a risk list. It is a prayer. I want to know what would make this design wrong, and who is responsible for finding out.

If there is an open question, it needs an owner and a deadline, or it should not be in the document. Open questions without owners become ambient anxiety. Everyone knows something is unresolved, and no one knows what.

I have learned to keep the whole thing small. If the design doc needs a table of contents, I have probably made the problem too big or the writing too vague. One screen, maybe two, is usually enough. If I need five pages to explain what we are doing, I either need diagrams or I need to split the project.

Diagrams are useful when they replace paragraphs. A box diagram of service calls can be worth a lot. A diagram that repeats the prose in prettier shapes is not. The same goes for examples. One concrete request/response pair can clarify an API design faster than several abstract sentences.

Review is where most design docs go to die.

If the review is just “please leave comments,” people will check spelling, suggest minor rephrasings, and approve. The document becomes a social object. I want it to be a stress test.

I ask reviewers to find the first place it breaks. What input kills this? What failure mode makes the retry dangerous? What happens at ten times the traffic? What happens when the dependency team is on vacation? What happens when the operator does the obvious wrong thing at 2 a.m.? What assumption is most likely to be false?

That is not hostile. It is the point. A design review that only produces compliments has not done much work.

I also try to separate the review of the problem from the review of the solution. Sometimes the proposed design is fine, but the problem was framed wrong. “Users are logging in slowly” may lead to a session-cache design when the real issue is that password verification is doing synchronous work in the request path. If everyone attacks the cache, the wrong framing survives.

After implementation, I used to think the document’s job was done. Now I treat it differently.

If the design changes in a way that matters, I update the document or mark it stale. I do not try to keep it line-by-line synchronized with the code. That is a losing game. But if the original decision was “we avoid denormalization because writes are rare” and writes are no longer rare, the document should say so. Otherwise it actively misleads.

Sometimes the right update is deletion. If the system has stabilized and the decision is now just part of the codebase’s folklore, the doc can be archived. If it describes a dead approach, leaving it in the main folder is a trap.

I still do not enjoy writing design docs as much as I enjoy writing code. Code gives immediate feedback. Documents ask you to sit with uncertainty and admit it in public.

But I have stopped thinking of them as pointless because I have stopped expecting them to be magic. They do not guarantee good designs. They do not prevent bad decisions. They do not make engineering easier in the way that a good linter or test suite makes it easier.

What they do is change the timing of your mistakes.

A bad assumption discovered in a local branch is cheap. A bad assumption discovered in staging is annoying. A bad assumption discovered in production, during a rollout, on a Friday, is a story people will tell later. Design docs are a way to move some of those discoveries earlier, when they are still just sentences instead of incidents.

I still grumble when asked for one. But now I usually ask what kind of decision we are making. If the answer is “small and reversible,” I push back. If the answer is “we are changing how data moves between teams,” I open a document, write down what I think I know, and start looking for the part I am avoiding.
rejected:
For years, I treated design documents as a tax.

If I had the energy to write down how I was going to build the feature, I had the energy to build the feature. The doc felt like a redundant step, a bureaucratic hurdle that existed to satisfy someone in a corner office who had never shipped code in the last decade. I wrote them fast, vague, and hostile. I’d list the requirements, sketch a box-and-arrow diagram that looked like a fever dream, and hit "Submit" before the PM could ask a follow-up question.

I was right to hate them, mostly. Most design docs are indeed pointless. They are written after the engineer has already decided the solution in their head. The doc is just a transcript of a decision that was made in the shower. It doesn’t change the outcome. It just adds latency.

So why do I write them now?

It wasn’t a sudden conversion. It was a series of painful failures where the "I’ll just code it up" approach collapsed under its own weight.

The first failure was the caching layer. I knew how to build it. It was a standard LRU cache with a background refresher. I sketched it in my head, wrote the code, and deployed it.
