# How to write positive peer feedback that isn’t just “they’re great”

The phrase “X is awesome” is not feedback. It is a conclusion with the evidence left out. If everyone you rate gets the same sentence, the review stops doing its job. It tells the person you like them, which may be true, and it gives their manager nothing they can use.

Useful positive feedback is different from praise. Praise says, “You are good.” Feedback says, “Here is what you did, here is what it changed, and here is why I noticed.” The second kind helps the person repeat the behavior. It also gives managers a reason to take the person seriously in calibration, promotion, and planning conversations.

## Write the scene, not the adjective

Adjectives like “great,” “reliable,” “collaborative,” and “strong” are easy to write and hard to verify. They also describe the person instead of the work.

“Maya is a great communicator” could be written about almost anyone. It does not tell Maya what to keep doing, and it does not tell her manager what kind of communication mattered.

A scene does the work:

> When the API outage hit on Tuesday, Maya posted a short status update every thirty minutes that said what was broken, what the team was trying, and what customers could do in the meantime. I could answer support questions without pinging her team, and the rest of us stayed focused instead of chasing rumors.

That paragraph contains the behavior—clear, frequent updates under pressure—and the effect—less noise, less dependency, more focus. The reader can see why “great communicator” was true.

Try to name the action: clarified, documented, pulled in, followed up, challenged, simplified, coordinated, prevented, unblocked. These are visible things. “Helpful” is not.

## Connect the action to an effect

A behavior by itself can sound like a job description. The effect is what makes it feedback.

If you don’t have a metric, use the smaller effects you actually saw: fewer meetings, less rework, faster decisions, clearer ownership, fewer escalations, a calmer room, a better document, a less ambiguous handoff.

“Sam left thoughtful comments on my draft” is nice. “Sam left comments that tied each section back to the original requirement, so I caught two scope problems before we took the proposal to the client” is useful. The second sentence tells Sam what kind of thinking mattered and gives the manager evidence that Sam improves work, not just participates in it.

If you only know the immediate effect, write the immediate effect. Don’t invent revenue impact. “This made my week easier” is weak unless you explain how.

Praising effort alone has the same problem. “They work hard” is not evidence of value. If the hard work produced a clearer plan, a safer launch, or fewer surprises, write that.

## Make the strength repeatable

Positive feedback should help the person know what to do more of. That means the strength has to be something they can choose, not a personality trait.

“Jordan is a natural leader” is flattering but not very actionable. What did Jordan do that looked like leadership? Did they set a direction when the group was drifting? Did they make a decision after gathering input? Did they take responsibility for a bad outcome and propose a fix?

> You took ownership of the integration delay by identifying the blocker, pulling in the two teams that needed to talk, and proposing a smaller scope for launch. That kept the project from stalling while the bigger question was still open.

Now Jordan knows the pattern: find the blocker, create the forum, propose a path. The manager sees judgment, scope, and follow-through.

You don’t have to end with “keep doing this.” If the behavior is named clearly, the instruction is already there.

## Give managers a signal, not a mood

Managers read peer reviews to test their own view. They want to know whether a strength is real, recurring, and relevant to the work.

If you saw one good instance, write one good instance. Don’t turn it into a permanent character trait.

> I haven’t worked with Priya long enough to say she is consistently reliable, but in the last two release cycles she gave clear go/no-go updates and flagged risks before they became surprises.

That is honest and useful. It distinguishes a pattern from a first impression.

If you have seen the behavior repeatedly, say so. “Every time we start a project, Priya writes down the open questions first” is stronger than “Priya is organized.” The manager can see that the organization shows up at the start of work, not just in tidy notes.

Words like “always” and “never” raise the burden of proof. “In the last two release cycles” is easier to believe and easier to use.

Also, be careful with praise that sounds like a warning. “They always stay late” or “they are always available” can be read as unsustainable or as a boundary problem. Write the professional behavior instead: “They made their availability explicit during launch, which let the team plan around it.”

If you are not sure an observation is fair, write the smallest true version: “In the planning meeting, they summarized the tradeoffs and proposed a next step.” That is defensible and still useful.

## What to write when there was no hero moment

Most useful feedback is not about a dramatic rescue. It is about the ordinary work that makes other people’s work easier.

Think about the moments someone made your job less annoying. Did they write the document that stopped the meeting from going in circles? Did they ask the question that exposed the real constraint? Did they hand off work so clearly that you didn’t have to reverse-engineer it? Did they correct a mistake privately and without drama?

> Ravi’s review comments are specific and tied to the requirement, not just style preferences. When he says a section is unclear, he usually points to the missing assumption and suggests a fix. I trust his comments enough to act on them immediately.

That is a strong positive review. It does not need “awesome.” It tells Ravi what kind of reviewer he is and tells the manager that Ravi raises the quality of the work he touches.

If you cannot think of an example, the problem may not be your writing. It may be that you have not paid enough attention to what the person actually does. Ask yourself: What would get harder if they stopped doing this? What did I stop worrying about because they handled it? What did I learn from watching them?

## A few rewrites

Before: “Alex is a team player and a great culture add.”

After: “When two engineers disagreed about the rollout plan, Alex restated each side’s concern and asked what evidence would change their minds. That moved the conversation from positions to tests.”

Before: “Dana is very responsive.”

After: “Dana responds to handoff questions quickly and includes the context I need to act, not just an answer. During the migration, that meant I didn’t have to wait a day to find out whether a dependency was real.”

Before: “I love working with Chris.”

After: “Chris makes ambiguity easier to work in. When our requirements changed, they wrote a short note separating what was settled, what was open, and who owned each open item. The team stopped re-litigating the same questions.”

The second versions are longer, but they are not more intense. They are more precise. Precision is what makes positive feedback feel real.

## A test before you submit

Before sending, check the paragraph against a few questions:

- Does it contain a specific moment, artifact, or repeated behavior?
- Could the same sentence be true of several people? If yes, make it narrower.
- Would it still mean something if the name were replaced with a different person’s? If not, it is a generic compliment.
- Does it name an effect on the work, the team, or the person reading it?
- Is it something the person can repeat?

If it passes, it is probably useful. If it fails, you likely have a feeling that has not yet been turned into evidence.

That is not a flaw in the coworker. It is a flaw in the review. “I love working with them” may be true, but it is the conclusion. The reader needs the evidence.

The problem with writing "X is awesome" is that it is un-actionable. It tells the manager nothing about how to keep the person, and it tells the employee nothing about what to keep doing. When you strip away the fluff, a positive review isn’t about praise; it’s about evidence.

To write feedback that sticks, you need to move from adjectives to artifacts. An adjective describes a trait; an artifact describes a behavior. "Reliable" is an adjective. "When the database migration failed on a Saturday, X was the only person who stayed up to rerun the scripts and document the failure for the post-mortem" is an artifact.

There are three specific types of positive feedback that actually matter in a performance cycle.

**1. The Multiplier Effect**
Managers hire people to solve problems, but they keep people who make other people better. Identify a specific instance where your peer lowered the barrier to entry for someone else. Did they write a clear runbook that stopped the on-call rotation from getting paged? Did they review a junior’s code with such patience that the junior understood the *why*, not just the *what*?

Instead of saying "X is a great mentor," write: "During the Q3 onboarding, X created a sandbox environment that allowed new hires to practice deployments without breaking production. This cut the time-to-first-pull-request by a week and reduced my own interruption count significantly." This tells the manager that X reduces organizational friction.

**2. The High-Stakes Call**
Competence is easy to spot when things are going well. Distinguishable talent is visible when things are going wrong. Did your peer make a hard call? Did they push back on a project that was doomed to fail, or did they take ownership of a mistake that wasn’t technically theirs?

If they stopped a bad launch, say so. "When the marketing team proposed the new pricing page, X flagged that the UX would break on mobile. They didn’t just point out the bug; they brought a mockup of a fix to the next day’s standup." This shows initiative and cross-functional awareness, which are often the exact traits missing from mid-level employees.

**3. The Invisible Work**
Most "great" coworkers do things that are technically below the radar because they are so normal to them. They answer the ambiguous Slack message. They update the stale documentation. They clear the blockers for the person in the next office.

Call out the invisible work explicitly. "X consistently updates the API documentation immediately after every endpoint change. I don’t have to guess what the new payload looks like; I just read the docs. This has saved the frontend team hours of debugging every sprint." This is concrete, quantifiable, and directly links their behavior to team velocity.

**The Format**

Stop writing paragraphs of praise. Use the Situation-Action-Impact (S-A-I) structure. It forces you to be specific.

*   **Situation:** What was the problem or context? (The server was down. The client was angry. The deadline was in two hours.)
*   **Action:** What did they specifically do? (They wrote the patch. They called the client. They automated the test.)
*   **Impact:** What was the result? (We saved the contract. We met the deadline. The team stopped making that mistake.)

If you can’t fill out the three lines, you don’t have a concrete example. You just have a vibe.

**What to Avoid**

Avoid superlatives. "Best," "greatest," "most hardworking" are empty calories. They are easily discounted by a manager who sees a dozen "great" reviews a year. Save the superlatives for the one person who actually is the best. Use the concrete details for everyone else.

Avoid generic praise of character. "X is kind" is nice, but it’s not a performance metric. "X always asks 'what else can I do to help?' before leaving a meeting" is a behavior you can reward.

Finally, check your calibration. If you write three reviews and they all sound the same, you are probably defaulting to the safe path. Dig deeper. The person who is "great" is usually great in one or two very specific, weird, or hard ways. Find that way. Describe it. That is the review your manager needs to justify a raise, and the review your peer needs to know they are on the right track.

I want to live entirely in the future. Not because I dislike the present, but because I have learned that the present is the only place where the future is still possible. Yesterday is already fixed. Tomorrow is still open. A person who builds a life out of yesterday is not preserving anything; they are paying interest on a form that no longer fits.

By “entirely” I mean no shrine: no room, no relationship, no habit, no tool, no identity is exempt from the question of whether it still serves the life I am moving into. This is not a denial of the body. I still eat in the present, sleep in the present, feel pain in the present. I mean that the orientation of the mind is forward. The past is evidence. The future is work.

Take a house. A house built for a family of six becomes a tomb when the children leave, if the rooms remain as they were. The future-oriented person repaints, closes a wing, turns a bedroom into a studio, moves out, buys a smaller place, or lets the extra rooms be used by someone who needs them. None of this is betrayal. The house was never a promise to the past; it was a temporary answer to a life. When the life changes, the answer must change, or it becomes a cage.

Or take a job. A worker who keeps doing by hand a task that a simple program can do is not being artisanal; they are choosing to spend scarce hours on pointless repetition. The new tool is not an insult to the old skill. It frees the skill for the part that still needs judgment. A writer who refuses a better editor is not loyal to writing. A driver who refuses a clearer map is not loyal to the road. When a tool removes a pointless friction, adopting it is a small act of respect for people’s time.

The present is always a little stale. It is the time when the old has worn in and the new has not been tested. Every stable thing is a fossil of an adaptation: a street pattern made for a different traffic, a job title describing a task that no longer exists, a custom that once solved a problem we no longer face. To treat the present as the highest reality is to mistake the surface of a moving thing for its destination.

I am not a consumer. The difference matters. A consumer wants the newest because it is shiny. I want the next because it may be truer. A new phone is not automatically better. A new diet trend is not automatically wisdom. A new business model is not automatically noble. But if a new method saves time, reduces harm, makes a task easier to learn, or lets a person with a disability do what others did easily, then refusing it out of loyalty to the old way is not virtue. It is a tax on the living.

The hardest objection is that a life always turned toward the next thing is a life without depth. If everything is provisional, nothing becomes real. If I am always becoming, I never arrive. If I abandon each form as soon as it ages, I become a collector of beginnings, a person with no home.

I am not sure how often a life can be revised before it loses its center. I suspect more often than most people allow, but the failure mode is real: a person who changes so often that no one can recognize them, or they cannot recognize themselves, has not found the future; they have lost the present. So the case I am making is not that novelty is good. It is that revision is necessary, and that the refusal to revise is a disguised form of fear.

Depth is not the same as permanence. A river is deep because it has moved through many channels, not because it stands still. A language is rich because it has absorbed new words and dropped dead ones. A person who has revised their views several times is not less serious than one who has never been challenged; they are more likely to know what they are talking about. To live in the future is to be present to the draft. A musician does not stop being in the present because the next phrase is already forming. A doctor does not neglect the patient because the literature is improving. A parent does not fail to love the child because the child’s needs will change next month. The future is not a place I escape to. It is the dimension of the now in which things are unfinished, and unfinished things are the only things that can be helped.

Many relationships die because the people in them refuse to meet each other’s future selves. They argue over the last version of the other. They keep score of a person who no longer exists. The future-oriented person says: you are changing, I am changing, the arrangement must change. That is not coldness. It is the minimum work required to keep a living bond alive. A friendship that can only discuss last decade is not a friendship; it is a shared archive. A marriage that cannot renegotiate chores, desires, work, and space will either become a performance or a prison.

Institutions need the same habit. A company that keeps an old hierarchy because it built the company is not honoring its founders; it is preventing the company from responding to customers, workers, and competitors. A city that bans new uses for old buildings preserves a photo instead of a neighborhood. A law that cannot be amended becomes a trap. The future-oriented institution has a regular question built into it: what does this form now cost, and what does it no longer serve?

There is a spiritual aspect, though I would not call it spiritual if that word makes it soft. To live in the future is to accept that I am not the final product. My tastes will embarrass me. My body will make new demands. My loyalties will be tested by circumstances I cannot now imagine. If I build a life that cannot bend, I am not building a life; I am building a monument to a person who is already changing. The next thing is not always better than the old thing, but it is the only thing that can be born.

So the practice is simple and unglamorous. Every year, look at the routines, tools, rooms, relationships, and rules that carry the most weight in my life. Ask whether they exist because they still work or because I remember when they first worked. If the answer is memory, revise. If a tool is only familiar, replace it. If a room is only a relic, use it for what is needed now. If a rule was made for a version of me who has already passed, let it go. Do this without drama. The future does not require a revolution. It requires that I stop defending the draft.

I do not want to be satisfied with the present as if satisfaction were a place where time stops. I want the pause to be a pause. When the next thing arrives, I will ask whether it is louder, newer, or more expensive, and then I will ask whether it lets me be less false. If it does, I will take it. If it does not, I will wait. Either way, I will not make the old thing a god. The old thing did its work. Now it has to get out of the way.

# The Manifesto of the Upward Drift

The past is a graveyard. It is full of dead ideas, failed relationships, and obsolete technologies. To look backward is to invite the dead into your living room. To live entirely in the future is to refuse that invitation. It is to recognize that the only time that matters is the time that is coming, because the only time you can change is the time that has not yet happened.

We do not chase the new out of vanity. We chase it out of necessity. The world is not static; it is a river. To stand on the bank is to drown. To swim upstream is to exhaust yourself. To float with the current is to be swept into the future. This is not escapism. It is survival.

### The Obsolescence of Yesterday

Every habit you keep from last year is a small tax on your potential. Every belief you held five years ago is likely a lie you have outgrown. The person you were in 2020 is a stranger who made bad decisions with less information. If you cling to them, you are clinging to a corpse.

The "next" thing is not just a product. It is a state of mind. It is the willingness to discard the toolkit you mastered yesterday because it is no longer sharp enough for the stone you must cut today. Mastery is a trap. If you master a skill, you become dependent on its permanence. The future-proof individual is the one who remains a beginner forever.

### The Joy of Anticipation

There is a specific pleasure in the unknown. It is the electricity of the unverified. When you buy a book, you do not read it immediately. You wait. You let the cover talk to you. You let the promise of the story settle into your bones. This is the only honest relationship we can have with reality. We are creatures of expectation. To live in the present is to live in a vacuum of anticipation, a void where the future has not yet arrived to fill the space.

To live in the future is to live in the fullness of possibility. The past is fixed. It is a single, narrow line. The future is a vast, branching tree. By orienting your life toward the branches, you expand your habitat. You make more room for the unexpected. You stop treating life as a problem to be solved and start treating it as a mystery to be solved.

### The Ethics of Forward Motion

Critics say we are fickle. They say we lack loyalty. They are right. We are fickle. But loyalty to what? To a company that will be bankrupt in a decade? To a ideology that has already failed its first major test? To a version of yourself that is no longer real?

True loyalty is to the trajectory. It is to the arc of your own improvement. If you stay in one place, you are not being faithful to your past self; you are betraying your future self. You are stealing from the person who will exist in five years. You are handing them a broken map.

### The Practice

How do you live this way?

1.  **Delete the archives.** Stop reading old journals. Stop re-watching old movies. Stop revisiting old arguments. The data is dead. Let it rot.
2.  **Learn the language before the text.** When a new technology or art form emerges, do not wait for the masterpiece. Learn the grammar. Learn the tools. Be the first to know how the brush works, before the painting is finished.
3.  **Bet on the unlikely.** The future is rarely a linear extension of the present. It is a jump. If you predict the future by extrapolating the past, you will be wrong. You must guess at the discontinuity. You must place your bets on the weird, the small, the currently invisible.
4.  **Forgive the delay.** The future will not arrive on schedule. It will be late. It will be messy. It will not look like the brochure. You must have the patience to wait for the new to become real, but not the patience to wait for the old to become good.

### The Final Truth

You will die. That is the only certainty. The past is the only thing you can be sure of, and it is the only thing that is gone. The future is the only thing you can influence, and it is the only thing that is real.

Do not mourn the yesterday. It is not yours anymore. It belongs to the dead. Take your eyes off the rearview mirror. Take your hands off the dashboard. Look out the windshield.

The road is ahead. The engine is hot.

Go.

Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. The premise is close enough, but it needs one correction: the same drivers, teachers, and customers often *can* use all of them, and that possibility changes everything. They are not indifferent. A driver chooses where to spend the next hour. A teacher chooses where to push a new course. A rider chooses between two phones screens showing different prices and wait times. But because they can leave, the platforms cannot simply own their supply or their demand. They have to earn both, repeatedly, in real time.

That is where peer-to-peer businesses stop being peer-to-peer.

At first, the business is a matching problem. There are people with cars, rooms, skills, or goods. There are people who want them. The platform removes search friction and adds a payment rail. The “peer” label is accurate then because the value is direct access: you can get a ride from a person, a lesson from an instructor, a table from someone with one. The platform is a bridge.

At scale, the value shifts from access to reliability. A city rider does not want “a person with a car.” They want a car in four minutes that is clean, goes where they say, and does not end with a support ticket. A student does not want “a teacher.” They want a course that is current, easy to follow, and likely to produce the skill they are trying to buy. Once the platform is large enough, the problem is no longer introducing two strangers. The problem is making a variable human supply base behave like a consistent service.

This is why Uber and Lyft look so similar. Both have upfront pricing, ratings, cashless payment, background checks, insurance arrangements, trip sharing, and in-app support. The features converged because they are table stakes. The durable difference is usually local and operational: which app has more available cars in this neighborhood at this hour, which one is surging less, which one’s drivers accept short trips, which one’s support actually refunds a charge. In a dense market, the customer becomes a live auditor of the platforms’ dispatching. If one app shows a lower price and a shorter wait, the brand matters less than the operation.

The same dynamic shows up on the supply side. If drivers can work for both, the platforms compete for their attention with incentives. Bonuses, peak-hour guarantees, low-fee windows, and completion rewards are not customer-facing products. They are labor-market tools. The driver’s time is inventory. The platform that can predict demand and pay the right price for that inventory gets more reliable service. That is not peer-to-peer thinking. That is yield management.

Customers multihome too, but less symmetrically. A rider may check both apps before a trip, but over time they develop a default. The default app has the saved card, the home and work addresses, the payment history, the habit. So the platforms also compete for inertia. They try to make themselves the path of least resistance: faster button, cleaner map, easier scheduling, better loyalty offer. In dense markets, price transparency keeps rents low. In thinner markets, coverage becomes the product. If one platform reliably works and the other does not, the customer stops checking.

This is where the “peer” begins to disappear. The rider does not care about the driver as a person. They care about the car class, the estimated arrival time, the price, and the rating. The driver is abstracted into a service unit. The platform brands the experience, sets the minimum standards, handles the dispute, and carries the reputational risk. If the trip goes badly, the customer does not say, “That independent driver was bad.” They say, “Uber failed me.” The peer is still there, but the company has become the account.

The teacher side is similar, but the economics shape the supply differently. Udemy and Skillshare are often compared as if they are the same kind of marketplace with different logos. They are not. Udemy is closer to a course store: individual courses, often bought at a discount, chosen by a specific problem. “Excel for accountants,” “Python for finance,” “Project management for new managers.” The course page has to sell a narrow outcome. Skillshare is closer to a subscription channel: the customer pays for access to a body of content, so the platform benefits from bingeability, series, and production polish. The marginal cost of another class is low, so the incentive is to keep the user inside the catalog.

That means the same teacher may make different products for each. A Udemy course may be longer, more searchable, and framed around a credential-like result. A Skillshare class may be shorter, more visual, and easier to consume as part of a design or creative habit. The teacher is not just “sharing knowledge with peers.” They are adapting to two different retail environments. The platform selects a species of supply.

This selection is one of the main things peer-to-peer businesses become at scale: curators. Early on, the long tail is the point. Anyone can list. But too much unfiltered supply hurts trust. Customers cannot evaluate every option, so the platform must rank, recommend, and remove. Ratings, completion data, production guidelines, thumbnail standards, category editors, and featured placements all do the same job: reduce the customer’s risk. The marketplace becomes a storefront with an algorithm as the head clerk.

The hardest objection to this view is that if the platforms converge, one should simply win. If Uber and Lyft are nearly the same, why do both survive? If Udemy and Skillshare are both course platforms, why not a monopoly? The answer is that the network effects are real but local, and the positioning can remain different enough to matter.

Rides are intensely local. A national brand with weak supply in a particular county is not very valuable. A driver in one city can work for both, which prevents either platform from fully capturing the labor pool. A rider in a dense area can punish weak service by switching within minutes. So two large platforms can coexist by each winning different pockets, different time periods, and different driver incentives. The competition is not global; it is block by block, hour by hour.

Courses are different. I am less confident that the course side settles into a stable duopoly. Rides have immediate switching and strong local density. Course purchases are slower, more identity-driven, and more dependent on trust in the platform’s taste. A subscription platform can become a brand people join for community and curation, not just catalog. A marketplace can win by being the place where a specific professional skill is cheapest to acquire. So the end state may be more fragmented, or it may tilt toward one generalist with the best recommendation engine and the deepest catalog. The pressure, though, is the same: from open peer supply to managed distribution.

There is also a trust problem that scale makes unavoidable. A small marketplace can survive on goodwill. A large one cannot. When the transaction volume is high enough, the worst cases become statistically certain: the assault, the damaged room, the fake review, the course that is outdated or misleading, the driver who argues, the instructor who overpromises. The platform then has to act like an institution. It needs verification, insurance, monitoring, minimum standards, support teams, removal policies, and legal defenses. It may avoid the legal label of employer, carrier, or publisher, but operationally it takes on many of the responsibilities.

That is why the organizational shape changes. A young peer-to-peer company is mostly product and growth. A scaled one is operations, risk, and local management. There are city teams adjusting driver incentives. There are safety teams reviewing trips. There are creator-success teams telling instructors how to structure lessons. There are trust-and-safety teams reading transcripts, photos, and complaints. The office becomes a control room for a distributed workforce that it does not formally employ.

This is the end state in plain terms: peer-to-peer businesses become traditional service businesses with a crowdsourced back end. They own the customer interface, the payment, the brand, the standards, and the liability. The peers own their labor, their content, and a slice of the pricing power that comes from being able to leave. The platform’s job is to make the peer’s variability acceptable to the customer.

Data often gets credited as the moat, but at scale the moat is usually less mystical. Both ride platforms see similar demand patterns. Both course platforms see similar browsing and completion behavior. The data helps, but it does not remove the physical constraint: a human has to drive the car, and a human has to make and teach the course. The advantage goes to the company that turns data into local reliability—more cars where needed, better courses surfaced, faster refunds, fewer bad actors, smoother onboarding.

So what do they end up looking like? They end up looking like franchisors without stores, or utilities with brands. The peer is not the customer’s main counterparty. The platform is. The customer buys a promise: a car now, a room that matches the photos, a lesson that works. The peer delivers it, but the company is responsible for making the delivery repeatable.

The “peer-to-peer” part becomes a story about origins. The business itself becomes something older: a service company trying to make independent supply dependable enough that strangers will pay for it without thinking too hard. The most successful versions are the ones where you forget the marketplace is there at all. The car arrives. The course plays. The refund appears. The peer is still doing the work, but the company has become the guarantee.
rejected:
The distinction between Udemy and Skillshare, or Uber and Lyft, dissolves at the scale of the individual participant. A driver in Chicago can toggle between apps depending on which one offers a surge bonus. A student in Berlin takes a course from one platform and another from the second. A teacher uploads the same video lecture to both. The "platform" is not a container for a community; it is a transient interface for a transaction.

When peer-to-peer businesses reach scale, they stop looking like networks and start looking like utilities. The network effects that once defined them—the idea that value grows non-linearly with the number of users—plateau. Once there are enough drivers to ensure a car arrives in four minutes, the marginal value of the fifty-millionth driver is zero. The value proposition shifts from "access to a unique network" to "reliability and price."

This shift triggers a brutal convergence in business models.

**The labor market becomes a commodity market.**
In the early days, platforms fought for talent because supply was constrained. Drivers were scarce; teachers were rare. They offered higher payouts to lock in loyalty. At scale, supply exceeds demand in most markets. The platform’s leverage flips. It no longer needs the driver; the driver needs the platform. Consequently, the take-rate (the percentage of the transaction the platform keeps) rises until it matches the cost of payment processing and customer service. The driver or teacher is no longer a partner; they are a variable cost. The only differentiator left is the algorithm’s ability to match supply to demand with minimal idle time.

**The "moat" is logistical, not social.**
A social network’s moat is the graph of relationships. If you leave Facebook, you lose your friends. A peer-to-peer utility’s moat is the friction of switching. If Uber and Lyft offer the same car for the same price in the same time, the customer chooses the one with the app already on their phone. This is not a product advantage; it is a behavioral inertia. The companies spend billions not on improving the car or the course, but on subsidizing the first ride or the first month to install that inertia. Once the habit is formed, the subsidy stops, and the price rises to market equilibrium.

**Quality control becomes a data problem, not a human one.**
At small scale, a peer-to-peer business is a trust network. You hire a plumber because a friend recommended them. At scale, you cannot vet individuals. You vet the aggregate. The platform replaces judgment with ratings. A 4.8-star rating is not a measure of excellence; it is a measure of statistical deviation from the norm. It tells you the driver is unlikely to be terrible. It does not tell you they are good. The result is a floor, not a ceiling. The experience becomes standardized, sanitized, and interchangeable. The "peer" in peer-to-peer is an abstraction. The customer does not know the driver’s name, background, or face. They are interacting with a node in a graph.

**The end state is a two-sided monopoly with a single price.**
In most major cities, one platform will dominate the ride-hailing market, and one will dominate the course marketplace. The second player will likely be acquired, spun off, or reduced to a niche. This is not because one is better. It is because the cost of maintaining two parallel logistics systems is inefficient. The market settles into a state where the platform is a tax on the transaction. The driver and the teacher are independent contractors, but they are structurally dependent on a single gatekeeper for income. The customer has choice in the abstract (they *can* download the other app), but in practice, they face a duopoly or monopoly that dictates price and availability.

The peer-to-peer revolution was a misnomer. It was a shift from vertical integration (where a taxi company owned the cars and employed the drivers) to horizontal coordination (where a software company coordinates cars and drivers who belong to themselves). The power did not go to the peers. It went to the coordinator. The scale of the business revealed that coordination is the valuable asset, not the connection.

prompt: Write an exploratory blog post, from the point of view of an engineer at a tech company, about the open questions you have about open source: when to use it versus building your own, why companies pay people to write it, and how you're supposed to evaluate it. It's fine to raise more questions than you answer.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Open Questions About Open Source

When I open the dependency graph for one of our services, the first thing I notice is that the service is mostly not ours. It will not start without a database, a logging library, a JSON parser, a date-time helper, a task queue client, a set of transitive dependencies I have never heard of, and several tools whose names I can only half-pronounce. I did not write most of that code. I have not read most of it. I do not know who is responsible for it, whether they are still working on it, or what happens next when the world changes underneath it.

That is the situation most software teams are in now. We do not choose “open source” as a philosophy. We choose it because the alternative is worse. If we need an HTTP client, we are not going to write a good one. If we need a Postgres driver, we are not going to write a safe one. If we need a container orchestrator, we are absolutely not going to write one. But the more we use these things, the more I find myself asking questions I cannot answer cleanly.

The first one is about when to use something and when to build it.

At our company, the default answer is usually: use open source unless the thing is core to the product or our requirements are so weird that we will spend most of our time fighting the tool. That sounds reasonable. It is also not very helpful, because the hard cases are not weird requirements. They are ordinary things that have become load-bearing.

A date library is an ordinary thing. A retry wrapper is an ordinary thing. An internal authentication helper is an ordinary thing. None of them is the product. But if one of them is wrong, or unmaintained, or abandoned, the cost can be much larger than the original code would have been. I have seen teams spend weeks untangling an internal abstraction because nobody remembered why it existed. I have also seen teams spend months maintaining an internal library that was only slightly better than the external one and much harder to upgrade.

The build-versus-use decision is not really a technical question. It is a question about who will carry the future cost. If we use an external project, we are betting that someone else will keep doing the boring work: updating dependencies, writing migration notes, responding to security reports, explaining breaking changes, keeping the build green on new compilers, answering the question that always comes up at the worst time. If we build it ourselves, we are betting that we will still care about the boring work in three years, and that we will have the people to do it.

That second bet is scarier than it sounds. Internal code does not get abandoned because the code is bad. It gets abandoned because the person who understood it left, and the next person is too busy to learn it. But external code can get abandoned too, and then you have the same problem with less context and a public audience.

I think the line is often drawn by leverage. If the component is a commodity and there are several credible options, using one is probably right. If the component is central to how the product works, building it may be right. The uncomfortable middle is where the component is not central to the product but is central to the engineering platform: the thing every service depends on, the thing nobody wants to own, the thing that becomes infrastructure by accident.

The second question is why companies pay people to write open source in the first place.

The obvious answer is that open source is a public good. That is true, but it does not explain a lot of behavior. Public goods are exactly the things markets underfund. If a company can get value from a project without paying enough to sustain it, why would it pay?

The real answers are messier. Companies pay people to work on open source because it helps them hire. Engineers want to work on things that matter outside the company, and contributions to well-known projects are a signal. Companies pay because it reduces fragmentation. If everyone uses the same database, the same container runtime, the same API gateway, the ecosystem gets thicker, the tooling improves, and the company has less custom glue to maintain. Companies pay because it gives them influence. A standard is worth something when you can help shape it. Companies pay because they sell support, or cloud hosting, or compliance, or integration, and the open source project is the top of the funnel.

Sometimes the company is the project. Kubernetes is a good example: many companies contribute because the whole cloud-native stack depends on it, and the project has institutional backing through the CNCF. Linux is another: there are enough companies with direct commercial interests that the kernel gets maintained even when any one company would underinvest. PostgreSQL is different. It has survived for decades with a largely volunteer core, which tells you that stable, conservative software can be maintained by people who care about the software itself.

But there is a third case that worries me more. The project is maintained by a company for which it is not the main business. It is important enough to need a maintainer, but not important enough to have a business model. The maintainer is an employee, but the project is a side obligation. The company benefits from it, but if the project becomes expensive or politically awkward, the company can change the license, reduce staffing, or move on.

Redis made that risk concrete when it changed its licensing terms in 2024. The ecosystem responded quickly, with Valkey emerging as a Linux Foundation-backed fork. That was a healthy sign: the community had enough shared interest to organize. But it also showed how much friction a license change can introduce. Forks are not free. They split contributors, duplicate work, and make users choose sides. A company that depends on the original may not get to enjoy the fork’s safety without doing something active.

So I keep coming back to the same question: is open source a commons, a vendor relationship, or a mix of the two? I think it is a mix, and the mix changes project by project. A library maintained by one unpaid volunteer is closer to a commons. A database maintained by a company that sells clusters is closer to a vendor. A tool maintained by a foundation with corporate members is somewhere in between, but the foundation can still be captured by the companies with the most money and the most engineers.

The third question is how you are supposed to evaluate all this.

We have checklists. License: is it permissive enough for us? Activity: are there recent commits? Releases: do they happen on a schedule? Issues: are they answered? Documentation: is it good? Security: is there a contact, a process, a history of patching? Dependencies: how deep is the tree? Governance: who can merge, and who can change the rules?

Those are all useful. None of them is enough.

Stars measure popularity. They do not measure whether the maintainer will still be around when the next language release breaks the build. Commit activity can mean healthy work or anxious churn. A project can have weekly releases and still be moving in the wrong direction. An issue tracker can look responsive and still be run by one person who is about to burn out. A project can have a security policy on its website and no real process behind it.

The best signal I have found is boring maintenance. Not the exciting feature, not the architecture diagram, not the conference talk. The boring stuff. How did the project handle a dependency update that everyone hates? How did it handle a CVE? Did it yank a release? Did it write a migration guide, or did it just bump the version and hope? Did the maintainers answer the question about the obscure platform, or did they close it as “not planned”? Did the last breaking change come with a deprecation path, or did it arrive as a surprise?

That is harder to evaluate because it is not usually visible in a dashboard. You have to read release notes, issue threads, pull requests, and sometimes the tone of the maintainer’s replies. You have to ask whether the project is being run as a service or as a hobby. Both can be fine, but they are different bets.

There is also a supply-chain problem that makes evaluation feel less like choosing a library and more like choosing a counterparty. A dependency is not just code. It is a claim that someone will notice when the world changes. If a maintainer’s account is compromised, if a package is typo-squatted, if a transitive dependency disappears, if a build tool changes its defaults, someone has to notice and do something. In a small project, that someone may be a person with a day job. In a large company, it may be a team with a budget. The difference matters.

I would like a standard way to see the project’s balance sheet. Who pays the maintainers? How much of their time is spent on it? What happens if one of them leaves? Is there a security contact who will actually answer? Is there a governance document that means something? Are the release artifacts reproducible? Does the project have a plan for the next breaking change, or only a plan for the last one? Almost no project publishes that information, because it is not flattering and it is not stable.

The hardest objection to all of this is that the model is unstable. Open source is a public good, companies free-ride, maintainers burn out, and the important projects survive because they are either lucky or commercially backed. That is a fair description of a lot of the ecosystem. If I take it seriously, I should stop asking whether a project is good and start asking whether it has a durable incentive structure.

But that is not the whole answer either. Too many critical projects are not products. They are standards, utilities, safety nets. If we treat every dependency like a vendor, we miss the fact that some of the most important software is maintained by people who are not trying to monetize it. If we treat it like charity, we miss the fact that maintainers need jobs, and jobs need companies with reasons to keep paying.

Maybe the right question is not “Is this project sustainable?” in the abstract. It is: “Who has a reason to keep this alive when we are no longer the loudest user?” That is a better question, but it is still a forecast. I can look at the contributors and the funding and the governance and the issue tracker, and I can make a judgment. I cannot make a guarantee.

That leaves the question I do not know how to answer. What should a company do when it depends on a project that is too important to abandon and too small to fund? Do we pay the maintainer directly and become a weird patron? Do we fork it and accept that we are now the maintenance risk? Do we hire the maintainer and lose the project anyway? Do we write our own version and pretend the problem is ours? Do we keep using it, update it carefully, and hope that the next person who cares shows up before the next breaking change does?
rejected:
I spent last week deciding whether to adopt a new state management library or write a 200-line reducer from scratch. The decision felt trivial, but the underlying logic is one of the hardest parts of modern engineering.

We treat open source as a public utility, but it behaves more like a marketplace with broken price signals. When you pull a dependency, you are taking a loan against a stranger’s future. The interest rate is invisible until the maintainer quits, the package gets compromised, or the license changes.

The "build vs. buy" question is usually framed as an efficiency calculation. *Is it faster to use X or build Y?* This is the wrong frame. The real question is about risk transfer.

When you build your own tooling, you own the risk. If it breaks, you fix it. If it becomes obsolete, you rewrite it. You have total agency. When you use open source, you transfer the maintenance risk to a community that has no contractual obligation to you. You gain speed today, but you assume a long-tail liability that is difficult to price.

This leads to the second mystery: why do companies pay people to write it?

The standard answer is that open source is a recruiting tool or a marketing channel. That’s true, but it’s not the whole picture. For many engineers, writing open source is a form of reputation capital. It is the only way to signal competence to the broader industry, not just your current employer. It is a portfolio that follows you.

But there is a darker incentive structure. If I work at Company A, and I spend 20% of my time maintaining a library that 50,000 developers use, Company A benefits from my productivity gains, but the library belongs to the community. If I quit, the library doesn’t quit with me. The knowledge is externalized. This creates a perverse incentive to pick projects that are high-visibility but low-maintenance, or to maintain projects that are critical enough to keep you employed but not so complex that you burn out.

So how do we evaluate it?

We look at stars. We look at download counts. We look at the last commit date. These are vanity metrics. They tell you that people have looked at the code, not that the code is good, secure, or sustainable.

I have started using a different heuristic: *Who pays the maintainer?*

If the maintainer is a full-time employee of a company that sells a related product, the project is likely stable. The company has a financial incentive to keep it alive. If the maintainer is a single individual with no corporate backing, the project is a bet on their personal longevity.

This doesn’t mean solo-maintained projects are bad. Some of the most critical infrastructure on the internet is maintained by people who do it for love or habit. But the risk profile is different. You are relying on a person, not an institution.

There is a third open question that I don’t have an answer for: the security model of trust.

In a proprietary world, you trust the vendor because they can be sued. In an open source world, you trust the code because you can read it. But nobody reads the code. We install packages and hope for the best. The supply chain is a black box. We have moved from trusting a company to trusting a cryptographic hash, but we haven’t built the tools to verify that hash against a human intention.

We are building our software on a foundation of goodwill. It works. It’s fast. It’s cheaper than the alternative. But I don’t think we fully understand what we are doing, and I’m not sure we will, until something breaks.

prompt: I just finished a book about Soviet economic planning and the mathematicians who tried to fix it. Write a long, thoughtful review that goes beyond the plot to what it teaches about planning, incentives and who ought to run a country.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I do not know the exact title, so I will not invent chapter details; I will review the argument that a book about Soviet economic planning and the mathematicians who tried to fix it carries. The central claim is easy to state and hard to resist: the Soviet economy was not saved by better equations because it was never primarily an equation. It was a hierarchy of ministries, factories, party committees, quotas, shortages, bribes, hopes, and fears. Mathematics could clarify parts of it. It could not replace the political question of who gets to decide, who bears the cost of error, and how mistakes become visible.

The tempting promise behind Soviet mathematical planning was real. Linear programming, input-output tables, cybernetic control, and computerized optimization were not fantasy. Leonid Kantorovich’s work in the 1930s on allocating scarce resources among competing uses was serious operations research, not Soviet ideological decoration. It won a Nobel Prize in 1975 because it was genuinely useful. If a factory has a fixed amount of steel, labor, machine time, and warehouse space, and if the possible products and technical coefficients are known, then one can calculate a better allocation than a tired planner with a pencil can find. The same is true of a railway timetable, a military supply chain, a hospital bed system, or a power grid. These are bounded problems with measurable constraints. The mathematicians who entered Soviet planning were not charlatans. They had found a powerful method and wanted to apply it to the largest system of all.

The mistake was to treat the national economy as if it were one of those bounded problems. A linear program needs an objective function. Maximize what? Steel? GNP? Welfare? Defense capability? Consumer satisfaction? If the answer is “social welfare,” someone must assign weights: how much leisure is worth relative to a ton of aluminum, how much a pair of shoes counts against a missile component, how much clean air should be valued compared with a new factory. In a market economy, prices perform a crude, noisy, and often unjust job of aggregating these choices. In a command economy, the weights are chosen by politicians and planners. That is not a technical failure. It is the technical consequence of politics. The computer can optimize the system, but it cannot tell the state what the people want, what is fair, or what future should be built.

The second missing element is the coefficients. The Soviet planning model treated the economy as a matrix of material balances: so many tons of metal require so much coal, so much electricity, so many worker-hours. The problem was that the matrix was not given by nature. It was reported by the very institutions the plan was supposed to discipline. A plant director did not submit data the way a sensor submits data. He submitted a position. If he revealed that his factory could produce more than the official target, the next target would rise. If he admitted a shortage, he would be blamed for poor management. If he exaggerated his capacity, he might get credit for overcoming difficulties later. The plan therefore became a negotiation in which every unit tried to secure inputs and weaken obligations. The “data” were not measurements of the economy so much as opening bids in a game.

This is where the incentive problem becomes concrete. Suppose a shoe factory is judged by the number of pairs produced. It produces pairs: thin, ugly, likely to fall apart. Suppose it is judged by quality. The ministry must define quality, inspectors must measure it, and the factory can learn to satisfy the test rather than the user. Suppose it is judged by profit. But if losses will be covered by the state, profit is not a real constraint. János Kornai’s term “soft budget constraint” captures the whole weakness. In a market, a loss is information: this use of resources is worse than some alternative, and the firm that made the mistake pays. In the Soviet system, a loss was a paperwork problem. The enterprise could request more money, better equipment, a lower target, or a transfer from another ministry. The signal that should have corrected behavior was absorbed by the state.

The mathematicians could not fix this by adding more variables, because the variables were strategic. A manager’s report was part of his action. If the plan demanded 100 million pairs of shoes, the interesting question was not whether the arithmetic for leather, labor, and soles was correct. The interesting question was whether the shoes would be wanted, whether they would fit, whether they would last, and whether the factory had hidden capacity to make the target look heroic later. The official statistics measured production, not consumption. They counted what left the factory gate, not what satisfied anyone. The result was an economy that could be very good at producing the things it was ordered to produce and very bad at discovering what people actually needed.

The black market and the dacha garden were not failures of the Soviet economy in the way a breakdown of a machine is a failure. They were the economy’s way of continuing to function. If the store had no meat, no decent fabric, no decent shoes, and no reliable way to get repairs, people developed private channels. They traded, bartered, cultivated plots, stored goods, and used personal connections. The official plan and the informal market were not two separate systems; they were one system with a public face and a private face. The plan allocated visible resources. The shadow economy allocated the rest. This coexistence shows that the planners did not control the whole process of coordination. They controlled only the part they could count.

The information problem is often summarized by saying that no central computer could process enough data. That is too simple. The Soviets had computers. They could have computed input-output tables. The deeper issue is that the relevant information was not waiting in files to be processed. Much of it was local, tacit, temporary, and created only by action. A small workshop might find a better way to machine a part. A supplier might learn that a customer’s real need was not the item on the order form but a modification of it. A new material might make an old product obsolete. A consumer might prefer a smaller, cheaper, more durable good to the standard model. In a market, these discoveries are tested through prices, competition, imitation, and failure. The cost of error is usually limited to the firm that made it. In a command system, the same discoveries require permission, reporting, standardization, and political approval. Errors are not localized; they enter the plan and become official.

This does not mean that the Soviet state was incapable of impressive coordination. It was not. The Soviet economy industrialized rapidly in the 1930s and after the war. It built heavy industry, railways, dams, universities, research institutes, and a military-industrial base that could challenge the United States. It put people into orbit. It supplied basic housing, education, and healthcare to hundreds of millions. These were real achievements, and any honest review must grant them. The point is that they were achievements of mobilization around narrow, measurable, politically prioritized goals. Building a bridge, a bomber, a reactor, or a railway line is easier to plan than deciding what ten million households should buy for breakfast, what software should be written, what style of coat will be fashionable, or which medical procedure gives the best result for a patient with a complicated case. The state can direct known tasks. It is much worse at discovering unknown ones.

The strongest objection to the usual verdict against planning is that markets can also be catastrophic, and that the post-Soviet transition showed this brutally. If central planning was so irrational, why did Russia in the 1990s experience collapse, inflation, corruption, and social devastation? Why did many people remember the shortages of the 1980s as a kind of order compared with the chaos that followed? The answer is not that planning was fine and markets were the problem. The answer is that institutions cannot be swapped in a few years. A market is not a set of prices appearing by magic. It requires property rights, courts that enforce contracts, competition law, functioning banks, auditable accounts, social insurance, and a state capable of stopping monopolies and banditry. The Soviet state was very good at commanding. It was not good at the different task of referee. When the command was removed faster than the referee was installed, the result was not a market economy but a lootable state.

China’s experience complicates the simple story in another way. China kept political control while introducing market incentives gradually: household farming, township and village enterprises, local competition, export processing, partial price liberalization, and state-owned enterprises pushed by output targets. It did not create a liberal democracy, but it did create real signals and real rewards for local initiative. The lesson is not that authoritarianism is compatible with prosperity in general, but that the boundary between planning and market can be moved. The state can retain control over some sectors while allowing competition in others. It can use performance incentives for managers without pretending to know what every consumer wants. The failure of Soviet planning was not the use of statistics, computers, or state investment. It was the attempt to make the state the final allocator of everything.

This leads to the political lesson, which is the one the book should teach most uncomfortably. Central planning does not merely require a central computer; it requires a central authority that can enforce the solution. If a ministry ignores the plan, the plan must have power to punish it. If a factory hides capacity, the state must have power to discover and expose the concealment. That means information about error must be controlled. A free press, independent courts, and open audit are not helpful accessories to a planning system; they are threats to it. They reveal shortages, waste, and failed targets. They allow local officials to complain without being labeled saboteurs. They make the costs of bad decisions visible to the people who must live with them. A planning state therefore tends toward secrecy, hierarchy, and political monopoly. The method of economic control shapes the method of political control.

The mathematicians’ models usually contained a fictional planner. This planner knew the true coefficients, had no private interest, could enforce the optimal solution, and did not need to be re-elected, promoted, or defended against rivals. The real planner was a ministry with a budget, a career, a reputation, and a stake in the plan’s success. If the model was wrong, admitting the error was dangerous. If the ministry’s forecasts were bad, the ministry lost influence. If the plan exposed a shortage, someone had to be blamed. Expertise did not remove politics; it became a form of politics. A mathematician with a model could defend a budget, justify a hierarchy, and resist criticism by appealing to the elegance of the system. The model did not make the planner neutral. It gave the planner a better language.

This is why the question “who ought to run a country?” cannot be answered by saying “the best experts.” Expertise is a tool, not a legitimacy. A country is not run the way a factory is run. A factory manager can be hired by owners, constrained by contracts, and replaced if performance fails. The state has a monopoly of force over the whole community. It decides who may be taxed, imprisoned, drafted, displaced, or ignored. For that reason, the distribution of political authority matters more than in any ordinary organization. The people do not need a council of genius to tell them what is good for them. They need institutions that make power temporary, local, visible, and replaceable.

That means several things at once. Elected bodies should decide collective ends, because no technical class has a natural right to choose the social goal. Independent courts should enforce rules, because if the same body makes the law, applies the law, and judges the result, error becomes obedience. Local governments should have real authority, because many problems are local and because local competition among officials creates a kind of accountability that a central ministry cannot replicate. A free press and open statistics should exist, not because bad news is pleasant, but because a government that cannot be corrected from outside will be corrected only by crisis. Professional bureaucrats should run day-to-day administration, but they should be answerable to political officials who can be removed, and to auditors who can expose failure.

The incentive structure of rulers is the whole point. If officials are secure regardless of performance, they will maximize security: budgets, status, ideology, and appearances. If they can be replaced, they must listen. If their decisions can be examined, they must prepare better information. If local rivals can outperform them, they must learn. If citizens can organize, protest, and vote, the state cannot treat people as parameters in a model. The Soviet planning system failed in part because it tried to make the population a variable to be managed. A constitutional order succeeds when it makes the rulers responsive to the people they govern, not because the people are wiser in the aggregate, but because the rulers are more likely to discover the truth when they cannot suppress it.

The book’s deepest lesson is therefore not that markets are a natural order and planning is an unnatural one. Markets are also institutions, and they can be corrupted by monopolies, finance, capture, and inequality. The lesson is that a society must choose where to draw the line between centralized direction and decentralized trial. The state can and should provide public goods, enforce standards, manage common resources, invest in basic research, and respond to emergencies. It can plan a vaccine campaign, a disaster relief effort, a grid upgrade, or a national defense system. But the more the economy depends on local knowledge, consumer choice, and innovation, the less a central plan can know what is happening. The moment the state tries to be the final judge of every exchange, it does not gain efficiency. It loses the feedback that would tell it when it is wrong.

The mathematicians who tried to fix Soviet planning were defeated not by stupidity but by scale and power. They had solved a real problem: how to allocate known resources more rationally within a bounded system. They had not solved the problem of a society that must create new resources, new wants, new knowledge, and new legitimacy while being governed by fallible officials. A country can be made more efficient in parts. It cannot be run from a central solution. The measure of a political order is not how cleanly it solves a fixed problem, but how well it finds problems, admits mistakes, corrects course, and allows ordinary people to live without begging permission from a ministry. The Soviet experiment shows what happens when the plan is treated as the whole truth and the people are treated as data.
rejected:
The central failure of Soviet economic planning was not a lack of intelligence, but a lack of information. This distinction is crucial because it shifts the critique from moral to epistemic. The planners were not stupid; they were brilliant. Many were the top mathematicians in the world. They understood linear programming, input-output matrices, and computational complexity. The problem was that they were trying to solve a system of equations with billions of unknowns using data that did not exist.

When a central authority attempts to allocate resources, it must know two things: the relative scarcity of inputs and the relative value of outputs. In a market economy, prices do this work for free. A rise in the price of copper signals that copper is scarce or that its value has increased. No one needs to know *why* the price rose. They only need to know that it did. The information is compressed into a single number that every actor can use to make local decisions.

In the Soviet model, this compression was impossible. The State Planning Committee, or Gosplan, had to determine the price of steel, the price of bread, and the allocation of raw materials across thousands of industries simultaneously. To do this, they needed to know the true cost of production for every firm, which depended on the efficiency of every worker, which depended on the incentives provided by the state. But the incentives were distorted by the plan itself.

This creates a circularity that no amount of computing power can break. If the state sets a low price for electricity to encourage industrialization, factories have no incentive to conserve it. They will consume it voraciously, not because they are wasteful people, but because the rational response to the given price is to use more. The data on electricity consumption that Gosplan receives is therefore not a neutral measure of demand; it is a measure of the distortion they just created. When they feed that data back into the model to adjust the price, they are refining their error.

The mathematicians who tried to fix this, such as those working on the Optimal Plan in the 1960s, realized this too quickly. They found that even if you could solve the linear program, the solution was unstable. A tiny change in an input constraint would require a total reorganization of the economy. The system was too rigid to be adaptive. It could optimize for a fixed target, but it could not learn.

This leads to the deeper lesson about incentives: information is not just data; it is action. In a market, price signals are generated by the actions of people making bets. When I buy coffee, I am not just consuming a bean; I am voting with my wallet on the relative value of coffee versus everything else I could have bought. That vote is aggregated by the market. In a planned economy, the "vote" is issued by the state. But the state does not consume the goods it produces. It has no personal stake in the quality of the boot or the durability of the tractor. It is an abstract entity trying to simulate the preferences of millions of specific individuals.

The result is a tragedy of coordination. The planner knows the aggregate goal—more steel, more grain—but not the local conditions. The factory manager knows the local conditions—his machine is broken, his workers are sick, his supplier is late—but not the aggregate goal. He only knows the quota. His rational move is to pad his quota requests to ensure he can meet the target with minimal effort. The planner, seeing inflated requests, tightens the quotas. The manager, seeing tighter quotas, pads his requests further. This is not corruption in the petty sense of bribery; it is a structural feedback loop of distrust. The system requires honesty to function, but it provides no reward for honesty.

This brings us to the question of who ought to run a country. The Soviet experiment demonstrated that a government cannot be a better manager than a market, but it can be a worse one. A bad manager at least has a board of directors or shareholders who can fire them. A central planner has no such check. If the plan fails, the plan is blamed, or the planner is replaced, but the structure remains. The incentive to misreport remains. The information deficit remains.

The lesson is not that all government is bad, but that government is bad at *coordination*. It is good at setting rules, enforcing contracts, and providing public goods that markets underproduce. It is terrible at allocating specific resources among competing private uses. When the state tries to do what the market does, it does it worse because it lacks the information that the market’s price system generates.

The book you read likely ends with the collapse of the Soviet Union, but the real ending is earlier. It is the moment the mathematicians realized that the computer was not the bottleneck. The bottleneck was the human mind’s inability to hold the whole picture. We are social animals who coordinate through decentralized signals, not central commands. To try to run a country like a factory is to misunderstand what a country is. It is not a machine to be optimized; it is a conversation to be managed. And you cannot manage a conversation by shouting the next word at everyone simultaneously. You have to let them talk to each other.

prompt: Tech companies keep lobbying for easier immigration for programmers, and critics say we should just train more Americans instead. Write a short, punchy essay taking a side in that argument.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I side with the critics, but not with their slogan. Tech companies are not asking for visas because the United States has stopped producing programmers. They are asking for a subsidy.

The H-1B is an employer-sponsored temporary visa. A firm must show a job in a specialty occupation, offer a wage at least equal to the prevailing wage, and take responsibility for the worker. The annual cap is 85,000 for most employers, but universities, nonprofits, and research firms are exempt, so the real flow is larger. That is already a lot. And yet the pitch is that American tech is dying from a shortage of code.

The numbers do not support that panic. The country awards more than 100,000 bachelor’s degrees in computer and information sciences every year. Add the workers already in the labor force, the people switching careers, the community-college and self-taught pool, and the claim that no American can write software becomes absurd. The real claim is narrower: some firms cannot get the exact experience they want, at the exact wage they want, quickly enough. That is a business cost, not a national emergency.

This is where the hardest objection lands. In a few narrow fields—machine learning, chip design, cryptography—the best people are global and mobile. If a country tries to lock them out, it loses. But the answer is not a general corporate visa program. It is targeted immigration: green cards for people who intend to stay, visas tied to specific scarce skills, and rules that let firms recruit genuinely exceptional talent without turning hiring into a staffing arbitrage.

The H-1B is not built for that. It is temporary and employer-bound, which gives the company leverage. It is selected by lottery when the cap is oversubscribed, which rewards firms that file thousands of applications and pay consultants to game the odds. And among the biggest users are IT services firms whose model depends on moving work between high-wage and lower-wage countries. When a company can rent a worker from abroad, it has less reason to train a junior at home.

So the critics are right, but too often they say it like a slogan: train more Americans. What that means in practice is unglamorous. Pay apprentices a real wage while they learn. Let community colleges teach the tools companies actually use. Make firms prove a job was open at a decent wage before they import. If a company wants a senior engineer, it should be willing to pay for a junior’s first two years. That is how domestic skill gets built.

Immigration is not the enemy. Cheap labor is. The question is not whether America should want smart people from abroad. It is whether tech companies should get to shift the cost of building their workforce onto everyone else.
rejected:
The "train more Americans" argument sounds patriotic, but it is economically incoherent. It assumes that software engineering is a craft that can be mastered in eighteen months by a motivated college student, and that the U.S. workforce is currently sitting on its hands while jobs go unfilled. Neither is true.

First, the supply side is broken at the top. We are not short on coders; we are short on *senior* coders. The entry-level market is flooded with bootcamp graduates and CS majors who can write a sorting algorithm but cannot design a distributed database. The companies lobbying for H-1B visas are not looking for interns. They are looking for engineers who have already spent five to ten years debugging legacy systems, managing technical debt, and learning which architectural decisions blow up in production. You cannot "train" that experience. It is accrued through time and failure, not curriculum.

Second, the "train them" crowd ignores the geographic mismatch. The U.S. education system produces graduates in places like Ohio, where tech infrastructure is thin. The work is in California, Texas, and New York. Moving a twenty-two-year-old from Columbus to San Francisco is a logistical and financial hurdle that a visa holder, who is already relocating for their career, does not face.

Critics argue that importing talent lowers wages for domestic workers. The data doesn’t support this. When a company imports a specialist to solve a problem that no domestic candidate can solve, the result is a higher-functioning product. That product generates revenue that flows back into the company, often raising the floor for everyone else. The alternative to hiring the best available engineer—domestic or not—is hiring the least bad available engineer. That is not a strategy for innovation; it is a strategy for mediocrity.
