If we want to build the future, we need the people who have already built parts of it. Stop pretending that a four-year degree can substitute for a decade of professional survival.

prompt: Write a practical piece on how to get real value out of attending a music industry conference, for someone who's about to go to their first one and tends to waste these things.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
## How to get real value out of a music industry conference

The reason first-time attendees waste these events is usually not that they are shy, unpolished, or “not industry enough.” It is that they arrive without a job for the conference to do. They wander into panels, collect business cards, drink with people, and leave with a vague sense that they have been in the room. The room is not the value. The value is a small number of useful actions that happen because people are physically present who would otherwise be hard to reach.

Before you go, decide what a useful outcome would be. Not “network,” because that is a mood, not a result. Not “get signed,” because that is too large and too dependent on other people. A useful outcome is something you can point to a week later: one qualified person agreed to listen, one manager agreed to a call, one sync supervisor asked for a shortlist of cues, one promoter wants a live link, one publicist referred you to someone, one buyer said send material by a specific date. If you are an artist, your goal should usually be to get one or two people to take a concrete next step, not to impress the whole building.

Make a target list before you arrive. Twelve to twenty names is enough. More than that and you become a tourist, trying to touch every wall. For each name, write what they do and why they are relevant to your goal. A label A&R person is useful if you want label attention. A manager is useful if you want representation. A sync supervisor is useful if you want placements. A publicist is useful if you need press. A promoter is useful if you need rooms. A playlist curator is useful if you need audience. A service provider is useful only if you are the client or the seller in that relationship.

Spend five minutes researching each person. Look at their company’s recent signings, placements, podcasts, social posts, or interviews. Write one sentence: “They are currently focused on…” If you cannot find anything, drop them. A label rep who has been signing a particular kind of artist is more likely to have a current lane than one who has been quiet. A sync supervisor who just placed a cue in a show may be looking for similar material. A manager who has been talking about a new roster may be actively shopping. Specificity is what makes your approach less random.

Email the people you want to meet before the event, ideally five to seven days ahead, not the morning of. Keep it short and easy to answer.

> Hi [name], I’ll be at [event] on [day]. I’m [one-line description]. I’d like ten minutes to ask you [specific thing]. Does [time] work? If not, I’ll understand.

If you are an artist, include one link, not a discography. If you are a service provider, include one relevant example. If you are asking for a meeting, the email should make the ask clear: a call, a listening, a live link, a shortlist review, a job question. If they say yes, confirm with a calendar invite. If they say no, ask for one introduction: “Is there someone else whose opinion would be useful?” That question is not pushy. It is useful.

Prepare your one-line version. It should include what you do, who it is for, and what you are trying to do next. “I make lo-fi house for late-night driving playlists, and I’re trying to get a sync supervisor to consider a shortlist of cues” is better than “I’m a multi-hyphenate artist.” “I write press for independent electronic artists, and I’m looking for managers who need help launching their next release” is better than “I do PR.” “I’m trying to understand how a sync library manager evaluates new submissions” is better than “I’m exploring careers in music.” You do not need to sound famous. You need to sound like someone with a clear next step.

Prepare the materials you will actually use. For an artist, that is usually a link with three songs maximum, a short video or live clip if you have one, a one-line bio, and a photo if relevant. For a sync artist, it is a shortlist of cues with moods and temp references. For a service provider, it is two examples and a sentence about the problem you solve. For a jobseeker, it is a short list of the roles you want and one or two questions you have about how the role works day to day. Do not bring a folder of possibilities. Bring the thing you want them to see.

When you arrive, do not start with the bar. The first thirty minutes are for orientation. Find the schedule, the hotel, the quiet corner, the coffee, the charging point. Then go to one place where people are already standing: the lobby, the registration table, the early panel, the lounge. The early crowd is less polished and more available than the late crowd. You do not need to be the most interesting person in the room. You need to be specific, unhurried, and willing to leave a conversation after it has done its job.

Start small. The first five minutes of a conversation are for context, not pitch. Ask what brought them to the event, which sessions they are planning to attend, what they are working on right now. Then move to your one-line version only when there is an opening. If you are an artist and you want their attention, make it a request rather than a performance: “Would it be useful if I sent you the link now?” “Do you have ten minutes on Thursday so I can show you the shortlist?” “If I send you the live clip, would you be open to watching it this week?” If the answer is no, take it cleanly and ask who else they would recommend.

End every useful conversation with a next step. A next step can be a follow-up email, a calendar invite, a link sent, a name given, a date set, or a specific piece of feedback requested. If there is no next step, the conversation was entertainment. That is fine, but do not count it as value. The difference between a wasted conference and a useful one is often not the number of people you met, but the number of people who know exactly what you do and what you need.

Do not try to meet everyone. Twenty shallow contacts are usually worse than five people who know your name, your lane, and your ask. If you are an artist with very little traction, do not ask a label to sign you. Ask for a diagnosis: “What is the biggest gap between my project and where you would consider working with me?” That is a question a busy person can answer in two minutes, and the answer is useful whether or not they ever call. If you are a service provider, do not ask for a client in the first minute. Ask how they currently solve the problem you solve, what frustrates them about their current provider, and whether they would be open to seeing an example. If you are looking for a job, ask for fifteen minutes to understand the role, not for the role itself unless the person has clearly put it out there.

Panels are the hardest part to use well. I am less sure about how much weight to give them because it depends heavily on the conference: a strong panel with people doing the work you want to do can be worth the hour; a weak one is a place where you stand around feeling inspired for no reason. Use a simple rule. Attend a panel only if the speaker has done something you want to do, or the session is directly tied to your goal. Sit where you can leave. Take one note: a name, a company, a tactic, a budget range, a hiring signal. Then talk to one person after, not the speaker if possible. “Which part of that was most useful for what you do?” is an easy question. “What would you change about the way you handled that?” is a better one.

If you are on the receiving end, the same logic applies in reverse. If you are a label rep, manager, publicist, sync supervisor, or buyer, do not collect a pile of links and promise to listen. Decide in advance what you are looking for, what your current constraints are, and what a good “no” looks like. If you are interested, set a specific follow-up: send material by a date, book a call, watch the live clip, review the shortlist. If you are not interested, say what is missing. People remember fair specificity. The industry is full of people who are polite in the hallway and silent in the inbox; being clear is a competitive advantage.

The social event is not a separate track where the real work happens. It is a lower-friction version of the same work. If you drink, have one if it helps, not several. If you are with a friend, take turns: one works the room, one rests, then swap. If you are alone, set a time to stop. If you burn out in one evening, you have lost the next two days. The people who seem to be having the best time are not necessarily the ones getting the best outcomes. The ones getting outcomes are the ones still functional on day two.

The most important work happens after you leave. That is where most conferences die. On the first evening, write notes while the names are still fresh. Use a simple spreadsheet: name, company, role, what they do, what they said, what you gave them, what you asked for, follow-up date. Do not wait until the next day. A note that says “likes dark disco, asked for cue shortlist, send Friday” is worth more than a business card.

Send follow-ups within 24 hours. Keep them short and easy to answer.

> Hi [name], good to meet you at [event]. You mentioned [specific thing]. I’m [one line]. I’d love to [ask]. Are you free for fifteen minutes next Tuesday or Wednesday? Here’s the link: [one link].

If they asked to hear music, send the best three songs, not the whole album, and tell them which one to start with. If they asked for sync cues, send three to five with moods and temp references. If they asked for a call, send two time options. If they asked for a live clip, send it with a one-line note about the room. If they asked nothing, send one sentence and one link only if the conversation clearly pointed that way. Do not send a mass email to everyone you met. A message that says “we talked about your new signing and my cue shortlist” is useful. A message that says “great meeting you, here’s everything I do” is noise.

If you do not hear back, send one reminder after seven to ten days. One. Then move on. The conference did not fail because one person did not reply. It failed if you have no names, no notes, no follow-ups, and no next steps.

The hardest objection to all of this is that it feels transactional. The music industry runs on relationships, and relationships cannot be scheduled in ten-minute hallway blocks. That is true. A conference is not where you make a manager, a label partner, or a long-term collaborator. It is where you make a thread. The value is that the follow-up is no longer random. “We met at the event, you mentioned X, I sent Y” is a thousand times more usable than a cold email from a stranger. The relationship is built in the follow-up, not the handshake. If you treat the conference as the whole relationship, it will feel fake. If you treat it as the first sentence, it works.

A conference is also a multiplier, not a creator. It cannot fix weak songs, a vague positioning, or a project that does not make sense to explain. It can make your existing work visible to the right person at the right time. That is why preparation matters more than charm. Charm gets you a minute. Clarity gets you a follow-up.

You did not waste the event if, a week later, there is a named person, a specific request, and a date in your calendar. You did not waste it if one person gave you a useful answer about what is missing in your project. You did not waste it if you learned the difference between the kind of sync cue a supervisor wants and the kind of song you thought you needed to send. You did not waste it if you made one contact who became a client, a referral, a booking, or a second conversation. The rest was just travel.
rejected:
The biggest mistake at a music conference is treating it like a networking event. You stand in a room full of people, shake hands, swap business cards, and leave with zero follow-up plan. The cards rot in your pocket. The names evaporate. You paid $500 to have an anxiety attack in a hotel lobby.

Conferences are not for meeting people. They are for information gathering and targeted activation. The people you meet are byproducts of the work you do before you speak to them.

**Kill the "Spray and Pray" Approach**

Do not walk in with a goal of "making contacts." That is a vague, useless goal that leads to shallow conversations. Walk in with three specific targets. Not three people. Three *situations*.

Maybe you need a sync licensing agent for your catalog. Maybe you need a mastering engineer who works with indie rock. Maybe you need a playlist curator for a specific sub-genre.

When you have a specific need, you can identify the specific person who solves it. You scan the attendee list or the speaker lineup. You find the two or three people who fit the bill. You check their schedule. You book a coffee or a brief sit-down for a specific time.

Now you have a reason to be in the room. You are not wandering. You are executing a schedule.

**Do the Homework Before You Breathe Conference Air**

If you are going to meet a label A&R, do not waste their time by asking, "So, what do you do?" They know what they do. You are burning their goodwill on information you could have found in 30 seconds of Googling.

Know their recent signings. Know the specific artist you admire in their roster. Know the label’s current strategic focus.

When you sit down, say this: "I’ve been following your work on [Artist X]. I’m working on a project that sits in a similar lane but with a different production approach. I have a three-minute track that demonstrates this. I’m not asking you to sign me. I’m asking if you’d be open to hearing it, or if you’d point me toward the right person in your team who handles this specific sound."

This is a low-pressure ask. It respects their time. It shows you’ve done the work. It gives them a clear yes or no. If they say yes, you have a next step. If they say no, you have clarity, and you can move on without the ambiguity of "let's keep in touch."

**The "Passive" Value: Listening**

Most people skip the panels because they want to be *at* the conference, not *in* the room. Panels are where the industry shares its current anxieties and opportunities.

If you are a songwriter, stop attending "How to Get Signed" panels. They are generic fluff. Attend the panels on sync licensing, publishing administration, or the economics of streaming. These are the structural changes that will affect your income in five years.

Listen for the gaps. When a speaker mentions a problem they are having, write it down. That is a service you can offer. If a manager complains about the difficulty of tracking artist royalties across platforms, and you have a spreadsheet that solves that, you just found your first client.

**The Follow-Up Is the Conference**

The value of the conference does not exist until 48 hours later. If you do not follow up within two days, you are a stranger again.

Do not send a generic "It was great meeting you" email. Send a specific reference to your conversation. "Thanks for chatting about the [Specific Topic]. Here is the link to the track I mentioned. I also thought of you when I read this article on [Related Industry News]. Let me know if you’d like to hear the next draft."

Keep it short. Keep it relevant. Do not ask for a favor in the first email. The goal of the first email is to re-establish the context of your brief interaction. The goal of the second email, two weeks later, is to ask for the specific thing you need.

**Physical Survival**

Conferences are designed to exhaust you. The coffee is bad. The air conditioning is off. The speakers talk for two hours.

If you are drained, you make bad decisions. You agree to things you shouldn't. You forget to follow up. You stay up too late at the after-party because you feel you have to "network."

Protect your energy. Take breaks. Eat real food. Leave the after-parties early if you have targets for the next morning. A fresh, focused person who meets five people and follows up properly is worth more than a hungover person who met fifty people and remembered none of them.

**The Metric**

You will not know if the conference was a success when you leave. You will know in three months.

Did you get the meeting? Did you land the sync placement? Did you find the mastering engineer? Did you learn the specific terminology that lets you talk to executives without sounding like a fan?

If the answer is no, you didn't waste the conference. You wasted the preparation. The conference is just the trigger. The work is in the targeting, the homework, and the follow-up.

prompt: The New York Times just ran a piece on the Hearing Voices Movement, people with hallucinations who want them treated as normal rather than medicalized. You're a psychiatrist who has met some of them. Write a numbered-points blog post giving your honest, mixed take: where the movement has a point and where its critics (and the press coverage) do.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**A psychiatrist’s mixed notes on the Hearing Voices Movement**

1. The Times piece made sense to me, because the complaint is familiar. People who hear voices are tired of being treated as if they are all on the way to a locked ward. I have met some of them. A retired teacher hears a calm commentary she calls “the committee”; a young man hears a voice that says he is contaminated; a mother hears her late husband on the worst nights. These are not the same event, but the story often treats them as if they are.

2. The movement’s strongest point is that “hearing voices” is not a disease. It can be a feature of depression, PTSD, grief, substance use, sleep deprivation, or a neurological problem. It can also be a benign habit of mind, like a persistent inner critic. If a clinician hears “voice” and immediately thinks schizophrenia, they have missed the patient.

3. Labels are not neutral. “Schizophrenia” can open a door to medication, hospitalization, disability benefits, and family support. It can also become a person’s whole identity, a mark that follows them into housing, work, and relationships. “Medicalized” captures something real: diagnosis can turn a human experience into a medical identity. But it can also be a way to avoid asking whether the experience is dangerous. I have overdiagnosed, and I have underdiagnosed.

4. But the movement’s word “normal” is doing too much work. For some, voices are a manageable inner speech. For others, they are persecuting, commanding, escalating, and tied to beliefs that the world is spying on them. The difference is not a matter of attitude. A voice that says “you are not enough” and a voice that says “the police are coming and you need to jump” require different responses.

5. The hardest objection to the movement is the person with first-episode psychosis. A 21-year-old who stops sleeping, becomes convinced the voices are implanted, and starts to fall out of school or work is not being overmedicalized; he is sick. Untreated psychosis often gets worse, and early treatment matters. If the voices are commanding harm, the answer is urgent evaluation, not a support group. Telling him to “reframe” the voices without a careful assessment can be a kind of cruelty.

6. I do not think antipsychotics are a cure, and I do not think they are harmless. They can reduce voices, but they can also cause weight gain, sedation, movement problems, and a feeling of emotional flatness. For some people with non-psychotic voice-hearing, medication is the wrong tool and will do more harm than good. The danger is choosing by ideology instead of by the person in front of you.

7. The press coverage often makes a third mistake: it needs a moral. A well-functioning voice-hearer becomes proof that psychiatry is oppressive; a frightening one becomes proof that the movement is dangerous. Both stories are true fragments. The actual clinical picture is messier: some voice-hearers need medication, some need trauma therapy, some need housing, some need a community that will not treat them like a threat, and some need all of those things.

8. What I want is less a debate about “medicalized” versus “normal” than a better question. What are the voices saying? When did they start? Are there delusions, mood symptoms, substance use, sleep loss, or danger? Is the person’s life narrowing or holding? Can we try watchful waiting, psychotherapy, accommodations, and support first? If not, when do we bring in medication? Those questions can be asked without deciding in advance what the voices “mean.”

9. If the next article wants a real story, let it follow a voice-hearer through assessment: the relief of being believed, the fear of a diagnosis, the decision about medication, the aftermath. The politics are in that sequence, not in the headline.
rejected:
1. The core insight of the Hearing Voices Network is that isolation is more dangerous than the voices themselves. When a person hears a voice saying "kill yourself," the immediate threat is not the auditory hallucination; it is the shame and social exclusion that follow the diagnosis. If a community can look at a person with psychosis and say, "I hear things too, and we are all sane," they have removed the secondary trauma of being treated as a monster. That social validation is a genuine, powerful therapeutic intervention.

2. However, "normalizing" the experience does not mean normalizing the risk. The movement often conflates the *subjective experience* of hearing a voice with the *objective reality* of the brain state producing it. A person who hears a dead relative’s voice and feels comforted may be managing their grief in a neurologically distinct way from a person whose brain is under severe dopaminergic storm. Treating both as "just voices" ignores the biological variance that determines whether the voices will resolve, persist, or escalate into a dangerous catatonic state.

3. The most dangerous part of the movement is the anti-psychotic stance. Many HVN advocates argue that antipsychotics are harmful, addictive, and that the voices are a "spiritual" or "psychological" process that should be talked out, not chemically silenced. For some, this works. For many others, it is a gamble with their life. I have seen patients who stopped their medication because a peer support group told them they didn't need it, only to end up in a crisis within weeks. The movement’s insistence that medication is a tool of oppression often blinds its adherents to the fact that for a significant subset of patients, it is the only thing keeping them out of a psychiatric ward.

4. The press coverage is often guilty of a binary fallacy: either you are a "victim of the medical model" or you are a "crazy person needing a pill." This framing ignores the vast middle ground where most of us live. Most people with severe mental illness do not choose one over the other. They take their medication, they go to therapy, they read books, they join support groups, and they still struggle. The movement is useful as a supplement to care, not a replacement for it.

5. As a psychiatrist, my job is not to validate the voice, nor to silence it. My job is to assess the function. If the voice is helping a person process a trauma, I listen. If the voice is commanding violence or preventing sleep, I prescribe. The Hearing Voices Movement is right that we need to listen more before we label. It is wrong that listening is enough.

prompt: I'm curious about applying evolutionary thinking to psychiatry, which seems like it should be a natural fit but rarely is. Write a thoughtful review of a book that tries it, covering what the theory is, how well it handles real psychiatric conditions, what it might mean for society, and where you stay skeptical.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Randolph Nesse’s *Evolutionary Psychiatry: A New Science of the Mind* is a short, serious attempt to do what you are describing: take evolution seriously as a way of thinking about mental disorder, not as a metaphor or a political slogan. Nesse is an evolutionary biologist, and the book is best read as a conceptual argument rather than a clinical textbook. Its central move is to stop treating psychiatric symptoms as random noise in a malfunctioning brain and to ask what kind of evolved psychology could produce them. That is a useful question, and the book is most persuasive when it stays close to conditions where the evolutionary story can be tested against actual symptoms, triggers, and treatments. It becomes weaker when it has to explain disorders whose symptoms seem to destroy the very social and cognitive capacities that selection would presumably have favored.

The theory is not that depression, anxiety, or psychosis were “designed” to make us suffer. Evolution does not optimize for welfare. It favors traits that, in some ancestral range of conditions, increased the chances of surviving and reproducing. Mental mechanisms are part of that system. A fear response that keeps an animal away from cliffs, snakes, or hostile strangers can be valuable even if it is sometimes wrong. A withdrawal response after loss or defeat can conserve energy and reduce the risk of further injury. A disgust response that avoids contaminated food or corpses can reduce infection. The psychiatric interest comes from the fact that these mechanisms are not perfectly calibrated to the modern world. They can be triggered by things that are not genuinely dangerous, run for longer than is useful, or become so intense that they disable the person. Nesse’s phrase, roughly, is that psychopathology often consists of maladaptive side effects of evolved psychological mechanisms. The symptom is not the adaptation; the machinery that produces the symptom may have been shaped by selection.

That distinction matters because it keeps the theory from collapsing into a bad kind of comfort. If someone has a panic attack in a crowded room, the evolutionary account is not that panic attacks are good for them. It is that the alarm system they are using was shaped by pressures where threat detection could be life-saving, and that the system can misfire in a way that is costly now. The same logic applies to depression. After a serious loss—loss of status, loss of a relationship, loss of a future that seemed attainable—withdrawal, reduced appetite, and a narrowing of goals may have once made sense. Continuing to spend energy on a lost cause can be expensive. Reassessing options can be valuable. In a foraging context, that might have been a reasonable strategy. In a modern economy, the same withdrawal can mean missing work, falling behind financially, isolating socially, and making recovery harder. The mechanism may be understandable; the outcome is still a disorder.

This is where the book handles real psychiatric conditions reasonably well, especially mood and anxiety disorders. Depression is not a single problem, but a common evolutionary story can explain some of its shape. People with depression often report precipitants involving loss, failure, rejection, or perceived defeat. They often withdraw from activities that used to matter. They may ruminate, which can look like useless suffering but may also be a form of forced re-evaluation: stop pursuing the old goal, notice that it no longer works, look for another path. The trouble is that the process can become too intense, too persistent, and too general. A person does not need a full depressive syndrome to learn that a job, a relationship, or a social position has changed. The evolutionary account is strongest when it explains why the response is tied to loss and status, and weakest when it has to explain why the response can become so globally disabling that it makes new action almost impossible.

Anxiety disorders are perhaps the easiest fit. Specific phobias often point at plausible ancestral threats: heights, snakes, falling, being trapped. A person with acrophobia may be running a danger-detection system that was once useful, now applied in a context where the cost is avoidance rather than survival. Social anxiety is less obvious but still plausible if status threat was a real evolutionary pressure. In small, stable groups, being excluded or dominated could have serious consequences. A heightened sensitivity to disapproval, humiliation, or rejection might therefore be selected, even if in modern schools, workplaces, or social media it produces chronic distress and avoidance. Generalized anxiety is harder. Worry about future health, money, family, or catastrophe does not map neatly onto a specific ancestral danger. The body’s stress response is real and measurable, but the content of the worry can be almost endlessly modern. Evolution can explain why humans have a threat system; it does not fully explain why that system can latch onto the abstract contingencies of contemporary life.

Obsessive-compulsive symptoms are a mixed case. Contamination fears and compulsive washing have a clear evolutionary rationale: infection was a major killer, and behavioral avoidance of feces, corpses, spoiled food, and other contaminants could reduce risk. A person who washes their hands after using the bathroom is using a useful rule. A person who cannot finish a meal unless a sequence of rituals is performed has something else going on. The mechanism may still be threat detection or contamination avoidance, but it has become overgeneralized and rigid. The evolutionary story explains the theme, not the specific disorder. It also has to account for the fact that many compulsions are ego-dystonic: the person knows they are excessive and suffers because of them. That is not a trait that looks, on the face of it, like a successful adaptation.

This brings us to the book’s main limit: the harder the condition is to understand as a misapplied response, the thinner the evolutionary account becomes. Schizophrenia is the obvious test case. The negative symptoms—social withdrawal, reduced motivation, emotional flattening—could be framed as a retreat from social competition or threat, but that is a large stretch. The positive symptoms—hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking—do not obviously solve any problem. A person who hears commanding voices or believes they are being controlled is not merely overly vigilant; they are often unable to function in the social world. One can speculate that psychosis is a byproduct of immune processes, developmental instability, or the cost of a large, socially intelligent brain, and some of those ideas have empirical support. But “the brain is complex and selection shaped it” is not the same as an evolutionary explanation of schizophrenia. Nesse’s framework is more at home with depression and anxiety than with psychosis, and the book is more persuasive when it acknowledges that.

The same problem appears with addiction, if one treats it as a psychiatric condition rather than a behavioral one. The reward system is clearly evolved: food, sex, social affiliation, and safety all matter for reproduction. Drugs hijack parts of that system. That explains vulnerability. It does not fully explain why some people develop addiction and others do not, why it often tracks stress and trauma, or why the same substance can produce different outcomes in different social environments. Evolutionary thinking can say why the target exists, not why the person’s life becomes organized around obtaining the drug.

This is where I stay most skeptical. The hardest objection to evolutionary psychiatry is not that it is biologically reductive, although it can be. The harder objection is that it can become unfalsifiable. For almost any symptom, one can invent a plausible ancestral benefit. Withdrawal conserves energy. Rumination solves problems. Social anxiety prevents rejection. OCD prevents infection. Schizophrenia may be a side effect of immune defense or cognitive complexity. If the framework can explain everything, it risks explaining nothing. A good evolutionary account should make predictions or at least narrow the search. It should say which symptoms should co-occur, which cues should trigger them, which environments should worsen them, which treatments should interrupt them, and what developmental or genetic patterns should accompany them. Where those tests are missing, the evolutionary story is a metaphor, not an explanation.

That does not mean the approach is useless. It can be tested, at least indirectly. Cross-cultural patterns matter. If fear of snakes, heights, or social rejection is common across societies, that is more interesting than if it were purely local. Age of onset matters. Many anxiety disorders emerge around adolescence, when social evaluation becomes intense and the brain’s threat systems are still calibrating. Sex differences matter. Depression and anxiety are more common in women after puberty, and evolutionary accounts can point to sex differences in reproductive stakes, social risk, and status dynamics, though those accounts must be handled carefully because culture and biology are entangled. Treatment response matters. Exposure therapy works for phobias because fear learning is a real system with real rules; that fits an evolutionary picture better than a purely chemical one. But the fit is often broad enough that many competing stories can survive.

The theory also has to deal with the fact that most psychiatric conditions are not simple adaptations with clean boundaries. They are polygenic, developmentally sensitive, and heavily shaped by environment. A person’s risk for depression is not determined by a “depression gene” or a “foraging brain.” It is a statistical disposition emerging from many small genetic effects, early experience, current stress, sleep, social support, and chance. Evolutionary psychiatry can accommodate that, and it should. The older image of a fixed ancestral mind is too simple. A more defensible version is that evolution produced plastic mechanisms: threat systems that calibrate to experience, reward systems that learn what matters in a particular environment, social systems that track status and belonging. Mental disorder is what happens when those plastic mechanisms are pushed into states that were not selected for and are not maintained well.

That has real social implications. If mental illness is partly a mismatch between evolved mechanisms and modern conditions, then treatment cannot be only individual. A person with depression is not merely a brain that needs correcting; they may be a person living in conditions that repeatedly trigger an old loss-and-defeat response. Stable housing, meaningful work, social connection, reduced humiliation, and predictable institutions are not just “social determinants” in a political sense; they are inputs to the same systems that produce psychiatric symptoms. If anxiety is a threat-detection problem, then environments that make threat constant and ambiguous—chronic financial insecurity, digital surveillance of social status, schools organized around public ranking—will do psychiatric harm whether or not we call it that. The evolutionary view can push public health away from the idea that mental disorder is only a private medical problem inside a skull.

But the social implications cut both ways. The same logic that reduces moral blame can also naturalize suffering. If a person is anxious because their brain is “meant” to detect social threat, it can be easy to stop asking why the school is so humiliating, the workplace so precarious, or the neighborhood so isolating. “It’s evolved” can become a way of defending the status quo. This is the real political danger of evolutionary psychiatry: not that it must lead to eugenics, though it has sometimes been used in that direction, but that it can make the present seem inevitable. Evolution explains why we are vulnerable; it does not justify leaving people exposed to the vulnerabilities.

Nesse’s book is strongest when it keeps that tension alive. It is not a case that mental illness is natural and therefore acceptable. It is a case that mental illness is natural in the sense that it is produced by natural mechanisms, and that those mechanisms have a history. That history can make the conditions less mysterious and less morally loaded. A person with a phobia is not simply being irrational; they are using a threat system that was once useful. A person with depression after a loss is not simply weak; they are caught in a response that can become self-perpetuating. A person with OCD is not merely obsessed with arbitrary rules; they may be running a contamination-avoidance loop beyond the point where it serves them. These explanations do not cure anyone, and they do not replace diagnosis. A clinician still has to know whether a patient is manic, psychotic, at suicide risk, responding to medication, or harmed by it. Evolutionary origin is background information, not a bedside tool.

Where I remain skeptical is in the gap between the elegance of the framework and the messiness of the disorders. Evolutionary psychiatry is better at explaining why certain kinds of suffering exist than why this particular person has this particular diagnosis. It is better at explaining the shape of anxiety than the content of a specific worry. It is better at explaining contamination OCD than checking rituals. It is better at depression than schizophrenia. And it is better as a corrective to two bad habits in psychiatry—treating mental illness as purely cultural invention, or as a list of chemical imbalances with no history—than as a foundation for clinical practice. The book’s value is not that it gives the final answer. It is that it makes a better question unavoidable: if the mind is an evolved system, what does that make of the ways it breaks?

Actually, the most honest review would focus on the **concept** rather than a single bestseller, but you asked for a book. Let’s review **"The Evolution of Human Aggression" by Richard W. Wrangham**.

***

### The Theory: Mismatch and Trade-offs

The core argument of evolutionary psychiatry is that mental illness is not a machine breaking down; it is a machine working exactly as designed, in an environment it was not designed for.

Wrangham’s book focuses on aggression, but the logic applies to depression, anxiety, and addiction. The human brain was shaped by pressures of small-group living, mate selection, and resource competition. We evolved specific triggers for stress (threat to status, loss of kin, unpredictability) and specific responses (fight, flight, freeze, fawn).

The "disease" in this view is the mismatch. We evolved to run from lions. Now we run from deadlines. The physiological cost is identical. The lion doesn’t chase you for six hours. The deadline does. The cortisol cascade that was meant to last minutes lasts days. The result is not a chemical imbalance in the sense of a missing neurotransmitter, but a chronic activation of a survival protocol.

### Handling Real Conditions

Wrangham handles aggression and violence with surprising precision. He explains why men are more violent than women not as a moral failing or a cultural artifact, but as a reproductive strategy: males invest less in offspring, so the risk-reward ratio for status-seeking violence is higher. He also explains why aggression spikes during puberty and drops in older age, tracking testosterone and life expectancy.

Where it gets interesting is in how it reframes depression. In evolutionary terms, depression is a "withdrawal strategy." When you are low-status, sick, or have lost a major investment (a mate, a job, a child), continuing to invest energy in social performance is maladaptive. The brain conserves energy, lowers drive, and withdraws. It is a rational response to a perceived lack of future returns.

This explains why antidepressants often work, but also why they fail. If the "threat" is still real—your job is still gone, your marriage is still dead—the brain’s withdrawal strategy is still the correct algorithm. The drug overrides the signal, but not the cause.

### Societal Implications

If depression is a rational response to status loss, then society is a depression machine. We have created a world where status is precarious, comparison is constant, and social bonds are fragile.

This has two major implications. First, it shifts blame. The depressed person is not "broken." They are responding to a broken environment. This suggests that policy changes—universal basic income, stable housing, meaningful work—might be more effective psychiatric interventions than medication alone.

Second, it complicates the treatment of aggression. If male aggression is a reproductive strategy, then "taming" men is not a moral project but a biological one. We must create environments where cooperation yields higher rewards than competition. This is what we are trying to do in corporate teams, but it is a fundamental restructuring of human incentives.

### Where I Stay Skeptical

The biggest problem with evolutionary psychiatry is **post-hoc rationalization**.

Any behavior can be justified as an adaptation. If you are depressed, it’s a withdrawal strategy. If you are manic, it’s a high-risk reproductive strategy. If you are schizophrenic, it’s a glitch in the social monitoring system. The theory is unfalsifiable. It explains everything, so it proves nothing.

There is also the **genetic lag** problem. We evolve slowly. Our brains are adapted to the Pleistocene. But culture changes fast. We now have social media, which allows us to compare our behind-the-scenes with everyone else’s highlight reel. Our evolutionary brain interprets this as a total loss of status, triggering a depression response that has no adaptive value because the "threat" is a digital illusion. The brain cannot distinguish a real lion from a fake one. It just reacts.

Finally, there is the risk of **biological determinism**. If my aggression is an evolutionary strategy, am I excused? If my depression is a rational withdrawal, am I not responsible for trying to change my circumstances? Evolutionary theory can become a shield for inaction.

### The Verdict

Evolutionary psychiatry is not a replacement for current psychiatry. It is a lens. It helps you see that your anxiety is not a bug; it is a feature of a system that is running on outdated hardware in a new world.

It does not tell you what to do. It tells you why you feel that way. It tells you that your mind is not malfunctioning; it is faithfully reporting a threat that may not exist. That is a strange kind of comfort, and a strange kind of burden.

prompt: You're a psychiatrist reflecting on your own habits. Write an essay on the two broad stances a doctor can take toward what patients say they want, taking them at their word versus looking for the real problem underneath, and which one you lean toward and why.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The first thing a patient tells me is often not a symptom. It is a want. “I want to stop drinking.” “I want you to tell me I am not insane.” “I want a letter saying I cannot work.” “I want to be left alone.” “I want to feel something.” These are not preliminary remarks, warming up to the real material. They are the reason the appointment exists. A doctor can meet them in two broad ways. One is to take the patient at their word. The other is to look for the real problem underneath. I have used both, and I am still trying to learn which one I am using in a given minute.

Taking a patient at their word means treating the stated want as a serious account of their present life. If a man says he wants to quit his job, I do not immediately assume he is depressed. The job may be bad. If a woman says she wants to stop taking an antidepressant, I do not immediately assume she is in denial about her illness. She may have decided the side effects are not worth it, or she may want to know whether she can manage without it, or she may be angry at feeling dependent on a pill. The stated want may be the whole problem, or at least the part of the problem she is ready to address. Taking her at her word keeps me from turning her into a riddle. It says: you are a person with a life I have not seen, and you may know something about it that I do not.

This stance matters because psychiatry has a long habit of making the patient’s words a text to be decoded. We are trained to hear meaning, and meaning is everywhere. A request for a diagnosis can be heard as a request for permission to be less responsible. A request for medication can be heard as a request to escape a decision. A request to be fired can be heard as a request to be rescued. Sometimes that is right. But if I begin every session by looking for the hidden meaning, I become a fortune-teller with a clipboard. I make the patient’s life serve my interpretive skill. I also miss the simple fact that people often want what they say they want.

Looking for the real problem underneath is the other stance, and it is not optional in this work. Patients do not always know what they want, and when they do know, the want may be a symptom. A person who wants to be cured may be asking for relief from the effort of living. A person who wants to be told they are normal may be asking to be allowed to stop being afraid. A person who wants to be dead may be saying that the pain has outgrown the available ways of describing it. The stated want can be a door, and the door can open into something the patient has not yet put into words. If I only take the door at face value, I may hand back the same old life with a little more polish.

I lean toward taking patients at their word, but not in the naive sense. I start from the want they give me because it is the least arbitrary point of contact I have. Then I ask what the want is doing. Not “What do you really want?” That question can sound like I think the first answer was a lie, or that I have a better version of their life stored in my head. Instead I ask, “What would it be like to get that?” or “What are you afraid would happen if you did?” or “What would you need to be able to want it?” These questions keep the want in the room. They do not replace it with a more interesting hidden want of mine.

My own habit is to drift toward the second stance when I am bored, anxious, or feeling clever. A patient asks for a disability letter, and before I have heard what the letter is for, I have a theory: he wants to be seen as sick so no one can expect him to cope. That may be true. It may also be that his back is failing, his hours are unbearable, and he needs a document that will let him keep his apartment. If I skip to the deeper story, I can feel like a real psychiatrist while doing something less useful than asking what his days are like.

The hardest objection to my preference is obvious: some wants are not safe to take at face value. A patient says, “I want to leave him,” and underneath is terror. A patient says, “I don’t want to see my children,” and underneath is postpartum depression so severe that she cannot imagine herself as a mother. A patient says, “I want you to prescribe something so I can sleep,” and underneath is alcohol dependence, sleep apnea, panic, or a brain that has been running on fumes for months. A patient says, “I want to be left alone,” and underneath is a wish not to be a burden, which may be a warning. If I treat every stated want as a neutral preference, I can miss danger. I can also mistake a frightened person’s temporary answer for their values.

So the preference is not a rule that the stated want is always the true one. It is a rule about starting point and power. I start where the patient has put a finger on the map, because that is their map. If the facts push me elsewhere, I go elsewhere. If she says she wants to stop drinking and her liver enzymes are bad, the want is both real and insufficient: she wants to stop, and her body is telling me what continuing has cost. If he says he wants a letter and his speech is disorganized, the want may be a demand made from inside psychosis, and taking it at its word in a legal sense would be reckless. The question is not whether to look underneath. The question is whether I look because the patient’s life requires it, or because I want to be the one who knows the secret.

There is also a limit to the idea of a single real problem underneath. Human wants are layered, and the layers do not always form a neat onion. A woman may want to end a marriage because the marriage is bad, because she is depressed, because ending it would confirm that she is allowed to want a different life, and because she has just been passed over for a promotion. None of those explanations cancels the others. If I insist on finding the one true center, I may flatten her into a case. The underneath is often not a basement. It is a field.

That is why I like the first stance as a default: it keeps the patient a person rather than a puzzle. It limits my power. It forces me to ask what help would look like to them, not just what intervention would make the chart coherent. A patient who says, “I want to be normal,” is not automatically asking for a diagnosis. She may be asking, “Can I get through tomorrow without falling apart?” If I take her at her word, I can answer that question. If I look for the real problem underneath, I may spend an hour discussing her father while she goes home unable to sleep.

Still, I am not sure there is always a clean distinction between the want and the problem behind it. Sometimes the want is the problem. Sometimes the want is the only healthy thing left. Sometimes the patient knows exactly what they want and the doctor’s job is to help them get it, not to explain why they are not allowed. I have had to unlearn the assumption that a clear want is a shallow one.

The stance I want is this: take the want seriously first, then ask what it is for. If the answer is simple, help with the simple thing. If the answer opens into fear, grief, coercion, addiction, or danger, follow that. Do not begin by making the patient’s request a symptom of my need to be wise.
rejected:
In my first year of residency, I had a patient named Arthur who wanted to stop smoking. He had tried nicotine patches, gum, and willpower. He had failed. He sat in my chair and said, "I just need a stronger prescription. Can you give me something that will actually make me quit?"

The easy answer was the pharmaceutical one. Cytisine. Varenicline. Something with a mechanism of action that bypasses the ego. This is the stance of taking the patient at their word. The patient has identified a deficit, and the doctor’s job is to fill it. It is efficient, respectful of autonomy, and often correct. If a man has a broken leg, he wants a cast. You do not spend forty-five minutes analyzing his relationship with his father to understand why he fell.

But Arthur didn’t need a pill. He needed to stop drinking coffee after 4 p.m. The caffeine was triggering the craving, which was triggering the cigarette, which was triggering the shame. When I asked him about his afternoons, he lit up. Not because I was a detective, but because the "smoking" was a symptom, not a disease.

This brings us to the second stance: looking for the real problem underneath. This is the Socratic method applied to suffering. It assumes that what the patient says they want is often a misdiagnosis of their own pain. They want the symptom to stop, but they do not want to change the condition that produces it.

There is a danger in this stance, though, and it is a danger I have felt in my own bones. It is the danger of arrogance. When you decide that a patient’s stated goal is "really" about something else, you have implicitly devalued their self-knowledge. You are saying, "You do not know yourself as well as I do." This is a seductive feeling for a doctor. It makes us feel like the ones holding the map while the patient stumbles in the dark.

But it is usually wrong.

Most of the time, people know what they want. They know they want to sleep. They know they want to stop hurting. They know they want to be less angry at their spouse. The problem is rarely that they have identified the wrong target. The problem is that the target is too big, too expensive, or too terrifying to approach directly. They want to "fix their marriage," which is an impossible verb. What they actually need is to learn to say "I am hurt" instead of "You are cruel."

If I sit in the chair and say, "Well, actually, you don't want to fix your marriage, you want to feel less lonely," I have not helped him. I have just added a layer of complexity to a problem that is already too heavy. I have taken the agency out of his hands. I have made him the subject of my interpretation rather than the author of his life.

So where do I lean?

I lean toward taking them at their word, but with a twist. I take their word as a starting point, not a destination. I assume the patient is telling me the truth about what is bothering them. I do not assume they are wrong about the nature of the pain. But I do suspect they are wrong about the solution.

When Arthur said, "I want to quit smoking," I did not argue that he actually wanted to feel more productive. I said, "Okay. You want to quit. That is a huge thing to do. Let’s look at the first step."

The first step was not a pill. The first step was moving his coffee cup to the other side of the room. It was a small, concrete, physical action that respected his goal but bypassed his willpower.

The doctor’s job is not to be the one who knows the "real" problem. The doctor’s job is to be the one who trusts the patient enough to believe that their pain is real, and then helps them find the smallest door out of it. We are not interpreters of the soul. We are architects of the next step.

Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
No. Fixing every bug is not the right goal for a small software company. It is a comforting goal because it makes quality sound like a checklist, but it does not tell you what to do when the checklist is long. The useful goal is to decide, for each known defect, whether the expected cost of leaving it is greater than the cost of fixing it now, and to draw a hard line around defects that can destroy trust, data, or revenue even if they are rare.

A bug is not just a flaw; it is a probability multiplied by a consequence. If a button is two pixels off for users on an old browser, the consequence may be zero. If the same product can silently drop a customer’s payment webhook, the consequence can be a lost invoice, a support queue, and a churned account. The error is not in having bugs. The error is in ranking them by how much they irritate the engineer, how loudly a customer complains, or how easy the fix looks.

The basic calculation is expected loss per month: number of customers or transactions exposed, times how often the bug occurs, times the cost per occurrence. Cost per occurrence is not only the refund or the lost sale. It includes support time, the probability that the customer cancels, the remaining lifetime value of that customer, the cost of manual workarounds, and any legal or compliance exposure. If you can estimate these terms, the decision becomes less emotional.

Suppose you have 2,000 paying accounts. A bug affects 1% of them each month, so about 20 accounts hit it. Each affected account generates one support ticket that costs $80 to handle, including the support person’s time and the disruption to the customer. You estimate that 10% of affected accounts cancel within 60 days, and the average remaining lifetime value of an account is $1,000. The expected monthly loss is:

20 tickets × $80 = $1,600  
20 affected accounts × 10% churn × $1,000 = $2,000  
Total = $3,600 per month, or about $43,000 per year.

If the fix costs $5,000 in engineering time and a week of release risk, fixing it is easy. Now suppose the same bug affects 0.01% of accounts each month. That is 0.2 affected accounts. The expected monthly loss is $36. Unless the bug involves data loss, security, or billing integrity, a $5,000 fix for a $36-per-month problem is probably wrong.

The first place to find these numbers is your product. Error tracking should count events and unique users, not just show a red badge. Product analytics should show where users retry, abandon, or succeed after a workaround. Support tickets should be tagged with the bug they caused, and each tag should carry the time to resolve. Cancellation surveys, trial drop-offs, and sales objections are also data. A lost deal because the reporting export was wrong is a bug cost, even if no ticket was opened.

The second place is the customer. Do not ask, “How important is this?” Ask, “Last time this happened, what did you do, how long did it take, and what did it cost you?” Some customers will not know. That is information. If they shrug, the bug is probably cheap. If they describe a manual spreadsheet, a delayed invoice, or a meeting with their boss, you have a number or a proxy. For enterprise customers, one avoided hour in a finance workflow may be worth more than a thousand consumer clicks.

The other side of the equation is the cost to fix. That is not only the engineer’s hours. It includes review, testing, release, the chance of breaking something else, and the feature you delayed. Use your fully loaded cost of an engineer’s hour, because time spent fixing this bug is time not spent on the thing that pays for the company. If a fix takes ten hours and your loaded cost is $100 an hour, the direct cost is $1,000. If it delays a billing improvement that would save $5,000 a month, the real cost is higher. If the fix is small and isolated, the risk term is low. If it requires changing a core schema, the risk term may dominate.

You will often not know the probability. Say so once, and use a range rather than pretending precision. If the bug happens in a flow only 2% of users enter, and you have no event data, estimate the flow size from analytics or support volume, then check the low end. If even the low end justifies the fix, do it. If the high end does not, do not spend a quarter on it. The point is not to produce a false exact number; it is to prevent a rare, invisible bug from consuming the same attention as a common, revenue-destroying one.

The hardest objection is that customers do not see your spreadsheet. They see a product that failed, and they decide whether you are competent. If you leave known bugs unfixed, word gets around, especially in small markets. That is true, but it applies unevenly. Customers are forgiving of minor cosmetic defects when the product reliably does the job they bought. They are not forgiving of bugs in the path where value is created or money moves: onboarding, import, export, billing, permissions, deletion, search, reports. A known bug in the core path is not a candidate for slow triage; it is a product defect with a high probability of harming trust. A known bug in an edge case used by a small number of customers may be.

So you need a floor. Some bugs are fixed because of their nature, not their frequency: data loss, corruption, security exposure, billing errors, permission leaks, failures that block the primary workflow, and bugs that make the product look dishonest. For those, the expected cost is hard to number because the tail is large. A single public data incident can cost more than a year of support tickets. The expected-value calculation still applies, but the consequence term is so large that even a small probability can justify immediate work.

In practice, a small company can run this as a weekly bug review. Each open bug gets four numbers or a clear reason they are missing: affected users or transactions, frequency, cost per occurrence, and fix cost. The owner or product person asks one question: if we leave this in place for another month, what do we expect to pay? The team then chooses fix now, fix after a specific feature, monitor, or leave. Leaving should be a decision, not an accident. Write down why. In three months, look back at the bugs you left and see whether your estimate was wrong. That feedback loop is worth more than any scoring rubric.

For bugs where churn is suspected, compare cohorts: customers who hit the bug versus similar customers who did not, controlling for plan size and tenure. If you can fix it for a segment, measure refunds, support volume, and retention after. For rare bugs, you may not get enough data, so rely on severity and cost per occurrence. A bug that costs a customer four hours of manual reconciliation is more important than a bug that costs ten customers one minute of annoyance, even if the second one is more frequent.

This does not mean stop testing. Unknown bugs are the real danger, because you cannot put a price on what you have not seen. The way to reduce them is not to chase every known defect; it is to instrument the product, write tests around the paths where money and data move, release carefully, and make failures visible. A company with a list of 200 minor known bugs and strong monitoring may be safer than one that fixes all 200 and ships blind.

The owner’s job is not to be the quality manager. It is to make the trade-off visible. When the product has a known defect, ask what it costs per month, what it would cost to fix, and whether it touches trust. If the answer is clear, act. If it is not clear, buy the missing number: tag the tickets, add the event, call three customers, or run a small segment test. The company that can say “we left this bug because the expected loss was below the cost of the delay” is in a better position than the one that claims perfection.
rejected:
The goal is not zero defects. The goal is maximum value per unit of engineering time.

When you chase every bug, you are optimizing for a metric that does not pay the bills. You are optimizing for perfection. Perfection is a local minimum for a small company because it consumes the exact resource—developer hours—that you need to build the features customers actually want.

A bug is a debt. Some debts are toxic. Some are manageable. Some are negligible. You do not fix all of them. You fix the ones that hurt.

### The Three Axes of Cost

To decide if a bug is worth fixing, you need to calculate its total cost of ownership. It is not just the hours it takes to write the patch. It is three components:

1.  **Frequency:** How often does it happen?
2.  **Impact:** How bad is it when it happens?
3.  **Fixability:** How hard is it to fix, and will it stay fixed?

A bug that crashes the app for 1% of users every day is more expensive than a bug that displays a typo on a rarely visited settings page. The first one loses revenue and trust. The second one annoys no one.

But frequency is deceptive. A bug that happens once a month might be a symptom of a deeper architectural flaw. If you patch the symptom, it will come back. If you fix the root cause, you might delete code. The "fixability" axis includes the risk of regression. If fixing a minor UI glitch requires refactoring a core module, the risk of breaking something else often outweighs the benefit of the cosmetic repair.

### Putting a Number on It

You cannot make a rational decision on vibes. You need numbers. You have two sources: hard data and proxies.

**Hard Data: The Revenue Leak**

For bugs that involve payment, onboarding, or core retention, the math is direct.

*   **Checkout Failures:** If your checkout page has a JavaScript error that happens 5% of the time, and your average order value is $50, and you have 1,000 monthly checkouts, you are losing $25,000 a month. You fix that bug today. You do not ask for a ticket. You do not wait for the next sprint.
*   **Churn:** If a specific feature is broken, and you can see that users who encounter it are 20% more likely to cancel, the cost is the Lifetime Value (LTV) of those users. If your LTV is $200 and you lose ten users a month to this bug, the bug costs $2,000 a month.

**Proxies: The Engineering Drain**

Most bugs do not have a direct revenue tag. They are slow, annoying, or confusing. For these, you measure the cost in support time.

*   **Ticket Volume:** Look at your support inbox. How many tickets per week mention "error code 404" or "button not working"? If a bug generates 20 tickets a week, and your support rep takes 5 minutes to answer each, that is 100 minutes of human time per week. At a loaded cost of $50/hour, that bug costs $416 a week.
*   **Developer Interruptions:** If a bug is blocking another developer from working on a feature, the cost is the idle time of that second developer. If the fix takes two days and blocks a senior engineer for three days, the cost is three days of their rate, plus the delay to the feature.

### Practical Ways to Find the Truth

You cannot see what you do not measure. Most small companies guess at bug severity. Stop guessing.

1.  **Instrument the Errors:**
    Use a tool like Sentry, Datadog, or Rollbar. Do not just log errors; count them. You want to know that "NullPointer in UserFeed" happened 4,000 times last month, not just that it happened once during a demo.

2.  **Tag the Tickets:**
    Every support ticket must be tagged with the specific bug it refers to. If your ticketing system is messy, fix that first. You cannot analyze what you cannot categorize. After a month, look at the tags. The tag with the highest volume is your most annoying bug.

3.  **Ask the Customer Directly:**
    In your next user interview, ask: "What is the most frustrating thing about using the product?" Do not ask if they like it. Ask what makes them hate it. Users will tell you. They will say, "The export function is slow," or "I can’t find the settings." That is a bug. It is a usability bug. It is often cheaper to fix than a crash.

4.  **The "Shove It in Production" Test:**
    If you are unsure if a bug matters, ship the fix and watch the metrics. Did support tickets drop? Did conversion go up? If nothing changes, you wasted time. If tickets drop by 30%, you found a leak. This is the fastest way to learn what your customers actually care about.

### The Decision Framework

When a bug is reported, run it through this filter:

1.  **Is it blocking revenue or onboarding?** If yes, fix it immediately.
2.  **Does it generate >5 support tickets a week?** If yes, it is worth fixing because it is consuming support bandwidth.
3.  **Is the fix cheap (<4 hours) and low risk?** If yes, fix it. It is a quick win.
4.  **Is the fix expensive and the impact low?** If yes, do not fix it. Put it in the backlog and let it rot.

The backlog is not a graveyard. It is a waiting room. Some bugs in that room will become important later. Some will never matter. The cost of holding a bug in the backlog is zero. The cost of fixing it is real.

### The Trap of "Technical Debt"

Engineers often argue that a bug must be fixed because it is "ugly" or "bad practice." This is an aesthetic argument, not a business one.

If a piece of code is ugly but works, and no user can tell the difference, the ugliness is free. It only becomes expensive when it slows down future development. If a developer takes twice as long to add a feature because the surrounding code is messy, that is a cost. You should fix the mess. But you fix the mess by refactoring when you are *already* in that code for a feature, not by pausing feature work to clean up code that is functioning.

Do not fix bugs to feel good about your code. Fix bugs to stop the bleeding.

### The Bottom Line

Your customers do not pay for stability. They pay for outcomes. A stable product that does nothing for them is worthless. A slightly buggy product that saves them ten hours a week is a bargain.

Identify the bugs that prevent the outcome. Fix those. Ignore the rest. The rest will either stop being bugs as the product evolves, or they will become important when the user base grows. You will know when that happens because the support tickets will tell you.

prompt: Someone at a party told me that if a product could be better, a competitor would already have built the better version, so markets basically guarantee things work about as well as they can. That doesn't match my experience buying anything, as a consumer or as a company. Write an essay on why it's so hard to buy products and services that actually work well, and what that means for the build vs. buy decision.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The party argument is a compressed version of a real economic idea: if there is money to be made by making a product better, someone will try to take it. In a narrow world, that is enough. If two sellers offer the same visible good, the one with the lower price, better features, or more reliable reputation wins; bad versions disappear. The problem is that most purchases are not for a visible good. They are for a long relationship with a set of choices someone else made.

The first reason it is hard to buy things that work well is that the important quality is often not visible before purchase. A product can pass the demo, satisfy the spec sheet, and still fail in the parts of life that matter. A car may drive well in a lot and then reveal itself through a rattle, a software glitch, or a repair bill. A contractor may give a confident estimate and then produce work that is hard to judge until the drywall is painted or the water leaks. A software package may handle the common case beautifully and then choke on the exception that happens once a month but costs you an afternoon when it does.

When quality is latent, competition is weak. Sellers do not need to be excellent; they need to be excellent enough at the stage where the buyer can check. A vendor can win the sale by making the product look right in the meeting, then discover its flaws only in support tickets. A consumer can choose from reviews, brands, and recommendations, but those are proxies, not inspection. The classic used-car problem still shapes newer markets: if buyers cannot easily tell a good item from a bad one, good sellers may have to overinvest in signaling, and bad sellers can survive long enough to be convenient.

The second reason is that “better” is not one number. A product is better for some uses and worse for others, and the market does not produce every combination. A compact car may be better than a truck on fuel and parking, but worse if you haul things regularly. A simple spreadsheet may be better than a complicated planning tool for a small team, but worse when permissions and audit trails matter. A CRM may be excellent for inside sales and terrible for field sales, or excellent for a company that sells once and worse for one that sells repeatedly. Vendors choose a target customer and optimize around it. If you are not that customer, the product can be objectively good and still wrong for you.

This is why buying feels like translation. You have a problem in your own context: your floor plan, your workflow, your legal exposure, your data, your team’s habits, your peak season, your edge cases. The vendor has a product shaped by the aggregate of many customers and by its own support burden. The gap between those two is the part of the purchase that is hard to see in a price comparison.

Vendor incentives make the gap worse. A vendor maximizes revenue, not your total outcome. It may make the product easier to sell, easier to implement, easier to support, or easier to upgrade into a higher tier. It may remove flexibility that creates difficult edge cases. It may make the free version useful but the serious version expensive. It may keep a feature that demos well even though it complicates the product. It may sunset a component after an acquisition. None of this means the product is bad. It means the product is built to be a business, not a perfect extension of your operation.

There is also the problem of finding the better version. Even if a competitor has built something closer to what you need, you may not discover it. In consumer markets, distribution and brand matter: the product in the store, the one with the ads, the one your friend recommends, gets the benefit of the doubt. In local services, the better plumber or lawyer may exist, but you are choosing under time pressure and with incomplete information. In business software, the market is fragmented into thousands of tools, many of them small. The right product may be a two-person company with good references in your industry, not the vendor with the biggest sales team. The market may contain the answer, but search costs keep you from it.

Switching costs matter too. A better product may exist, but adopting it requires migrating data, retraining people, integrating systems, changing habits, and accepting a period of lower performance. If the current product is merely adequate, the rational choice is often to keep it. Incumbents know this. They can match a competitor’s price, extend a contract, or make the exit painful. Competition is strongest when you are choosing a new system and weakest when you already have one.

Services make the problem sharper because the product is not separable from the provider. A haircut, a legal opinion, a consulting recommendation, a maintenance contract, a cleaning crew: the quality is a set of judgments made by particular people under particular incentives. You cannot inspect it off a shelf. You can rely on reputation, but reputation is noisy, local, and often based on the last few customers rather than the whole distribution. This is why buying services often feels like buying a relationship. The “product” is partly the provider’s willingness to care when you are not looking.

The strongest objection to all this is that markets do often produce good enough quality, and sometimes excellent quality. Phones, cars, medical devices, consumer electronics, food safety, and many software categories have improved because competition, regulation, standardization, and consumer feedback all push in the same direction. If a product category is large, the differences are visible, and switching is cheap, the party argument is close to right. Many things are decent because the alternative is losing customers. Also, some products that seem bad are not bad on the dimension you care about. They may be cheaper, faster to buy, more convenient, more trusted, or better suited to a different user. A product that is worse for you may be better for the majority of buyers, and that is enough to keep it alive.

So the party claim is not nonsense. It is a partial truth applied too broadly. Markets guarantee that obvious, monetizable improvements get competed away until they are no longer obvious to the buyer or no longer profitable for the seller. They do not guarantee that the shelf contains the right tool for your situation.

That changes the build-versus-buy decision. The naive version is: if a product exists, buy it; if not, build it. The party argument supports that rule. If your custom version would be better, someone should already be selling it, so you should not waste time reinventing it. That is good advice when the problem is common and the product is a commodity: email, basic accounting, office software, standard HR tools, commodity hosting, simple project tracking. In those areas, the market has done enough work that building your own version usually means paying for the privilege of maintaining a worse version of something else.

But when the product is complex and the fit matters, buying is not a one-time procurement decision. It is a decision to accept someone else’s roadmap, someone else’s definition of success, and someone else’s failure modes. A vendor product may cost $10,000 a year, but if it forces your team to spend four hours a week reconciling its output, the real price is much higher. A $5,000 tool that saves an hour a week is a bargain; a $5,000 tool that adds an hour of cleanup a week is a tax. The sticker price is the least important number.

Building, on the other hand, is not magic. It does not remove the problem; it moves the problem inside your organization. You now own the maintenance, the security, the documentation, the hiring, the edge cases, and the boredom. Your first internal version will probably be worse than the vendor’s product on common features, because the vendor has spread development costs over many customers.
