You may also discover that the thing you thought was unique was actually a known problem with known solutions, and that you have now built a dependency on your own past choices.

The better rule is to ask who should own the problem. Buy when your needs are in the common case, when you can evaluate the product before committing, when the cost of misfit is small, and when the capability is not central to your competitive advantage. Buy when a pilot on your own data can show whether it works. Buy when references can speak to the failure modes, not just the happy path. Buy when the exit cost after two years is something you can estimate and accept.

Build when the capability is core to what you sell, when the requirements are stable enough to learn but changing in ways a vendor is unlikely to follow, when the cost of misfit is high, and when you can afford to maintain the result. Build when the “product” is mostly glue between systems you already own and the vendor version would require you to reshape your operation around its assumptions. Build when the thing you need is so specific that a vendor would have to build it for you alone, which means it is not really a product market at all.

Often the right answer is in between. Buy the hard, generic parts and build the thin, specific layer. Buy a database, a payment processor, an identity system, a document store, a reporting engine, and build the workflow that connects them to your actual business. Or buy a service instead of a product when the problem is judgment rather than computation: a maintenance contract, a managed team, a specialist firm. The point is not to avoid the market. The point is to stop treating the market as a place where the right version of your problem is waiting for you to compare prices.

The party claim should be revised, not rejected. Markets guarantee that obvious improvements get competed away. They do not guarantee that what is for sale is what you need. The build-versus-buy question is therefore not whether a product exists. It is whether you can buy a version of the problem that is close enough to yours without becoming dependent on the seller’s version of the solution.
rejected:
The person at the party is describing a market that does not exist. They are applying the logic of price discovery to the discovery of quality. In competitive markets, prices converge because the good is fungible. A gallon of gasoline is a gallon of gasoline. If your station charges $3.50 and the one down the street charges $3.20, you drive down the street. The market punishes the expensive seller instantly.

Quality is not fungible. A "better" product is often a different product entirely, or a product that requires a specific context to reveal its value. If a software vendor builds a workflow that is 10% faster but requires a two-week migration of legacy data, the 10% speedup is invisible to the buyer until after the migration is complete. By then, the switch is locked in. The competitor has not built the better version; they have built a version that is easier to sell.

This divergence exists because the seller and the buyer have different objectives. The seller wants to maximize the number of units sold. The buyer wants to minimize the friction of using the product. These goals align only when the product is simple enough that its value is obvious on first contact. For complex goods—enterprise software, industrial machinery, financial services, legal structures—the value is latent. It appears only after integration, training, and time.

The seller knows this. Therefore, the seller optimizes for the demo, not the deployment. They build the features that look impressive in a sales call: the dashboard, the API documentation, the case study. They underinvest in the unglamorous parts that determine daily utility: error handling, edge cases, performance under load, and the clarity of the user interface. When a buyer evaluates a product, they are evaluating the seller’s marketing, not the product’s engineering.

The market does correct this, but slowly and unevenly. Reputation builds over years of churn. A bad product keeps customers for a while because switching costs are high. By the time the reputation collapses, the seller has already extracted maximum value. The "better" competitor emerges only when the incumbent’s customer base becomes large enough to support a viable alternative. This lag is the source of the frustration. You are buying in the present, but the market is grading you on the past.

This creates a specific failure mode for the build-versus-buy decision. The standard advice is to buy if the product is a commodity and build if it is a core differentiator. This is too simple. The real question is: how much of the product’s value is visible to the buyer?

If the value is visible, buy. If you need a CRM and you can see the interface, if the reports are standard, if the pricing is transparent, the market has done its work. The differences are small, and the risk of building your own is higher than the risk of buying a mediocre off-the-shelf tool.

If the value is latent, the calculus changes. If you need a workflow that touches three other systems and requires a custom logic layer, the vendor is selling you a promise. They cannot verify that promise for you because they do not know your specific context. You are buying a black box. In this case, "buying" is really an act of faith. You are outsourcing a problem that you do not fully understand to a company that does not understand your business.

The build option is not always superior. It is expensive, slow, and requires maintenance. But it has one advantage the buy option lacks: it makes the problem visible to you. When you build, you are forced to confront the edge cases. You see where the data breaks. You understand the actual constraints of the workflow. This knowledge is the asset. The code is secondary.

So the decision is not about the product. It is about the information asymmetry. If the gap between the demo and the reality is small, buy. If the gap is large, and that gap lies in the core of your operation, build. Not because you are better at engineering than the vendor, but because you are the only party with an incentive to make the latent value real. The vendor’s incentive ends at the signature. Your incentive begins after it.

prompt: I tried a Kaggle competition, landed nowhere near the leaderboard, and now I'm wondering if I'm just bad at machine learning. You do ML as your actual job. Can you write a blog post about how real-world machine learning work compares to Kaggle?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
**Kaggle is a modeling contest. Most ML jobs are data and product problems.**

The first thing I do when a real machine learning project starts is not open a notebook. I ask who owns the label. If the label is wrong, late, or nobody can define it, the model is already in trouble. Kaggle competitions usually do not ask that question. They hand you rows, columns, a target, and a metric. The world is frozen. Your job is to move a number.

That difference matters. A Kaggle dataset is a contract: the schema is stable, the test set is drawn from the same distribution, the metric is fixed, and the answer is a submission file. In a company, the data is a process. A customer table changes grain when a product team adds a new entity. A billing system emits a record after the fact. An app event arrives with a user ID that only matches the CRM after a support agent fixes it. There are access controls, privacy reviews, and retention limits that do not appear in a competition file. A lot of real ML is SQL, joins, backfills, and arguing about whether a row represents a customer, an order, or a session. The model may be small; the data work is not.

The target is another place where Kaggle and production diverge. In a churn competition, “churn” is a column. In a business, it might mean canceled within 90 days, but cancellations are disputed, refunds happen, a customer cancels and returns, and the finance team wants the label to align with revenue recognition. If the model is used to offer a discount, the model changes the future: people it targets may not churn, so the label for next month is contaminated by the intervention. A Kaggle test set does not usually react to your predictions.

Evaluation changes too. Kaggle gives you a score, often AUC or log loss. Real systems care about decisions. A fraud model is not judged by how well it ranks all transactions. It is judged by how many alerts an analyst can review, how many fraud dollars are caught, and how many good customers are blocked. A fraud score may need to be returned before a payment is authorized, which can mean tens of milliseconds, not a batch job. A ranking model may improve click AUC while reducing revenue because it shows items users click but do not buy. A medical risk score may need calibration, not just ranking, because clinicians must compare a patient’s predicted probability to a treatment threshold. In production, the metric is often the thing the business can pay for, and the proxy metric in the notebook is only a guide.

There is also a deployment boundary. A Kaggle model only has to run on the competition data and produce predictions. A production model has to run on new data at a certain latency, with features computed the same way in training and serving, with logs that let you reproduce a prediction, with a rollback when the upstream table changes, and with monitoring that tells you when the input distribution has moved. I have seen projects where the model was trivial but the feature pipeline was the actual system: a score had to be available before a checkout page rendered, and the feature store had to survive a schema migration without silently changing the meaning of a column. If a model cannot be served, monitored, and updated, it is a notebook, not a service.

There is also a difference in what wins. Kaggle rewards squeezing the metric. Real work often rewards narrowing the problem. If a decision table with three features explains most of the value, a complex model may be a liability because it is harder to explain and more likely to fail quietly. The winning change is often a better label, a cleaner join, or a threshold chosen with the business, not a new architecture.

Kaggle does teach some real things. It is a good place to learn baselines, cross-validation, overfitting, feature engineering, and the difference between a public leaderboard and a private one. For some jobs, the modeling intensity is close to Kaggle: search ranking, ad bidding, recommendation, fraud scoring, and other high-volume problems where small metric gains are worth real money. In those areas, the skills transfer. But the top of a leaderboard is also a contest artifact. Teams make many submissions, browse kernels, ensemble models, exploit the public/private split, and spend more time on the competition than a normal employee can. In a competition with thousands of teams, being outside the top ten is not a meaningful skill test. A low rank can mean you lacked the contest-specific tricks, not the ability to build a useful system.

The honest objection is that a clean dataset is a controlled test of modeling fundamentals. If you cannot avoid leakage, build a reasonable baseline, or understand why your validation is misleading, that is a problem in real work too. I do not know your code or how much time you had, so I cannot tell whether your rank came from missing fundamentals or missing contest leverage. But the rank itself is not a general diagnosis. It measured how well you optimized one score on one frozen dataset, under competition rules, against people with specific incentives and resources.

Real ML is messier and less glamorous. It is defining the right question, finding the right data, making the label honest, integrating the model into a workflow, and living with it after the launch. A person can be a poor Kaggle competitor and still ship a reliable model because they ask better questions, understand the system, and do not overfit to a metric. The useful question after a bad rank is not “Am I bad at machine learning?” It is “What did that competition actually measure, and is that the job I want?”
rejected:
Kaggle competitions are a different sport. They are not machine learning. They are pattern matching on a closed dataset with a known metric, executed by a team with unlimited compute and no deadline, aiming to squeeze 0.1% out of a model that already works.

Real ML is engineering.

In a competition, the data is clean, labeled, and static. The problem is defined by the leaderboard. You submit a pickle file. You know when you win: when your score stops moving.

In your job, the data is a mess of CSVs, SQL views, and API responses that break every Tuesday. The labels are often wrong, delayed, or missing entirely. You don’t know the true metric because the business definition of "churn" changes based on who is asking. You aren’t trying to beat a baseline; you are trying to answer a question the data may not contain.

The most important skill in production ML is not architecture. It is data hygiene. I have spent more time debugging a timezone offset in a timestamp column than I have tuning hyperparameters. A neural network with a perfect architecture trained on skewed, leaky, or dirty data is worse than a logistic regression on clean data. Kaggle rewards you for finding the magic combination of learning rates and batch sizes. Real work punishes you for trusting the source.

There is also the issue of feedback loops. On Kaggle, you get a score. In production, you deploy a model, and then you wait weeks or months to see if it actually improved the business outcome. You have to build the instrumentation to know if you failed. You have to handle drift. You have to retrain when the world changes, not just when you run out of ideas.

Finally, there is the constraint of cost. Kaggle participants use free GPUs for days. In a company, every inference has a price tag. You will often be asked to replace a deep learning model with a decision tree because the latency requirement is 50 milliseconds and the budget is fixed. You are not trying to win a gold medal. You are trying to stay within a budget while solving a problem that is only 60% solvable.

If you are bad at Kaggle, it might mean you are good at real work. The competition tests your ability to optimize a proxy. Real work tests your ability to navigate ambiguity. The fact that you didn't rank high means you didn't spend enough time overfitting to a noise floor. That is a useful trait to have when you can't afford to overfit to a metric that the stakeholders will redefine next quarter.

prompt: I keep seeing devs who just have the LLM write code and paste errors back to it until it works, without really thinking. Models are getting good enough that maybe that's fine? Is there any future where that approach actually pays off for them?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
It pays off when “works” is cheap to check and the code is not going to be load-bearing.

A developer who asks a model to write a script that renames files, runs it, pastes the traceback, runs it again, and then checks that the folder now contains the right names is not necessarily being lazy. The code is disposable, the blast radius is one directory, and the real test is visible. In that situation, the model is a fast way to skip syntax and boilerplate. The human’s thinking is in choosing the input, running the script, and noticing when the output looks wrong. If the model can get that right in five minutes, spending twenty minutes deriving the path logic by hand may be worse.

The approach stops paying off when the absence of errors is not the same as correctness.

Ask a model to add retries to a webhook handler. It writes code that calls the endpoint again on failure. No compile error. Local test passes. But if the provider retries after a timeout that actually succeeded, the second call creates a duplicate order. The error-pasting loop never sees this because nothing red appears. The model is optimizing for the visible failure, usually the last exception, not for the invariants of the system: idempotency, ordering, partial failure, authorization, data migration safety.

That is why “paste until green” can be dangerous even when the developer is otherwise competent. A lot of software bugs are not crashes. They are wrong totals, stale cache, race conditions, missing indexes, N+1 queries, permission checks that only run on one path, migrations that succeed but lock tables, UI state that desynchronizes after a refresh. LLMs are good at producing plausible code for the happy path. They can also fix failures in ways that hide the problem: wrap it in try/except, cast to any, add a sleep, hardcode the test value, delete the assertion, make the dependency optional. Each of those can make the immediate error disappear and make the later failure harder to trace.

A 200-line script can often be trusted by reading it and running it on a few cases. A 2,000-line service cannot be trusted the same way unless you have tests and a model of its behavior. As the code grows, the cost of a plausible-but-wrong patch grows. If a mistake costs five minutes to find, the loop is fine. If it costs a week of on-call, a refund queue, or a bad migration, the loop is not enough.

The strongest case for the lazy version of this workflow is that the feedback channel is improving. Models will not just read stack traces; they will run the app, write tests, inspect logs, run fuzzers, compare screenshots, and propose fixes. If that works, the human may only need to state the goal and approve the diff. I think that future is coming for a large class of tasks. For internal tools, web pages, data pipelines with sample data, and simple CRUD apps, agentic coding may make the prompt-error loop almost sufficient, because the loop will contain much more than errors.

But that does not remove the hard part; it moves it. Someone has to decide what the acceptance criteria are. If the model writes the tests, it can write tests that match its own implementation rather than the intended behavior. If the human cannot articulate the difference between “the page loads” and “a user cannot claim a coupon twice,” the system will optimize the wrong target. The verification problem is the bottleneck. In high-stakes code, the expensive question is not “how do I make this compile?” but “what property must be true under failure, scale, and adversarial input?” A better autocomplete does not answer that.

So there is a future where this approach pays off for developers, but it is a future with two kinds of work.

One kind is disposable or low-risk: scripts, local tools, prototypes, one-off migrations, dashboards, internal automations, code whose failure can be detected quickly and rolled back cheaply. There, the best developer is the one who can turn a fuzzy want into an executable check and let the model grind until it passes. The developer who is good at this will ship a lot, and much of it will not matter enough to require deep architectural care.

The other kind is durable: payment systems, auth, storage, compilers, medical devices, infrastructure, large shared codebases. There, the developer who only pastes errors will eventually produce a system that is expensive to change and frightening to touch. They may ship faster now, but they are leaving a bill. The bill shows up when someone else has to add a feature, or when the model cannot figure out why the tests pass but the production behavior is wrong.

For early-career developers, there is an additional risk: atrophied calibration. If you never learn why the first attempt failed, you cannot predict the next one. The model can be a tutor, but only if the developer pauses long enough to notice the pattern. A developer who can say “this failed because I assumed the array was sorted” is learning. A developer who just says “try again” is renting competence.

The approach is fine when the code is small, the stakes are low, and the output can be checked. It becomes a trap when the code becomes part of a system and the only test is “no exception.” Models getting better will widen the first category a lot. They will not make the second one disappear. The developers who benefit from LLMs will spend less time thinking about syntax and more time specifying what success means, designing checks, and deciding what happens when the system fails.
rejected:
The approach is not "fine." It is a failure of engineering, not a workaround for it.

When a developer pastes an error back to an LLM without understanding the root cause, they are outsourcing the most critical part of programming: debugging. Debugging is not just about fixing the bug; it is about building a mental model of the system. If you do not know why the code failed, you do not know if the fix is correct. You are flying blind.

The model is a brilliant intern who has read the entire history of software but has never shipped a product. It knows the syntax. It knows the common pitfalls. It does not know your business logic, your data constraints, or the specific way your users are breaking your API.

There is a future where this pays off, but it looks nothing like what you are seeing.

In that future, the developer acts as a compiler. They write precise, constrained specifications. The LLM generates the code. The developer reviews the diff, not for syntax, but for logic. They check:
*   Does this handle the edge case we discussed?
*   Does this respect the separation of concerns?
*   Is this code maintainable by a human six months from now?

If the code fails, the developer does not paste the stack trace. They analyze the stack trace. They form a hypothesis. They ask the LLM a targeted question based on that hypothesis. "The null pointer exception occurs at line 42. I suspect the user object is undefined during initialization. How can I assert that it exists before this function runs?"

The difference is agency. The first developer is a passive conduit for tokens. The second developer is an active engineer using a powerful tool.

The models are getting good enough to write the code. They are not getting good enough to understand the context. The gap between "code that runs" and "code that works" is filled by human judgment. That gap is not closing. It is widening because the volume of code being generated is increasing, and the volume of human oversight is not.

If you continue to paste errors until it works, you are not building software. You are building a fragile artifact that will break in ways you cannot predict because you never learned why it broke in the first place.

prompt: My mom says she raised me so I owe her everything, including taking care of her when she's old. How far does a debt like that actually go?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The first thing to separate is the true part from the false part. The true part is that your mother did real work. If she raised you, she probably spent years on labor that was unpaid, exhausting, and partly unrewarded: feeding, clothing, supervising, worrying, paying, making decisions, sacrificing convenience. You benefited from that. A person who recognizes that fact has good reason for gratitude, loyalty, and a willingness to help.

The false part is “everything.” A debt that includes everything is not a debt; it is a claim of ownership. It says your time, money, body, relationships, and future belong to her because she helped create and maintain you. But you are not a product she can claim. You are a person with your own limits, your own obligations, and your own right to a life. The moral question is not whether you owe her nothing. It is how much a person can be owed by another person without being destroyed.

That limit matters because old-age care is not one thing. It can mean a phone call on Sunday. It can mean driving her to appointments, helping her sort mail, paying for a cleaner twice a month, staying with her during a hospital stay, or researching care options. It can also mean moving in, becoming a full-time caregiver, giving up a job, supporting her financially while your own life stalls, or spending twenty hours a week managing her medicine, meals, transport, and moods. Those are not the same obligation wearing different clothes. They have different costs.

A useful test is proportionality. If your mother needs a small amount of help and you can give it without serious harm to your own life, refusing is callous. If she is lonely and a visit would cost you an evening, the debt of gratitude pulls strongly toward visiting. If she needs money for a medication and you can afford it, not helping is hard to defend. But if “taking care of her” means you must live with her full-time for the next fifteen years, abandon your own children, drain your savings, and accept constant emotional pressure, that is no longer a reasonable payment on a debt. That is a demand that you stop being an independent adult.

The strongest objection to drawing any line is obvious: parents are vulnerable. Old age brings illness, dementia, income loss, and isolation. If adult children can say, “I feel gratitude, but I am not required,” what prevents children from leaving parents to rot whenever care becomes inconvenient? That is a real risk, and it is one reason filial obligations feel heavier than ordinary debts. A parent who raised you is not a stranger. If you are her only family and she cannot care for herself, you are morally closer to the problem than almost anyone else. Walking away while you could reasonably help would be a serious failure, not a neutral choice.

But even that strong case does not make the obligation infinite. A moral demand can be severe without being absolute. If your mother is in danger and you are the only person available, you may have to act quickly, spend money, make unpleasant decisions, and take on more than you wanted. The fact that the burden is heavy does not mean it can be unlimited. If full care would ruin your health, your marriage, your ability to support your own children, or your mental stability, the moral problem changes. You are then not being asked to pay a debt; you are being asked to sacrifice your whole life. At that point, the right response is usually to share the burden: hire help, involve other relatives, use community services, apply for public benefits, arrange institutional care, or negotiate a limited role.

The legal answer is different from the moral one, and it depends on where you live. In many U.S. states, adult children are not generally required by law to pay for a parent’s care unless they have signed a guarantee, become a legal guardian, or fall under a specific support statute. Some states have old “filial responsibility” laws, but they are uneven and often not the main tool for ordinary elder-care decisions. In other countries, family law may impose maintenance duties on adult children for parents in need. If you are her legal guardian or conservator, you have fiduciary duties to manage her affairs in her interest. If you co-signed a loan or a facility contract, you may be personally liable. Those legal roles create real obligations, but they are defined by law and by the documents you signed, not by the general fact of being her child.

The quality of the upbringing matters too. “I raised you” is not a magic phrase that automatically creates maximum obligation. If she provided steady love, safety, and sacrifice, the moral weight of what she did is large. If “raising” mostly meant basic survival while she was neglectful, cruel, or exploitative, the debt is thinner. You can still have reasons to be cautious, compassionate, or legally responsible toward an aging parent, but the claim “you owe me because I birthed and housed you” is much weaker when the care was poor. Gratitude is proportional to the good actually received.

There is also a practical problem with unlimited filial debt: it gives the parent a veto over your life. If you owe her everything, she can argue that you should not have children because they would compete with her, not move away because she will be old, not marry someone she dislikes because your loyalty belongs to her, not keep money because she may need it someday. Once a relationship operates that way, the child is not an adult with duties; the child is a dependent with resources. That is why the boundary has to be drawn before the crisis forces you to draw it badly.

So what does the debt actually require? It requires that her needs not be invisible to you. It requires that you take her aging seriously instead of pretending it will happen to someone else. It requires that you help in ways that are fair given your means, your other responsibilities, and her actual needs. It requires that you not use independence as an excuse to abandon her if you are the person best placed to step in. It also requires that you advocate for her, tell the truth about her condition, and make arrangements that protect her dignity.

What it does not require is self-erasure. You do not owe her your peace of mind as a permanent tribute. You do not owe her unlimited financial support if it would impoverish you. You do not owe her your silence when her demands become manipulative. You do not owe her a life organized around her fear of aging. If she is competent, her wishes matter; you cannot force care on her or make decisions for her simply because she is your mother. If she is not competent, your role may become decision-maker, but even then your duty is to her interests, not to obeying every demand she made while she was still clear.

A concrete way to think about it is to define the outer edge of what you can do. You might be able to contribute a fixed amount of money each month, visit weekly, help with major decisions, coordinate care, stay for a few days during transitions, or be the person who notices when something is wrong. You might not be able to live with her, be available around the clock, pay for private care indefinitely, or put her needs above your own children’s. Both parts of that sentence can be true at once.

When your mother says you owe her everything, the worst answer is usually “I don’t owe you anything,” because it denies the real debt. The best answer is more specific: “I owe you a great deal because of what you did for me. Here is what I can actually give.” Then you say what that is, and you hold the line. The debt goes as far as serious, proportionate responsibility. It does not go as far as making her the owner of your life.
rejected:
Your mother’s claim rests on a category error. Raising a child is a legal and moral obligation, not a transaction. When she chose to have you, she assumed the responsibility to feed, shelter, and protect you until you could support yourself. She did not invest capital with an expectation of return; she fulfilled a duty. Therefore, there is no "debt" in the financial or contractual sense that you can be charged for repaying.

However, this does not mean you owe her nothing. It means the nature of the obligation shifts from repayment to reciprocity.

The obligation of care is not a debt; it is a moral expectation based on mutual love and shared history. Most children, out of genuine affection, do want to help their parents in old age. This is not because they are paying off a bill, but because they value the relationship. The problem with the "debt" framing is that it weaponizes guilt. It suggests that your compliance is the only variable that determines whether you are a "good" person.

There is a hard limit to what is reasonable, and it is defined by your own capacity. You cannot be expected to sacrifice your own stability, mental health, or life plans to manage her care, especially if she has other resources or family members. If she has other children, the burden is shared. If she has money, she should use it. If she is in good health, she should remain independent.

If you try to care for her because you feel you *owe* it, you will likely resent her. If you care for her because you *love* her, you will be able to set boundaries without feeling like a criminal. The distinction matters. A daughter who refuses to move back to take care of her mother is not a debtor in default; she is a person making a difficult choice about her own life. A daughter who agrees to help, but insists on hiring aides and limiting her own time, is not cheating on a contract; she is defining the terms of a loving relationship.

The debt metaphor is a tool for control. Recognize it for what it is, and then decide what you actually want to give, not what you think you must pay.

prompt: I sell my small software product both as a downloadable desktop app and as a web app. Is it actually worth keeping the desktop version around?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Probably not, unless the desktop version is doing a different job for a segment of customers who pay for that difference. For a small product, the default should be one product. A desktop app is not a second window; it is a second product: installers, OS versions, code signing, auto-updates, local file permissions, antivirus false positives, users who never update, and a support queue that says “works on my machine” in ways web tickets rarely do. If you are one person or a tiny team, that second product is where the schedule goes to die.

Put a number on it. Say maintaining desktop takes six hours a week: packaging, update bugs, OS regressions, answering version-specific questions. If your time is worth $50 an hour, that is about $1,200 a month. If the desktop version serves 100 paying customers at $10 a month, it brings in $1,000 before support. If those customers also generate more tickets than web users, the desktop version is not a revenue line; it is a cost center wearing a revenue line’s clothes. The threshold changes with your pricing and team, but the arithmetic is unforgiving.

Desktop earns its place when the job is local. Batch-processing files on disk, reading a database, watching folders, working offline, using global hotkeys, running in the background, keeping sensitive data off your server: these are real advantages. A tool for converting local video, analyzing code repositories, migrating files, or handling private documents may be primarily a desktop product. A shared project board, simple converter, content tool, or anything centered on an account is usually better as a web product. If the desktop app is mostly an icon that opens the same web experience, ask what the icon buys. If the answer is offline access and a launcher, an installable web app may cover enough.

Browsers have gotten better at local work. They can store data, request file access, use hardware security keys, and be installed. They still cannot do everything a native app can: arbitrary filesystem access, reliable background processing, system tray behavior, global shortcuts, deep OS integration, and some performance paths. But those capabilities matter only if your users need them. Do not carry a native client because it could do things; carry it because customers leave without them.

The strongest argument for keeping desktop is that desktop users are more serious. They downloaded an installer, maybe paid a one-time price, and they stay. That can be true. A small, loyal cohort can still be a bad business if it consumes disproportionate support. Ten percent of revenue that causes thirty percent of tickets is a tax. The relevant comparison is not web users versus no users; it is the incremental profit from desktop users versus the engineering hours they require. If desktop users have lower churn and higher lifetime value, the case improves. If they are just harder to serve, the case weakens.

If the desktop version is sold as a one-time license, be even stricter. You are selling perpetual support. The customer may keep using an old version for years, and you will still field questions about it. A subscription desktop client is easier to justify because the revenue continues while you maintain it. A one-time desktop client is a separate product with a long tail, and small companies often discover they are supporting software they no longer control.

I do not know your metrics, so I cannot say yes or no for your product. The way to find out is to stop pretending desktop and web are equal citizens. Freeze new desktop features. Keep security fixes, crash repairs, and critical bug fixes. Tell users that new capabilities will appear in the web app first. Then measure for a quarter. Compare cohorts: revenue per user, renewal or repeat purchase, support tickets, time to first value, and the reason people say they need desktop. If desktop is twenty percent of revenue and ten percent of effort, keep it. If it is ten percent of revenue and thirty percent of effort, retire it. If a meaningful group leaves because they need offline files or local privacy, you have found a real niche. If they leave because they wanted an icon, you have saved yourself a second product.

The middle path is often right: maintenance mode. A stable desktop app that receives fixes but no new features can preserve a useful segment without dragging the roadmap. That is better than either pretending desktop is a peer or deleting it abruptly. The practical test is simple: if you cannot explain in one sentence what the desktop version does that the web app does not, and the customers who want it do not clearly pay for that difference, let it stop growing.
rejected:
The short answer is no, unless your product does something specific that the web cannot.

The cost of maintaining two codebases, two distribution channels, two security postures, and two support queues is not trivial. It is a constant tax on your time. For a small product, that tax usually eats the margin.

The web version wins on:

*   **Updates:** You fix a bug and it’s live for everyone in minutes. Desktop requires users to download, install, and restart.
*   **Data integrity:** Your database is in one place. You don’t have to worry about a user’s local `SQLite` file getting corrupted, deleted, or out of sync with your server.
*   **Onboarding:** There is no friction. A link works.
*   **Security:** You control the environment. You don’t have to worry about a user running an old, vulnerable version of your app on a machine that hasn’t been patched in years.

The desktop version only wins if your product requires:

*   **Local file system access:** If your tool processes large local video files, drives, or specific hardware that a browser sandbox restricts.
*   **Offline reliability:** If your users are in environments with unreliable internet and your app is critical to their workflow (like a point-of-sale system or a field survey tool).
*   **Performance on heavy local computation:** If your software runs complex local AI models or simulations that are too slow to send to a cloud server.

If your product is a SaaS-style tool—dashboards, project management, customer communication, content management—the desktop version is legacy weight. It creates support tickets ("I can’t install it on my Mac") and fragments your user base.

The only reason to keep it is inertia: you’ve already built it, and users are used to it. That is not a business reason. That is a comfort zone.

Unless you have one of the three technical necessities above, stop updating the desktop version. Announce that the web version is the future. Let the desktop version rot gracefully.

prompt: You run an accelerator that picks companies after a short interview. Why do funding rounds take months to close, and does it really have to be that way?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
A short interview can tell you whether a founder is sharp, coachable, and likely to execute. It cannot tell you whether the business will survive the next 18 months. A funding round is not just a selection event; it is a transfer of a large, illiquid sum into a company with incomplete information and new control rights. The months are mostly the time needed to turn a good impression into a defensible bet.

There are three separate delays in a round: deciding, negotiating, and paying. The decision phase is diligence. The negotiating phase is terms, valuation, board seats, pro rata rights, information rights, drag-along, liquidation preference, and the legal documents that put all of that into enforceable form. The paying phase is signatures, board approvals, wire transfers, and sometimes tranched closings. People say “the round took four months” when really it was three different processes stacked together.

Diligence is real, even at early stage. Suppose a founder has 40 customers, $15,000 of monthly revenue, and a strong demo. Your interview can tell you if the founder will listen. It cannot tell you whether two of those customers are friends of the founder, whether the code lives in one person’s laptop, whether the cap table has an old angel with a 3x liquidation preference, or whether the main client can cancel in 30 days. A $2,000,000 investor needs those answers because the downside is large and the position will be held for years. The accelerator can afford to be wrong in a way the venture fund often cannot: the accelerator’s check is smaller, the batch provides immediate feedback, and the accelerator does not usually take the kind of control rights that make a bad round painful to manage.

Then there is the investor’s internal life. A fund is not one person making a decision. A partner may like the company, but the fund may need investment committee approval, a check against its allocation, a conversation about whether it is too concentrated in that sector, and a legal review of the documents. That is bureaucracy, but it is also the mechanism by which a fund avoids one partner’s enthusiasm becoming the fund’s bad quarter. The delay is not always stupidity. Sometimes it is the price of having a group make a large irreversible bet.

The negotiation phase is where months become easiest to see and hardest to justify. A lead investor sets terms, but the syndicate is not a clone of the lead. One investor may want a side letter. Another may have different outside counsel. The founder may be comparing two leads. The company may be trying to create a competitive process without signaling weakness. The lawyers work in batches. The founders are running the company and answering diligence questions between product meetings. Every party has a reason to wait a little longer.

Timing matters too. Startups are noisy. Revenue can jump in a quarter and fall in the next. Churn can look stable for two months and then reveal a problem. A founder may wait for one more cohort of customers, one more renewal, one more product metric. An investor may wait to avoid being the only one who believes the story. A round that drags becomes a signal: if it does not close, something may be wrong. That can be rational, but it can also become a self-fulfilling tax on uncertainty.

Does it have to take months? For a pre-seed or seed round, usually no. A fast round is possible when the company has a data room ready before it starts talking, when the investor is comfortable making small checks, when the terms are standard, when the process is run with a deadline, and when someone is willing to be the lead. A 30-day seed process is not fantasy: identify 10 to 15 plausible investors, give them the same materials, let them ask questions in parallel, get term sheets inside 10 days, use standard documents, and close in three to five weeks. Accelerators are good at this partly because they have already done the first screen and created the deadline.

But speed has a cost. If the process is too fast, investors may pay too much, miss a legal problem, or accept terms they later regret. If the founder is rushed, the company may take a lead whose money is not as good as it looked. Convertible instruments can remove pricing from the early step, but they do not remove diligence; they mostly postpone the hard conversation. For a $30,000,000 growth round, months are more defensible because the check is bigger, the board matters more, the documents are more complex, and the investor may need to understand the business model, contract structure, and integration risk in more depth.

The hardest objection to the whole thing is that a lot of round time is not discovery. It is commitment management. Investors need to feel they chose the company rather than were forced into it. Founders need to feel they had options. The process gives both sides cover. That cover is useful in a small way: it reduces regret and gives time for red flags to surface. But when it becomes ritual, it is just expensive waiting.

So the answer is not that rounds should be fast because accelerators are fast. They should be as fast as the risk can be verified. For early-stage companies, that is usually weeks, not months. For later-stage companies, it may be longer. The useful question is not whether the round is slow, but whether the time is being spent learning or merely waiting.
rejected:
You are running an accelerator, which means you have already solved the hardest problem: you have validated the founder and the product. You are handing over a check, not a thesis. Yet the money still takes 45 to 90 days to hit the bank account.

The delay is not about diligence. It is about bureaucracy and leverage.

**The Bureaucracy**
When a VC fund writes a check, they are spending other people’s money. That triggers a cascade of internal friction that has nothing to do with the startup’s quality.
*   **The IC Process:** The partner who likes the deal has to present it to the Investment Committee. They need a slide deck. They need to anticipate questions from partners who were not in the room during the interview.
*   **Legal Drafting:** The term sheet is signed in days, but the definitive agreement (the Stock Purchase Agreement) is a negotiation. The VC’s lawyers want specific indemnities, reps, and warranties. The startup’s lawyers (or the founder, if they are saving on legal fees) push back. Every redline adds a week.
*   **The Check:** Finally, the money is wired. It takes a few days to clear.

**The Leverage**
This is the part that feels personal. VCs know that a startup cannot function without cash. They know that if they drag their feet, the founder will accept worse terms.

A founder with six months of runway has zero leverage. A founder with two months of runway is desperate. If the VC knows you are desperate, they will slow down the process. They will ask for "more diligence" even though you just showed them the data. They will leave you on read for three days. They know that in those three days, your anxiety will make you agree to a lower valuation or a more restrictive board seat.

**Does it have to be that way?**

No. But it only changes if the structure changes.

The acceleration model works because it compresses the timeline. Y Combinator, Techstars, and others do this by standardizing the deal.
1.  **Standard Terms:** They do not negotiate the Stock Purchase Agreement. You take the standard SAFE or the standard term sheet, or you don't get in.
2.  **Small Checks:** The check is small enough that the IC process is trivial. The risk is below the threshold that requires a committee.
3.  **Speed as a Feature:** They treat speed as a competitive advantage. If you can get the founder to work on the product in 10 days, you save them money. You save yourself money.

For a large VC fund doing a $5 million Series A, the bureaucracy is a feature, not a bug. It is a control mechanism to prevent partners from making emotional mistakes with large sums of capital. You cannot remove it without removing the accountability.

But for a seed or pre-seed check? The delay is pure friction. If you are running an accelerator, you should kill the legal negotiation. Use a standard SAFE. Wire the money the day the term sheet is signed. Make the speed of capital part of the value proposition. The founder doesn't need your diligence; they need your speed.

prompt: people always say 'greed is good' and it makes me cringe. is there any version of that claim that actually makes sense?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The cringe is probably a useful signal. “Greed is good” sounds like someone announcing that taking from you is a civic virtue. That version does not make sense. But if you translate the phrase from moral praise into a claim about institutions, something survives: people will work, take risks, and pay attention to other people’s needs when they can profit from doing so, and systems that ignore that fact often become brittle, corrupt, or inefficient.

The first move is to separate “greed” from “self-interest.” Greed usually means wanting more without a stable limit. Self-interest is broader: a person wants to feed their children, keep a job, pay for medical care, avoid humiliation, build something they are proud of. The slogan collapses these. A parent working two jobs is not the same moral creature as a financier who engineers a bonus for destroying value. But both are acting on their own interests. The defensible claim is not that insatiable greed is admirable; it is that ordinary self-interest, under the right rules, can be directed toward useful ends.

Adam Smith’s famous point about the butcher, the brewer, and the baker was not that greed is noble. It was that you get dinner not because they love you, but because they understand that serving you serves them. That is a modest and important observation. Human beings are not angels. If a system depends on everyone doing the right thing for strangers out of pure goodwill, it will usually fail. People need reasons. Profit is one reason. So are wages, reputation, fear of punishment, pride, and love. The mistake is to assume that only the last four count, or that profit is the only reliable one.

A concrete case helps. Suppose a city needs groceries at 7 p.m. on a Friday. You could rely on the grocer’s love of community. Sometimes that exists. But the more dependable explanation for the stocked shelves, the open register, and the person restocking the cereal aisle is that the store wants revenue, the workers want pay, and the customers want convenience. The profit motive makes the store count costs, notice what people buy, and adjust when tastes change. If a new neighborhood appears, or if half the customers start buying different products, the store has a reason to find out. A system organized purely around benevolence lacks that feedback loop.

But the mechanism is not greed. It is competition. If many sellers want your money, they must serve you to get it. If one seller has power, the same self-interest turns into extraction. Imagine a town with one bus line. If the real cost of a ride is two dollars and the company can charge ten without losing all its riders, it may do so. Passengers have no alternative. Now imagine three bus lines competing for the same riders. The price is pushed down, service quality matters more, and the company has a stronger reason to listen to complaints. The underlying human motive—wanting revenue—has not changed. The institutional arrangement has.

That is why the slogan fails when it leaves out the conditions. “Greed is good” only sounds plausible when the greedy actor is also constrained: by rivals, by law, by reputation, by the need to repeat the transaction. Without those constraints, greed is just predation with better branding. A company that pollutes a river because cleanup is expensive is not doing the public a favor by maximizing profit. A lender that hides terms from borrowers may make money once, but if the market learns what it does, it becomes harder to do business. A monopoly that raises prices and lowers quality is not “serving demand”; it is taxing the people who cannot leave.

There is also the question of externalities, which is the technical name for costs that someone else bears. A factory may profit by dumping sludge into a creek instead of treating waste. The profit is real, but it is partly made from other people’s health, fishing, and property. The market transaction looks efficient from the factory’s ledger and catastrophic from the town’s. The sensible response is not to pretend greed is virtuous. It is to make the factory pay for the damage, enforce property rights, or regulate the harm. The profit motive can then work again, but only after the costs have been put where the decision-maker can see them.

Sometimes the high price that feels greedy is actually doing useful work. In a snowstorm, taxi fares may surge. That is easy to hate, especially if you are stranded. But if the fare stayed normal while demand spiked, many drivers would stay home, because the risk and effort would not be compensated. The high price is what calls cars onto the roads. It allocates scarce vehicles to the people who most need them at that moment. The policy lesson is not “greed is good.” It is that if you suppress a price signal, you need another way to allocate scarcity; otherwise you get queues, favoritism, or no supply at all.

As advice to an individual, though, “greed is good” is usually bad. Most valuable relationships are repeated games. A greedy partner, employer, supplier, or friend may win a few exchanges, but they become expensive to deal with. Trust is a form of capital. People pay less, cooperate more, and reveal more information when they believe the other side is not trying to skin them. A firm known for sharp practice often finds that good employees leave, customers defect, and investors demand a discount. The greedy move can pay in a one-shot encounter. In a long life, it often raises the price of everything.

The hardest objection is not that greed can lead to bad outcomes. That is obvious. The harder point is that if the defensible version is really just “incentives matter,” then “greed is good” is still the wrong sentence. It moralizes a structural fact. It turns a warning about human nature into a license for selfishness. It also underestimates the amount of good that comes from non-greedy motives: teachers who stay late, engineers who care about quality, parents who sacrifice, neighbors who help after a disaster. Those things do not fit neatly into a profit-and-loss statement, but they are not irrelevant to how well a society works.

So the claim can be saved only by shrinking it. In a competitive market with enforceable contracts, honest information, and rules that make people internalize the harms they cause, the pursuit of profit is often a powerful way to get people to do things that benefit others. They must anticipate needs, control waste, take responsibility for quality, and bear the consequences of failure. That is genuinely valuable. But it is not a reason to praise greed as a character trait. It is a reason to design institutions that can use self-interest without being ruled by it. Your cringe is the right response to the boast. The underlying idea survives if you stop calling it a virtue and start treating it as a force to be channeled.
rejected:
The phrase "greed is good" is a misquote that captures the spirit of the 1990s but misses the economic argument entirely. The actual defense of self-interest in classical liberalism is not that greed is a virtue, but that it is a predictable force that, when channeled through competitive markets and the rule of law, produces outcomes that benefit the many.

Adam Smith didn’t say greed is good. He said that a butcher provides us with dinner not out of benevolence, but out of self-interest. This is a descriptive claim, not a prescriptive one. It observes that humans are motivated by self-interest, and therefore, institutions should be designed to harness that motivation rather than fight it.

If you try to suppress self-interest through central planning, you don’t eliminate it; you just give it different, usually less productive, outlets. A corrupt official seeking personal enrichment will enrich themselves by extracting rent from businesses rather than by innovating products. A competitive entrepreneur seeking personal enrichment enriches themselves by making things cheaper or better. The difference is the incentive structure.

So, the version of the claim that makes sense is: **In a system with property rights and competition, individual pursuit of profit is a more efficient engine for wealth creation than top-down allocation.**

This doesn’t mean individuals should be greedy. It means that a society benefits from allowing individuals to be self-interested, provided those interests are aligned with creating value for others. If your only way to get rich is to trick someone, the market eventually punishes you by taking your business away. If your way to get rich is to solve a problem, the market rewards you by giving you customers.

The cringe comes from conflating the *mechanism* with the *moral*. We don’t say "the rain is good" because it waters crops; we say the rain is effective. Self-interest is a force. Markets are the irrigation system.

prompt: We're an early-stage startup and I honestly don't know what number we should be tracking or what 'good' looks like. How should we think about growth?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Track the number that tells you whether your next user is worth acquiring. If you are too early to know that, track the number that tells you whether the product is being used enough to become worth acquiring. That distinction matters because early-stage teams often pick a number that feels exciting, not a number that forces a decision.

Growth is not a single dial. It is a loop: someone discovers you, tries you, gets value, comes back, pays or tells someone else. If the loop is broken, the number that looks best will mislead you. A paid campaign can make signups grow while retention dies. A referral program can make invites grow while conversion dies. A founder can personally onboard 20 customers and make revenue look real while the process cannot scale. The useful metric is not the biggest number. It is the number at the weakest link.

Ask where users stop. If most people stop before doing the core action, track activation. If they do the core action but do not return, track retention. If they return but do not pay, track willingness to pay. If they pay but do not stay, track churn. If they stay but you cannot find more of them, track acquisition. Pick the first broken link, not the one that makes the dashboard look impressive.

For most early-stage products, the first number is not growth rate. It is cohort retention: of the users who arrived in week one, how many are still using the product in week two, week five, and week thirteen? Total users can hide a terrible business. If you start with 1,000 users and lose 500 a month, adding 600 new users makes the total grow, but the business is not compounding. Cohorts show whether the new water is staying in the bucket. If you can get 1,000 signups but only 50 are active after 30 days, the next 10,000 signups will produce 500 actives. That is not a growth engine. It is a churn machine.

If you are pre-revenue, the best early proxy for retention is activation. Define the action that means the user got real value. For a resume tool, it might be exporting a finished resume. For a habit app, it might be completing three habits. For a B2B project tool, it might be inviting a teammate or creating a project with actual content. Track the percentage of new users who do that action in the first session or first week. The exact percentage depends on the product, but the logic does not: if only a tiny slice of users reach value, you have a product or onboarding problem before you have a distribution problem. If 10% activate and 5% of those users come back next week, spending money on acquisition will mostly buy you a larger leak. If 50% activate and a meaningful share return without being nagged, you have something worth distributing.

Once retention exists, track the source of new users. The number I would watch closely is the fraction of new users who come from existing users: referrals, shared links, invites, word of mouth, community. If it is zero, you are renting every user. If it rises from 0% to 10% to 25%, the product is becoming easier to grow. This is often the earliest clean signal of product-market fit: not that people say they like it, but that their behavior brings others in.

If you are monetized, add the money number. The most useful one is CAC payback, not raw CAC. CAC payback tells you how many months of customer contribution it takes to recover the cost of acquiring that customer. Suppose a customer pays $100 per month and costs $20 per month to serve. Contribution is $80. If CAC is $800, payback is 10 months, before accounting for the fact that some customers will churn before you get paid back. If churn is 5% per month, the average customer lifetime is roughly 20 months, so 10-month payback is plausible but not luxurious. If CAC is $2,000, payback is 25 months, and you are financing growth with customers who may leave before you break even. This is why “our CAC is $300” is not an answer. It becomes an answer only when paired with contribution margin, churn, and expansion.

The other money number is net revenue retention by cohort. It asks whether existing customers are a stable base, a shrinking base, or an expanding base. If a cohort starts with $10,000 of monthly revenue and three months later produces $9,000 after churn and contraction, net revenue retention is 90%. That is a leak. If it produces $11,000, retention is 110%, and the business can grow from the base even before new sales. For early B2B software, I would be uncomfortable below 100% for long. Around 100 to 110% is healthy. Above 120% is strong, though category and pricing model matter.

The right metric changes with the model. If you are a marketplace, do not track total users as the main number. Track liquidity on the scarce side: the percentage of listings that receive a valid inquiry in seven days, the percentage of buyers who find what they want in the first session, the percentage of supply that transacts in a month. If you have 10,000 consumers and 50 drivers in a city, consumer growth may make the experience worse, not better. If you have 1,000 drivers and no demand, adding more drivers increases costs and disappointment. The growth problem is not “more users.” It is making one side useful enough that the other side stays.

If you are sales-led B2B, the early number is often not signups but conversion. Track meetings to opportunities, opportunities to pilots, pilots to paid contracts. If 50 qualified conversations produce one close, the problem may be product-market fit, pricing, buyer selection, or sales motion, not marketing. More meetings will not fix a broken close. If the close rate improves as you narrow the ideal customer profile, that is a strong signal you are finding the segment for whom the problem is urgent.

If you are consumer, track frequency and return, not just installs. A user who opens the app once is not a customer. Track day-one, day-seven, and day-thirty return, and sessions per week among retained users. The exact benchmarks vary wildly by category, but the pattern is the test: does a cohort settle into a habit, or does it decay to zero? If day-seven retention is low, a paid install campaign is just buying a larger graveyard.

What “good” looks like is less about a universal threshold and more about the shape of the curve. Bad growth is when every new user requires more founder effort: more personal onboarding, more manual support, more targeted outreach, more custom work. Good growth is when the time to go from 100 to 200 activated users falls while your hours per user fall. Bad growth is when retention is flat and you are buying your way upward. Good growth is when retention improves as you refine the audience and the first-run experience. Bad growth is when CAC falls only because you are reaching less qualified users. Good growth is when CAC is stable or rising while retention, contribution margin, or expansion improves.

A number is good when it makes the business more self-reinforcing. If you can predict next month’s active users from this month’s, you have some structure. If you can price an ad channel because you know what a retained customer is worth, you have leverage. If you can hire a marketer or salesperson because the process already works, you have a machine. If the metric only moves when you personally push it, you have a job, not a growth engine.

One caution: early numbers are noisy. With small cohorts, one or two users can move a percentage wildly. Do not make major decisions from a single week. Use four-week rolling cohorts, compare similar stages of the user journey, and treat the line as a direction until the sample gets bigger. If 3% of 200 users refer a friend, that is interesting, not truth. If 30% of 3,000 users return after 30 days, that is more likely real.

The hardest objection is that investors, founders, and momentum all point to growth rate, and retention feels slow. That is true, but growth rate can be a warning sign in disguise. Fifty percent monthly growth sounds great until you learn that 70% of users churn in the first month. The number is not growth. The number is growth that survives. A slower rate with improving retention and organic pull is usually more valuable than a fast rate that requires constant fuel.

For the next 30 days, build one simple table: cohort, new users, activated, active next week, active next month, paid, referred. Define activation concretely. Pick the first column where the percentage is too low. Make that your main metric until it improves. If you cannot instrument it, you are not ready to optimize it. If you can instrument it and it is bad, resist the urge to scale acquisition. Fix the link first.
rejected:
At the early stage, you are not optimizing for growth yet. You are optimizing for learning speed. The only metric that matters right now is the rate at which you are testing hypotheses about your customer.

Most early-stage founders make two errors. They pick a vanity metric (total downloads, website visits) because it feels good to watch the number go up, or they pick a bottom-line metric (revenue, churn) because they are terrified of dying. Both are useless for decision-making. Total downloads doesn't tell you if anyone wants to pay. Revenue is too noisy and slow to move to guide your weekly product changes.

You need a metric that is a direct proxy for value. This is often called the "North Star" metric, but it should be a specific, singular action that represents the moment a user gets value from your product.

Identify the "Aha!" moment.
*   If you are a project management tool, it is not "sign up." It is "created a board with three tasks."
*   If you are a dating app, it is not "downloaded." It is "exchanged five messages with a match."
*   If you are a B2B sales tool, it is not "tried the demo." It is "imported a contact list."

Once you have this action, you track two things:
1.  **Activation Rate:** What percentage of new users perform this action? If it is low, your onboarding is broken.
2.  **Time to Value:** How long does it take them to get there? If it takes three days, you are losing them before they realize you are useful.

"Good" looks like a steep upward curve in activation rate over a short period of weeks. You are not looking for a high absolute number. You are looking for a slope. If you change your landing page, your onboarding flow, or your product core, and the activation rate jumps from 10% to 20%, you have found a lever. That is a win.

Do not look at retention yet. You cannot retain people who don't know why they signed up. Do not look at paid acquisition. You cannot scale a leaky bucket. Do not look at revenue until you have at least 50-100 users who have hit that "Aha!" moment.

If you are struggling to find the "Aha!" action, you do not have a product yet. You have a feature. Go talk to users. Ask them what problem they are trying to solve and what specific outcome would make them feel the problem is solved. That outcome is your metric.

Growth is a byproduct of solving a real problem for a specific group of people. If you are not growing, you are not solving a real problem, or you are not talking to the right people. Fix the product-market fit first. The growth metrics will take care of themselves once the product is good enough that users tell their friends.

prompt: Two senior people on our open source project keep arguing about whether a section of the docs is clear. Each thinks their rewrite is better. How do you actually settle that kind of thing?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
You settle it by turning the argument into a small experiment, because “clear” is not a property of prose. It is a relation between prose and a particular reader trying to do a particular thing.

First write one sentence about what the section is supposed to accomplish. Not “explain the feature,” but something like: “After reading this, a new user can enable retries with three attempts and one-second backoff,” or “After reading this, a maintainer can tell whether a failing test is caused by the cache or by the network layer.” If the two rewrites serve different versions of that sentence, the real disagreement is about audience or scope, and that should be decided first. A section in a quickstart should not be judged by the standards of a reference page.

Then test the two versions against that sentence with a few plausible readers. Do not ask them, “Which one is clearer?” People will hedge, split the difference, or praise the one written by the more senior person. Instead, give them a task. For a how-to section, ask them to do the thing. For a conceptual section, ask them to predict what happens in two or three cases. Record what they ask, where they get stuck, and what they get wrong. Three or five people is not enough to rank subtle differences in style, but it is often enough to show that one version consistently produces the wrong command, the wrong mental model, or the same confused question.

If you cannot recruit real readers, do the next best thing. Have each author write down the specific failure mode of the other’s version: “This wording makes people think the flag is optional,” “This example hides the default value,” “This uses a term we define three pages later.” Then have a third person, preferably not one of the two authors, check those claims against the text and, if possible, against one or two outside readers. This forces the argument to move from taste to consequences.

If both versions pass the test, stop trying to decide which is more beautiful. Choose the one that is easier to maintain: shorter, consistent with the terminology already used in the docs, less dependent on a private metaphor, and less likely to break when the feature changes. If both versions fail, the answer is not to pick the lesser evil; it is to rewrite both, because the section is probably missing an example, an assumption, or a distinction that neither author noticed.

The hard case is when the only available judges are the maintainers themselves, and they already know the system. Then their judgment is biased, because they can fill gaps that a newcomer cannot. In that situation, agree on a tie-breaker before looking at the prose: clarity for new contributors, consistency with the CLI, fewer moving parts, or fit with the surrounding pages. Ship the result with a short note in the issue: what was tested, what was unknown, and what evidence should reopen the decision. A documented, reversible decision is usually better than a long debate over two competent paragraphs.
rejected:
Stop asking which one is "better." "Better" is subjective and invites ego. Instead, ask which one achieves the goal with less friction.

The goal of documentation is not to be liked; it is to prevent the user from getting stuck. You settle this by measuring the result, not the prose.

**The Usability Test**

Find three people who have not seen the code in weeks. Give them the specific task that the documentation section describes. Do not let them ask you questions. Let them struggle.

Watch where they get stuck.
*   If they miss a step, the docs missed a step.
*   If they use the wrong command, the docs buried the right command.
*   If they give up, the docs failed.

Run this test on both rewrites. The version where people succeed faster and with fewer confusions is the winner. It does not matter if that version uses passive voice or awkward phrasing. If it works, it is correct.

**The "Five-Second Rule" for Complexity**

If the task is simple, the documentation should be skimmable. If the task is complex, the documentation should be linear and step-by-step.

Senior engineers often write documentation for other senior engineers. They skip obvious steps because they have internalized the mental model. The junior user does not have that model. If your senior contributor says, "They should know that," they are wrong. They do not know that. If the doc requires the reader to infer context, it is a failure.

**The Tie-Breaker: Maintenance Cost**

If both versions pass the usability test with similar scores, pick the one that is cheaper to update.

Documentation that is tightly coupled to specific UI labels or variable names will rot. Documentation that describes intent and flow will survive. If one rewrite is a literal transcript of the error messages and the other explains *why* the error happens, choose the second one. It will still be true when you change the error message string next quarter.

**The Decision**

Show the test results to the two senior contributors. Say, "Version A had two failures; Version B had none. We are using B."

If they still argue, it is because they are not arguing about the docs. They are arguing about who is right. In that case, the project lead makes the call based on the data, and the discussion ends. Code and docs are tools. If a tool breaks the user, it is broken, regardless of how elegant the handle is.

prompt: I just found out there are already a few companies doing basically what I want to build. Am I too late? Should I drop the idea?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
No—finding a few competitors is not the same as being too late. It is the first useful piece of information. The question is no longer whether the idea exists; it is whether you can win a specific slice of it.

I don’t know what you are building, so I can’t tell you whether the market is full. But the existence of a few companies does not decide it by itself.

If nobody is doing it, that can mean you are early, or it can mean the job is not important enough for people to pay for. A few companies is often a better sign: someone has already shown that customers will pay, but the market has not been sorted out.
