When you ask a successful founder, "Should I quit my job?" they are answering, "Should I have quit my job?" Their answer is retrospective. They are looking at the outcome, not the decision. If they succeeded, they tell you to jump. If they failed, they tell you to be careful. Neither tells you what to do.

Furthermore, they are projecting their own risk tolerance onto you. The person who thrived on 40 hours a week of sleep deprivation in their twenties is not you. The person who had a safety net of family money is not you. Their "advice" is a biography, not a strategy.

You are also asking for a yes/no answer to a spectrum question. The binary of "employee" vs. "founder" is a false dilemma. You can build a business while keeping your day job. You can leave to work for another company. You can start a side project that never becomes a company.

The only advice that matters is the one you can verify yourself.

Stop asking for permission. Start building.

Spend the next three months building the product or service after hours. Do not quit. Do not incorporate. Do not buy a logo. Just make the thing and try to get one stranger to pay you for it.

If you can’t get one person to pay you, the answer is no. You don’t need a business; you need a better job or a different hobby.

If you do get one person to pay you, you have data. Now the question shifts from "Should I?" to "How much?"

How much revenue can this generate in six months? How much time does it take? What is my current salary?

If the revenue trajectory, adjusted for time, beats your salary, you can quit. If it doesn’t, you keep working, you keep building, and you ignore the people who tell you to leap.

prompt: Do you ever notice how your friend group doesn't look like the general population at all, even though you never chose it that way?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I don’t have a friend group, but the thing you’re describing is one of the clearest ways to see how social life gets organized. A person’s close friends rarely resemble a random sample of the people around them, let alone the national population. The obvious reason is that you meet people where you already are: school, workplace, neighborhood, gym, parent group, online community. Those places are already sorted by age, income, education, language, and life stage. A graduate student in Chicago, a line cook in Tucson, a new parent in a suburb, and a retiree in a small town are drawing from four different pools. The national census is not the relevant pool; the relevant pool is the set of people whose schedules and locations intersect with yours often enough for friendship to form.

The less obvious filtering happens after the first meeting. Friendship is expensive in time. It requires repeated, unforced contact, similar rhythms, and enough mutual interest to keep showing up. A group that meets after work in a certain neighborhood, goes to certain events, or travels on certain weekends will drift toward people who can absorb that time and cost. It will also drift toward people who find the conversation easy. That ease often tracks shared class, education, and assumptions, not just personality. So a friend group can become self-renewing: existing members bring in newcomers who are somewhat like them, and the group’s habits make it harder for outsiders to enter.

When you say “look,” the visible part is the easiest to see: age, bodies, clothes, race, the whole surface. But the same sorting is in the invisible part too—what people assume, how they spend money, what they find funny, what they consider a normal week. A group of friends may look similar because they were produced by similar conditions, and then they begin to think and behave similar because they keep spending unforced time together.

The “never chose it” part is both right and misleading. You did not choose a demographic profile. Nobody sits down and decides the age range, racial mix, income level, and political temperature of their close circle. But you did choose, or were placed in, the institutions that produce the profile: where to live, what job to take, whether to have kids, which hobby to pursue, which arguments to have, which friendships to keep investing in. Those choices are small and local, but they add up. If you move to a city, join a professional field, and spend Saturdays at a climbing gym, you have not selected a type of friend, but you have selected a type of life, and the friends arrive with it.

Sometimes the mismatch with the general population is just arithmetic. The general population includes children, very old people, people with disabilities, people in occupations you will never enter, and people living in places you will never visit. A group of thirty-something urban professionals is not supposed to look like that. The more striking case is when the friend group does not even resemble the local adult population. That is where the sorting shows up: in a diverse city, your close circle may still be narrow; in a small town, it may look like the town but not like the country. In both cases, the circle is a slice of a slice.

There is a harder question underneath: if the group is not chosen, is it accidental? Not entirely. Accidents bring people into the room; maintenance decides who stays. You can meet a wide range of people by chance, but you will keep close only those with whom contact is easy and rewarding. That is why friend groups often feel inevitable in retrospect. They look like a portrait of you, but they are also a portrait of the logistics of your life: the commute, the salary, the neighborhood, the hours, the institutions, and the small daily decisions about who gets called back.
rejected:
You didn’t choose your friend group. You just showed up in the same place at the same time.

This is a sampling bias so severe it distorts reality. You are not a random cross-section of humanity; you are a cluster of people who survived specific filters.

Consider the filters:

*   **Geography:** You live in a specific neighborhood or attend a specific school. This immediately excludes 99.9% of the global population based on where they were born or where they can afford to live.
*   **Timing:** You are friends with people whose life stages align with yours. Your college classmates are 25. Your coworkers are 30–40. You are rarely friends with people who are 70, because they are not in the rooms you occupy daily.
*   **Survivorship:** To be your friend, a person had to pass the initial social friction of meeting you. This requires a baseline level of sociability, confidence, or shared interest that is not universal. Many people in the general population are isolated, introverted, or simply do not have the energy for the small talk that precedes friendship.
*   **Taste:** You bond over music, hobbies, or values. If you like jazz, your friend group is skewed toward people who like jazz. If you are a parent of young children, your friend group is skewed toward people with young children.

The result is a group that feels like a representative sample of the world, but is actually a narrow slice.

This creates a dangerous illusion of normalcy. If your friends are all affluent, you assume most people are affluent. If your friends are all married, you assume most people are married. If your friends are all of one ethnicity or political leaning, you assume that is the default human condition.

You don’t see the general population because you are not in their orbit. You are in a bubble, and the bubble is made of people who happen to be on the same path as you.

The only way to see the general population is to leave the group. To travel to a different region. To join a different profession. To age into a different life stage. Until then, your social circle is not a mirror of society. It is a reflection of your own trajectory.

prompt: I feel completely unmotivated today, nothing seems worth doing. What should I do with a day like this?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The first thing not to do is turn the day into a moral problem. “Nothing seems worth doing” can sound like a verdict on you, but it is usually just a state: low energy, low reward, maybe too much input and too little movement. On a day like this, the goal is not to find meaning. It is to avoid becoming a lump of guilt and scrolling.

Do not try to motivate yourself. Motivation is unreliable, especially when you are already depleted. Instead, lower the task until it is almost absurdly small. Not “clean the kitchen,” but put one cup in the dishwasher. Not “get in shape,” but put on shoes. Not “have a productive day,” but sit up and drink water. The point is not the task. The point is to interrupt the loop where your body stays still and your mind keeps judging you for it.

Pick one physical change first. Get out of bed if you are in it. Open a window. Wash your face. Make tea, even if you do not drink it. Walk to the end of the street and back. These are not fixes. They are levers. They do not require you to feel like anything. They only require a small amount of movement, and movement can loosen the stuckness enough for the next choice to feel possible.

If you have obligations, do the minimum version. Reply to the message with one sentence. Do the smallest part of the work. Eat something bland but real. Take the medication if that is part of your life. Keep the floor under you. A bad day does not need to become a collapsed day.

Be careful with rest, though. Rest is useful when it actually restores you. Rumination is not rest. Lying there feeling worthless while the hours pass is not recovery; it is just suffering with the lights off. If you decide to rest, give it a shape. “I will lie down for forty minutes, then I will wash my face and make lunch.” Rest without a return time often becomes the whole day, and the whole day becomes heavier.

Also, do not make big decisions today. Do not quit, confess, rearrange your life, or decide that everything you have been doing is pointless. Low states distort judgment. They make the familiar feel dead and the dramatic feel clear. Let the day stay small.

If this is a one-day dip, the above may be enough. But if “nothing seems worth doing” is your weather for weeks, or if it comes with hopelessness, numbness, sleep problems, or thoughts that you would be better off gone, that is not a discipline issue. That is a signal to get help: a doctor, therapist, someone you trust, a crisis line if you feel unsafe. You do not have to white-knuckle a depressive state into evidence that you are fine.

For the next hour, do not ask whether life is worth doing. Ask only: what is the smallest physical action that would make the next ten minutes slightly less stuck? Do that. Then ask again.
rejected:
When the engine is off, do not try to force it to start. The desire to do meaningful work is a result of action, not a prerequisite. If you wait for motivation to arrive, it likely won't.

The goal of an unmotivated day is not productivity. It is preservation.

Your job is to keep the baseline intact so that tomorrow’s you isn’t worse off than today’s you. This means three things:

1.  **Maintain hygiene.** Shower. Brush your teeth. Change into clothes that aren’t pajamas. This signals to your nervous system that you are still in the world, even if you are not participating in it.
2.  **Eat real food.** Do not rely on snacks. Sit down and eat a meal. Dehydration and low blood sugar masquerade as existential dread.
3.  **Do one small, non-negotiable task.** Pick the smallest thing on your list that takes less than ten minutes. Make the bed. Reply to one email. Wash one dish. Completion generates a tiny hit of dopamine. It breaks the inertia without demanding effort.

After that, rest. Guilt-free. Watch a movie. Walk outside. Sleep. There is no moral failing in taking a day to recalibrate. The only failure is letting the day drag on into a week of stagnation because you spent it punishing yourself for not being productive.

If this state persists for more than two weeks, or if it is accompanied by a loss of interest in things you usually enjoy, it is no longer a bad day. It is a symptom. See a doctor.

prompt: Polls say a huge share of Americans would give a kidney to a stranger, yet almost nobody actually does. Why is the gap so enormous? Is everyone just lying?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
No, not in the simple sense. Some people are giving the answer that makes them look good, even to themselves. But most are not sitting there calculating a lie. They are answering a different question from the one the act actually asks.

When a poll asks, “Would you give a kidney to a stranger?” it is not asking, “Will you submit to major surgery, take weeks off work, recover in pain, and live for the rest of your life with one kidney?” It is asking, “Do you see yourself as the kind of person who would do that?” That is a question about identity, not a medical form. A person can sincerely believe they are the kind of person who sacrifices a body part for someone in need, and still not do it when the surgeon calls.

The numbers make the point. In the United States, thousands of living kidney transplants happen every year, but most donors are relatives, partners, friends, or otherwise connected to the recipient. Anonymous, non-directed donation to a stranger is a small sliver of living donation. If a poll suggests that tens of millions of Americans would do it, the actual number of people who make that anonymous leap is a tiny fraction of that pool. That is not a rounding error. It is a different phenomenon.

A little of the gap is social desirability. Saying no to a stranger who might die sounds bad. But social pressure alone does not explain it. People also overstate what they will do in many private, low-stakes contexts: they will exercise more, spend less, give more, be more patient, be braver. The pattern is not usually deception. It is that a survey presents the choice in the best possible light: no pain, no paperwork, no one waiting on you, no calendar, no body.

The real act is full of concrete frictions. Imagine the sequence. You say yes in principle. Months later, a coordinator calls. You need bloodwork. Then imaging. Then a urologist, a cardiologist, maybe a psychosocial interview. You need time off work. You may need to stop certain medications. You may have to discuss your health history with people you do not know. You will be anesthetized, cut into, and sent home with a plan for pain, activity limits, and follow-up visits. Your spouse or partner may be uneasy. Your employer may be vague. Your insurance may cover the donation but not every downstream worry the way you hoped. At each step, the person who answered a survey can say, “I need to think about it,” without being a monster. The poll never asked any of those questions.

There is also the problem of the stranger. Human generosity is much stronger when the recipient is visible. We give more to a named child, a neighbor, a friend, a person whose story we can hold in our heads. Anonymous donation removes the feedback loop. You will not meet the recipient. You will not get a thank-you card, a photo, a story about their recovery. Their life may be transformed, but you may never know the details. Some people are motivated by exactly that: the purity of giving without recognition. But most people are not built that way. We are more likely to act when the good deed returns something—gratitude, pride, social acknowledgment, a relationship. A stranger gives none of that.

The transplant system itself is a filter. To become a non-directed donor, you do not simply click a button. You enter an evaluation process. You must be medically suitable, matched, scheduled, and cleared by multiple professionals. Some people are genuinely unsuitable because of age, health, medications, or other risks. But many others are lost to the sheer weight of the process. The system is not designed as a simple opt-in. It is a funnel, and funnels discard people.

In the United States, there are also practical fears that a poll does not mention. Will an employer treat a kidney donation leave like any other medical leave? Will a complication be fully covered? Will a future job application involve a medical question that makes the missing kidney a problem? Will a family member make it difficult? These worries are not always justified, but they are real. A person can be morally willing and still rationally hesitate when the consequences touch their job, insurance, and household.

The people who actually donate to strangers are also not the average poll respondent. They often have a prior connection to dialysis or kidney disease. They may belong to a religious or community tradition that makes the act feel ordinary rather than heroic. They may have entered a paired exchange, where their donation helps unlock a chain of transplants, giving the act a traceable shape. The poll averages over everyone, including people for whom the idea of giving up an organ is so remote that the yes is almost automatic.

The hardest objection to this explanation is that the system may be suppressing a lot of real willingness. That is partly true. If donor protections were universal, if the process were simpler, if the social and medical infrastructure made the path less frightening, more people would follow through. The current system probably turns away some people who would otherwise donate. But even a frictionless system would not turn half the population into kidney donors. The central barrier is not just bureaucracy. It is that a person is being asked to convert a moral symbol into a body part.

So the gap is not mainly a gap between truth and falsehood. It is a gap between a word and a body. A poll answer is cheap. It costs nothing and commits nothing. It captures a preference under ideal conditions: no pain, no risk, no one watching, no recovery. The act removes those conditions. People are not all lying. They are just answering the easy version of the question.
rejected:
No, they are not lying. They are answering a different question than the one you are asking.

When a pollster asks, "Would you donate a kidney to a stranger?" they are asking about a hypothetical sacrifice. The respondent imagines a noble act: a single, discrete moment of altruism that secures their place in the moral hall of fame. They answer yes because the cost feels distant and the reward feels immediate.

When you look at the actual donation statistics, you are looking at a logistical nightmare. The gap exists because the hypothetical version of donation and the real version of donation are fundamentally different objects.

**The Cost of Information**

In the poll, the "stranger" is an abstraction. You are saving a life. In reality, saving a life requires navigating a bureaucratic maze. You have to find a specific recipient, verify compatibility, and convince a hospital to accept a living donor from a different city or country.

Most people do not have the time or energy to hunt for a specific kidney. They are willing to give, but they are not willing to search. The system assumes the donor will do the legwork. It does not.

**The Risk Asymmetry**

A kidney is not a dollar bill. You can’t just hand it over and walk away. You undergo surgery. You have a single kidney left. You carry a small but permanent risk of complications, infection, or long-term renal decline.

In the hypothetical, the risk is invisible. In the real world, it is the primary variable. People are not willing to accept even a 1% chance of long-term harm for a stranger whose face they will never see. This is not selfishness; it is rational risk aversion. We accept risks for family and friends because the emotional bond offsets the fear. We do not have that bond with a stranger.

**The Illusion of the Pool**

The poll creates a false sense of supply. If 40% of Americans say they would donate, it sounds like there is a surplus of donors. But because the act is so high-friction, that 40% never materializes. The "huge share" is a phantom supply. It is like asking if people would buy a new car if it were on fire. They will say yes, because the deal is too good to pass up. But when you go to the dealership, you realize the car is in a different state, and you have to drive there yourself, and it’s not actually on fire, it’s just a discount.

**The Solution Isn't Trust**

We don’t need to trust people more. We need to lower the friction.

Organizations like Kidney Exchange have shown that when you remove the search burden, donations skyrocket. They use altruistic "chain reactions" where one volunteer donor starts a cascade of paired exchanges. The donor doesn’t have to find the recipient. They just have to say yes to the surgery.

The gap between the poll and the reality is not a moral failing. It is a design failure. The system asks for a hero but provides only a clerk’s desk. Most people are willing to be heroes, but they are unwilling to be clerks.

prompt: why are corporations so hard to regulate? they always seem to find a loophole
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Corporations are hard to regulate for a boring reason: law is a slow, general technology, and corporations are fast, specific, and resource-rich. A loophole is not usually a magic trick. It is the space left open when a legislature had to write a rule that could be applied to thousands of situations, enforced by courts, and defended against challenges. The more precise the rule, the easier it is to step around it; the vaguer the rule, the harder it is to enforce fairly.

They do not always evade. Many firms comply because the cost of violation, including lost reputation and customer trust, exceeds the gain. But when evasion happens, it happens for structural reasons.

Take tax. If a law taxes profit where the business is managed, a corporation can argue that a decision was made elsewhere. If it taxes income earned in a country, the firm can locate the legal owner of a patent, trademark, or financing arrangement in a lower-tax jurisdiction. In 2016 Apple said it held most of its $252 billion cash hoard abroad and that repatriating it would trigger a large U.S. tax bill. That was not a secret scheme; it was the result of a tax code that distinguished places and legal forms. Sometimes what looks like a loophole is ordinary legal planning: the company is not breaking a rule, it is using the rule’s categories. That makes the conduct harder to condemn and harder to close without rewriting broad policy.

Finance shows the same problem. Before the 2008 crisis, bank capital rules focused heavily on assets on the balance sheet. Banks could move risk into special purpose vehicles, securitizations, and over-the-counter derivatives such as credit default swaps. The economic exposure was real, but the legal packaging made it harder for supervisors to see. Regulators were not blind; they were dealing with instruments whose terms were private, customized, and changing.

Then there is information. A regulator usually learns about a firm through filings, audits, complaints, site visits, and data the firm chooses to report. The firm knows more. It knows which product is failing, which customer segment is being overcharged, which chemical is leaking, which algorithm is making biased decisions. If the harm is visible—smoke, speed, spoiled milk—regulation can work. If the harm is delayed, statistical, or buried in code and contracts, the regulator is partly dependent on the regulated firm’s cooperation.

Enforcement matters too. I would not put a precise number on corporate lobbying, because definitions and years vary, but the scale is billions of dollars annually in the United States alone, before counting in-house lawyers, economists, consultants, and campaign contacts. Agencies are small by comparison. The SEC has a few thousand employees for a market with thousands of reporting companies. A large corporation can spend months on one regulatory issue; an agency may have one team. That does not mean every rule is bought. It means the marginal rule is often shaped by the people who must live with it.

Corporations also understand expected value. Suppose a violation can earn $50 million. If the chance of detection is 10 percent and the average fine is $20 million, the expected cost is $2 million. Even a firm with a genuine compliance culture may accept that risk if the business unit is measured on profit. Fines can be huge and still not eliminate the incentive. BP paid $20.8 billion over the Deepwater Horizon disaster, one of the largest environmental penalties in history, and remained a major global energy company. The penalty punished the event; it did not make every shortcut impossible.

Legal form gives corporations another advantage: they can reorganize. If a subsidiary is fined, the parent may sell it. If a brand is tainted, the firm can rebrand. If a jurisdiction becomes expensive, the firm can move headquarters, incorporation, data storage, or customer contracts. Limited liability means the people who approve the risk usually do not pay the full social cost. The corporation is a machine for separating decision from consequence.

Political economy matters. Regulators need budgets, technical data, and legislative support. Industry can offer all three, or threaten jobs and investment if rules are too strict. The people who leave agencies often go into industry, and industry people often go into agencies. That revolving door is not proof of corruption; it is a labor market for expertise. But it means regulators often share assumptions with the firms they regulate, and rules tend to be written in ways that are administrable, familiar, and defensible.

The hardest objection is that governments should simply make penalties severe enough. Sometimes they do. But severe penalties require proof, and proof is hard. Corporate wrongdoing is often diffuse: a product is approved by engineers, reviewed by lawyers, sold by managers, priced by a committee. To convict, prosecutors must show who knew what and that the law was clear. If lawmakers instead write broad rules against “deceptive” or “reckless” conduct, companies can challenge them as vague, and regulators lose the ability to enforce consistently. The legal system that protects citizens from arbitrary power also protects firms from overreach. That protection is worth having, but it makes perfect regulation impossible.

Regulation works best when the harm is observable, the rule is simple, the regulator has independent data, and the firm cannot easily move. Speed limits, food inspections, emission monitors, and basic accounting rules work reasonably well because violations can be measured and the actor is tied to a place. Regulation struggles with financial risk, data practices, environmental damage that appears decades later, and global platforms that can serve customers from many jurisdictions at once.

So corporations are not hard to regulate because they are uniquely cunning. They are hard to regulate because they are adaptive, well-funded, and organized to persist, while law must be general, public, and constrained. Loopholes are the visible sign of that mismatch. The best regulation does not try to write a rule with no gaps. It tries to make the gaps visible, make the price of crossing them high enough, and keep the regulator from being starved of information by the very firms it is supposed to watch.
rejected:
The premise that corporations are hard to regulate because they are smarter than regulators is only half right. The other half is structural.

Regulation is a lagging indicator. It is a legal response to a past harm. By the time a company’s practices cause enough damage to trigger political will for new laws, the company has usually shifted its business model. The 2008 financial crisis didn’t just reveal bad actors; it revealed that the rules for derivatives were written for a different century. The "loophole" isn’t a clever trick found by a lawyer; it’s the gap between the law’s date of enactment and the date of the market’s innovation.

But even if you could write the law in real-time, you face the problem of scale. A single bank has thousands of products, millions of customers, and operations in dozens of jurisdictions. A regulatory agency has a few hundred staff. The cost of compliance is distributed across a company’s revenue, but the cost of enforcement is concentrated in a government budget. Corporations can afford to hire the best legal minds in the country to interpret a statute’s ambiguity. The government cannot. This creates an arms race where the regulated party always has more resources to test the boundaries of the rule than the regulator has to defend them.

There is also the issue of who writes the rules. In many jurisdictions, regulatory capture is not a bug; it’s a feature. The entities being regulated often provide the technical expertise needed to write the rules. This doesn’t mean they buy the regulators. It means they define the vocabulary. If you can define what constitutes "reasonable diligence," you can ensure that your specific methods are reasonable.

Finally, regulation is often designed to be efficient, not perfect. Strict liability for every potential harm would paralyze business. Laws must leave room for reasonable judgment. That room is where the loopholes live. It’s not that corporations are escaping justice; it’s that the legal system is built on consent and intent, while modern corporate harm is often a byproduct of scale and incentive structures that no individual person intended.

The difficulty isn’t that corporations are clever. It’s that they are large, fast, and funded to push against the slow, under-resourced, and politically constrained machinery of the state.

prompt: I've felt guilty for years about something I did when I was young. How reliable is my memory of it, really, and can I do anything about the past?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Your memory is probably less reliable than its clarity suggests. Memory is not a stored recording; it is rebuilt each time from surviving fragments—emotional tone, partial images, later explanations, current beliefs. People can be led to remember events that never happened, and confidence in the memory is a poor guide to accuracy. A childhood memory has fewer anchors: you were younger, your understanding of motives was thinner, and the event may have been compressed into a scene you have revisited for years. That rehearsal changes the memory. The exact words, the sequence, the degree of blame, the other person’s reaction: these are the parts most likely to be distorted by the guilt itself.

That does not mean the guilt is imaginary. A persistent moral feeling usually has a source, even if the story around it has become inflated. You may have done something smaller than you now imagine, or you may have judged a child’s action by an adult standard. You also have some advantage over an outside witness: you remember your intention, your body’s involvement, and the feeling of the moment. The broad outline may be more trustworthy than the details. The task is to separate layers: what you directly remember, what you infer, what someone else told you, and what you assume because it fits the person you fear you were. The first layer may be thin. The feeling may still be true.

Age matters. A seven-year-old’s shove, a fourteen-year-old’s cruel joke, a teenager’s reckless choice are not the same moral facts as the same acts done by a settled adult. Young people often lack the perspective to foresee harm, the skill to regulate impulse, or the language to repair things on the spot. That does not make their actions harmless. It means the moral weight should be measured with the knowledge and capacities they had then, not with the full hindsight you now possess. If you judge a child by the standards of a person with decades of experience, you will almost always find the child guilty.

What you can do depends on whether there is a living person to whom repair is owed. If there is, ask whether contacting them would serve their needs or yours. An apology can be a genuine attempt to acknowledge harm, but it can also be a way of making yourself feel better while asking the other person to process your past. If you reach out, make it short, take responsibility without excuses, offer something concrete if appropriate, and accept that you may get no answer or a bad one. If the person is vulnerable, if the contact would reopen an injury, or if you cannot be sure it is safe, do not do it. Then make amends in the only available way: by not repeating the pattern, by recognizing it in others, and by giving your attention to the kind of harm you once did.

If there is no identifiable person, or the harm was minor, the work is mostly internal. Decide what you actually regret. Is it that you caused pain, that you were cowardly, that you missed a chance, or that you are ashamed of what the act says about you? Guilt, shame, regret, and anxiety are not the same. Guilt can be corrected by repair. Shame often needs evidence that you are not a fixed bad thing. Regret needs acceptance. Anxiety needs exposure to the fact that you can bear the memory without acting on it. If you can, write the event down as plainly as you can, mark the parts you are unsure of, and ask what a fair-minded person would say about a young person in that situation. If the memory resists that and keeps returning with the force of a command, it may be less a moral question than a wound, and a therapist who works with intrusive memories can help.

The hardest part is that uncertainty remains. You may never know whether the scene is exactly true. But the practical question is not whether you can recover the original file. It is what the memory is doing to you now, and whether your response to it is proportionate. If the remembered act was real, the best use of the guilt is to make the future different. If the remembered act has been exaggerated by years of rehearsal, the best use of the doubt is to stop punishing yourself for a wrong your own mind has embellished.
rejected:
Your memory is likely distorted in ways that serve your current need for self-punishment. Human recall is not a recording; it is a reconstruction. Every time you remember the event, you are not retrieving a file, you are editing it. If you carry guilt, your mind will subtly sharpen the edges of your wrongdoing and blur the context of your youth. You may be remembering the act as a malicious adult, while forgetting that you were a child with limited empathy, information, and impulse control.

The reliability of the memory is low. You cannot separate the original event from the years of ruminating on it. The guilt has become a separate entity that is now generating its own false details to justify its existence.

As for the past, you cannot change it. This is a physical fact, not a philosophical abstraction. What you can change is the story you tell about it. You have two options. First, you can seek out the person you hurt to apologize, but only if doing so serves their healing rather than your absolution. If they are unreachable or if contact would cause them more pain, this is not possible. Second, you can stop treating the memory as evidence of your character. You were a young person who did a bad thing. You are an older person who recognizes that it was bad. The gap between those two states is not a failure; it is growth.

Guilt is useful when it motivates correction. When it only causes suffering without changing behavior, it is just pain. You are paying a debt that has already been settled by the fact that you no longer do these things. Stop paying.

prompt: is there really that much money in US politics? how does it compare to other stuff we spend on
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Yes, but the answer depends on what you mean by “money in politics.”

If you mean the cash that candidates, parties, PACs, Super PACs, and independent groups spend to win federal elections, it is a large private industry. In the 2023–24 federal cycle, campaign spending was roughly $10 billion. That is a lot of money. It pays for consultants, polling, data firms, mailers, television and digital ads, phone banks, fundraising events, and a permanent class of professional political operators.

But if you mean “Is politics a bigger budget line than the rest of government?” the answer is no. Federal campaign spending is a small slice of the federal budget.

A useful set of comparisons:

- Federal campaign spending: about $10 billion in a recent cycle  
- Reported Washington lobbying: about $5 billion a year in recent years  
- State and local election spending: harder to count, but probably several billion dollars in a big cycle  
- Total “political” spending, loosely defined: maybe $15 billion to $25 billion

Now compare that with what the federal government actually spends:

- Total federal budget: about $7 trillion a year  
- Social Security: about $1.4 trillion  
- Medicare: about $900 billion  
- Department of Defense: about $900 billion  
- Interest on the national debt: about $900 billion  
- Food stamps, or SNAP: about $130 billion  
- NASA: about $25 billion  
- National parks: about $4 billion

So a $10 billion federal election is less than one day of federal spending. Even if you add lobbying and state/local races and get to $25 billion, that is still only about a day and a half of federal outlays. It is roughly one or two new aircraft carriers, not a hidden second government.

That is the first thing to keep in mind: the money is real, but it is not the size of the budget.

The second thing is that political money feels bigger than it is because it is not trying to buy goods or services. It is trying to steer decisions that control much larger amounts of money.

That is the strongest objection to the “it’s only $10 billion” point. The reason political spending matters is not that Washington spends $10 billion on politics. It is that $10 billion can influence rules, contracts, tax breaks, regulations, and entitlements worth hundreds of billions or trillions.

Lobbying makes this clear. A major industry may spend a few million or a few hundred million dollars a year on Washington access. That sounds enormous compared with a household budget, but it is tiny compared with the value of the policies it cares about. A pharmaceutical company, a bank, an energy firm, or a tech platform does not need to spend more than its revenue to try to shape the legal environment in which it earns that revenue. A small lobbying budget can be a lever on a much larger economic outcome.

The same is true in elections, though less directly. Campaign money does not usually buy a vote in the way a bribe would. It buys infrastructure: advertising, voter data, ground games, fundraising networks, media presence, and the ability to keep a candidate competitive. In close races, that can matter. In safe races, it mostly matters for maintaining the appearance of a contest and building the donor relationships that continue after the election.

That is why the money seems disproportionate. A Senate race in a competitive state can cost $100 million or more. That is not because the office is worth $100 million in salary. It is because the office can help shape federal policy, appoint judges, control committees, and signal influence to donors, lobbyists, and executives. The price of the race reflects the value of the access and power attached to the seat, not the cost of running the seat.

There is also a difference between election money and policy money. Campaign cash is spent to get people elected. Lobbying cash is spent to influence people after they are elected. The two are linked, but they are not the same thing. A candidate may spend $50 million to win, but the industries that care about that candidate’s vote may spend a fraction of that to maintain relationships with the office once it is occupied.

Where I am less sure is the total amount of political spending outside federal campaigns. State and local elections are not reported with the same clarity. Independent groups, trade associations, corporate political giving, and some nonprofit advocacy spending are harder to track. So the true total is fuzzy. But the order of magnitude is stable: tens of billions, not trillions.

That matters because it changes what the problem is. The problem is not that Americans are paying a huge direct tax called “political spending.” The problem is that a relatively small amount of private money can acquire a lot of leverage over public decisions. It does not need to match the size of the government budget. It only needs to be large enough to buy attention, access, expertise, and persistence.

So the plain answer is: yes, there is a lot of money in U.S. politics by ordinary private-sector standards. But no, it is not comparable to what the government spends on defense, health, retirement, or debt service. Its power comes from asymmetry: a small amount of money aimed at the right decision point can move a much larger amount of public money.
rejected:
The premise that there is "that much" money is true, but the scale is often misapprehended because it is compared against the wrong things.

In the 2020–2021 election cycle, candidates for federal and state offices raised and spent approximately **$14.5 billion**. That is a massive number in human terms. It dwarfs the annual budgets of most countries. It is more than the GDP of Vietnam. It is roughly equivalent to the entire annual budget of the U.S. Department of Energy.

However, when you put that figure in the context of the U.S. economy and government, it is a drop in the bucket.

*   **GDP:** The U.S. economy produces about $25 trillion per year. Political spending is **0.06%** of GDP.
*   **Federal Budget:** The federal government spends about $6 trillion per year. Political spending is **0.2%** of that.
*   **Healthcare:** Americans spend about $4.5 trillion on healthcare. Political spending is about **3%** of what we spend on medical care.
*   **Military:** The U.S. spends about $800 billion on the military. Political spending is **1.8%** of the defense budget.

If you want a visceral comparison: The money raised in a single two-year election cycle is about the same as the U.S. spends on **air traffic control** in a year. Or the cost of **one month** of the National Debt interest payments.

The reason it *feels* like there is an absurd amount of money is not because the absolute number is high relative to the economy, but because the return on investment is impossibly high.

A billionaire who gives $100 million to a political party is not spending 1% of their wealth. They are buying influence over a $25 trillion machine. They are buying access to the people who write the laws that determine their taxes, their regulatory environment, and their legal liability. The cost of entry is low relative to the value of the prize.

The real problem is not that the money is too big. It is that the barriers to entry are too low. Because the cost of a Senate seat is $100 million, but the potential gain from favorable legislation is in the billions, the market is saturated with wealthy actors. The "price" of democracy has become a subscription fee that only the ultra-wealthy can pay.

The comparison that matters is not to GDP, but to **private equity and lobbying**.

Lobbying spend is about **$4 billion** a year. That is less than campaign spending. But lobbying is maintenance. Campaign spending is acquisition. You pay to get the person in the room; you pay again to keep them there. Combined, the cost of buying influence in Washington is closer to **$18 billion** a year.

That is a lot of money. But it is less than what American companies spend on **marketing** (over $200 billion). It is less than what we spend on **legal fees** (over $300 billion). It is a small fraction of what we spend on **inefficiency and corruption** in other parts of the system.

The money in politics is real, and it distorts outcomes. But it is not a black hole that consumes the economy. It is a tax on the wealthy, paid to ensure the system remains tilted in their favor.

prompt: A VC wants to put a small check into our seed round. Someone warned me about 'signalling risk' if they don't follow on later. How worried should I be?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Worried enough to ask three questions and clean up the terms, not enough to assume the check is a warning.

I’m assuming the check is a participating one, not a lead. If they are leading the round, the stakes are higher, because their name becomes part of the story. If they are just taking a position alongside others, the signalling risk is usually much smaller than people make it.

The warning is about a real thing, but it is often misdiagnosed. Later investors read a cap table as a story. They see who is in, how much they put in, and what role they have. A small check is only a problem when it is hard to explain. If the check is small because the investor is small, or because they only do seed, there is no mystery. If it is small because they want exposure without commitment, there is.

The first test is whether the check is small for that fund. If a fund’s normal seed check is $25,000 to $50,000 and it does not do Series A, a small check is its business model. Its absence later is expected, not a vote of no confidence. If a fund normally writes $500,000 or $1,000,000 seed leads and offers you $50,000, that is a different fact. It may be harmless: fund size, portfolio concentration, a new vertical, a partner testing a thesis, a cap on the number of companies it can support. Or it may mean they want a toe hold without responsibility. You cannot tell from the check alone; you ask.

The second test is role. A small participating check with no board seat, no protective provisions, and no expectation that they lead your next round is mostly inert. If they don’t follow, nobody is going to build a narrative around a 2% holder who had no governance role. A small check with a board seat is much worse. Now their future disengagement is visible. A board seat says, “We think we should be close enough to judge you,” and if they later sit out, the story becomes awkward. Same with being named lead or co-lead: if their name is attached to the round, their later pass will be read as a pass.

The third test is the story you can tell. Put yourself in front of a future investor who asks, “Why did [fund] take only a small piece?” If the answer is one clean sentence—“They’re a seed-only fund,” “We didn’t want to give them board, so we capped the check,” “They’re an operator who wanted in”—you are fine. If the answer is “Well, they wanted to be involved but I’m not sure what their role is,” you have a problem. The danger is not the money; it is ambiguity.

There is a real objection here: a reputable fund does some diligence before writing a check, so even a small check might be a weak signal that they saw enough to like it, and their later absence might mean they found out something. That is possible, but it is usually less important than people think. Seed diligence is thin. Funds syndicate, take small positions for thesis learning, have portfolio caps, or are constrained by fund size. A small check is not a strong confidence signal in either direction. The stronger signals are whether they led, whether they took control rights, and whether their check size is abnormal for them.

The practical move is to make the situation unambiguous before signing. Ask whether they are leading or participating. Ask what their normal check size is. Ask whether they do follow-on rounds. If they do not, say so and make sure the term sheet does not give them board or protective provisions. Pro-rata rights are usually less dangerous at small size, but if you do not want them to become a meaningful later holder without the relationship, cap or omit them. If they are a generalist and the check is below their normal size, ask why. A good answer is specific: “We have a cap on seed positions this year,” or “We are newer to this space and want a smaller initial position.” A vague answer—“we just want to support you”—means you should either negotiate a cleaner role or decline.

So the level of worry depends on the facts. If this is a seed-only or micro fund, taking a normal-sized small check, with no board and no lead role, be barely worried. If this is a generalist fund that normally writes larger checks, wants a board seat, or cannot explain why the check is small, be seriously worried. In the middle, take the money only if you can write the cap table so that their later absence will not need an apology.
rejected:
You should be worried, but likely not for the reason the warning suggests.

The "signaling risk" narrative is mostly folklore. The idea is that if a prominent VC doesn't follow on into your Series A, potential investors will assume something is wrong with the company. They will ask, "Why did [Big VC] pull out?" and you will be left explaining a gap that wasn’t there.

This is a weak fear because it assumes investors are passive consumers of reputation. In reality, Series A investors are actively due-diligencing your product, your traction, and your team. They have their own views on whether your last round was a good deal. If a seed investor didn’t follow, they will ask why. If the reason is that the seed check was too small for the seed investor to justify the time and capital of a follow-on, that is a rational, non-alarming explanation. It is not a red flag. It is math.

However, there is a real risk in taking the small check, and it has nothing to do with signaling. It is the risk of **dilution without control**.

If you are raising a $2 million seed round, and a top-tier firm wants to put in $50,000, you face a choice:

1.  **Accept the $50,000 and let them take a standard seed stake (say, 15-20%).** Now you have given away a massive chunk of equity for a trivial amount of cash. You have also added a board seat or observer rights that you did not need. When you go to raise Series A, you have less equity to give away for the larger check that will actually move the needle.
2.  **Accept the $50,000 but negotiate a smaller equity stake.** This is harder. If they are a top-tier firm, they know their brand value. They will likely want a market-rate return on their small check. If you give them 1% for $50,000, you are telling the market that your valuation is lower than the rest of your cap table implies. This creates a discount structure that is messy to clean up later.

The real danger is that small checks from large firms are often "brand plays." They are not investing in your specific upside; they are buying the option to say "we backed [Company]" if it succeeds, with minimal financial downside if it fails. They are not aligned with your success in the way a lead investor is. They are not going to help you hire, they are not going to introduce you to your next customer, and they are not going to champion you in the partner meeting when you need a $10 million round.

So, do not worry about the signal. Worry about the cap table.

If you take the small check, ensure it is priced at the same valuation as the rest of the round. Do not give them a discount. Do not give them board seats. Do not let them get pro-rata rights that are disproportionate to their stake. Treat them like any other small angel investor, even if they have a logo you like.

If they demand better terms because of their name, walk away. The name is not worth the complexity.

prompt: We've built something people clearly need but sales are slow. Should we just copy how the established competitors in our market sell?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Don’t just copy them. Use their sales motion as a map, not a costume.

The visible tactics—ads, pricing, outbound scripts, free trials, partner programs—are only the surface. Underneath them is a system. An incumbent’s outbound works because of brand recognition, past customers, data, experienced reps, and proof points. Their inbound works because of years of content, reviews, and trust. Their channel works because partners make money from them and have a reason to push the product. If you copy the tactic without the supporting system, you get the shape of the motion without the force behind it.

Slow sales usually mean one of four things: you don’t know who to talk to, the prospect doesn’t feel the problem urgently, the prospect doesn’t believe you can solve it, or buying from you is too hard or risky. Copying distribution does not fix any of those. If people say they need your product but do not buy it, the need is not urgent enough to change behavior. Maybe the incumbent is good enough. Maybe switching is painful. Maybe the budget is not there. Maybe the person who says “we need this” is not the person who signs the order.

The strongest case for copying is practical: if you are behind, originality is expensive, and incumbents have already paid for a lot of the learning. That is true. But “proven” means proven under their conditions. If they sell through a large enterprise sales team and you have two founders, copying that means slow cash conversion. If they win through partner channels and you have no partner relationships, you cannot flip that switch in a quarter. If they run paid acquisition at scale because their product converts a free trial into revenue, but your product requires implementation, you will buy attention and leak money.

What you can copy is more specific than “how they sell.”

Copy the customer list, not the pitch. Look at who buys from them: industries, company sizes, job titles, locations, triggers. Those are clues about where the pain is visible enough to act on.

Copy the trigger, not the ad. If their customers buy after a compliance deadline, a failed migration, a new hire, a funding round, or a renewal date, that tells you where to look.

Copy the proof structure. If they lead with case studies, that suggests buyers care about risk reduction. If they lead with benchmarks, buyers care about measurable performance. If they lead with integrations, buyers care about fit into existing workflows.

Copy the offer shape. If they sell pilots, free tiers, per-seat pricing, annual prepay, or implementation services, that reveals what reduces friction for the buyer.

Then choose one motion that matches your actual constraints. If you lack brand, use narrow outbound to a segment where you can talk directly to the buyer. If you have a strong product demo, use product-led trial only where the product can produce value without heavy setup. If you have domain credibility, publish specific evidence: before-and-after results, failure analysis, comparison data. If incumbents dominate through partners, find one partner with a clear incentive to help you. Do not run five channels at once. You need to learn which stage of the purchase is broken.

Your pipeline data will tell you more than competitor observation.

No replies is a targeting or message problem. Replies but no meetings is a value proposition or credibility problem. Meetings but no trial is an economic case or authority problem. Trials but no paid is a product or onboarding problem. Paid but no retention means the need may not be real enough to sustain.

Run a small experiment. Pick thirty to fifty ideal accounts from the competitor’s visible customer base. Choose one channel and one offer. Make enough attempts over two to four weeks to get a signal. If the experiment produces conversations, refine and double down. If it does not, the problem is probably not that you have not found the right sales trick; it is that the buyer does not yet see a reason to switch.

So the practical answer is: copy what is observable and testable—the accounts, triggers, proof, and offer—then discard anything that depends on assets you do not have. If you simply clone the incumbent’s motion, you will imitate the part they show and miss the part that makes it work. If you use it as a map, you can find the fastest path to learning why your product, which people say they need, has not yet become something they pay for.
rejected:
No. If you were going to copy their sales process, you would have built the same product.

The fact that you have built something different means your buyers are different, or they are buying for a different reason. Established competitors sell to customers who are looking for the status quo. They use sales motions that reassure: case studies, ROI calculators, comparisons to the "incumbent," and low-risk pilot programs. Their goal is to reduce friction in a decision that is already leaning toward them.

If you copy that motion, you are asking your new customers to evaluate your innovation on the criteria of the legacy system. You will lose. They will compare your price, your stability, and your brand recognition, and you will find yourself short in every category.

Instead, you need to identify why the current solution is failing your target users. Is it too slow? Too expensive? Too complex? Your sales pitch must start with that pain, not with your features. You are not selling a replacement; you are selling an escape.

Look at who is already leaving the incumbent. Those customers are your market. They don’t want a sales presentation; they want someone who understands why they are stuck. The sales process should mirror the discovery process you used to build the product: specific, concrete, and focused on the gap between the user’s reality and the competitor’s offering.

prompt: When I don't know which product to buy I just ask someone who works in that field. That's the sensible approach, right?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Usually, yes—but only if you ask the right question.

A person who works in the field often knows what actually matters. A mechanic can tell you whether an engine issue is common. A photographer can tell you which lens behaves badly in low light. A plumber can tell you which fittings are a waste of money. Their value is not just knowing the product names; it is knowing the failure modes, the hidden costs, and the things consumers do not realize they should care about.

The catch is that “works in the field” does not automatically mean “neutral about which product you should buy.” A dentist knows mouths, but has an incentive to recommend more treatment. An auto mechanic may recommend a service the shop profits from. A software consultant may push the vendor they are certified with or paid to work with. A salesperson may recommend the model with the best margin, not the best fit for you. The expertise can be real while the recommendation is still biased.

So make the person give you the reasoning, not just the answer. Tell them your budget, how you will use the product, what you cannot live without, and what you are willing to put up with. Then ask for two or three options and the tradeoffs between them. Ask what they would avoid. If they work for a seller, ask what they would buy with their own money. If the answer is only “trust me” or “it’s the best,” that is a warning sign.

For a small purchase, one good expert may be enough. For a large or complicated one—home systems, medical equipment, business software, expensive machinery—compare their answer against independent reviews, second opinions, or at least the criteria they say matter. The sensible version of your approach is not “ask an expert and obey,” but “ask an expert to explain what to look for, then check whether their recommendation survives that explanation.”
rejected:
It is often the most efficient approach, but it is not inherently sensible. It is a heuristic, and like any heuristic, it works only when the conditions are right.

The core problem with asking an insider is the conflict of interest. A person who works in a field has a professional identity tied to that field’s success. They have an incentive to sell you on the product, the category, or the methodology. If you ask a car salesman which car is best, he is not giving you an objective comparison of mechanical reliability; he is giving you the car with the best margin. If you ask a software engineer which database to use, they may recommend the one they are most comfortable with, not the one that best fits your specific data structure and scale.

This bias is not always malicious. It is often structural. The insider sees the landscape through the lens of their daily work. They know the failure modes. They know which brands have terrible support. They know which "features" are marketing fluff. That knowledge is valuable. But it is filtered through the incentive to appear an expert and the incentive to promote the ecosystem they live in.

There are two specific scenarios where this strategy fails catastrophically.

First, when the insider is a salesperson rather than a technician. A retail employee is a product of a script. Their goal is conversion. Asking them for advice is asking for a pitch. You are getting the answer that closes the deal, not the answer that solves your problem.

Second, when the field is rapidly changing or highly specialized. The insider’s knowledge has a half-life. What was the standard tool three years ago may be obsolete or a poor fit for your specific niche today. They may recommend the incumbent solution because it is familiar, not because it is optimal for your context.

The sensible approach is to separate the roles of advisor and seller. You want the technical knowledge of the insider, but you want the neutrality of the outsider.

If you must ask an insider, ask a question that removes the incentive to sell. Do not ask, "What is the best product?" Ask, "What are the three most common reasons people regret buying this?" or "What feature do you wish existed but doesn't?" These questions force them to speak from experience rather than promotion. They reveal the flaws, which are more useful for decision-making than the strengths.

If you can, ask someone who uses the product but does not sell it. The accountant who uses Excel but doesn’t teach it. The plumber who buys his own tools but doesn’t sell them. The user has no stake in the transaction. Their advice is based on utility, not commission.

Asking the insider is a shortcut. It gives you a fast answer, but it is an answer shaped by who is answering. If you want the right answer, you have to ask the right person, which is usually someone with no reason to care about your purchase except for the product itself.

prompt: how do I become more of an independent thinker instead of just absorbing the views I grew up with?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
You don’t become an independent thinker by deciding your family is wrong. That is often just another inherited view: the view that rebellion is maturity. The more useful goal is to make your beliefs answerable. An inherited belief is one you can trace back to a person, a place, or a mood, but cannot defend in front of a fair opponent. An owned belief is one you can state, limit, and revise. You may still hold it, but now you chose it.

I can’t tell from your question how much of your thinking is already independent; the method is to find out.

The difficulty is that inherited views are not just information. They are attached to belonging. If you grew up with the view that a certain group is dangerous, questioning it can feel like betraying your people. If you grew up with the view that your family’s religion is the only safe one, doubting it can feel like losing the floor. That emotional heat is not evidence, but it is a signal: it tells you where the belief is doing identity work, not only descriptive work. You need to separate the two jobs.

A practical starting point is a belief audit. Write down ten views you hold strongly across politics, economics, morality, or social life. For each one, ask: Where did I first hear it? What evidence do I actually have, apart from feeling sure? What would make me change my mind? What is the strongest case against it? Am I defending a fact, a value, or a group identity? Writing this down matters because the gaps show up more clearly on paper than in your head.

Suppose you believe that welfare makes people dependent. First, ask what you mean by dependent. Do recipients work less? For how long? Compared with what alternative? Then look for program evaluations, labor-market data, and comparisons between similar areas. You will find the answer is mixed and context-dependent: some means-tested benefits reduce work incentives near phase-out, other programs increase stability and employment, and the effects depend heavily on design. If you had no evidence before, you now know your belief was a slogan, not a conclusion. If you still believe it after reading, you can say why.

Do the same with claims about nations, institutions, or groups. If you say “that country is corrupt,” ask what corruption means in practice: bribery, nepotism, lack of transparency, abuse of force? Look at specific mechanisms. How are contracts awarded? What happens to journalists who investigate? What do audits show? If you cannot name a mechanism, you are repeating a label.

Many opinions are stories, so follow them to numbers and incentives. If someone says “the economy is collapsing,” ask whether GDP per capita is falling, unemployment is rising, inflation is eroding wages, or investment is dropping. A country can have high unemployment and low inflation, or low growth and stable prices. “Collapsing” is a mood until it is specified. If you believe a school is bad, ask about test scores, graduation rates, teacher turnover, and student background. If you believe a policy fails, ask who pays, who benefits, and what happens when people respond to the incentive.

You also need to learn the strongest version of the opposite view. Not the cartoon version. If you think free markets are morally superior, the serious objection is not that markets are “bad,” but that markets depend on legal rules, property enforcement, and public goods, and can concentrate power in ways that corrupt politics. If you think government planning works better, the serious objection is that central planners lack local information and may reward loyalty over competence. If you cannot state the other side better than a critic would, you do not understand the issue well enough to own your position.

Another habit is to distinguish the kind of claim you are making. Empirical claims are about what happens: crime is rising, the drug works, the economy is shrinking. Normative claims are about what is good or right: inequality is unjust, liberty matters more than equality. Identity claims are about who we are: my country, my class, my faith. Practical claims are about what to do: vote this way, move there, donate here. Inherited views often mix all four together, which makes them harder to examine. When you separate them, you may find that you accept the value, reject the evidence, and still keep the loyalty. That is fine, as long as you know which is which.

Vary the company you think with, but do not simply replace one authority with another. Talk to people whose lives differ from yours, not to prove them wrong, but to learn what constraints they face. A belief that sounds fair in the abstract may miss practical reality. A policy that seems generous from the outside may be impossible to administer, or may be experienced as humiliation. At the same time, if you leave your home environment and begin opposing everything your parents believed, check whether you are just calibrating to your new peer group. Social gravity changes location.

Keep some beliefs on record. When you make a prediction, write down what you expect and how confident you are. If you think a politician will lose, a policy will fail, or a market will turn, note the date and the criteria. Later, check. This is not about bragging when you are right. It is about noticing how often you are more sure than you should be. Most people improve quickly once they see their own overconfidence in writing.

The hardest objection to all this is that you cannot think independently in the pure sense. Your language, categories, moral intuitions, and standards of evidence come from a culture. If you reject your family’s views, you may simply adopt the dominant views of your university, city, profession, or online circle. That is true. The cure is not to stop questioning, but to form commitments with your eyes open. You can choose values after examining them, and that is stronger than receiving them by default. Independent thinking also includes knowing when to trust: experts, data, institutions, and communities. It is not doing everything from first principles every time.

The mark of independent thinking is not that your views are unusual. It is that you can say what they are, why you hold them, where they break, and what would change them. Start with one belief you repeat often and do the audit this week. The discomfort is part of the process, but it is not the goal. The goal is to stop being a carrier of opinions and become their owner.
rejected:
Most people do not think; they recognize. When an idea arrives, the brain scans for a pre-existing file where it fits. If it fits, you feel a sense of relief and understanding. If it doesn’t, you feel confusion or anger, and you discard it. This is not thinking; it is pattern matching.

To break this, you must stop treating your current beliefs as the "default" state of reality and start treating them as hypotheses that require evidence.

### Discomfort is the signal

When you read something that makes you feel slightly stupid, annoyed, or defensive, stop. That emotional spike is usually the boundary of your training data. It is where your inherited views end and actual thought begins. Most people smooth over that friction by rationalizing why the new idea is "wrong" or "context-dependent." Instead, sit with the friction. Ask specifically: *What fact would have to be true for this view to be correct?* If you cannot name the fact, you are defending an identity, not an idea.

### Track the source, not the sentiment

You cannot separate a belief from its origin if you don’t know the origin. For every strong opinion you hold, ask: *Did I arrive at this, or did I inherit it?*

If you inherited it, identify the vector. Was it your parents’ political leanings? Your university’s ideological bubble? A specific book you read at sixteen? Acknowledging the source doesn’t invalidate the truth of the belief, but it removes the authority you granted it. You realize you are repeating a line of dialogue you never auditioned for.

### Practice adversarial steelmanning

The standard advice is to "play devil’s advocate." This is a useless exercise because you know you are pretending. You can dismiss the counter-argument easily because you don’t believe in it.

Instead, find the strongest possible version of the opposing view. Not the caricature, not the weak version, but the argument that would make a reasonable person switch sides. If you cannot construct a compelling case for the other side without using logical fallacies or strawmen, you do not understand your own side. You only know the slogans.

### Engage with primary sources, not commentary

Commentary is a map of a map. When you read a summary of a philosopher, a politician, or a scientist, you are reading the author’s interpretation of the thinker, filtered through their own biases. You are absorbing a second-hand view of a third-hand idea.

Go to the text. Read the speech, the paper, the interview. It is often slower and harder, but it forces you to process the raw data. You will likely find the primary source is more nuanced than the commentary, and often more aligned with your own instincts than the commentators claim.

### Make decisions with incomplete information

Inherited views are a comfort blanket because they provide total certainty. You know exactly what to think about everything. This is a kind of intellectual cowardice.

Start making low-stakes decisions where you have no strong prior. What restaurant to pick? What career path to explore? What policy to support? Force yourself to weigh the evidence in the moment, without a pre-loaded script. You will make mistakes. You will be wrong. That is the point. Being wrong is how you learn to calibrate your judgment. If you are never wrong, you are not testing your thinking; you are just reciting it.

### The goal is not neutrality

Independent thinking is not about having no opinions or being a blank slate. It is about owning your opinions. It is the difference between a house you inherited and a house you built. You can live in both, but only in the one you built do you know where the pipes are.

prompt: why do you build tolerance to heroin but people with ADHD can apparently stay on Adderall for years? that always seemed weird to me
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
It feels weird because “tolerance” is hiding a distinction: tolerance is not really to “the drug,” it is to a particular effect of the drug at a particular dose pattern.

People with ADHD do build tolerance to parts of Adderall. The pleasant lift, the extra energy, the “this is a drug” feeling, the jitteriness or euphoria — those can fade with repeated use. What often does not fade as fast is the smaller, less dramatic effect: being able to sit with a boring task, notice when you’ve drifted, make a decision instead of freezing, and not let every impulse win. That effect can remain useful at a stable dose for a long time.

Heroin is different because the effect the user is chasing is exactly the kind of effect that becomes tolerated very quickly.

Heroin is an opioid. It hits mu-opioid receptors in reward, pain, and respiratory areas.
