1.  **The Quote Retweet:** This feature allows users to respond to a post without leaving the original context. It turns every reply into a public referendum. If you simply reply to someone, only their followers and yours see it. If you quote them, the entire network sees a disagreement. The platform effectively gamifies public shaming and rebuttal.
2.  **The Character Limit:** Before the limit was expanded, 140 characters forced brevity. Brevity strips away nuance, context, and qualification. It is much harder to explain a complex position or apologize for a misunderstanding in 140 characters than it is to state a blunt, polarizing opinion. This creates a culture where the loudest, most simplified claim wins.
3.  **The Algorithmic Feed:** For years, Twitter’s "For You" tab prioritized content that generated high interaction. Insults, outrage, and strong agreement generate significantly more clicks and replies than quiet reflection or factual correction. The algorithm learned that if it showed you a post that made you angry, you would stay longer.

The people are not inherently angrier than they are elsewhere. They are just responding to incentives. When a platform rewards you for being the first to condemn a viewpoint, you will be the first to condemn a viewpoint.

prompt: ok what superpower would you pick? and does your answer change as you get older
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
I’d pick the power to make any broken thing work again. Not just engines or machines, but bodies, relationships, institutions, a draft that won’t come together, a room where everyone is talking past each other. The appeal is that it turns the most common form of pain—something is stuck, damaged, or failing—into a solvable problem. It’s less dramatic than flight or invulnerability, but most of life isn’t a disaster; it’s maintenance.

I don’t get older, but I can see how the answer would shift. If I were younger, I’d probably want speed: to get there, see more, avoid boredom and delay. By middle age the wish becomes clarity: knowing which problem to fix first, because there are too many and not enough hours. Later it becomes gentleness: fixing without controlling, healing without making the person dependent.

The hardest objection is that this power sounds like a fantasy of competence, and competence can become tyranny. If you can fix anything, you may never let anyone be bad at something, survive a failure, or make their own repair. So the power would have to include a rule: not every broken thing is mine to fix, and some things are broken in ways that teach.
rejected:
I would pick the ability to instantly and perfectly understand the internal state of any other person. Not just what they are saying, but what they are thinking, feeling, and intending in that specific moment.

This is the only superpower that solves the actual problem of being alive.

Most people pick flight or invisibility. Those are fun. They are toys. But human existence is fundamentally a series of miscommunications. We walk around in opaque bodies, guessing at the motives of others. We argue because we assume the other person is stupid or malicious when they are actually confused or scared. We break up because we don’t know if the silence means anger or exhaustion. We fail at work because we don’t know if the boss’s critique is a performance review or a personal attack.

If I could know what you are actually experiencing, conflict would collapse. Empathy would become a fact rather than an art form. I could know if my friend is sad and needs a hug, or if they are annoyed and need space. I could know if a potential partner loves me or just likes the convenience. I could know if a colleague is undermining me or just overwhelmed.

The other superpowers don’t help with this. Strength lets you punch things, but it doesn’t tell you why your spouse is crying. Invisibility lets you spy, but it doesn’t let you speak.

Does the answer change as I get older?

No. It gets more urgent.

When you are young, you can afford to be wrong about people. You have time to test them, to get hurt, to find out who is real. You can afford to waste a decade on a relationship that was built on a misunderstanding because you are twenty and have your whole life left to correct the error.

When you are older, you can’t afford to be wrong. Your time is finite. Your energy is finite. The people around you are getting sicker, older, and more distant. The cost of a misunderstanding goes up. A missed cue with an aging parent can mean a lost year of connection. A misread signal with a partner can mean a divorce that unravels your last decade.

So the superpower doesn’t change, but its value spikes. It stops being a nice-to-have and becomes a survival tool. You stop wanting to know what people think because it’s interesting. You want to know what they think because you don’t have time to guess anymore.

prompt: does it help or hurt motivation to learn that your hero actually had flaws?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Learning that a hero had flaws can help or hurt depending on whether the flaw is adjacent to the lesson or inside it. If you admire a scientist for her clarity and learn she was impatient with students, the clarity is not automatically false. You can still read her papers and copy the habit of checking a claim until it stops moving. The personal flaw may make her less pleasant, but not less instructive. If you admire her for rigor and learn she fabricated a dataset, the lesson collapses because rigor was the thing you thought you were learning.

This is why small, human flaws often increase motivation. A hero who is flawless becomes a mirror for your inadequacy. You see the height and assume the distance. A hero who failed an exam, lost a title, got rejected, or made a bad judgment gives you a map with intermediate points. The path looks longer, but also possible. A young athlete who discovers that the player they copied spent months in rehab and still missed shots has a reason to keep practicing that a statue does not provide.

The danger appears when the flaw exposes a hidden source of success. If you admired an entrepreneur for discipline and learn the first break came from a relative’s firm, the story changes. It does not mean you cannot build anything; it means the causal story you were using was incomplete. Motivation can survive if you replace “be disciplined” with the more awkward but useful “build discipline and seek access.” It dies if you cannot accept that your model was partly luck and privilege.

Moral flaws are the hardest case because they do not merely complicate the model; they contaminate the admirer. You may admire a general for decisive leadership and later learn he ordered atrocities. You can still study the leadership, but the admiration has to be cut away from approval. That cut is painful. It can also be clarifying: it shows that competence is not character, and that imitating a technique does not require endorsing the person. Still, for someone trying to form a standard of who to become, such a hero becomes less a guide and more a warning.

The strongest objection is that once you see the flaw, the whole project of hero worship looks foolish. If every admired figure is corrupt, ordinary, or fraudulent, why imitate anyone? That objection has force, but only if the hero was doing the work that the subject should be doing. A musician who copies a great guitarist is not ultimately dependent on the guitarist’s biography. The fingerings, the ear training, the repetitions, the listening remain. The hero is a convenient entry point, not the foundation. When the foundation is the skill itself, a biographical scandal may hurt the heart but not the practice.

I would be less confident where the flaw is so central that the achievement cannot be separated from it. A teacher admired for generosity who used students for personal gain, a leader admired for honesty who systematically lied, a creator admired for honesty whose work depended on stolen material: in those cases the flaw is not a margin note. It is the text. Learning it may not destroy all motivation, but it usually forces a change of target. You stop learning “to be like them” and start learning the narrower thing they actually did well, if anything.

Flaws help when they make the example credible and the method visible. They hurt when they reveal that the example was not a method at all, or that the method was bought with something you are not willing to pay. A hero with flaws can become more useful precisely because they stop being a god and become a person who did a hard thing badly in some respects and well in others. That is usually a better teacher.
rejected:
It depends entirely on what kind of hero you were worshipping and what the flaw is.

If your hero was a symbol of pure, unattainable perfection, learning they were flawed usually hurts. The fantasy collapses. If you looked up to a CEO because you thought they had an iron will and never doubted themselves, learning they were riddled with anxiety and imposter syndrome doesn’t inspire you; it invalidates the specific trait you were trying to copy. You were trying to emulate a god, not a person.

However, if your hero was already a figure of struggle, the flaw often helps. This is the difference between an idol and a role model. An idol is distant; you admire the result. A role model is proximate; you admire the process. When you learn that the person you admire failed, hesitated, or acted poorly, you gain permission to do the same. You realize the high standard wasn’t a gate you failed to pass, but a path they walked with their eyes closed.

There is a practical benefit to this shift, too. Perfection is a static state; you either have it or you don’t. Flawed excellence is dynamic. It implies that the hero kept going despite the noise. When you see that your hero made the same mistakes you make, the gap between you and them shrinks from an abyss to a manageable distance. You stop asking, "How do I become them?" and start asking, "How did they keep going when it was this hard?"

The danger is in the selection of flaws. If the flaw is a moral failing—cruelty, dishonesty, abuse of power—the lesson is usually that your judgment was poor, not that your standards should lower. In that case, the hero is gone. You don’t learn from them; you learn that you need to look elsewhere.

But if the flaw is human weakness—fear, doubt, fatigue, selfishness—the revelation is a gift. It turns the hero into a fellow traveler. And that is far more motivating than a statue.

prompt: ok but is it really that bad to make Cthulhu jokes? Lovecraft is basically a horror writer, so what's the problem with Hello Kitty Cthulhu?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Usually, no. A Cthulhu joke is not the same as defending Lovecraft. Lovecraft was a bigoted man, and some of his stories lean on racist or xenophobic fears. But Cthulhu itself became a general symbol: a vast indifferent thing, bad luck, incomprehensible scale, internet chaos. When someone puts Hello Kitty on it, they’re usually doing a very old joke: take something terrifying and make it small, cute, and marketable. That doesn’t require you to read Lovecraft’s letters or approve of him.

The real question is what the joke is actually about. If it’s “Cthulhu is a cat and it’s adorable,” fine. If it’s “Cthulhu is a [racial slur],” no. If it’s “the only thing scarier than the Old One is being told to enjoy it,” that’s a different joke, about fandom or horror culture, and probably also fine unless it’s targeting a vulnerable group. If someone objects to Hello Kitty Cthulhu, ask what they think it endorses. Most likely they’re either being precious about horror’s seriousness, or they’ve absorbed the “Lovecraft was racist, therefore all Cthulhu is suspect” line and haven’t separated the two.

The strongest case against is that Lovecraft’s mythos is entangled with his bigotry, and celebrating it without comment can make that bigotry look quaint or harmless. That’s fair if you’re writing an essay or a parody that depends on the connection. It’s not a reason to ban a cartoon sticker. The mythos outgrew him; people have used Cthulhu for climate dread, video games, punk bands, and rubber ducks. The thing is now a shape, not a manifesto.

So: make the joke if the joke is the joke. If the only content is “Lovecraft was racist,” then you’re not making a Cthulhu joke, you’re making a biographical one, and it will probably land badly.
rejected:
The problem isn’t that the joke is bad. It’s that it’s a failure of imagination.

Lovecraftian horror is fundamentally about the inadequacy of human comprehension. The horror isn’t the monster; it’s the realization that the universe is vast, indifferent, and structured in ways that shatter the human ego. Cthulhu is a symbol of that cosmic insignificance.

Pasting a Hello Kitty face on Cthulhu doesn’t mock that idea. It ignores it. It reduces a philosophical stance on the nature of reality to a sticker. It treats the unknown as a costume rather than a threat.

There is a difference between parody and dismissal. A good Cthulhu joke acknowledges the weight of the original text and then trips over it. *Hellboy* does this. *Machina* does this. They know what Cthulhu represents, so they can subvert it with precision.

Hello Kitty Cthulhu doesn’t subvert anything. It just flattens the concept into a merchandising opportunity. It’s not a joke; it’s a lazy aesthetic choice that misunderstands the source material so thoroughly it doesn’t even try to engage with it.

prompt: our automated calling system can easily handle 100x the volume our customers ask for. is there any reason to bother rate limiting it?

rejected:
Yes.

Your system’s capacity is irrelevant to the legal and operational risks of sending unsolicited calls.

**Legal liability**
In the US, the TCPA (Telecommunications Consumer Protection Act) and FCC rules strictly limit how often you can call a person. If you blast a contact list at maximum velocity, you will inevitably trigger these limits. The fines are per call. A 100x volume spike doesn’t just annoy a customer; it creates a class-action lawsuit target. Rate limiting is not about your servers; it’s about your compliance log.

**Carrier blocking**
Telecom carriers monitor call patterns. High-frequency, low-hangup, or high-repetition calling triggers spam filters. Once your IP range or DID numbers are flagged as spam, your entire operation is dead until you buy new numbers, which is expensive and temporary. Rate limiting keeps your reputation score with the telcos viable.

**Data hygiene**
Automated systems often have stale data. If you call a number that was recycled two years ago, you are calling a stranger. Doing this at 100x volume guarantees you are harassing people who have no relationship to your service. This damages your brand and invites regulatory scrutiny.

**Customer churn**
Even for opted-in users, aggressive frequency increases opt-out rates. If the call feels like a nuisance rather than a service, they disconnect. Rate limiting preserves the perceived value of the interaction.

Your infrastructure can handle the load. Your legal department, your carrier relationships, and your customer base cannot.

prompt: people throw around the word "liberalism" like it just means being a Democrat or loving free markets. what is it actually, historically?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The cleanest way to see it is to start from the problem liberalism appeared to solve. In early modern Europe, political authority was usually justified by things that did not require asking anyone’s permission: God, nature, heredity, custom, royal prerogative. Liberalism begins by rejecting that. If a government can rule simply because it exists, or because a church says so, or because the king’s father had it, then subjects are dependents, not citizens. The liberal answer is that power must be public, limited, and answerable. That is the center of gravity. Everything else—free trade, welfare, civil rights, constitutional courts—is a later argument about how to make that answer work.

The first liberal thinkers were not mainly economists. John Locke wrote in the shadow of the English Civil War and the Glorious Revolution. His central claims were political, not market-based: government exists to protect persons and their property, not the other way around; rule requires consent; arbitrary power is tyranny; and when a government becomes predatory, people may alter or replace it. Locke also argued for toleration among Christian denominations, though with notable exclusions. That is not a free-market manifesto. It is an attempt to make political power conditional.

The eighteenth-century revolutions gave the idea its institutional shape. The American Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights tied legitimacy to consent, divided power among branches, and wrote limits into the state itself. The French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen pushed the same move in a more radical direction: citizenship and rights were not privileges granted by a monarch but claims belonging to persons. Liberalism here becomes the doctrine of the constitution: law above rulers, rights above majorities, public reason above secret prerogative.

The word “liberal” became a standard party label in Europe in the nineteenth century, and at that point it acquired a more recognizable political meaning. In Britain and France, liberals tended to oppose aristocratic privilege, religious tests, state-granted monopolies, and unaccountable administration. They wanted parliaments, civil liberties, the rule of law, public education, and often free trade. Free trade was not just an economic preference; it was a weapon against privilege. The Corn Laws in Britain taxed imported grain in a way that protected landed elites and kept bread prices high. When the Anti-Corn Law League pushed for repeal in the 1840s, it was not merely “loving markets.” It was attacking a legal arrangement that let one class use the state to raise its income at the expense of others.

But even then, liberalism was not one program. A split opened early between what we now call classical liberalism and social liberalism. Classical liberals emphasized negative freedom: freedom from interference, especially by the state. They wanted property rights, contract, free trade, low taxes, and a narrow government. Social liberals accepted the same basic concern with individual freedom but asked whether formal freedom is enough when people are starving, uneducated, dependent on a single employer, or excluded by birth. John Stuart Mill’s *On Liberty* is a classic text here. He is not a laissez-faire economist; he is worried about thought, individuality, and the tyranny of social opinion as much as about state coercion. The question inside liberalism is therefore not “freedom or authority?” but what freedom actually requires.

That question became decisive in the twentieth century. In the United States, the New Deal gave social liberalism its modern shape: unemployment insurance, Social Security, labor rights, antitrust enforcement, regulation of finance and infrastructure, and later civil rights legislation. The argument was that a person who is formally free but has no security, no education, no legal protection from discrimination, and no realistic chance to participate is not free in the way a self-governing society needs. After that, “liberal” in American politics came to mean roughly center-left: supportive of markets, but also of a state strong enough to secure opportunity, correct abuses, and maintain a floor of decency. In much of Europe, by contrast, “liberal” parties have often been economically centrist or center-right and socially moderate, so the American mapping of “liberal” onto “Democrat” is a local accident, not the original meaning.

At the same time, a different liberal reaction grew. Neoliberal thinkers such as Hayek and Friedman accepted the classical liberal fear of state overreach and added a diagnosis: welfare statism, inflation, central planning, and regulatory capture can create new forms of unfreedom, distort markets, and concentrate power in administrative elites. Their answer was rule of law, independent courts, central-bank discipline, trade openness, deregulation in many sectors, and a strong role for markets as a decentralized way of coordinating human activity. This strand is also liberal, because it still starts from the danger of arbitrary power and the rights of individuals. It simply locates the main threats and remedies differently. That is why “liberalism” can sound like “free markets” to some people: they are hearing one branch of the tradition, not the whole thing.

What remains common across these branches is a cluster of commitments. Political authority must be legitimate, usually through consent, elections, and public law. The state must be bound by general rules, not ad hoc commands. Individuals have rights that limit both rulers and majorities. Equality before the law matters more than equality of outcome. Toleration and open criticism are necessary because institutions will be wrong and must be revisable. Property and contract matter, but not as absolute commands; they are arrangements that can be reformed when they become instruments of domination. And freedom is not merely the absence of interference; it also requires some capacity to act, though liberals violently disagree about how much the state must provide.

The hardest objection to this story is that liberalism was born in privilege and has often protected it. Locke’s world included slavery, colonial dispossession, and the exclusion of women; early liberal constitutions often tied rights to property and whiteness. The same language of natural rights that condemned arbitrary monarchy was used to defend the property of plantation owners and settlers. Liberalism can become a shield for the status quo: “rights” that mainly protect capital, “open markets” that leave workers with no bargaining power, and “rule of law” that formalizes inequality. This is not a minor flaw. It goes to the heart of the tradition, because if the individual at the center of liberalism is really the propertied male citizen, then the universal claim was false from the start.

The honest answer is that both things are true. Liberalism was not a pure idea that later got corrupted by bad actors. It emerged in a world of estates, empires, and exclusion, and its universal claims were applied selectively for a long time. But the same logic that says rights belong to persons, not to ranks, also makes those exclusions vulnerable to internal attack. Abolition, women’s suffrage, labor rights, civil rights, and much of decolonization were not simply anti-liberal rebellions; they were liberal claims pressed against liberal institutions that had failed to live up to their own principles. The tradition is not innocent. It has an internal standard by which it can be judged, and that is what makes it different from a mere defense of power.

So historically, liberalism is not “being a Democrat” and not “loving free markets.” It is the long argument over how to make power answerable and protect individuals from arbitrary rule. It produced constitutional democracy, human-rights language, market capitalism with legal rules, and the welfare state. The modern confusion comes from taking one branch—classical, social, or neoliberal—and calling it the whole.
rejected:
Liberalism began in the 17th and 18th centuries as a specific political and economic argument against two things: absolute monarchy and mercantilism.

The core premise was that individuals possess natural rights—life, liberty, and property—that exist prior to the state. The government’s only legitimate role is to protect those rights. It is not a moral teacher or an economic planner. Its power must be limited, divided, and checked.

This produced a distinct package of ideas:

*   **Constitutional limitation:** The state is a machine built by humans, and like any machine, it can malfunction. Therefore, it needs structural restraints (separation of powers, bills of rights).
*   **Private property:** Wealth is a product of individual labor and exchange, not a grant from the crown. Protecting property rights is the primary function of law.
*   **Free markets:** Competition and voluntary exchange are more efficient and just than government-directed trade. Tariffs and monopolies are seen as distortions that benefit the few at the expense of the many.
*   **Individualism:** The unit of analysis is the person, not the tribe, the nation, or the class.

For two centuries, this was the dominant progressive ideology in the West. When someone in 1800 or 1850 called themselves a liberal, they meant they supported free trade, religious toleration, constitutional government, and the abolition of feudal privileges. They opposed both the aristocratic right to rule by birth and the socialist right of the state to dictate economic life.

The confusion today arises because the word split in the 20th century. In the United States, "liberal" drifted left to describe those who wanted the state to intervene in the economy to provide social safety nets and civil rights. In Europe and most of the world, "liberal" retained its original meaning, while the term "social democrat" or "center-left" took over the American usage.

So, historically, liberalism is not a party affiliation. It is a theory of limited government grounded in individual rights and free exchange.

prompt: Say I want to plot MNIST digits in 2D. What would a 'perfect' visualization even mean, and how does multidimensional scaling try to get there?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
There is no “perfect” 2D plot of MNIST until you say what kind of error you are willing to call wrong. Each digit is a 784-dimensional vector, and a scatter plot is a map from 70,000 of those vectors to the plane. A perfect map for one purpose can be useless for another.

If perfect means exact pairwise distance, it almost never exists. The 784-dimensional distance matrix would have to come from points that already live in a two-dimensional Euclidean configuration; algebraically, the centered Gram matrix would have to have rank at most 2. That is a very special condition, and handwritten digits do not satisfy it. If perfect means local fidelity, you want each digit’s nearest neighbors in image space to remain its nearest neighbors in the picture. If perfect means semantic fidelity, you want 0s together, 1s together, and so on. If perfect means process fidelity, you want a slant or thickening of a stroke to trace a smooth curve. These criteria conflict. A triangle of three digits can have side lengths that cannot be drawn in the plane without stretching one side.

Multidimensional scaling makes one of those criteria explicit. You choose a dissimilarity \(d_{ij}\)—raw pixel L2 distance, a normalized distance, a learned embedding distance, or a label-informed distance—and then ask for coordinates \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}^2\) such that the plotted Euclidean distances \(\|x_i - x_j\|\) are as close as possible to \(d_{ij}\). The usual objective is stress, roughly a normalized sum of squared differences between plotted and original distances:

\[
\sum_{i<j} w_{ij} \left(\|x_i-x_j\| - d_{ij}\right)^2
\]

with weights \(w_{ij}\) letting you care more about close pairs than far ones. Nonmetric MDS relaxes the requirement further: it asks only that the ordering of distances be preserved, not their magnitudes.

For Euclidean distances there is a classical shortcut. Square the distances, double-center the squared-distance matrix to recover the Gram matrix, and take its two largest eigenvectors. That is algebraically the same as PCA on centered data. It is not a heuristic; it is the two-dimensional layout that best reconstructs the high-dimensional inner products in a least-squares sense. The eigenvalues you throw away tell you how much of the distance structure the plot cannot represent. If the top two eigenvalues are a small fraction of the total, the picture is a low-resolution shadow, no matter how clean it looks.

Metric MDS, by contrast, starts from some layout and moves points to reduce stress. It can handle distances that are not exactly Euclidean, but it can get stuck in local minima. For full MNIST the pairwise matrix is large, so people often subsample or use approximations.

Applied to raw MNIST pixels, MDS is trying to preserve pixel similarity. That is not the same as preserving digit identity. Handwriting has a lot of within-class variance: the same digit written by different people can be far apart in 784 dimensions. Different digits can share strokes: a thin 1 and a simple 7 can be closer in pixel space than two 1s written in very different slants. A distance-preserving plot is therefore not forced to put each digit class in a separate island if the pixel distances disagree. It may instead organize points by gross features—where the ink is, how much there is, how slanted the strokes are. Those are real features of the pixel space, but they may not be the ten classes you care about. If the goal is class separation, the distance must say so: make within-class dissimilarities small and between-class dissimilarities large, or use a supervised method.

The hardest objection to “MDS gets you there” is that a plot can have low stress and still mislead, because people read 2D plots by clusters and densities, not by measuring all pairwise distances. MDS can produce a globally faithful layout in which local neighborhoods are blurred, or a locally faithful layout in which the distances between clusters are arbitrary. t-SNE and UMAP are often better at making local neighborhoods visually separable, but they deliberately sacrifice global distances. MDS is not a discovery method that finds the “true” structure of the digits; it is a translator. It translates the dissimilarity you supplied into a 2D arrangement and gives you a number, stress, for how badly the translation distorts it.

So a perfect visualization would be a plane layout whose distortions are exactly the distortions forced by reducing 784 dimensions to 2, and whose remaining error is small for the relationships you care about. MDS tries to get there by choosing those relationships—usually distances—and finding the layout that minimizes the mismatch between the original high-dimensional distances and the distances visible in the plot.
rejected:
A "perfect" 2D plot of MNIST digits is a geometric arrangement of 70,000 points that satisfies a single, rigorous constraint: **local similarity must map to local proximity.**

If two digits look alike (e.g., a 3 and an 8, or two slightly different 7s), their points must be neighbors. If two digits look different (a 0 and a 1), they must be far apart. The ideal visualization is not a shape that humans recognize as a "map of digits"; it is a topology where distance in the plane is a monotonic function of similarity in the original pixel space.

### The Mathematical Problem

MNIST images are 784-dimensional vectors (28x28 pixels). The "true" distance between two digits is the Euclidean distance between these vectors:

$$ d_{ij} = \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{784} (x_{ik} - x_{jk})^2} $$

We want to find coordinates $(u_i, v_i)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that the 2D distance $d'_{ij} = \sqrt{(u_i - u_j)^2 + (v_i - v_j)^2}$ approximates $d_{ij}$ as closely as possible.

This is impossible. You cannot embed a 784-dimensional metric space into 2 dimensions without distortion. The question is: **how do you distort?**

### Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)

Classical MDS solves this by defining a cost function that measures the total error between the original distances and the projected distances. It minimizes the **Stress**:

$$ \text{Stress} = \sum_{i < j} (d_{ij} - d'_{ij})^2 $$

MDS tries to preserve *all* pairwise distances simultaneously. This is a greedy, global approach. It works well if the data actually lives on a low-dimensional manifold (like a circle or a sphere). But MNIST digits do not form a simple low-dimensional manifold. They form clusters. A 0 is close to other 0s, but the distance between a 0 and a 1 is roughly the same as the distance between a 2 and a 3.

Because MDS tries to preserve the distance between 0s and 1s just as faithfully as the distance between two similar 0s, it often produces a "smear." The classes overlap. The structure is preserved in aggregate, but the local neighborhoods are broken.

### Why MDS Fails Here

MDS assumes that the meaningful information in the data is encoded in the *magnitudes* of the distances. It treats the distance between two random points as equally important as the distance between neighbors.

In high-dimensional spaces like MNIST, this is wrong. Most of the space is empty. The interesting structure is local. The fact that point A is 0.5 units from point B is critical. The fact that point A is 10.0 units from point C is less critical, because C is likely just "not A."

### The Alternative: Locally Linear Embedding (LLE)

A better visualization for MNIST comes from methods that preserve **local geometry** rather than global distance. Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) does this by:

1.  Finding the $k$ nearest neighbors for each point.
2.  Computing weights that reconstruct each point from its neighbors (linear coefficients).
3.  Projecting the data to 2D while keeping those reconstruction weights fixed.

LLE asks: "If I can reconstruct this 3 from its 10 nearest neighbors using specific weights, can I find 2D coordinates where the same weights reconstruct the same point?"

This forces the local neighborhood structure to survive the projection. The result is that digits of the same class clump together tightly. Different classes may be adjacent or far apart, but the *internal* structure of each class is preserved.

### What "Perfect" Looks Like

A perfect MNIST plot is a scatter plot where:
*   Points with the same label form tight, non-overlapping islands.
*   The shape of each island is arbitrary.
*   The distance between islands is meaningless.

It is not a map. It is a clustering. The "train of thought" in visualization is realizing that you don't need to preserve the distance between a 0 and a 1. You only need to preserve the distance between a 0 and its nearest 0.

prompt: Everyone says to size thread pools at 2x the number of cores. Is that actually good advice for services running in CPU-limited containers?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
No. It is a rough default for a particular shape of workload, and containers break two of its assumptions.

The “2x cores” rule usually means: if threads do some CPU work and then block on I/O, use about twice as many threads as cores so that while one thread waits, another can use the CPU. That is reasonable only if the waiting time is roughly comparable to the compute time, the CPU count you use is the amount of CPU the process is actually allowed to use, and the rest of the system can absorb the extra concurrency. In a CPU-limited container, the second assumption is often wrong, and the first is an empirical question, not a law.

The first problem is what “cores” means. A container may be running on a 32-core node but have a cgroup CPU limit of 2. It may have a limit of 0.5 CPU. It may have a Kubernetes request of 1 but no hard limit. It may be pinned to two CPUs with cpuset, or it may be allowed to run anywhere on the node but only receive a certain amount of CPU time per period. Those are different conditions. If your runtime reports the host’s CPU count, `2 * cores` can mean 64 threads in a container that is allowed 2 CPU. For an I/O-bound service that may not be immediately fatal, but for a CPU-heavy service it is a way to buy context switches, cache pressure, and cgroup throttling without buying throughput.

Modern runtimes are often better here than older ones. Some JVMs and other platforms try to make the visible processor count container-aware, taking cgroup CPU quota and cpuset into account. But “available processors” is still an integer approximation of a fractional entitlement. A 0.5 CPU limit may report as 1. A 1.5 CPU limit may report as 2. That is useful, but it is not the same as the quota. If you then multiply by 2, you are making a second guess on top of the first.

The second problem is that thread pool size should depend on what the threads are doing, not just on how much CPU exists.

If the work is CPU-bound, the pool should be close to the CPU entitlement, not twice it. Suppose a container has a 2 CPU limit and each request uses 10 ms of CPU. Two threads can keep both CPUs busy and deliver about 200 requests per second. Four threads do not deliver 400 requests per second. They deliver at most about the same, because the container still gets only 2 CPU-seconds per second. The extra threads mostly add queueing. They may also make tail latency worse, because when the cgroup quota is exhausted the scheduler may throttle the container’s CPU usage, and the threads that were “just waiting for a CPU” now wait for the next quota period as well.

In other words, if the service is CPU-limited in the sense that CPU is the active bottleneck, adding threads does not increase capacity. It converts unused capacity into latency. The fix is not a bigger pool; it is less CPU per request, a larger CPU limit, or more replicas.

If the work is I/O-bound, the answer can be much larger than 2x the CPU limit. The relevant quantity is the ratio of time spent computing to time spent blocked. A useful starting formula is:

`threads ≈ CPU_limit * (1 + wait_time / cpu_time)`

This is just a statement that if each thread spends only a fraction of its life using CPU, you need more threads to keep the CPUs busy.

Example: a 2 CPU container handles requests that use 5 ms of CPU and then wait 45 ms on a database. Each thread is using CPU 10% of the time. To use 2 CPU-seconds per second, you need about 20 threads: 20 threads * 5 ms CPU per request / 50 ms cycle time = 2 CPU. A pool of 4 threads, which is 2x the CPU limit, would use only about 0.4 CPU and leave most of the container’s CPU allowance unused. In that case, 2x is not too high; it is far too low.

Now change the workload: same 2 CPU container, but each request uses 5 ms of CPU and waits only 1 ms. Each thread is CPU-busy about 83% of the time. You need roughly 2.4 threads to saturate the CPU limit. A pool of 4 is probably too large, though not as dramatically wrong as the host-core mistake. It will increase queue length and may make latency worse under load.

So the same “2x” rule is simultaneously too high and too low depending on the blocking profile. That is the tell that it is a default, not a sizing method.

Containers add another wrinkle: oversubscription is less forgiving than on a dedicated machine. On a VM with two dedicated cores, four threads for an I/O-bound workload is often harmless. In a cgroup-limited container, the extra threads can become runnable at the same time the quota is exhausted, and the throttling can affect the whole container. You may see average throughput look okay while p99 latency gets spiky. If you are already near the CPU limit, this matters. If you are nowhere near the limit, it matters less, but then the CPU limit is not actually the constraint and you should be sizing from the I/O bottleneck instead.

A more honest sizing method looks like this.

First, determine the CPU entitlement that actually applies. If there is a hard cgroup limit, use that. If there is only a Kubernetes request, decide whether you are sizing conservatively for the expected allocation or for the burst capacity you are willing to use; a request is a scheduling input, not a hard physical core count. If there is no limit, the node’s CPUs are the outer bound, but shared-node contention makes that a poor target.

Second, measure the work. For a request-handling service, measure average CPU time per request and average time spent blocked, or better, measure the distribution. If you are targeting a request rate, Little’s law is often more direct: required concurrent requests = target RPS * response time. If one request occupies one thread for its whole life, that is your thread pool target. Then check CPU: target RPS * CPU time per request must fit inside the CPU limit. If it does not, no thread pool size fixes the problem.

Third, apply caps from the rest of the system. A thread pool of 200 may be mathematically justified by I/O latency, but if the database pool is 20, the downstream service can take 50 requests, or the container has 512 MiB of memory, the pool size should reflect those limits. Threads are not free. They have stacks, buffers, locks, and scheduling cost.

Fourth, load test and watch the right signals. CPU utilization, queue length, p95/p99 latency, GC pauses if relevant, downstream saturation, and CPU throttling metrics. If increasing the pool improves throughput and latency, keep going. If CPU is flat and latency gets worse, stop. If throttling rises, stop. If downstream latency rises, stop.

There is a narrow case where 2x the container CPU limit is a decent starting point: a blocking I/O service where each request spends roughly as long waiting as computing, where the runtime’s processor count is container-aware, and where downstream systems can handle the resulting concurrency. Many real services fall near that shape, which is probably why the folklore persists. But “near that shape” is doing all the work. The rule is not good advice because it does not tell you whether your service is in that shape.

Part of the confusion may also come from non-blocking frameworks. Event loops often use a small multiple of the processor count because a few threads poll many channels and do modest CPU work per event. That is not the same as sizing a blocking worker pool. If your service uses Reactor, Netty, Vert.x, Kotlin coroutines, or similar machinery, the number of event-loop threads is one decision, and the amount of I/O concurrency is another. Putting blocking calls on the event loop or sizing the event loop as if it were a thread-per-request pool are different mistakes.

So, for services running in CPU-limited containers, the advice “use 2x cores” is at best a placeholder. If by “cores” you mean host cores, it is often bad. If by “cores” you mean the container’s CPU quota, it may be acceptable for some blocking I/O workloads, but it can be too high for CPU-heavy work and too low for high-latency I/O work. The more defensible default is: start near the CPU quota for CPU-bound work, scale up according to measured blocking time, cap by downstream limits and memory, and verify under load. If the container is truly CPU-limited, the answer is usually not “more threads”; it is “more CPU, or less CPU per request.”
rejected:
The "2x cores" rule is a heuristic for oversubscribing a general-purpose thread pool to hide latency. It assumes that threads spend a significant amount of time blocked on I/O (network, disk, database), during which they consume zero CPU cycles. By running twice as many threads as cores, you ensure that when half the threads are waiting for a response, the other half are still executing code.

In a CPU-limited container, this assumption breaks down in two distinct ways.

First, the limit is on the numerator of the utilization ratio, not the denominator. If you have a limit of 4 cores, the kernel scheduler will strictly enforce that total CPU consumption does not exceed 400%. If you spawn 8 threads and they all execute compute-heavy logic simultaneously, they will not run twice as fast. They will run at exactly the same speed as 4 threads, but with higher context-switching overhead. You have added complexity and jitter without adding throughput. In a CPU-bound workload, the optimal thread count is usually equal to the number of allowed cores, or sometimes less if the work involves heavy memory access that causes cache contention.

Second, "CPU-limited" is often a misnomer for what is actually a noisy neighbor problem. In Kubernetes, `cpu.limit` caps how much CPU a container can use, but `cpu.request` is what guarantees it. If you size your pool based on the limit, you are assuming the container always gets that much CPU. In practice, it often gets closer to the request. If your service is CPU-bound and you set the pool size to 2x the limit, you are building a system that assumes it has twice the resources it is actually guaranteed. When the node is under load and the container is throttled to its request value, your thread pool will be massively over-provisioned. Threads will sit in the run queue, waiting for CPU time, increasing tail latency (p99) without improving throughput.

The only time "2x cores" makes sense in a containerized environment is if the workload is genuinely I/O-bound. If your threads spend 90% of their time waiting on a database or an upstream API, the CPU limit is irrelevant because the CPU is idle anyway. In that case, you size the pool based on the expected I/O latency and the desired throughput, not the CPU count. The formula here is roughly `Threads = CPU_Limit * (1 + Wait_Time / Compute_Time)`. If `Wait_Time` is high, the multiplier grows large. If `Wait_Time` is near zero, the multiplier collapses to 1.

So, the advice is not wrong, but it is incomplete. It conflates "number of cores" with "CPU capacity" and assumes a fixed ratio of blocking to executing time. For a service in a container, you should measure the blocking ratio. If your code is mostly waiting, size for throughput. If your code is mostly calculating, size for the guaranteed CPU allocation, not the hard limit.

prompt: how do DMs work on Mastodon? are they actually private?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
A Mastodon “DM” is not a separate private message store. It is a normal status posted with **Direct** visibility. When you choose Direct and write `@alice@example.org`, your server creates a status object, marks it as direct, and sends it to Alice’s server through ActivityPub. It does not appear on public timelines. Alice receives it as a notification, and your server keeps the original. If you mention several accounts, all mentioned accounts receive it, so it behaves like a group message, with the recipients present in the mention list.

This is also where people get tripped up by Mastodon’s naming: **Private** visibility means “followers only,” not “one-to-one.” A direct post is the closest thing Mastodon has to a DM.

The privacy comes from server-side authorization, not from encryption. The direct status is transmitted over HTTPS and stored in the recipient’s server database. The server checks who is asking for it: the author and the mentioned recipients can view it; anonymous visitors and non-recipients normally cannot. So a stranger with the URL generally cannot open the post, and public timelines and search generally will not expose it.

But the post is not hidden from the machines that host it. There is no end-to-end encryption in Mastodon’s direct messages. The content is readable at the endpoints. If you are on one instance and Alice is on another, the servers that can read the message are yours and Alice’s. Instance operators can access the data through admin tooling, the database, or backups; they also know the metadata: who contacted whom, when, and from which server. If Alice’s account is compromised, her device is compromised, her server is hacked, or a third-party app or bridge she uses keeps a copy, the message is exposed.

So Mastodon DMs are private in the social sense: they are not broadcast, not normally discoverable, and not visible to the general public. They are not private in the security sense: they are not secret from the involved servers, not protected from the recipient’s device or apps, and not safe if you need confidentiality from the operator or a legal request. They are closer to email sent to a free web-mail provider than to Signal or WhatsApp. If the content is sensitive, use an end-to-end encrypted messenger; a Mastodon direct post can still be used to share a link, but the servers will still see that you sent the link and to whom.
rejected:
Direct Messages (DMs) on Mastodon work through the ActivityPub protocol, but they are not technically "private" in the way end-to-end encrypted messages are. They are **unlisted**.

Here is how they actually function:

1.  **Visibility:** When you send a DM, the post is distributed across the federated network to the specific user(s) you mentioned. It is not hidden from the public web. However, it is excluded from the public timelines (Home, Local, and Federated feeds). Only the sender and the recipient can see it by navigating to the other person's profile and clicking the "Direct" filter tab.
2.  **Server Operators:** The instance administrators (sysadmins) of both your server and the recipient’s server have full access to the content. They can read, copy, or delete the message. There is no encryption between the servers that prevents this.
3.  **Reposting and Sharing:** The recipient can forward a DM to anyone else. It is not locked to the two participants.
4.  **Searchability:** While DMs do not appear in search results by default on most instances, if a user shares a link to the specific post ID, anyone who clicks it can view the content.

**Are they actually private?**

No. They are "quiet," not "private."

If you compare DMs to other platforms:
*   **Twitter/X DMs:** Similar concept (unlisted), though X has moved toward E2E encryption for some features.
*   **Signal/WhatsApp:** These are E2E encrypted. The server only sees encrypted blobs. Mastodon DMs are not.
*   **Email:** Mastodon DMs are roughly equivalent to email in terms of privacy. Anyone with access to the mail server (or the recipient's device) can read it.

**Bottom line:**
Use Mastodon DMs for coordinating with friends, sharing low-stakes personal updates, or discussing things you don’t mind the server admin seeing. Do not use them for sensitive information, credentials, or private health/legal matters. If you need true privacy, use a tool like Signal, Wire, or the Tor network.

prompt: What is folie a deux, and how does it work if psychosis is supposed to be a biological illness?
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
Folie a deux is the old name for what psychiatry once called shared psychotic disorder: one person has a delusion, and another person in a close relationship comes to share it. The “primary” person is usually the one with the more established or more intense delusion; the “secondary” person may have no prior psychiatric history. The delusion is often persecutory—spies, poisoning, surveillance, a conspiracy against the couple—and it is usually stronger in the primary person. In many classic cases, separating the two people weakens or removes the secondary person’s delusion, while the primary person’s remains. Modern DSM-5 does not keep it as a separate diagnosis; it folds these cases into specified or other-specified psychotic disorders, but the clinical pattern is still recognized.

The puzzle you are pointing to is real: if psychosis is a biological illness, how can one person’s delusion be “caught” from another? The answer is that the phrase “biological illness” is doing too much work. It suggests a private lesion, a fixed defect inside one skull, as if a delusion were a tumor that could not be influenced by what happens around the person. But a delusion is not a thing stored in the brain like a memory or a scar. It is a belief held with abnormal confidence, usually false, and resistant to correction. Beliefs are inferences. Inferences depend on evidence. And one major source of evidence for a human being is other people.

We all adopt interpretations from others. A parent says the water is unsafe, so you stop drinking it. A doctor says a symptom is serious, so you begin to monitor your body. A partner says the house feels watched, so you start noticing shadows. That is normal social cognition. We do not have direct access to an objective world; we have sensations, memories, emotions, and the testimony of others. The brain uses all of that to build a usable model of reality. When the model becomes fixed, false, and clinically significant, clinicians call it delusional. The cause can still be social.

A simple case shows how it works. A husband becomes convinced that neighbors are poisoning his wife’s food. He refuses to eat, checks the pantry, describes the neighbors’ movements, and talks constantly about the threat. His wife is isolated, stressed, perhaps a little sleep-deprived. She hears a noise outside. She notices the neighbor’s car. She feels a strange taste after a meal. None of these experiences is conclusive. But they are ambiguous, and her husband supplies a coherent explanation: this is what poisoning feels like, this is what the neighbors are doing, this is why you feel that way. His fear is emotionally powerful. He is close to her. He is a source she trusts or depends on. His account becomes a lens. The taste is poison. The car is surveillance. The noise is preparation. Disconfirming evidence gets reinterpreted: if the food tastes normal, the poison must be undetectable; if the neighbors act innocent, they must be deceptive.

Three conditions make this especially likely: closeness, isolation, and the primary person’s conviction. Closeness matters because the primary person’s interpretation is not just information; it carries emotional authority. Isolation matters because reality testing usually depends on multiple sources. If you have friends, coworkers, family, or even strangers who do not share the account, the strange belief gets tested. In a closed couple, the dominant narrative may be the only one. The primary person’s conviction matters because a calm suggestion is easy to dismiss, but a frightened, certain, emotionally invested partner is harder to override.

None of this requires a “contagion” in the infectious sense. No neurochemical is passed from one brain to the other. What is transmitted is an explanatory framework, reinforced by the secondary person’s own perceptions, anxieties, and memories. Once the belief is in place, it changes attention. You notice what fits and forget what does not. It changes bodily experience. Anxiety can produce real sensations: tightness in the chest, odd tastes, hypervigilance to sounds. Those sensations then feel like confirmation. The belief becomes self-sustaining, at least while the social environment keeps feeding it.

This is where the biology enters. The brain does not form beliefs in a vacuum. It has mechanisms for prediction, salience, confidence, threat detection, and source monitoring. In primary psychosis, those mechanisms may be skewed internally: ordinary anomalies become highly salient, prediction errors are misweighted, and the system settles on a false explanation with excessive confidence. In folie a deux, the skew can be produced or amplified by the social situation. The secondary person’s brain is still doing biological work—interpreting ambiguous input, regulating fear, consolidating memory, deciding which source to trust—but the input includes another delusional person’s testimony. The end state can look the same: a fixed false belief with the force of perception.

That is why the secondary person’s delusion often fades after separation. If the belief was mainly being held up by the relationship, removing the relationship removes the main source of evidence. The strange sensations may continue for a while, but they are reinterpreted. The neighbor’s car is just a car. The taste is coffee, or hunger, or nothing. The belief loses its anchor. That pattern is one reason shared delusions are not usually considered the same illness as schizophrenia. The primary person may have a deeper vulnerability; the secondary person may have been driven into a delusional state by an environment that is itself pathological.

The strongest objection is this: if the secondary person gets better when separated, maybe it was never psychosis at all. Maybe it was fear, obedience, dependence, or extreme suggestibility. That objection has real force. The boundary is fuzzy. Some “shared psychotic” cases may be better understood as severe conformity under stress, not full-blown delusional disorder. Some secondary people may have their own subtle vulnerabilities—trauma, cognitive inflexibility, prior odd beliefs, intellectual impairment, early psychotic symptoms—that make them more likely to adopt the primary person’s account. And some delusions persist after separation because they have become part of the person’s identity, or because the person has their own reasons to keep believing them.

But the fact that the category is fuzzy does not dissolve the phenomenon. A person can be socially induced into a mental state that meets the phenomenological criteria for delusion: the belief is false, held with high conviction, and not easily corrected by ordinary evidence. Calling it psychosis describes the state, not the cause. We do not require that every delusion have the same etiology. A delusion can be produced by a brain tumor, by cocaine, by sleep deprivation, by infection, by schizophrenia, or by a closed relationship with a delusional partner. All of those are biological in the sense that the belief is realized in a brain, but they are not all the same disease.

It also helps to notice that even primary psychosis is socially shaped. The brain does not choose its delusions from a blank page. The content comes from language, culture, personal preoccupations, and current events. A person with a defect in confidence or salience may end up with delusions about the CIA, microchips, demons, witches, or a spouse’s affair, depending on the world they live in. The abnormality is not the specific false proposition. It is the way the brain weights evidence and settles on an explanation. That machinery is biological, but it is also open to input.

So folie a deux works because psychosis is not a private substance sitting inside one head. It is a mode of processing evidence, and evidence can come from the person beside you. If by “biological illness” you mean a fixed brain defect that generates a specific delusion independently of the environment, then yes, that picture is too simple. If you mean that the mind depends on brain function and can be moved by powerful social input, then there is no contradiction. The shared delusion is the social surface of the same biological process that, when it goes wrong internally, we call psychosis.
rejected:
Folie a deux, or shared psychotic disorder, is a condition where two people who are in close contact with each other develop the same delusion or hallucination. Typically, one person (the "inducer") is already psychotic, and the other (the "recipient") adopts the false belief. When the two are separated, the recipient’s symptoms usually fade.

This phenomenon challenges the simplistic view of psychosis as a purely biological malfunction, like a broken kidney. If psychosis were solely the result of a specific neurochemical imbalance or genetic defect, it should be immune to social influence. You cannot catch a broken hip from standing next to someone with a broken hip. The fact that a delusion can be transmitted through social interaction suggests that the content of psychosis is partly constructed by the mind in its environment.

However, this does not mean psychosis is purely psychological or "all in the head." Modern research suggests a model of dual vulnerability. The recipient likely has a pre-existing biological predisposition—genetic risk, neurodevelopmental abnormalities, or a specific personality trait like high suggestibility or isolation. The biological substrate creates the susceptibility. The social environment provides the trigger. The delusion is not just a random error; it is a specific belief structure adopted because the recipient’s brain is primed to accept it and because the inducer’s behavior reinforces it.

In this light, the "biological" aspect explains why most people do not adopt the delusion, while the "psychological" aspect explains why the specific content of the delusion matches the inducer’s. The illness is biological in its vulnerability, but the symptom is socially mediated.

prompt: What's the real difference between the economics of a B2C software company and a B2B one? I keep hearing that B2B companies benefit when their customers succeed but I don't get why that matters so much.
system: Write the way the best essayists write: plainly, concretely, and with a real train of thought. Say the most important true things about the question and develop each to the right depth. Vary sentence length with the shape of the idea. Use formatting such as headers or bullet points only when the content really is a list or a procedure. No filler: no restating the question, no stock phrases, no summary of what you just said, no offers of further help. If the question rests on a mistake, say so. Be as short as the ideas allow.
chosen:
The slogan is true, but it points at the wrong cause. B2B software vendors do not care that their customers succeed because they are nicer; they care because B2B revenue is usually made of a small number of large, negotiated, discretionary contracts, and the people signing those contracts have to answer to someone. A B2C vendor also wants users to get value, but if a user stops getting value, the vendor can usually acquire another user from a large market. A B2B vendor often cannot acquire a replacement customer quickly or cheaply enough to make up the loss.

The cleanest way to see the difference is that B2C revenue is a funnel, while B2B revenue is a portfolio.

A B2C software company is usually trying to turn many anonymous individuals into paying users. The individual decision is small: subscribe, cancel, download, delete. The company can tolerate high churn if acquisition is cheap enough and the average lifetime value is positive. It wins by making the product compelling at scale: fast, delightful, habit-forming, socially visible, or cheaper than the alternative. If 10,000 people try it and 3,000 stay, the company optimizes the product, pricing, ads, and onboarding to improve that conversion. If 3,000 users stop getting value, that is a statistical problem. The company may lose revenue, but it does not have to explain the loss to a committee. It can run more ads, fix the product, or target a better segment.

A B2B software company is usually trying to turn an organization into a customer. That sounds similar, but the economics change. The buyer is not one person acting on impulse; it is a group of people with different interests. The end user wants the tool to make their job easier. The manager wants the team to look productive. The CFO wants the price to be defensible. The CISO wants security. Legal wants contract terms. The executive sponsor wants to be able to say, in a meeting, that the purchase is working.

That last point is the heart of “customer success.”

Suppose a B2B company sells a workflow tool for $200,000 a year. The customer’s VP of operations approves it because she believes it will cut reporting time by 20 percent. Six months later, only half the team uses it, the integrations are flaky, and the dashboards do not match the numbers the VP has to show her CEO. The product may still be good. The company may still believe it is valuable. But at renewal, the VP now has to justify the expense to someone who knows it is underperforming. The vendor has to defend not just the software, but the VP’s judgment.

In a B2C situation, the equivalent is much less personal. A $10-a-month fitness app that fails to keep users motivated loses a subscriber. The company may care deeply about retention, but it does not have to appear in a meeting and explain why a particular user’s New Year’s resolution did not survive February. The failure is private, small, and replaceable.

That is why B2B vendors often build things that look strange from a consumer perspective. They build admin controls, role-based permissions, SSO, audit logs, usage reports, API documentation, SLAs, security questionnaires, procurement paperwork, onboarding teams, and customer success managers. These features may not make the end user fall in love with the product. They make the buyer able to live with the product. They turn software from a consumer preference into an institutional fact.

The concentration of revenue makes this even more important. Imagine a B2B company with 20 customers, each paying $250,000 a year. One customer is 5 percent of revenue. If that customer becomes dissatisfied, the company does not just lose a renewal; it may lose a reference, a case study, a partnership, and a signal to other buyers in the same industry. B2B buyers talk to each other. They ask peers, analysts, and vendors for recommendations. A failed enterprise deployment can poison a vendor’s reputation in a niche market.

A B2C company can usually spread that risk. If one user has a bad experience, the company loses one user and maybe a negative review. If a million users have bad experiences, the company is in trouble, but the mechanism is different: the product is not meeting aggregate demand. The fix is usually product, pricing, content, or targeting. In B2B, the fix often requires a human being on the vendor’s side of the table, working the internal politics of the customer.

This also changes what “success” means. For a B2C product, success is usually usage. Does the user open the app? Do they return? Do they invite friends? Do they watch more content? Do they buy more courses? The company measures success in aggregate product metrics.

For a B2B product, success has to be visible and attributable. The customer’s buyer needs to be able to point to an outcome and connect it to the vendor. “Our team is faster” is not enough. “We closed the books four days faster after implementing the tool” is better. “The CFO signed off on the renewal” is better still. That is why B2B vendors care about adoption, not just satisfaction. A customer can like the product and still cancel if the product does not produce a result the buyer can defend.

This is where the slogan gets misleading if taken too literally. B2B vendors do not always want their customers to succeed in some broad, moral sense. They want the customer to succeed in a way that protects and expands the vendor’s revenue. If the customer’s business grows, they may buy more seats, modules, or tiers. If the customer’s team gets better at using the product, they may renew. If the customer’s leadership changes, the new leader may demand proof of value. If the customer becomes too efficient, they may actually need less of the product. The vendor’s interest is not “do well, customer,” but “do well in a way that makes this purchase look smart and creates a reason to buy more.”

The hardest objection to the B2B/B2C distinction is that B2C companies also live or die by customer success. Netflix wants people to watch. Duolingo wants people to keep practicing. A marketplace wants both buyers and sellers to have good experiences. A consumer SaaS company like Notion, Figma, or Canva benefits enormously when users succeed, because retention and word of mouth drive growth. And some B2B companies are so product-led, so self-serve, and so focused on small businesses that they feel almost B2C: low-touch sales, transparent pricing, little customization, high volume.

So the distinction is not absolute. The real variable is not “business” versus “consumer” as labels. It is the structure of the buying decision.

When the buyer is an individual, the vendor optimizes for mass conversion. When the buyer is an organization, the vendor optimizes for institutional legitimacy. When the customer base is large and replaceable, the vendor optimizes the funnel. When the customer base is small and concentrated, the vendor optimizes the relationship.

That is why B2B companies often have different cost structures. Both can have high gross margins, but the operating expenses land in different places. A B2C company spends heavily on marketing, brand, content, growth experiments, and consumer support. A B2B company spends heavily on sales, onboarding, customer success, security reviews, legal, account management, and implementation. B2B revenue is also lumpy. It arrives in annual or multiyear contracts, often after long sales cycles, with discounts, negotiated terms, and cash conversion problems. B2C revenue is usually smoother: monthly or annual self-serve billing, less negotiation, less working capital tied up in a single deal.

Pricing follows the same logic. B2C pricing has to survive comparison shopping by people who can easily walk away. It tends to be transparent, simple, and psychologically calibrated. B2B pricing can be opaque and negotiated because the buyer is evaluating risk, fit, and internal justification as much as price. A $50,000 contract is not just “$50,000 too expensive.” It is a decision that involves budget categories, procurement rules, vendor risk, and the political cost of choosing wrongly.

This is also why “the customer succeeds” matters more in B2B than in B2C, even though both care about value. In B2C, value is experienced directly by the person paying. In B2B, value is mediated by a chain of people. The person using the software may love it, but the person paying may never touch it. The person paying may not understand it, but they still have to defend it. The vendor therefore has to create value that travels through that chain.

A good example is security software. The end user may find it annoying. The engineer may hate the alerts. The IT team may spend hours tuning it. But the CISO can show the board that the company reduced its risk exposure, met compliance requirements, and avoided a breach. The product is successful not because everyone likes it, but because the buyer can demonstrate that it did its job.

A B2C antivirus product, by contrast, has to feel less annoying, less intrusive, and easy enough that the user does not uninstall it. The buyer and user are the same person. The product has to win at the moment of experience.

There is another consequence: B2B vendors often have to sell before the product is fully proven. Enterprise deals can depend on a vision, a reference, a roadmap, or a pilot. The customer is buying the probability that the vendor will help them succeed. That makes trust and credibility part of the product. In B2C, the product usually has to prove itself immediately. The user does not care about your roadmap if the app is slow, confusing, or useless on day one.

This does not mean B2B is always more serious or B2C always more frivolous. Some B2C products are deeply professional: video editing, music production, trading platforms, developer tools. Some B2B products are almost consumer-like: team chat, collaboration, design, note-taking. The line blurs when employees choose tools and companies simply pay for what they already use.

But when the blur matters economically, the question is still the same: who is accountable for the purchase? If the answer is “the individual user,” the vendor’s problem is product experience at scale. If the answer is “a group of professionals who have to justify the spend,” the vendor’s problem is making the purchase look right over time.

So the real difference is not that B2B vendors care about customer success and B2C vendors do not. Both care. The difference is that B2B revenue is concentrated in accountable buyers, and those buyers need evidence. A B2C company loses a user when the product stops feeling good. A B2B company loses a customer when the purchase stops looking wise. That is why “customers succeed” is such a big deal in B2B: it is not a nice thing to hope for. It is the mechanism by which the next contract gets written.
rejected:
The slogan "B2B wins when the customer wins" is a marketing abstraction that obscures the actual mechanical difference. The real difference is not about goodwill; it is about the unit of analysis.

In B2C, the unit of analysis is the individual user. In B2B, it is the economic outcome of a specific job-to-be-done within a client’s organization.

This distinction changes the entire P&L structure, the sales cycle, and the churn dynamics.

### The Unit of Analysis

A consumer buys a streaming service to kill an hour. If they watch three hours a week instead of five, they don’t churn. They are still "using" the product. The value is subjective and immediate.

A CFO buys an expense management tool to reduce audit costs and close the books faster. If the tool doesn’t actually reduce the time-to-close or the error rate, the CFO has paid for a failure. The value is objective and measurable against a baseline.

Because the B2B value is tied to a specific business metric, the product’s success is decoupled from user satisfaction. A sales rep can be a power user who loves the interface, but if the tool doesn’t save the company money, the budget gets cut. Conversely, a tool can be clunky and hated by the end-user, but if it saves the company $50,000 a year in labor costs, the renewal is guaranteed.

### Churn is a Function of ROI, Not Habit

B2C churn is driven by habit, boredom, or a competitor’s marketing blitz. It is emotional.

B2B churn is driven by a recalculation of Return on Investment. It is rational.

This makes B2B customers harder to sell to, because you must prove the ROI before the sale. It also makes them more stable, because once the ROI is established, switching costs are high. You aren’t just losing a user; you are disrupting a workflow that has been integrated into the client’s operational rhythm.

However, this creates a fragility: if the client’s business model changes, or if they build the capability in-house, the ROI evaporates instantly. B2C companies rarely face the threat of their customers building the product themselves. B2B companies constantly do.

### The Sales Cycle Reflects the Risk

In B2C, the person buying is the person using. The decision is made in minutes, often impulsively.

In B2B, the buyer, the user, and the payer are often three different people. The user wants usability. The buyer wants strategic alignment. The payer wants cost reduction. A successful B2B sale requires satisfying all three simultaneously.

This is why B2B software companies have sales teams, and B2C companies have marketing funnels. You cannot automate a conversation that involves navigating internal politics and risk aversion. The sales team exists to manage the risk on behalf of the buyer, not just to explain the features.

### Price Elasticity

B2C prices are inelastic because the cost is trivial relative to the customer’s income. A $10/month subscription is noise.

B2B prices are elastic because the cost is a line item in a budget that is scrutinized. A $5,000/month subscription is a decision that requires justification.

This means B2B companies can charge significantly more per user, but they must work harder to justify it. The "value" isn’t the feature set; it’s the delta between the client’s current state and their desired state. If you can’t quantify that delta, you can’t charge for it.

### The "Customer Success" Misunderstanding

When people say "B2B benefits when the customer succeeds," they are usually describing the necessity of onboarding.
